US$72k cement dispute heads back to court after respondent withdraws opposition

by Staff Reporter

1 hr ago |

61

Views

BULAWAYO - A High Court case in which cement manufacturer PPC Zimbabwe is accused of failing to deliver 330 tonnes of cement despite receiving full payment is set to return to court after one of the respondents withdrew opposition to the matter's reinstatement.

Justice Bongani Ndhlovu is expected to rule on November 6 on an application by Erksales Hardware to have the matter reinstated after it was previously removed from the court roll.

PPC Zimbabwe is cited as the first respondent, while one of its employees, Nicole Botha, is cited as the second respondent.

According to a High Court notice dated October 20, Botha has withdrawn her notice of opposition to the reinstatement application.

"Take notice that the second respondent has withdrawn its notice of opposition with each party bearing its own costs," reads part of the notice.

The dispute, registered under case number HCBC835/26, centres on allegations by Erksales Hardware that PPC Zimbabwe failed to deliver 11 truckloads of cement weighing 30 tonnes each despite allegedly receiving full payment for the consignment last year.

The cement is valued at approximately US$72,600 at current market prices.

According to court documents, the cement was allegedly purchased through a PPC sales representative but was never delivered.

Erksales Hardware subsequently sought compensation through the courts, but the matter was initially dismissed after opposition by the respondents.

The company then filed an application seeking reinstatement of the case.

Should Justice Ndhlovu grant the reinstatement application, PPC Zimbabwe and Botha will be required to answer the allegations during subsequent court proceedings.

Erksales Hardware is represented by Mashayamombe and Company, while PPC Zimbabwe is represented by Moyo and Nyoni Legal Practitioners. Botha is represented by Calderwood, Bryce Hendry and Partners.

The allegations remain disputed and have not yet been tested before the court.

The development comes months after another company, Tri Oceans, reportedly pursued legal action against PPC Zimbabwe in a separate matter before the parties reached an out-of-court settlement.

title: Mnangagwa courts Russian investment as Zimbabwe assumes COMESA leadership
categories: Africa Report; Business; Crime & Courts; Politics; Top Stories

Cabinet said on Tuesday that Mnangagwa used the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow to promote Zimbabwe as a regional production and trade hub linking investors to markets […]
content_text:
HARARE — President Emmerson Mnangagwa has sought to position Zimbabwe as a gateway for Russian investment into southern and eastern Africa following the country’s assumption of the COMESA chairmanship.

Cabinet said on Tuesday that Mnangagwa used the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow to promote Zimbabwe as a regional production and trade hub linking investors to markets under COMESA, the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and the African Continental Free Trade Area.

Zimbabwe assumed the one-year chairmanship of the COMESA Authority at the bloc’s 25th Summit of Heads of State and Government, held on October 22.

Zambia was elected vice-chair, while Kenya assumed the role of rapporteur.

During the Russia-Africa Summit, Mnangagwa held high-level engagements with Russian President Vladimir Putin and leaders of African regional organisations.

He also met representatives of Russian institutions, including PSB Bank, as part of efforts to deepen economic cooperation.

Cabinet said the President emphasised the need for partnerships that would link Africa’s resources and markets with Russia’s industrial and technological expertise.

Mnangagwa also participated in the summit’s Economic and Humanitarian Forum, which featured industrial and scientific exhibitions.

The government said Zimbabwe’s COMESA leadership would strengthen the country’s influence in regional economic affairs and advance its investment promotion objectives.

However, Cabinet did not announce the value of any investment commitments or identify specific projects secured during the engagements.

The government said its regional leadership would be used to promote industrialisation, cross-border trade and stronger regional value chains.

Zimbabwe’s COMESA chairmanship is expected to run for one year.

title: Tatanga and Modaso Plan 228MW Renewable Energy Project in Zimbabwe
summary: HARARE — Zimbabwe’s energy sector could receive a significant boost from plans by Tatanga Energy and Modaso Energy to develop a 228-megawatt hybrid renewable power plant in the Guruve-Mazowe area, combining wind, solar and battery storage to supply electricity to the domestic market. content_text:
HARARE — Zimbabwe’s energy sector could receive a significant boost from plans by Tatanga Energy and Modaso Energy to develop a 228-megawatt hybrid renewable power plant in the Guruve-Mazowe area, combining wind, solar and battery storage to supply electricity to the domestic market.

The proposed project will comprise 128MW of wind generation and 100MW of solar capacity, supported by battery storage, with projected annual output of approximately 550 gigawatt-hours (GWh). The development is expected to strengthen electricity supply while adding renewable generation capacity to a power system facing persistent demand and reliability challenges.

Modaso Energy is part of Geneva-based MISA Group. Standard Bank has been appointed to arrange project debt, with a term sheet already agreed, an important step towards securing the financing required for construction.

The project is expected to supply electricity primarily to ZESA, while Zim GreenCo has signed Heads of Terms for a long-term power offtake arrangement. Financial close is targeted for mid-2027, with commercial operations scheduled to begin in 2029.

Zim energy developer Tatanga Energy and Modaso Energy, part of Geneva-based MISA Group, have announced plans for a 228MW hybrid plant in Guruve-Mazowe.

It will combine 128MW wind, 100MW solar and battery storage, generating 550GWh annually.

Standard Bank will arrange project debt, with a term sheet agreed. ZESA is expected to be the main power buyer, alongside Zim GreenCo, which has signed Heads of Terms for a long-term offtake contract.

Financial close is targeted for mid-2027, with operations expected in 2029.

— newZWire (@newswireZW) November 3, 2026

The proposed investment has implications beyond electricity generation. Reliable power is a critical input for Zimbabwean manufacturers, mining companies, agricultural processors and other businesses whose operating costs and production schedules are affected by supply interruptions. Additional generation could reduce reliance on expensive alternative power arrangements and improve the predictability of industrial operations.

The combination of wind and solar is also intended to diversify generation sources, while battery storage could help manage fluctuations in renewable output. The commercial value of the storage component will depend on its capacity, operating configuration and ability to deliver electricity when generation from the two renewable sources is lower.

NewZWire has highlighted the importance of private-sector investment in addressing Zimbabwe’s electricity constraints, as energy availability remains a key consideration for industrial recovery and investment decisions. The proposed Guruve-Mazowe development adds to the pipeline of projects seeking to mobilise private capital for domestic power generation.

The Zimbabwe Mail notes that the project’s economic contribution will depend on more than its installed capacity. Financing completion, grid connection, transmission infrastructure, construction costs and the bankability of power purchase arrangements will determine whether the proposed output can be delivered commercially.

With financial close still targeted for 2027 and operations expected in 2029, the development remains at the planning and financing stage. If implemented as scheduled, the 228MW project would provide additional renewable electricity and support efforts to expand Zimbabwe’s domestic generation base.

The squad includes experienced players Takudzwanashe Kaitano, Clive Madande, Johnathan Campbell, Roy Kaia and Dion Myers, alongside former Under-19 players Shelton Mazvitorera and Panashe Taruvinga.

title: Zimbabwe joins 39 states at African Human Rights Commission’s 89th session in Dakar
categories: Herald; Africa; Local News; National; National News; News
summary: Thupeyo Muleya-Beitbridge Bureau ZIMBABWE was among 39 African states that participated in the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human…
content_text:
Thupeyo Muleya-Beitbridge Bureau

ZIMBABWE was among 39 African states that participated in the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR)held in Dakar, Senegal, last month.

The session, held in accordance with Article 64(2) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, read together with Rule 27 of its Rules of Procedure (2020), had its private session online from September 21 to October 1, followed by the public session in person at the King Fahd International Conference Centre in Dakar from 12 to 21 October.

According to the final communiqué released at the end of the session that was chaired by the Chairperson of the Commission, Commissioner Idrissa Sow assisted by Vice-Chairperson Commissioner Hatem Essaiem.

The opening ceremony, according to the Communiqué, was officially opened by Senegal’s Minister of Justice Moussa Sarr on behalf of Senegal President Bassirou Diomaye Faye.

“During the ceremony, several key statements were delivered by AU and international officials, including Ms Hannah Foster on behalf of the NGO Forum Steering Committee, Prof James Mouangue Kobila of NANHRI, and Mr Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African union Commission,” read part of the communique.

“A total of 1 662 participants took part in the Session who include185 representatives of 39 States Parties; 25 representatives of African union bodies; 85 representatives of international and intergovernmental organisations; 96 representatives of national human rights institutions; 957 representatives of African and international NGOs among others.”

Zimbabwe was represented at the State level, while the Zimbabwe Human Rights Commission (ZHRC) was among 14 NHRIs that made statements on the human rights situation in their respective countries.

Other NHRIs that presented included those from Algeria, Burundi, Egypt, Kenya, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa and Chad.

The ACHPR said during the private session, the Commission considered and adopted decisions on sixteen (16) communications: Eight (8) communications on the Merits; Seven (7) communications on Admissibility; and One (1) request for review of a decision on the Merits.

“The Commission also approved the referral of one communication to the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights in the context of its complementary relationship with the Court,” said the Commission.

It also adopted a thematic resolution on the biennial vote of the United Nations General Assembly calling for a moratorium on the use of the death penalty — an issue Zimbabwe has been seized with following the abolition of the death penalty in December 2024.

The Commission raised concern over delays by States in submitting periodic reports under Article 62 of the African Charter.

“It was noted that eight (8) countries are up to date; five (5) countries are at the examination stage; six (6) countries have one (1) report overdue; ten (10) countries have two (2) reports overdue; two (2) countries have three (3) reports overdue; eighteen (18) countries have more than three (3) reports overdue; and five (5) countries have not yet submitted their initial reports,” said the Commission

“The Commission also deliberated on five thematic panels, including Situation of Human Rights Defenders in West Africa, Advancing the Rights of Women and Girls in Africa, and The Impact of Water and Basic Sanitation on the Living Conditions of Detainees in African Prisons.

“In addition, the Commission took note of the report on budgetary and staff matters, including the implementation of programmes and the budget, recruitment, the Commission’s permanent headquarters, temporary replacement office premises, performance management, staff welfare and training.”

The Commission said it had welcomed the proposal by the Mozambican delegation to host the next ordinary public session in the first half of 2027.

title: Air Force of Zimbabwe unveils entrance arch in honour of Air Chief Marshal Josiah Tungamirai
summary: Story by Learnmore Jenya THE restoration of Zimbabwe’s pre- and post-independence military history is extending to national defence institutions, with government sustaining the legacy of liberation icons through the renaming and development of military installations. The official opening of an entrance arch at Josiah Tungamirai Air Force Base in Gweru has added another landmark in […] The post Air Force of Zimbabwe unveils entrance arch in honour of Air Chief Marshal Josiah Tungamirai first appeared on ZBC NEWS .
content_text:
Story by Learnmore Jenya

THE restoration of Zimbabwe’s pre- and post-independence military history is extending to national defence institutions, with government sustaining the legacy of liberation icons through the renaming and development of military installations.

The official opening of an entrance arch at Josiah Tungamirai Air Force Base in Gweru has added another landmark in honour of the country’s first black Air Chief Marshal.

The Air Force of Zimbabwe has unveiled an entrance arch at Josiah Tungamirai Air Force Base in Gweru, completing a historical process of recognising the late liberation stalwart.

The installation further entrenches his legacy within the institution he once commanded, drawing appreciation from his family, who view the gesture as an enduring tribute to his contribution.

His son, Cde Thomas Tungamirai, thanked Government and all those involved in the project, saying the recognition will preserve important chapters of the country’s history.

“I would just like to thank the President and everyone else who was involved in this auspicious occasion. This is a great honour, and it will evoke memories and history of this country as we look towards a wonderful future for the Air Force of Zimbabwe.

His daughter, Ms Retina Mberikwazvo, said the honour would be remembered by future generations.

“I am humbled. It is an honour achieved through the great works of a dedicated, humble and honest man called Josiah Tungamirai. It is going to outlive generations to come.”

Another son, Honourable Tawanda Tungamirai, said the family appreciated the recognition accorded to their father.

“Before 2017, our father had not been given such a great honour. We want to thank the Second Republic for recognising him and giving him this great legacy.”

The renaming of the base in 2017 under Statutory Instrument 139 marked a major step in restoring the country’s military heritage.

“I am filled with a great sense of joy to be here today to complete the historical chapter of renaming this Air Force Base. In 2017, under the wisdom of the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces, Dr Emmerson Mnangagwa, this base was renamed after the first black commander of the Air Force of Zimbabwe and liberation stalwart, the late Air Chief Marshal Josiah Tungamirai. I am pleased that the structure before us is a work of art and a worthy honour to the late Air Chief Marshal,” Commander Air Force of Zimbabwe, Air Marshal John Nzvede said.

Air Chief Marshal Josiah Tungamirai died in 2005 and was accorded national hero status, with his remains being interred at the National Heroes Acre.

title: Jairos Jiri ablution facilities refurbished
categories: Herald; Local News; National; National News; News
summary: Online Reporter THE Jairos Jiri Centre in Southerton has received a major facelift after the Bridging Gaps Foundation (BGF) rehabilitated its ablution…
content_text:
Online Reporter

THE Jairos Jiri Centre in Southerton has received a major facelift after the Bridging Gaps Foundation (BGF) rehabilitated its ablution facilities to improve the dignity and living conditions of learners with disabilities.

The facilities were handed over in Harare on Tuesday during a ceremony presided over by Bridging Gaps Foundation Chief Executive Officer Mr Mberikwazvo Chitambo.

BGF is a philanthropic organisation funded by prominent businessman Dr Kudakwashe Tagwirei.

The foundation refurbished all 23 toilets at the centre, installed six gas-powered geysers for hot water, resolved all electrical faults, repaired switches and plugs, and installed new bathroom tiles and mirrors. The comprehensive project also included the installation of hand-wash basins and bathtubs, re-tiling of shower cubicles, internal and external repainting, and the fitting of new water storage tanks, booster pumps, and optimized drainage systems.

Speaking at the handover, Mr Chitambo stated that the intervention was guided by a precise needs assessment to restore basic human dignity.

“For children who depend on others for aspects of their daily care, the quality of these facilities matters deeply,” Mr Chitambo said, praising the patience of the institutional caregivers. “When we undertook the needs assessment at this Centre, our responsibility was to listen carefully and understand where our support could make a meaningful difference.”

He added that BGF is working with five partner children’s homes under its Path to Self-Reliance initiative to help vulnerable institutions strengthen corporate management and build financially secure futures.

Jairos Jiri Association National Executive Director Mrs Grace Kamanga revealed that the facilities had degenerated into a severe health and safety hazard prior to the intervention.

“Before these renovations, the state of the ablution facilities had become a matter of great concern,” Mrs Kamanga said. “The flushing systems had ceased to function effectively, forcing learners and staff to resort to the use of buckets of water to flush toilets. Some learners had no choice but to use dishes and buckets for bathing.”

She commended BGF and Mrs Tagwirei for their unwavering commitment to persons living with disabilities, noting that the gesture honours the legacy of national pioneer Mr Jairos Jiri, MBE, while aligning with Vision 2030 and the mantra of leaving no one and no place behind.

The Jairos Jiri Association currently treats and transforms the lives of more than 16,000 persons with disabilities annually through community-based rehabilitation, specialized education, and vocational training frameworks.

title: Zimbabwe launches US$14,33m Pandemic Fund country project to strengthen health security
categories: Herald; Health; Local News; National; National News; News
summary: Herald Reporter Zimbabwe has launched a US$14,33 million Pandemic Fund country project to strengthen early detection, laboratory diagnostics, workforce capacity and emergency…
content_text:
Herald Reporter

Zimbabwe has launched a US$14,33 million Pandemic Fund country project to strengthen early detection, laboratory diagnostics, workforce capacity and emergency preparedness and response across the human, animal and environmental health sectors.

Supported by the Pandemic Fund, the three-year project (2026–2028) will leverage US$49 million in partner co-financing and US$91,8 million in Government co-investment.

These are distinct financing categories, reflecting wider support for Zimbabwe’s pandemic preparedness and response capacity.

The project will help the country identify and respond to emerging threats before they escalate, while also reinforcing coordination across human, animal and environmental health institutions.

Together, these investments are expected to strengthen the ability of national institutions, frontline services and communities to manage outbreaks while maintaining essential services.

Led by the Government, the project will be implemented by the African Development Bank Group, the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), working with relevant ministries and other national and international partners.

The country grant will support five complementary areas of intervention namely; disease surveillance, laboratory systems and early warning, health workforce development, governance and emergency preparedness, and community engagement and innovation.

Under disease surveillance, the project will expand event-based, environmental, community-based and cross-border surveillance using digital tools, automated weather stations, social listening and community feedback. It also aims to establish five public health emergency operations centres to strengthen multisectoral coordination.

Under laboratory systems, the project aims to upgrade 25 laboratories—five national and 20 subnational—to strengthen rapid diagnostics, antimicrobial resistance testing, genomic sequencing, biosafety and laboratory quality management.

On health workforce development, it is expected that more than 10 000 professionals across relevant sectors will receive training in integrated disease surveillance and response, emergency preparedness, risk communication and community engagement.

Under governance and emergency preparedness, the project will support annual simulation exercises, relevant health emergency reviews and strengthened risk assessments at points of entry to improve readiness and cross-sector coordination.

On community engagement and innovation, the peoject will have community-led monitoring, multilingual awareness campaigns and digital learning platforms are expected to reach up to two million people, strengthening public understanding, trust and participation in disease prevention.

Zimbabwe is also one of eight countries taking part in a separate Southern Africa multi-country Pandemic Fund initiative implemented by WHO. This regional grant of approximately US$35,8 million is distinct from Zimbabwe’s US$14,33 million country grant and supports climate-sensitive early warning, laboratory systems, workforce capacity and cross-border coordination.

Delivering the keynote address at the launch, Health and Child Care Minister Dr Douglas Mombeshora, said: “As we pursue Vision 2030 and implement the National Development Strategy 2, protecting public health must be recognised as a fundamental national development imperative, essential for safeguarding our livelihoods, economy, and public services.

“Because health threats do not respect administrative or international boundaries, pandemic preparedness requires a Whole-of-Government and whole-of-society effort through the One Health approach.

“By aligning human health, animal health, agriculture, environment, local government, research, and private sectors around a shared mandate, we ensure our preparedness systems are resilient, unified, and capable of protecting the lives of all Zimbabweans.”

UNICEF Zimbabwe Representative Ms Etona Ekole said effective pandemic preparedness must go beyond technical infrastructure and place communities, particularly children and other vulnerable populations, at the centre of national response systems.

“The first signs of an outbreak are often detected not in a laboratory, but in a community. Preparedness is therefore not only about investing in laboratories, surveillance systems and emergency operations centres.

“It is also about ensuring that families have access to trusted information, that communities are empowered to act early, and that essential health services remain available when emergencies strike. Every child deserves to be protected, and no community should be left behind.”

The African Development Bank Group’s Country Manager for Zimbabwe, Ms Eyerusalem Fasika, said: “Securing Zimbabwe’s single-country grant from the Pandemic Fund marks a decisive shift from reactive containment to proactive protection.

“This grant strengthens the country’s ability to identify and contain health threats before they escalate. The African Development Bank is proud to partner with the Government, the Pandemic Fund and fellow Implementing Entities on this project.”

Dr Patrice Talla, FAO Subregional Coordinator for Southern Africa, who is also FAO Representative for Zimbabwe, said: “Many of the pathogens with pandemic potential emerge at the interface between people, animals and the environment. This investment will strengthen Zimbabwe’s capacity to detect, prevent, and respond to threats where they arise, through stronger animal health systems, integrated surveillance and the application of the One Health approach.

“FAO is committed to supporting the Government and its partners to build resilience that protects lives, livelihoods and food systems.”

Dr Desta Tiruneh, WHO Representative in Zimbabwe, said: “These investments offer an opportunity to translate the lessons of COVID-19 and other health emergencies into stronger systems and greater protection for communities across Zimbabwe. By bringing together human, animal and environmental health sectors, we can detect threats earlier and respond faster, with communities as essential partners in preparedness and response.”

The Pandemic Fund is a multilateral financing mechanism hosted by the World Bank that supports countries and regions to strengthen pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Zimbabwean-born Chris Dzikiti becomes most senior nurse at UK regulator
categories: Diaspora; News; Care Quality Commission; Chris Dzikiti; healthcare; mental-health nursing; NHS; NMC; Nursing and Midwifery Council; united kingdom; Zimbabwean diaspora; Zimbabwean nurses
keywords: Care Quality Commission; Chris Dzikiti; healthcare; mental-health nursing; NHS; NMC; Nursing and Midwifery Council; united kingdom; Zimbabwean diaspora; Zimbabwean nurses
summary: Zimbabwean-born nurse Chris Dzikiti has become the most senior registered nursing professional at the UK’s Nursing and Midwifery Council.
content_text:
LONDON – Zimbabwean-born nurse Chris Dzikiti has taken up one of the most influential professional roles in British nursing, becoming the most senior registered nursing professional at the Nursing and Midwifery Council.

Dzikiti is now serving as the NMC’s Executive Director of Professional Practice, placing him at the regulator’s top table as it oversees standards affecting 867,935 nurses, midwives and nursing associates across the United Kingdom.

The NMC announced his appointment in April and said at the time that he would begin the role in June. Its current senior-management register now lists him among the organisation’s executive directors.

Dzikiti, who was born in Zimbabwe and spent the first 20 years of his life there before moving to the UK in 1999, has been a registered nurse for almost 25 years.

His appointment represents a significant achievement for Zimbabweans working in Britain’s health and social-care sectors, where thousands have built careers as nurses, carers, doctors and other healthcare professionals.

Zimbabweans consistently rank among the most represented overseas nationalities in the NHS nursing workforce. NHS England figures showed that 3,852 nurses and health visitors identified as Zimbabwean in June 2025, making Zimbabwe one of the leading nationalities represented in the profession outside Britain.

Leading professional standards

As Executive Director of Professional Practice, Dzikiti leads the NMC directorate responsible for setting and maintaining standards for nursing and midwifery education and professional practice.

His responsibilities include safeguarding, education quality assurance, employer outreach, registration and revalidation.

He will also play an important role in the NMC’s programme to modernise professional standards across the nursing and midwifery sectors.

The regulator is reviewing practice-learning requirements for students and developing a new Code and refreshed revalidation process, which are expected to take effect in autumn 2027.

It has also accelerated plans to introduce advanced-practice proficiency and education standards, bringing the proposed delivery date forward from March 2028 to October 2027.

The changes will affect how nurses, midwives and nursing associates are educated, registered, assessed and supported throughout their professional careers.

Dzikiti said when his appointment was announced that he had always believed in the importance of professional standards, continued learning and reflective practice in delivering safe and compassionate care.

“I am excited about the opportunity to contribute to this important work at a critical time for the professions,” he said.

He also expressed his desire to work with nurses, midwives, nursing associates and other healthcare stakeholders to strengthen professional practice and promote inclusive, compassionate and equitable care.

Extensive regulatory experience

Dzikiti joined the NMC from the Care Quality Commission, where he most recently served as Interim Chief Inspector of Mental Health.

In that position, he was responsible for the CQC’s regulation, inspection and oversight of mental-health services across England.

During his time at the commission, he also served as Interim Chief Inspector of Healthcare, Executive Director of Operations and National Director for Mental Health.

Before joining the CQC, Dzikiti held senior positions at NHS England and NHS Improvement. His work included leading a national programme aimed at retaining NHS professionals and supporting the delivery of government health commitments.

He has also worked at the integrated-care-system level and as a global-health consultant at Health Education England, which was responsible for planning, recruiting, training and educating the NHS workforce before its functions transferred to NHS England.

Earlier in his career, Dzikiti worked as a senior nurse manager at East London NHS Foundation Trust.

His professional background is rooted in mental-health nursing. He completed his mental-health nurse training at City University London in 2002 and later pursued postgraduate studies, including work in transcultural psychiatry.

‘A real coup’ for the regulator

NMC Chief Executive and Registrar Paul Rees MBE described Dzikiti’s recruitment as “a real coup” for the regulator.

Rees said Dzikiti’s experience at the CQC and across the wider nursing and regulatory sectors would help ensure that the voices of nurses, midwives and nursing associates were represented within the NMC’s senior leadership.

Dzikiti succeeded Professor Donna O’Boyle MBE, who retired in June after serving as Acting Executive Director of Professional Practice from April 2025.

O’Boyle described her time as the NMC’s most senior registrant as a privilege and said Dzikiti was joining the organisation at an important stage in its renewal.

The NMC is rebuilding after a difficult period involving concerns about its organisational culture, regulatory performance and the handling of fitness-to-practise cases.

Its current reform programme includes modernising professional standards, strengthening safeguarding, improving registration decisions and addressing racial disparities within nursing and midwifery regulation and education.

The organisation’s latest figures show that more than a third of the professionals on its register are now Black, Asian or from other ethnic-minority backgrounds.

A record 293,778 of its 867,935 registered professionals fall within those groups, underlining the growing diversity of the nursing and midwifery workforce Dzikiti will help regulate.

For Zimbabwean healthcare professionals in Britain, his elevation provides visible representation at the highest professional level of one of the UK’s most important healthcare regulators.

Nehanda Radio has contacted the NMC for further information about Dzikiti’s priorities and whether his directorate intends to undertake work specifically addressing the experiences of internationally educated registrants.

Story by Tafara Chikumira

INGUTSHENI Central Hospital is expanding its agricultural activities after securing five boreholes to increase food production, support patient rehabilitation and improve the institution’s self-reliance.

The hospital uses farming activities as part of its occupational therapy programme, giving patients opportunities to participate in practical work and acquire skills that may support their reintegration into society.

Ingutsheni Central Hospital Senior Medical Officer Ms Nyasha Chunda said the programme was helping patients develop practical skills while supporting their physical and psychological rehabilitation.

“We are saying that for a patient to be fully rehabilitated, they need physical exercise, psychological therapy and a purpose in life. We are giving them a skill that they can use once they leave this facility, and it helps them deal with the issue of discrimination they usually face when they return to society,” she said.

The agricultural programme is also helping the hospital meet some of its food requirements amid budgetary constraints and an increase in patient admissions.

Ingutsheni Hospital Chief Executive Officer Dr Nemache Mawere said produce from the farm was supplementing the institution’s food supplies.

“Of late, we have experienced an increase in admissions. The farm therefore helps to feed the patients. We rely solely on budget allocations, which are sometimes not enough, as we do not charge user fees. The garden comes in handy, as its produce helps us a lot,” she said.

The hospital plans to expand its farming operations to 10 hectares, with a focus on drip irrigation to improve water efficiency.

Ingutsheni Hospital Farm Manager Mr Nkosilathi Mpofu said the institution had received support from Government and development partners to improve its water supply.

“Government helped us drill three boreholes while Howmine drilled one and we got another one from an NGO,” he said.

The expansion is expected to increase the hospital’s capacity to produce food while strengthening the role of agricultural activities in its patient rehabilitation programme.

title: ARDA Targets 100,000 Hectares in Major Push to Shield Zimbabwe From El Niño Drought
summary: ARDA delivered 187,704 metric tonnes of summer cereals from the 2025/26 agricultural season and a further 60,529.3 tonnes of winter wheat to the GMB, bringing its combined deliveries to 248,233.3 tonnes. Source
content_text:
Agriculture

ARDA Targets 100,000 Hectares in Major Push to Shield Zimbabwe From El Niño Drought

ARDA delivered 187,704 metric tonnes of summer cereals from the 2025/26 agricultural season and a further 60,529.3 tonnes of winter wheat to the GMB, bringing its combined deliveries to 248,233.3 tonnes.

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

Staff Reporter

The Agricultural and Rural Development Authority (ARDA) is targeting 100,000 hectares under its 2026/27 summer cropping programme after delivering more than 248,000 tonnes of cereals to the Grain Marketing Board (GMB), as the country intensifies efforts to build strategic grain reserves ahead of a potentially difficult agricultural season.

ARDA delivered 187,704 metric tonnes of summer cereals from the 2025/26 agricultural season and a further 60,529.3 tonnes of winter wheat to the GMB, bringing its combined deliveries to 248,233.3 tonnes.

Of the summer cereal deliveries, 31,293.46 tonnes were channelled towards immediate milling requirements and price stabilisation, helping to support grain availability on the domestic market.

Winter wheat harvesting is still underway, having commenced two weeks ago, with the authority indicating that most of the harvested crop remains on farms undergoing bagging and grading, while some fields are yet to be harvested.

The deliveries come as Zimbabwe prepares for an anticipated El Niño-induced drought, with authorities stepping up efforts to strengthen national food reserves and expand agricultural production to cushion the country against potential crop failures.

Under its 2026/27 summer production programme, ARDA is targeting 100,000 hectares across its estates, A1 and A2 joint venture growers, irrigation scheme business units and clustered smallholder farmers.

Of the targeted hectarage, 60,000 hectares will be placed under irrigation, while the remaining 40,000 hectares will be planted using climate-smart varieties as part of efforts to sustain production under increasingly unpredictable weather conditions.

The programme is expected to contribute towards strengthening domestic cereal supplies and replenishing the Strategic Grain Reserve, which remains central to the country’s capacity to respond to drought-related food shortages.

Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development Minister Dr Anxious Masuka recently warned that Zimbabwe was almost certain to experience below-normal rainfall during the 2026/27 agricultural season, with the Meteorological Services Department classifying it as a drought year.

Speaking at the 74th graduation ceremony at Gwebi College of Agriculture, Dr Masuka said the warming of the central South Pacific Ocean associated with El Niño was expected to exceed three degrees Celsius, pointing to a particularly strong weather phenomenon.

“So now we are almost 100 percent certain that we will have below-normal rainfall for Zimbabwe,” he said.

Despite the unfavourable forecast, the minister assured the nation that Government was implementing measures to safeguard food security, revealing that the GMB had purchased 345,000 tonnes of various cereals by the previous day.

The figure exceeds the 328,000 tonnes of grain distributed during the devastating 2024 drought, when the country relied heavily on imports and emergency interventions to meet domestic food requirements.

“As of yesterday, we had actually purchased at the GMB 345,000 metric tonnes of various cereals. In 2024, when we had the worst drought, we distributed 328,000 metric tonnes,” he said.

“So we are well on our way to ensuring that should there be this unfortunate event, we will have enough of the strategic grain reserve to feed everyone.”

Government’s broader drought preparedness programme includes strengthening national and household grain reserves, promoting climate-smart agriculture, implementing livestock drought mitigation programmes and improving early-warning systems.

Under the livestock intervention, authorities plan to establish drought mitigation centres serving every seven to eight villages. The facilities are expected to have permanent water sources, livestock feeding infrastructure, sales points and disease-control services to help farmers manage their herds during periods of prolonged dry weather.

Dr Masuka also called for improved post-harvest management, raising concern over maize losses that can reach 30 percent after harvesting.

He urged farmers and households to minimise food wastage and embrace innovation as the country prepares for the anticipated weather challenges.

“Let’s invoke the Munhumutapa spirit, that entrepreneurial spirit, that innovation, so that Zimbabwe can come out stronger from this drought,” he said.

Meanwhile, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development, Professor Obert Jiri, has urged farmers against panic planting or abandoning their fields over fears of an El Niño-induced drought, emphasising that seasonal forecasts should inform preparedness rather than trigger premature agricultural decisions.

Prof Jiri said farmers should concentrate on conserving soil moisture, diversifying their crops and taking advantage of favourable rainfall whenever it occurs.

“Farmers need to be ready and make the most of every drop of rain,” he said.

He urged farmers to closely monitor local weather conditions, assess soil moisture levels and seek guidance from agricultural extension officers before making planting decisions.

The authorities’ message is that while the anticipated drought presents significant risks to agricultural production, preparations must focus on maximising available water resources, protecting livestock, reducing post-harvest losses and ensuring that available grain stocks are sufficient to meet national requirements.

title: Cheaper HIV Prevention Injection Could Benefit Zimbabwe
summary: HARARE — The approval of a lower-cost generic version of lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injection designed to prevent HIV infection, could improve access to preventive treatment across low- and middle-income countries, including Zimbabwe, where the cost and availability of prevention services remain important public-health and economic concerns. The US Food and Drug Administration has granted tentative […]
content_text:
HARARE — The approval of a lower-cost generic version of lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injection designed to prevent HIV infection, could improve access to preventive treatment across low- and middle-income countries, including Zimbabwe, where the cost and availability of prevention services remain important public-health and economic concerns.

The US Food and Drug Administration has granted tentative approval to a generic version developed by India’s Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, according to the Associated Press (AP). The development could accelerate access in as many as 120 low- and middle-income countries, with the medicine expected to cost approximately US$40 per person annually in the markets covered by the initiative.

Lenacapavir is administered twice a year, offering an alternative to daily pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) pills. Two major clinical studies found that the injection nearly eliminated new HIV infections among participants at high risk, according to AP. Its less frequent dosing could also help address adherence challenges associated with daily medication.

The generic was developed through an arrangement involving Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and South Africa-based Wits RHI. Six generic manufacturers have secured royalty-free licensing agreements with Gilead Sciences, the original developer, to support wider production in specified countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America.

For Zimbabwe, the development presents a potentially important opportunity to strengthen HIV prevention while reducing the long-term economic burden associated with new infections. Greater access to effective prevention could help protect the country’s workforce, reduce future pressure on public healthcare expenditure and support productivity among economically active communities.

However, lower manufacturing costs do not automatically translate into immediate availability. Zimbabwe would still need to establish the relevant regulatory pathway, procurement arrangements, financing and distribution systems before the injection could be incorporated into national prevention programmes. The available licensing arrangements also do not, by themselves, establish when the generic will reach the Zimbabwean market.

The Zimbabwe Mail notes that the economic significance extends beyond the price of the medicine. Affordable prevention depends on sustainable public-health financing, reliable supply chains, diagnostic capacity and the ability of healthcare providers to reach communities at risk. These requirements will determine whether the scientific breakthrough produces measurable benefits for Zimbabwe.

The generic approval follows a period in which demand for lenacapavir in lower-income markets has exceeded supply, with Gilead previously the sole supplier. The company’s branded version, Yeztugo, carries a US list price of US$28,218 annually, although that price is not the expected cost of the generic in the targeted markets.

AP reported that generic lenacapavir must be preceded by HIV testing, with further testing required before each injection. This is important because administering the drug to someone with an undiagnosed HIV infection can contribute to drug resistance. Reported side effects include injection-site reactions, headaches and nausea.

The approval is therefore a significant step, but not the end of the process. Health organisations involved in the initiative say governments and donors must still secure funding to purchase the medicine and build the systems needed to deliver it at scale.

For Zimbabwe, the potential gains will depend on whether affordable supply can be translated into an accessible national prevention programme. The breakthrough could strengthen the country’s HIV response, but procurement, regulatory approval and sustained financing will determine how quickly its benefits reach patients.

title: Zimbabwe Wheat Harvest Nears 600,000 Tonnes as Output Rises
summary: HARARE — Zimbabwe is on course for a wheat harvest of at least 600,000 tonnes after farmers collected 568,581 tonnes from 83% of the area planted this season, strengthening the country’s food-security position and creating fresh opportunities for millers, food processors and agricultural suppliers. Agriculture Permanent Secretary Professor Obert Jiri said 108,569 hectares had been […]
content_text:
HARARE — Zimbabwe is on course for a wheat harvest of at least 600,000 tonnes after farmers collected 568,581 tonnes from 83% of the area planted this season, strengthening the country’s food-security position and creating fresh opportunities for millers, food processors and agricultural suppliers.

Agriculture Permanent Secretary Professor Obert Jiri said 108,569 hectares had been harvested out of 130,316 hectares planted during the 2026 winter season, with average yields of 5.2 tonnes per hectare. The Government is targeting completion by Friday, 6 November, ahead of forecast rainfall that could damage standing crops and compromise grain quality.

Authorities have deployed 482 combine harvesters, collectively covering an estimated 14,000 hectares a day, as they seek to bring in the remaining 21,747 hectares. Mashonaland West leads provincial production with 163,918 tonnes, followed by Mashonaland Central at 140,579 tonnes and Mashonaland East at 104,070 tonnes.

The expected harvest would exceed the initial planting target of 125,000 hectares, reflecting continued investment in irrigation, mechanisation and improved agricultural production. More importantly for the domestic economy, industrial wheat demand has increased from less than 360,000 tonnes three years ago to more than 552,000 tonnes annually, according to Jiri.

That growth has implications beyond food security. A larger domestic wheat supply provides local millers with a stronger sourcing base, potentially reducing exposure to imported grain and foreign-currency costs. It also supports downstream businesses involved in flour production, bread manufacturing, biscuits, pasta and other processed foods.

A harvest of 600,000 tonnes would imply a theoretical surplus of about 48,000 tonnes against the stated annual industrial requirement. However, the balance will depend on final deliveries, grain quality, storage losses and the specific varieties required by processors. Zimbabwe continues to import specialised hard wheat for blending and industrial applications that domestic production does not yet fully satisfy.

The distinction is commercially important. Higher volumes alone will not eliminate imports if locally produced wheat does not meet millers’ protein, strength and processing specifications. Greater coordination between farmers, seed suppliers, millers and agricultural researchers could help align production with industrial requirements and retain more value within the domestic supply chain.

The Zimbabwe Mail notes that sustained wheat self-sufficiency could also improve planning for food manufacturers by making local raw-material supplies more predictable. For farmers, reliable demand from millers offers an incentive to invest in irrigation equipment, machinery, seed and fertiliser, while transporters and grain-storage operators stand to benefit from increased volumes moving through the agricultural supply chain.

FurtherAfrica has previously highlighted the importance of agricultural training and industry partnerships in improving productivity and developing climate-resilient farming technologies. The wheat harvest reinforces the economic value of connecting agricultural expertise with commercial production, particularly as the country seeks to improve yields and manage weather-related risks.

The Government has said it wants to sustain self-sufficiency and eventually develop export capacity. But any exportable surplus will need to be assessed against domestic quality requirements, strategic reserves and the timing of local demand. The immediate priority remains completing the harvest before rainfall threatens the crop.

Zimbabwe’s wheat performance is increasingly becoming an industrial as well as an agricultural story. Its longer-term contribution will depend on whether higher farm output translates into competitive processing, reliable supplies and reduced dependence on specialised imports.

title: Constitutional Court Reserves Judgment on Challenge to Amendment No. 3
summary: By Chenesai Mugwadi The Constitutional Court on Monday reserved judgment in a case challenging the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act, 2026, which removed the direct election of the President. The matter, Case CCZ278/26, was filed by Eliphas Kawa and Hazvineyi Machingura, who are seeking direct access to the Constitutional Court for a declaration […]
content_text:
By Chenesai Mugwadi

The Constitutional Court on Monday reserved judgment in a case challenging the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act, 2026, which removed the direct election of the President.

The matter, Case CCZ278/26, was filed by Eliphas Kawa and Hazvineyi Machingura, who are seeking direct access to the Constitutional Court for a declaration that provisions of the amendment are invalid.

No date has been set for delivery of judgment on the preliminary issue of direct access.

What the Amendment Does

The Amendment Act, signed by President Emmerson Mnangagwa on 7 July 2026, repealed and replaced Section 92 of the Constitution.

Previously, the President was elected directly by registered voters in a general election.

Under the new provision, the President is elected by members of Parliament sitting jointly as the Senate and National Assembly.

The amendment also expands the Senate from 80 to 90 members, providing for 10 additional senators appointed by the President on the basis of professional skills and competencies.

The Challenge

The applicants argue that the removal of the right to directly elect the President infringes Section 67 of the Constitution.

They argue that the section provides for political rights, and that such a fundamental change required approval by referendum in terms of Section 328.

The State is opposing the application.

The amendment has attracted multiple legal challenges.

The Court will first determine whether the applicants meet the threshold for direct access before considering the substantive constitutional issues.

If upheld, the new system will replace direct presidential elections with an electoral college model based in Parliament.

title: Gwebi College Partnerships Drive Zimbabwe Agricultural Innovation
summary: HARARE — Zimbabwe’s efforts to strengthen agricultural production and food security are receiving support from closer links between training institutions and private-sector companies, with Gwebi Agricultural College emerging as an example of how education can feed skills, technology and expertise into the commercial farming sector. In a report published by FurtherAfrica, it says partnerships between […]
content_text:
HARARE — Zimbabwe’s efforts to strengthen agricultural production and food security are receiving support from closer links between training institutions and private-sector companies, with Gwebi Agricultural College emerging as an example of how education can feed skills, technology and expertise into the commercial farming sector.

In a report published by FurtherAfrica , it says partnerships between Gwebi, universities and agricultural businesses were helping graduates gain practical workplace experience while developing technologies aimed at addressing production challenges.

The college graduated 86 students in 2026, recording a 99% pass rate. One graduate, Abide Chitiyo, received the Overall Best Student Award with a Distinction and subsequently joined Seed Co as an agricultural extension officer. His work focuses on climate-resilient farming techniques and agronomic practices intended to improve productivity among smallholder farmers.

The partnerships operate within Zimbabwe’s Education 5.0 framework, which combines teaching with research, innovation, community engagement and industrialisation. The University of Zimbabwe’s Associateship Scheme now covers eight agricultural colleges, broadening the academic links available to agricultural training institutions.

The commercial significance extends beyond graduate employment. FurtherAfrica reported that Gwebi students have developed digital irrigation controls, climate-smart mushroom production systems, a small-scale Juncao grass shredder and simplified water and animal-feed systems. Such innovations could offer opportunities for agricultural equipment suppliers, technology companies and processors if they can be developed into affordable products and adopted at scale.

For Zimbabwean businesses, the model could help address a persistent gap between agricultural research and commercial application. Farmers need practical technologies that improve water efficiency, reduce production costs and support climate adaptation, while agribusinesses require trained personnel capable of translating technical knowledge into better yields and more reliable supply.

The wider investment environment also presents opportunities. The €14 million Agroecological Transitions for Horticulture in Arid Zones programme, launched by the European Union and the International Fund for Agricultural Development in 2026, is designed to support resilient horticulture, productivity and market access in Zimbabwe, Zambia and Botswana through 2030.

Zimbabwe’s reported progress towards its 660,000-tonne wheat production target also points to demand for agronomists, extension officers and agricultural services. Government crop-monitoring figures cited by FurtherAfrica placed output at approximately 569,000 tonnes at the time of its report.

The Zimbabwe Mail understands that the economic value of these partnerships will depend on whether training and student innovation translate into measurable improvements in farm productivity, commercial investment and domestic supply chains. Wider adoption of locally developed irrigation and processing technologies could create business opportunities while reducing reliance on imported equipment.

However, the transition from college projects to commercially viable products is not automatic. It requires financing, testing, manufacturing capacity, maintenance networks and access to farmers. The longer-term test for Gwebi’s industry partnerships will be whether they produce technologies that can be deployed beyond the college and graduates who can deliver measurable gains across Zimbabwe’s agricultural value chain.

title: Parliamentary committee recognises GeoPomona’s role in waste emissions management
summary: Story by Owen Mandovha A PARLIAMENTARY committee has recognised the role of the GeoPomona Waste Management Facility in managing emissions from solid waste, following a tour of the site in Harare. The Parliamentary Thematic Committee on Climate Change, led by its Chairperson, Senator Prisca Mupfumira, visited the facility on Tuesday to assess its waste management […] The post Parliamentary committee recognises GeoPomona’s role in waste emissions management first appeared on ZBC NEWS .
content_text:
Story by Owen Mandovha

A PARLIAMENTARY committee has recognised the role of the GeoPomona Waste Management Facility in managing emissions from solid waste, following a tour of the site in Harare.

The Parliamentary Thematic Committee on Climate Change, led by its Chairperson, Senator Prisca Mupfumira, visited the facility on Tuesday to assess its waste management processes and contribution to efforts to limit greenhouse gas emissions.

Organic waste can produce methane as it decomposes, particularly when it breaks down in conditions with little or no oxygen. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming.

During the tour, Senator Mupfumira said the committee was satisfied with what it had observed, highlighting the technology being used to contain emissions.

“We are glad that this project indeed met our expectations from what we anticipated. We are the first Thematic Committee on Climate Change in the 10th Parliament demonstrating how Government places climate change interventions as a top priority. The emissions from solid waste are harmful and the technology deployed here is top notch to limit gas emissions hence the Committee is excited at this project,” she said.

Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, Senator Sengezo Tshabangu, who also took part in the tour, said plans to replicate the project in Bulawayo would proceed.

Bulawayo has for years faced challenges associated with its Ngozi Mine dumpsite.

“Last week, the council was here to appreciate how the project is unfolding and I can tell you that there is no going back in the implementation of this project, as the Minister of Finance told me that there is no extra cost to the residents, so this is not even an issue,” he said.

GeoPomona Waste Management Company Chief Executive Officer Dr Dilesh Nguwaya also announced plans to introduce a one-bin-per-household policy as part of efforts to expand the company’s waste collection and processing capacity.

“We are providing one bin per household to ensure that we expand our waste management capacity. This will also increase our feed to the sorting plant and the energy generation plant,” he said.

The proposed policy is expected to increase the volume of waste delivered to the facility’s sorting and energy generation plants.

title: NEW: Gweshegweshe’s death a loss to Zimbabwe’s creative and cultural landscape — Minister Sanyatwe
categories: SundayMail; Local News; National; National News; News
summary: Online Reporter THE death of actor William “Gweshegweshe” Matenga is a significant loss to Zimbabwe’s creative and cultural landscape as he was…
content_text:
Online Reporter

THE death of actor William “Gweshegweshe” Matenga is a significant loss to Zimbabwe’s creative and cultural landscape as he was a multi-talented and accomplished artist whose contribution to acting, television, film and journalism enriched the country’s cultural heritage and helped shape its storytelling tradition, Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture Minister Anselem Sanyatwe has said.

Matenga succumbed to hypertension on Saturday morning.

He was 68.

In a condolence message today, Minister Sanyatwe expressed profound sadness at the loss of a man whose life and career reflected a journey of service, creativity and dedication to his country.

“His passing is a significant loss to Zimbabwe’s creative and cultural landscape. He was a multi-talented and accomplished artist whose contribution to acting, television, film and journalism enriched the country’s cultural heritage and helped shape its storytelling tradition,” Minister Sanyatwe said.

Minister Sanyatwe

“He leaves a huge void in the nation’s creative industry, particularly within the film and television fraternity, where his distinctive talent, experience and contribution to the development of the performing arts will be deeply missed.”

Matenga was born on September 9, 1958 in Buhera, Manicaland province.

He was not only a household name in the arts but also a liberation war veteran.

Following Zimbabwe’s independence, he served in the military before pursuing his passion for the creative arts.

His formal artistic journey began in 1984 when he joined the Screen Talent Drama Club.

Eager to hone his craft, he further developed his professional skills through studies in Media and Journalism at Harare Polytechnic.

His versatility extended beyond the screen into journalism, where he contributed articles to Spotlight on Zimbabwe, a magazine formerly published by the Ministry of Information.

Matenga’s artistic footprint extended far beyond Zimbabwe’s borders.

Before becoming a local icon, he featured in notable international productions, including King Solomon’s Mine in 1985 and Steve Biko in 1987.

However, it was his subsequent performances alongside the late Lazarus Boora, popularly known as Gringo, that cemented his place in the hearts of Zimbabwean audiences across generations.

His role in the celebrated Gringo drama series and Gringo Troublemaker made him a beloved figure in local pop culture.

Despite Matenga’s death, Minister Sanyatwe added, his remarkable body of work remains an enduring legacy that will continue to inspire emerging actors and generations of creatives.

title: Tanzania delegation hails NAC’s integration of NCDs into HIV Care
categories: Herald; Africa; Health; Local News; National; National News; News
summary: Trust Freddy-Herald Correspondent A DELEGATION from Tanzania’s AIDS Trust Fund has commended Zimbabwe for pioneering the integration of Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) into…
content_text:
Trust Freddy- Herald Correspondent

A DELEGATION from Tanzania’s AIDS Trust Fund has commended Zimbabwe for pioneering the integration of Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) into its HIV and tuberculosis health delivery.

The team, comprising the board and management of the AIDS Trust Fund, is in Zimbabwe on a week-long learning visit to benchmark the country’s domestic health financing model.

It is led by board chairperson Mr Sabasaba Mwoshingi and Tanzania AIDS Commission executive director Dr Adam Mrisho, who is also ATF board secretary.

After touring Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals, where the National AIDS Council (NAC) injected over US$2 million to upgrade the renal unit and blood bank, and a mobile clinic in Epworth, Dr Mrisho said Zimbabwe had shown how HIV platforms can be leveraged to tackle rising NCDs.

“Today we toured one of the central hospitals where we saw the installations and operations of the renal unit. We congratulate NAC Zimbabwe for such a remarkable gesture,” he said.

“In the SADC region, we are having more people living with HIV than before, so integrating non-communicable diseases and HIV is paramount in our services.”

He said integrating conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, renal disease and cancers like cervical cancer into HIV care was now critical as people living with HIV live longer on treatment.

“Renal disease is a very serious disease that needs someone to really go through a lot. By having that facility at the central hospital, it really saves several people, not only people living with HIV but also the general community,” he said.

Dr Mrisho singled out Zimbabwe’s decision to offer renal services free of charge as a regional outlier.

“This is free of charge, which is different from most SADC countries. This gives a good example of proper use of the AIDS Levy fund. It is something we can try to replicate in other parts of the world,” he said.

In Epworth Overspill, where NAC supports mobile health services in partnership with ZimbosAbantu Healthcare on Wheels, the delegation saw integrated SRH, NCD and HIV services being offered at a market-side clinic.

“It is very promising to see that services are brought to the community. It saves the community through integrated SRH, NCDs and HIV services,” Dr Mrisho said.

He said the visit brought to life this year’s World AIDS Day theme: access.

“Ending AIDS starts with access. That is very key and we have seen it in a practical way here in Zimbabwe,” he said.

“Congratulations to NAC Zimbabwe and the Government of Zimbabwe for making sure all these essential services are accessed by all communities.”

title: Muzarabani village head jailed for 9 years over unlawful possession of Pangolin scales
categories: Herald; crime and courts; Local News; National; National News; News
summary: Prosper Dembedza-Herald Correspondent HARARE magistrate Ms Lisa Mutendereki has slapped Mazonde village head Johannes Mazonde with a mandatory nine-year imprisonment sentence after…
content_text:
Prosper Dembedza- Herald Correspondent

HARARE magistrate Ms Lisa Mutendereki has slapped Mazonde village head Johannes Mazonde with a mandatory nine-year imprisonment sentence after finding him guilty of unlawful possession of pangolin scales.

Mazonde, who serves under Chief Kasekete, was convicted following an anti-poaching sting operation conducted by police in the capital.

The court heard that on 27 October 2026, at around 7:00 am, Detective Constable Manzini from the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) Minerals, Flora and Fauna Unit received intelligence indicating that the traditional leader was in possession of pangolin scales and was actively seeking buyers in Harare.

Detective Constable Manzini obtained the accused’s mobile contact number and initiated a call, posing as a potential buyer.

The detective successfully arranged to meet Mazonde at Eastgate Mall in central Harare to conclude the transaction.

Det Manzini subsequently teamed up with Detective Sergeants Kemusi and Mututu to conduct surveillance at the shopping complex. At approximately 8:05am, Det Manzini contacted Mazonde to rendezvous at the main entrance.

Upon the suspect’s arrival, the undercover detectives intercepted him, identified themselves using their official service cards, and explained their mission.

Detective Sergeant Kemusi requested the accused to produce any wildlife product in his possession.

Mazonde extracted a black plastic bag from the left pocket of his blue jacket and handed it over to the team.

A physical search of the container uncovered 29 pangolin scales wrapped inside two separate black plastic bags.

When requested to produce a valid licence or permit authorising the legal possession of the items, Mazonde failed to do so, leading to his immediate arrest.

Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority officials were summoned to the CID offices, where they examined and authenticated the 29 seized pieces.

Pangolins are a strictly protected endangered species under the Parks and Wildlife Management Act, which carries heavy custodial penalties for possession or trafficking.

title: ZANU PF Women’s League donates food hampers to children’s homes
categories: Herald; Local News; National News; News; Politics
summary: Joseph Madzimure-Zimpapers Politics Hub THE ZANU PF Women’s League has handed over food hampers to 40 children’s homes across Zimbabwe to support…
content_text:
Joseph Madzimure- Zimpapers Politics Hub

THE ZANU PF Women’s League has handed over food hampers to 40 children’s homes across Zimbabwe to support underprivileged communities in line with the President’s mantra of leaving no one and no place behind.

The league selected four children’s homes in each of the country’s ten provinces to receive essential commodities, including rice, sugar, and cooking oil.

In Harare, the initial distribution covered several institutions, including the Matthew Rusike Children’s Home, Chinyaradzo Children’s Home, and the Tamuka Foundation.

ZANU PF Secretary for the Women’s League Cde Mabel Chinomona challenged citizens to cultivate a culture of philanthropy ahead of the holidays, revealing that the grain consignment had been secured through international diplomatic channels.

“As we are approaching the festive season, we should have a culture of giving back to the underprivileged society,” Cde Chinomona said. “We have sourced rice from China to give back to the vulnerable society in Zimbabwe. I sourced the rice from our Chinese friends.”

Cde Chinomona commended the long-standing bilateral relationship between Zimbabwe and China, noting that the alliance dates back to the days of the liberation struggle.

“Today, we are handing over bags of rice donated by our Chinese friends for distribution,” she added.

“Long live our friendship between Zimbabwe and China. Long live President Mnangagwa. Long live ZANU PF. Long live Chinese President Xi Jinping. When I approached them for food to give to the underprivileged communities, they showed us that a friend in need is a friend indeed. The Chinese people say, ‘Give a man a fish, and you feed him for a day’. Today, we have given our mothers and children rice, and we have fed them with love. On behalf of the Women’s League and the beneficiaries, we say thank you.”

She emphasised that the ruling party remains structurally committed to caring for vulnerable groups to ensure national food security is achieved in line with Vision 2030 and the Second National Development Strategy (NDS2). She also appealed to Zimbabweans to increase social support for elderly communities.

ZANU PF Secretary for External Affairs Cde Betty Kaseke highlighted that the league will extend its outreach programme to several additional children’s homes before Christmas and New Year.

Representing the beneficiaries, Matthew Rusike Children’s Home official Reverend Linneclink Mutendzwa commended the league for sourcing the food relief.

“We are happy to receive food for the children at various children’s homes. We really appreciate the support,” Rev Mutendzwa stated, adding that the commodities would significantly ease the day-to-day operational challenges institutions face when catering for residents over the festive season.

INCREASE GUMBO MIRROR REPORTER

MWENEZI – A 47-year-old peace broker was assaulted and allegedly killed by a man he tried to refrain from beating another at a beerhall at Chizenge Shopping Centre on Saturday evening. content_text:
Story by Patience Nyagato

FOUR children’s institutions in Harare have received food hampers from the ZANU PF Women’s League as part of a festive season outreach programme targeting 40 institutions across the country.

The initiative, spearheaded by the party’s Secretary for Women’s Affairs, Cde Mabel Chinomona, is expected to reach beneficiaries in all 10 provinces.

The four institutions that received donations on Tuesday were Matthew Rusike Children’s Home, Harare Children’s Home, Chinyaradzo Children’s Home and Tamuka Foundation.

The hampers included basic food supplies such as rice, cooking oil and sugar, with each institution reportedly receiving more than 250 kilogrammes of rice.

Speaking during the handover, Cde Chinomona encouraged communities to support initiatives that promote self-reliance and economic productivity, alongside assistance for vulnerable groups.

“Last year, we donated 600 sewing machines to women. I am told this home is making detergents. I applaud that because it is our vision to have people become productive, and that is how factories come to be. This is our party policy: we should help the less privileged. Our President has always taught us to leave no one and no place behind, in line with Vision 2030. I want to thank our friends from China who made this donation possible by donating rice to us,” Cde Chinomona said.

The beneficiaries welcomed the assistance, saying it would help meet some of the needs of children under their care.

Matthew Rusike Children’s Home National Director, Rev Linrlelink Mutendzwa, said the institution cared for 59 children, including five university students.

“We are so excited because you have extended a hand to us. We have 59 children, with the youngest being six years old. We also have five university students. We appreciate this gesture and hope you will continue doing this for our less privileged children in society,” Rev Mutendzwa said.

Tamuka Foundation spokesperson Tatenda Manyenya said the donation would support more than 20 children under the organisation’s care in Kuwadzana.

“We are so happy. We have more than 20 children in Kuwadzana and this donation will go a long way in supporting the children under our care,” Manyenya said.

The Women’s League says the festive season outreach programme will extend to other provinces, with a target of supporting 40 childcare institutions nationwide.

Story by Puleni Siampepu

ZAKA residents and businesses are set to benefit from improved access to environmental services following the commissioning of new Environmental Management Agency (EMA) district offices in the area.

Before the facility was completed, residents and stakeholders had to travel to Masvingo to access services such as Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) consultations and environmental licensing.

The new offices are expected to bring these services closer to communities while strengthening EMA’s environmental monitoring and public awareness activities.

Chief Ndanga welcomed the development, saying it would improve access to environmental information and enable the agency to extend its outreach programmes to previously difficult-to-reach communities.

“With the EMA office now open, our people will now access information nearer to their homes and EMA will find it easy to carry out its outreach campaigns to areas that were previously difficult to reach.”

Masvingo Provincial Director for Coordination Ms Rosemary Chingwe, who represented the Minister of State for Provincial Affairs and Devolution, Cde Ezra Chadzamira, said the new facility and the provision of service vehicles would improve the delivery of essential services in rural areas.

“The province has some areas that are not easily accessible, therefore the official handover of service vehicles is equally significant. They will enable environmental officers to conduct inspections and monitor compliance with environmental legislation, respond to environmental incidents and intensify awareness campaigns even in communities that are difficult to reach.”

Minister of Environment and Climate Honourable Evelyn Ndlovu, represented by Ambassador Zenzo Nsimbi, said the project reflected Government’s commitment to decentralisation, improved public service delivery and stronger institutional capacity at local level.

“A functional district office with good workplace and logistical enablers in the form of a vehicle will allow the agency to respond more effectively to environmental challenges, monitor compliance, promote environmental awareness and work closely with communities, local authorities, traditional leaders and other stakeholders.”

The establishment of the district office is expected to strengthen EMA’s presence in Zaka, improve environmental compliance monitoring and enhance engagement with communities and local authorities.

title: Boy (10)’s tumour responds to UK drug, more supplies needed
summary: PETRONILLA MUKAMURIMIRROR REPORTER HARARE – A 10-year-old boy battling a neck tumour is showing signs of improvement after starting treatment with a drug sourced from the United Kingdom (UK), but his family needs US$2 196 to secure further supplies.Kudakwashe Tabarira has shown a reduction in the size of the tumour since he started taking Trametinib […]
content_text:
PETRONILLA MUKAMURI MIRROR REPORTER

HARARE – A 10-year-old boy battling a neck tumour is showing signs of improvement after starting treatment with a drug sourced from the United Kingdom (UK), but his family needs US$2 196 to secure further supplies. Kudakwashe Tabarira has shown a reduction in the size of the tumour since he started taking Trametinib 0.5mg, which costs US$1 098 per supply. His father, Benedict Tabarira, told Masvingo Mirror that the medication had improved his son’s condition, restoring some of his independence. “Ever since the medicine was administered to Kudakwashe, the tumour is reducing in size. He can now eat on his own and walk on his own,” said Tabarira The family is appealing for US$2 196 to buy medication for November and December to sustain the progress. “We are grateful for the assistance we received from well-wishers. If supplies for two months are secured, I believe he will get better,” he said. The appeal follows previous fundraising efforts through Masvingo Mirror Helpline in July and August 2026, when the family needed money for scans and medication. Tabarira said the family raised US$750 by selling two cattle for US$350 and US$400, while well-wishers from the Masvingo United Residents and Ratepayers Alliance (MURRA) contributed the remaining US$446 needed for the first batch of medication. Kudakwashe was diagnosed with Neurofibromatosis Type 1, a genetic condition that causes changes in skin pigmentation and tumours to develop on nerve tissue. His medical problems began in 2017 when a growth was discovered under his tongue. It was surgically removed, but another tumour later developed on his neck. Doctors advised the family to wait until he was five years old before removing the tumour. However, the Covid-19 pandemic and travel restrictions disrupted plans for further treatment. His condition progressively affected his mobility and strength, leaving him unable to walk or feed himself without assistance. The family is appealing to well-wishers to help secure medication for the next two months. Those willing to assist can contact Benedict Tabarira on 0785356120 or Masvingo Mirror Helpline on 0716895703 or 0775036812.

title: Great Dyke Cycling Tour Puts Spotlight on Zimbabwe’s Mineral Wealth
categories: News; Munyaradzi Hwengwere; Nedbank Tour de Great Dyke; Zimbabwe
summary: The 2026 Nedbank Tour de Great Dyke begins on Thursday bringing together cyclists, mining companies, government officials and community stakeholders for a three-day event celebrating the country’s mineral wealth, tourism and community development.
