title: Zimbabweans call for tax on idle agricultural land
categories: National; Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube; idle agricultural land; tax
summary: Some sections of Zimbabwe have, as part of submission to the 2027 National Budget public hearings, suggested the introduction of a land tax targeting owners who leave agricultural land idle. The submissions have put spotlight on issues of land utilisation, agricultural productivity and the potential impact on rural communities. The proposal, which seeks to make […]
content_text:
Some sections of Zimbabwe have, as part of submission to the 2027 National Budget public hearings, suggested the introduction of a land tax targeting owners who leave agricultural land idle.

The submissions have put spotlight on issues of land utilisation, agricultural productivity and the potential impact on rural communities.

The proposal, which seeks to make it more expensive to hold land without putting it to productive use, was presented by Chairperson of the Parliamentary Portfolio Committee on Budget, Finance and Investment Promotion, Lincoln Dhliwayo, during a pre-budget seminar in Bulawayo last week.

Dhliwayo said participants had called for a review of the existing two percent land tax cost, arguing tax on unused land could encourage beneficiaries of the land reform programme to put their properties to productive use.

“Then another proposal had to do with the land tax. In this case, the participants were saying to try and make sure people do not leave land idle, they have to be charged a certain amount so that it becomes costly to keep idle land,” said Dhliwayo.

“Once we make it costly to keep idle land, then everyone will try to make sure that that land is productive.”

He said the seminar had proposed reviewing the two percent land tax, leaving it to the Ministry of Finance to determine the appropriate amount or percentage.

The proposal received a cautious response from Finance Minister, Professor Mthuli Ncube, who said he would consult the Minister of Lands and Rural Development, Vangelis Peter Haritatos, on the possibility of introducing the measure.

“Very interesting proposal on land tax rather than, you know, maybe introducing a ‘use it or lose it’ principle. We are saying that if you don’t use it, we’ll tax it,” he said.

“It’s an interesting proposal. I shall also have a conversation with the Minister for Lands, Minister of Lands and Rural Development Vangelis Peter Haritatos, on this and see if it’s something that we can introduce just to force our citizens to use the land that was hard fought for.”

The proposal comes amid longstanding concerns about the utilisation of agricultural land following Zimbabwe’s fast-track land reform programme, which redistributed land previously held by commercial farmers to indigenous Zimbabweans.

However, the suggestion has also raised questions about how such a tax would be implemented, particularly whether it would apply to communal landholders and how the government would distinguish between deliberate non-utilisation and circumstances beyond a farmer’s control.

Zimbabwe Communist Party secretary-general Ngqabutho Nicholas Mabhena warned introducing land taxation without careful consideration of its historical implications could revive painful memories of colonial-era taxation, which was among the grievances that fuelled resistance to colonial rule.

Mabhena said taxation imposed on indigenous people during the colonial period, including hut, land and cattle taxes, had contributed to the grievances that ultimately fed into the liberation struggle.

“One of the factors that led to the liberation struggle can also affect communal farmers. Some of the grievances that people had were hut tax and land tax, cattle tax,” he said.

He questioned whether the proposed measure would extend to communal land, warning that some rural households might not have the financial resources or capacity to utilise their land fully.

“It’s not clear from the submissions whether this will affect communal land as well, because some rural folk may be incapacitated to use their land,” said Mabhena.

His concerns point to the need for clarity on the proposed tax’s scope, particularly given the different land tenure arrangements and economic circumstances across Zimbabwe’s farming communities.

During colonial rule, taxation was also used as an instrument of economic and political control. Hut and poll taxes imposed on indigenous Africans compelled many households to seek wage employment to meet their tax obligations, while land policies entrenched racial inequalities in access to agricultural resources.

The Land Apportionment Act of 1930 formalised racial divisions in land ownership, reserving large areas of prime agricultural land for the white minority while restricting the majority of indigenous Africans to overcrowded and often less productive reserves.

Although the current proposal is presented as a measure to promote agricultural productivity rather than as a mechanism of coercion, Mabhena’s concerns highlight the importance of making sure any new tax does not disproportionately burden rural households with limited resources.

Beyond land taxation, the pre-budget consultations also highlighted challenges affecting agricultural production, particularly the late distribution of farming inputs and delayed payments to farmers who deliver their produce to the Grain Marketing Board (GMB).

Dhliwayo said farmers had complained that government-supported agricultural inputs, including those distributed under presidential input schemes, often arrived too late in the season to be useful.

“Many times you would find that those presidential inputs or inputs that are given to our farmers, they may come late in January when the farming season is almost over,” said the legislator.

He said participants had called on the Finance Ministry to make sure funding for agricultural inputs was released in time for farmers to prepare for the planting season.

The consultations also heard concerns about delayed payments by the GMB, which Dhliwayo said were undermining farmers’ ability to recover production costs and prepare for subsequent agricultural seasons.

“Whenever they submit their harvest or their product, then they are paid too late. They cannot cover their costs. They cannot go back to their farms,” he said.

He called for farmers to be paid promptly after delivering their produce to encourage continued production.

The seminar also proposed expanding irrigation infrastructure and water harvesting initiatives to improve agricultural productivity especially in areas vulnerable to changing rainfall patterns.

Other submissions included calls for tougher penalties against counterfeit imports, particularly fake food, medicines and agricultural inputs, to protect public health and consumers.

The Ministry of Finance is expected to consider the submissions as it prepares the 2027 National Budget.

title: Zimbabwe Manufacturing Investment Surpasses Mining in Q3 2026
summary: HARARE — Zimbabwe’s manufacturing sector attracted US$1.219 billion in proposed investment during the third quarter of 2026, overtaking mining for the first time in the latest investment figures, according to an analysis by Equity Axis. The figures, drawn from investment licences issued by the Zimbabwe Investment and Development Agency (ZIDA), show that manufacturing secured 49 […]
content_text:
HARARE — Zimbabwe’s manufacturing sector attracted US$1.219 billion in proposed investment during the third quarter of 2026, overtaking mining for the first time in the latest investment figures, according to an analysis by Equity Axis .

The figures, drawn from investment licences issued by the Zimbabwe Investment and Development Agency (ZIDA), show that manufacturing secured 49 licences, compared with 78 for mining, which attracted proposed capital of US$1.065 billion. Manufacturing therefore accounted for 46.8% of the US$2.606 billion investment pipeline approved during the quarter, against mining’s 40.8%.

Equity Axis said the figures point to growing interest in industrial production but cautioned that investment approvals do not necessarily translate into additional output, jobs or exports. The average proposed manufacturing investment was approximately US$24.9 million, almost twice mining’s US$13.6 million per licence.

The development comes as Zimbabwe’s industrial sector continues to recover. The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries reported that manufacturing capacity utilisation reached 55.9% in 2025, up from 52.3% in 2024, while industrial output increased by 13% and employment rose by 6%.

However, Equity Axis highlighted persistent constraints, including high operating costs, unreliable infrastructure, limited affordable finance and dependence on imported raw materials. Imported inputs accounted for approximately 54% of manufacturers’ raw-material requirements in 2025, underlining the challenge of translating higher investment into stronger domestic value addition.

The investment pipeline also raises questions about the extent to which new manufacturing projects will support mineral beneficiation. Zimbabwe recorded US$5.013 billion in mineral sales between January and 27 October 2026, with lithium and platinum group metals accounting for about 81.9% of the total, according to the Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe.

Equity Axis noted that without project-level information, it was not possible to establish how much of the newly licensed manufacturing investment involved mineral processing, factory expansion, rehabilitation or entirely new industrial facilities.

The distinction is significant because approved investment can take time to reach production. ZIDA’s monitoring figures for projects tracked at the end of 2025 showed US$1.547 billion in realised investment against projected expenditure of US$5.058 billion, representing a realisation rate of about 31%.

The Zimbabwe Mail understands that the latest figures will place greater focus on the implementation of approved projects, particularly their financing, commissioning schedules, employment commitments and expected export contribution. Manufacturing’s lead over mining marks a notable shift in the investment pipeline, but its wider economic significance will ultimately depend on how much proposed capital is converted into productive industrial capacity.

title: Opinion: Zimbabwe’s economy is growing, but is it rebuilding?
summary: By Dr Shame Mugova Zimbabwe’s economy is growing again. Inflation has fallen, the exchange rate has become more stable, and economic activity is recovering. The economy expanded by 8.3% in 2025, while the International Monetary Fund projects growth of 5% in 2026. These improvements deserve recognition. But they raise a more fundamental question: is Zimbabwe […]
content_text:
By Dr Shame Mugova

Zimbabwe’s economy is growing again. Inflation has fallen, the exchange rate has become more stable, and economic activity is recovering. The economy expanded by 8.3% in 2025, while the International Monetary Fund projects growth of 5% in 2026.

These improvements deserve recognition. But they raise a more fundamental question: is Zimbabwe rebuilding its productive economy, or merely recovering economic activity within a substantially weakened economic structure?

Consider Harare’s traditional industrial areas of Workington, Southerton, Graniteside and Willowvale, or Bulawayo’s Belmont and Donnington. These were once important centres of manufacturing, engineering and industrial employment. Many factories closed during Zimbabwe’s prolonged economic difficulties. Others survived but reduced production, while some former industrial premises have been repurposed for warehousing, wholesale trade and other commercial activities.

Commercial activity may have returned to some of these properties, but has manufacturing returned?

A former factory converted into a warehouse can generate employment and income. Yet it does not necessarily replace the machinery, technical skills, industrial jobs and supply chains previously associated with manufacturing.

This distinction receives insufficient attention in Zimbabwe’s economic debate. Inflation and GDP growth dominate the discussion, while less attention is paid to the productive capabilities the country has lost and what is being built in their place.

Recovery is not the same as transformation

The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries reports that manufacturing output increased by 13% in 2025, while capacity utilisation improved from 52.3% to 55.9%. Approximately 35% of surveyed manufacturers invested in expanding productive capacity.

These are encouraging developments. However, they also indicate that approximately 44% of installed capacity among surveyed manufacturers remained unused.

More importantly, capacity utilisation measures the performance of existing businesses. It does not account for factories that permanently closed years earlier.

A surviving manufacturer can increase production while the industrial district surrounding it remains substantially diminished.

Zimbabwe entered the 1990s with considerable manufacturing capabilities in textiles, food processing, engineering, chemicals, metal products and other industries. Not all were efficient or internationally competitive, but they supported formal employment, technical expertise and extensive supplier networks.

Economic transformation should not mean reopening every factory of the past. Some industries were technologically outdated or dependent on protection.

The relevant question is whether lost capabilities are being replaced by modern, competitive industries that generate sustainable employment, increase productivity and produce higher value goods.

When farms stopped feeding factories

Perhaps the clearest illustration of Zimbabwe’s structural transformation is the weakening of connections between agriculture, manufacturing and retail.

Cotton provides an important example.

A functioning cotton industry does not end at the farm. Cotton moves through ginning, spinning, weaving, fabric manufacturing, garment production and clothing retail. Each stage creates employment, investment opportunities and demand for related services.

Zimbabwe once possessed substantial capabilities across this production chain.

Over time, textile and clothing manufacturing contracted sharply, while imported new and secondhand clothing became increasingly important in domestic markets.

Today, vendors selling imported clothing provide livelihoods for many families. Their activities are economically meaningful, but they cannot fully replace the employment and industrial linkages associated with domestic textile production.

The experience of Truworths illustrates this wider transformation.

Once an extensive clothing retail business with domestic manufacturing connections, Truworths entered corporate rescue and was delisted from the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange in July 2025.

Its difficulties involved several factors, including consumer purchasing power, operating costs and competition. Nevertheless, its decline demonstrates how weaknesses in domestic production can become intertwined with the difficulties facing formal retail businesses.

Agriculture presents similar questions.

Zimbabwe produces maize, wheat, soya beans and other commodities that support food processing. Yet domestic supplies remain vulnerable to agricultural shocks.

According to ZIMSTAT’s Food Balance Sheet, maize import dependence increased from 7% in 2022 to 73% during the drought affected year of 2024. Soya bean import dependence reached 62%, while wheat stood at 38%.

These figures do not represent permanent import requirements. Agricultural output has since recovered in several crops. Rather, they expose the vulnerability of domestic production and supply chains.

Why should a country with significant agricultural potential remain so vulnerable to disruptions in food production? How much investment is going into irrigation, storage, agricultural processing and reliable domestic supply systems?

A recent example further illustrates the challenge.

In September 2026, the Competition and Tariff Commission initiated a safeguard investigation following concerns raised by National Foods about rising pasta imports. Imported pasta accounted for approximately 87% of Zimbabwe’s domestic market in 2025, while import volumes increased from about 49.5 million kilograms in 2024 to 58.1 million kilograms in 2025.

National Foods had commenced domestic pasta manufacturing in February 2024. Its concerns raise an important question about the conditions under which emerging domestic manufacturers can compete with established imported products.

The investigation has not established that imports caused the company’s difficulties. Nevertheless, the case demonstrates the challenge of developing local manufacturing in a market already dominated by foreign suppliers.

Imports are not inherently undesirable. International trade can lower prices, increase competition and improve consumer choice. Protecting inefficient industries indefinitely would impose costs on households and businesses.

The concern arises when imports replace productive capabilities that could be competitively developed domestically, without new industries emerging to create alternative employment and export opportunities.

The objective should be competitiveness, not protection for its own sake.

From supermarkets to roadside vendors

The transformation is also visible in Zimbabwe’s retail economy.

Established supermarket chains have faced increasing pressure, while tuckshops, informal wholesalers and roadside vendors have become important distribution channels.

In November 2025, OK Zimbabwe reported closing 11 stores, with three more undergoing closure. The company also highlighted difficulties involving suppliers and stock availability.

It would be misleading to blame informal traders alone. Formal retailers face operating costs, financing constraints and changing consumer behaviour. Informal outlets may offer competitive prices, greater convenience and quantities suited to household budgets.

Nevertheless, the changing retail landscape raises questions about the quality of employment and household purchasing power.

A household with stable monthly earnings can plan expenditure, purchase essential products in larger quantities and build savings.

A household dependent on irregular income may purchase only what it can afford that day.

Both participate in economic activity, but their financial security differs substantially.

Similarly, a person who loses factory employment and starts selling imported goods remains economically active. Yet the transition may involve lower productivity, unpredictable earnings and weaker employment benefits.

Informal enterprise is not inherently unproductive. Many successful businesses begin informally. The concern is when informal trading becomes the principal alternative to formal jobs that the economy is struggling to create.

A busy marketplace should therefore not automatically be interpreted as evidence of rising prosperity. It may reflect entrepreneurial dynamism, economic necessity, or both.

The investment problem beneath the recovery

There is another indicator that deserves much greater attention than it receives in discussions of Zimbabwe’s recovery: gross fixed capital formation.

This measures investment in fixed assets such as machinery, equipment, buildings and infrastructure.

Historical World Bank data show that Zimbabwe’s gross fixed capital formation reached approximately 24.6% of GDP in 1995. By 2024, it was approximately 7.9%.

Although changes in national accounting and GDP measurement require caution when making historical comparisons, the figures point to a substantial decline in investment intensity.

This matters because economies do not grow sustainably through consumption and trading alone. They must accumulate productive capital.

Factories require machinery. Farmers need irrigation equipment. Railways require locomotives and maintained tracks. Manufacturing businesses need modern production systems, reliable electricity and efficient logistics.

Investment also needs to replace depreciating assets before productive capacity can expand.

A country may experience a construction boom while still investing inadequately in machinery and industrial production. Residential buildings are valuable assets, but they do not automatically replace lost manufacturing capabilities.

The distinction is between an economy that is spending and an economy that is building the productive capacity required to generate future income.

The question is therefore not simply how much investment is taking place, but where that investment is going and whether it is improving productivity.

Who is financing economic reconstruction?

Rebuilding productive capacity also requires finance.

Factories need machinery, technology, reliable infrastructure and working capital. Expanding industrial production frequently requires financing that can be repaid over several years.

Yet Zimbabwe’s financial system remains relatively shallow.

The IMF’s 2025 assessment estimated private sector credit at approximately 4.3% of GDP and identified limited banking intermediation.

Banks can be profitable, adequately capitalised and financially stable without supplying sufficient long term investment finance.

The capital market provides another potential financing channel, but Zimbabwe’s listed corporate sector has experienced substantial delistings and relatively few new operating company listings.

The Victoria Falls Stock Exchange has facilitated important capital raisings through its United States dollar denominated market. However, transferring an existing company from the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange to the VFEX does not, by itself, generate new productive investment.

What matters is the amount of fresh capital businesses actually raise and invest.

If banks provide limited long term credit and relatively few enterprises raise equity through public markets, how will Zimbabwe finance the next generation of manufacturing businesses?

The issue extends beyond money circulating in the economy. It concerns whether savings and financial resources are reaching productive enterprises capable of creating employment and future output.

The railway test

Infrastructure provides another revealing measure of economic reconstruction.

Zimbabwe’s railway system once transported substantial quantities of minerals, agricultural commodities and industrial products.

In 1998, annual railway freight exceeded 12.4 million tonnes. Zimbabwe’s National Development Strategy 2 reports that freight had fallen below 3 million tonnes in recent years, representing a dramatic deterioration in the role of railway transport.

Some freight has shifted to road transport, and the decline cannot be attributed entirely to industrial contraction. Nevertheless, it reflects a major weakening of railway transport’s contribution to the national economy.

The consequences extend beyond the railways themselves.

Manufacturers and mining companies face transport costs, while heavier dependence on road freight increases pressure on highways.

The prolonged deterioration and ongoing rehabilitation of the Bulawayo to Victoria Falls road demonstrate the wider importance of reliable infrastructure for tourism, mining and commerce.

Industrial competitiveness depends not only on what happens inside factories, but also on electricity reliability, water availability, transport efficiency and the cost of moving goods to markets.

A country cannot sustainably industrialise while these supporting systems remain inadequate.

Growth that depends on rainfall

The anticipated 2026/27 agricultural season provides an important test of Zimbabwe’s economic resilience.

The economy grew by only 1.7% in 2024 when severe drought affected agricultural production. Better rainfall contributed to the substantial recovery in 2025.

Now, with forecasts warning of possible El Niño related drought conditions, the IMF expects growth to moderate from 5% in 2026 to 3.5% in 2027.

This is not a forecast of economic contraction. However, it highlights the continuing vulnerability of national economic performance to agricultural conditions.

Agriculture will always remain sensitive to rainfall. Even advanced economies experience production losses during severe droughts.

The difference lies in their ability to absorb shocks.

An economy with extensive irrigation, diversified manufacturing, reliable electricity, productive services and developed financial institutions is better equipped to sustain economic activity when agricultural output falls.

Zimbabwe’s vulnerability is amplified because rainfall affects more than crops. Poor agricultural seasons reduce rural incomes, increase food import requirements and can disrupt hydroelectric power generation.

The consequences spread through manufacturing, commerce and household consumption.

The question is therefore not simply whether agricultural production will recover after the next favourable rainy season.

It is whether Zimbabwe is building an economy capable of sustaining growth when rainfall is poor.

Where is the economy growing?

There are genuine areas of expansion.

Mining has benefited from investment and favourable commodity prices. New steel and mineral processing projects offer opportunities for industrial development. Agriculture, construction, telecommunications and selected manufacturers continue to generate output and investment.

These developments should not be dismissed.

But their contribution to national transformation depends on the productive relationships they establish with the wider economy.

Does mining growth create sufficient demand for domestic engineering firms, machinery manufacturers and skilled labour?

Does agricultural expansion support food processing, packaging and industrial employment?

Does construction stimulate domestic production of building materials?

Are mineral export earnings and diaspora remittances being converted into productive investment, or are substantial amounts flowing into consumption, imported goods and property?

Consumption and housing investment are valuable economic activities. The issue is whether enough resources are also being directed towards investments that strengthen future productive capacity.

An economy can experience visible construction, busy trading centres and rising export earnings without generating an equally broad improvement in industrial employment and household incomes.

Growth becomes more transformative when expanding sectors create opportunities for others.

Beyond GDP and inflation

Zimbabwe should continue monitoring inflation, exchange rates and GDP growth. They remain essential measures of macroeconomic performance.

But they should be complemented by indicators that reveal whether the economy’s productive foundations are strengthening.

How many factories are operating? How much investment is going into industrial machinery and infrastructure? Are manufacturing employment and productivity increasing?

How much agricultural production is processed domestically? Are exports becoming more diversified? How much long term finance is reaching productive businesses?

Are railway freight volumes recovering? Are traditional industrial towns attracting sustainable new investment? Are ordinary households experiencing improvements in real earnings, purchasing power and employment security?

These questions should be central to evaluating economic progress.

Zimbabwe’s recent macroeconomic improvements provide an opportunity to address longstanding structural weaknesses. Greater stability can support investment, but stability should be treated as the foundation for transformation rather than its completion.

The objective is not to recreate the industrial economy of the 1990s. It is to develop modern productive capabilities, strengthen connections between sectors and create an economy capable of generating sustainable prosperity.

Zimbabwe can record falling inflation while factories remain underutilised. It can report GDP growth while formal employment opportunities remain limited. It can earn substantial export revenue while depending heavily on imported goods and vulnerable infrastructure.

These outcomes are not contradictory. They describe different dimensions of the economy.

The real test of Zimbabwe’s recovery is not how quickly GDP grows after a favourable harvest or commodity boom. It is whether the country is accumulating productive capital, increasing labour productivity, creating sustainable employment and improving real household incomes. Above all, it is whether Zimbabwe is building an economy capable of sustaining prosperity when favourable conditions disappear.

Dr Shame Mugova is a Lecturer in Finance at Birmingham City University. He writes on finance, economic policy, governance and development, with a particular interest in Zimbabwe and Southern Africa. He writes in his personal capacity.

title: Zimbabwe’s Platinum Boom: The Wealth Is Being Extracted. Where Is the Development?
summary: A country cannot claim resource sovereignty while the communities that host its mineral wealth remain poor. By Timothy Mutsekwa The Contradiction Beneath the Boom Zimbabwe’s platinum industry presents a question that should trouble anyone who believes natural resources ought to serve the public good: how can a country export billions of dollars’ worth of minerals […]
content_text:
A country cannot claim resource sovereignty while the communities that host its mineral wealth remain poor.

By Timothy Mutsekwa

The Contradiction Beneath the Boom

Zimbabwe’s platinum industry presents a question that should trouble anyone who believes natural resources ought to serve the public good: how can a country export billions of dollars’ worth of minerals while communities living beside the mines continue to struggle for clean water, decent roads, schools, and basic services?

This is the uncomfortable reality at the heart of our platinum boom. The contrast is not merely an unfortunate public-relations problem for mining companies; it exposes a deeper failure in the relationship between mineral extraction, public revenue, and national development.

In 2025, Zimbabwe’s mining export earnings reached a record US$8.5 billion, up from US$5.9 billion in 2024. Yet in communities surrounding major platinum operations, the everyday experience of development remains painfully uneven. Children still face long, gruelling journeys to school, while access to clean water and adequate sanitation remains elusive.

We must understand these figures carefully. Export earnings are not company profits; company profits are not taxes and royalties paid to the state; and public revenue is not the same as benefits actually reaching communities. But that distinction strengthens rather than weakens the argument. We need to account for each stage of the value chain and explain what the country, its workers, and its mining communities are actually receiving.

Corporate Charity Is Not Public Policy

The question is not whether mining companies do anything for host communities. Some do. Unki, for example, has spent an average of US$1.5 million a year on community development over five years, including drilling boreholes and supporting local schools. Such projects make a real difference, but corporate social responsibility-however welcome-cannot be a substitute for comprehensive public policy.

A mining company should not become the de facto provider of essential public services simply because the state has failed to deliver them. Nor should a community’s access to water, roads, or classrooms depend on the discretion of company management or the goodwill of corporate executives. The state must collect what is due, local authorities must be equipped to provide services, and communities must have a meaningful voice in deciding how development priorities are funded.

The critical issue is whether Zimbabwe has built a transparent, enforceable system that converts mineral wealth into lasting public benefit. How much tax and royalty revenue is collected from each operation? What incentives, exemptions, or concessions reduce the public take? How much is allocated back to the districts that bear the environmental and social costs? What has actually been delivered, rather than merely promised?

Without accessible, mine-by-mine disclosure, citizens are left with headline export figures on one side and visible deprivation on the other. Suspicion naturally fills the gap where public accounting should be.

Indigenous Ownership Must Mean More Than Changing Shareholders

Our unfinished debate about indigenous ownership must also be confronted honestly. Resource nationalism is not an illegitimate aspiration. A country endowed with platinum, gold, lithium, and other valuable minerals has every reason to seek greater domestic participation in ownership, financing, technology, and strategic decision-making. We should naturally want more of the value generated by our resources to remain inside the country.

However, changing the nationality of shareholders is not, by itself, economic transformation. Indigenisation cannot be declared a success if ownership is concentrated among a politically connected minority while workers, local suppliers, and host communities remain marginalised. The relevant question is not simply whether a Zimbabwean owns shares in a mine. It is whether everyday Zimbabweans are building productive businesses, acquiring high-level skills, accumulating assets, and participating meaningfully in the industries that extract and process the country’s resources.

Resource sovereignty must mean more than a change in the identity of the beneficiaries. It must mean a fundamental structural change in the economy: creating domestic capital, deepening local supply chains, supporting technological learning, and enabling Zimbabwean firms to move beyond low-value activities. Crucially, it must also mean that the public can scrutinize the terms on which national resources are exploited.

Beneficiation Needs an Industrial Strategy

Zimbabwe has a legitimate interest in processing more of its platinum at home and capturing a greater share of the value generated along the supply chain. Exporting raw or less-processed minerals leaves refining and higher-value industrial activities elsewhere. But beneficiation is not a mere slogan that can replace a coherent industrial strategy.

Processing requires reliable electricity, capital, infrastructure, skills, technology, and access to global markets. Government must actively create the conditions for viable investment, rather than simply issuing demands that ignore practical constraints.

Our objective should be a phased, credible programme:

Expand domestic processing where commercially and technically viable.

Intentionally develop local suppliers and technical capabilities.

Invest heavily in training, technical education, and supporting infrastructure.

Use mining as a platform for secondary industries that can endure after individual deposits are exhausted.

Mineral wealth is finite; the productive capabilities built with it should not be.

A Practical Programme for Accountability

To turn this around, we can and must take several practical steps:

Publish Mine-by-Mine Data: Publicly disclose all taxes, royalties, dividends, concessions, and other payments made to the state by each mining operation.

Disclose Community Commitments: Require both companies and public authorities to publish community-development commitments, precise budgets, and completed projects.

Establish Transparent Local Funds: Create local development arrangements governed by published allocation rules, independent audits, and genuine community participation.

Strengthen Environmental Monitoring: Implement accessible complaints mechanisms so that pollution, displacement, and social harms are promptly investigated and remedied.

Link Revenue to Long-Term Strategy: Connect mineral revenues directly to an infrastructure and industrial strategy, rather than absorbing them into general government expenditure without public accounting.

These measures should not create parallel systems where companies decide which communities deserve development. Local development funds must complement a properly funded system of local government, not replace it. Their purpose is to make the distribution of benefits transparent and accountable, while preserving the state’s primary responsibility to provide public services.

The Ultimate Test of Resource Sovereignty

Zimbabwe’s platinum boom must be judged by more than production volumes, export receipts, or the headline value of new investment announcements. It must be judged by whether our country is accumulating long-term productive capacity; whether our workers have decent jobs and opportunities to advance; whether local businesses can enter and grow along the supply chain; whether host communities enjoy improved services and a safe environment; and whether our public institutions can fully account for the revenue generated in the nation’s name.

The central contradiction is plain: mineral abundance will always coexist with widespread deprivation when ownership, taxation, public expenditure, and industrial policy fail to reinforce one another. A country may possess world-class deposits and modern mines yet remain a marginal participant in the value created from its own resources.

The true test of resource sovereignty is not who holds the mining licence, who appears at the commissioning ceremony, or whose name is attached to a corporate social responsibility project. It is whether control over natural resources produces accountable institutions, domestic productive capacity, and a materially better life for our people.

We do not merely need a platinum boom. We need a development settlement in which the wealth extracted from beneath our soil can be clearly seen, measured, and felt above it.

title: NoTo2030: Fambi Turns Up Heat On ZANU PF And Zimbabwe’s Political Establishment
summary: By A Correspondent|National Progressive Democrats (NPD) president Togara Fambi has launched a scathing attack on ZANU PF, accusing the ruling … Continue reading "NoTo2030: Fambi Turns Up Heat On ZANU PF And Zimbabwe’s Political Establishment"
content_text:
By A Correspondent|National Progressive Democrats (NPD) president Togara Fambi has launched a scathing attack on ZANU PF, accusing the ruling party of leaving Zimbabweans politically confused amid the country’s deepening political uncertainty.

In a strong message last week, Fambi questioned the political direction of the country and challenged Zimbabweans to critically examine the individuals and political forces claiming to have the capacity to remove President Emmerson Mnangagwa from power.

“Zimbabweans have been tossed around by ZANU PF Party and they are now politically confused,” Fambi said.

He further questioned whether the politician being presented as capable of unseating Mnangagwa had the political credentials and capacity to deliver on such claims.

“Is this the politician whom you are saying can remove Emmerson Dambudzo Mnangagwa? What are we saying,” he asked.

Fambi, a former Zimbabwe Republic Police Assistant Inspector, has positioned himself as a vocal critic of corruption, alleged looting and political malpractice, while advocating for an alternative political direction through the NPD.

The opposition leader has also alleged that he is being tormented by the regime for speaking out against corruption and the exploitation of national resources.

His latest remarks reflect growing political contestation over the country’s leadership, opposition strategies and the prospects of ending ZANU PF’s hold on power.

Through the NPD’s political messaging, Fambi continues to push back against the proposed 2030 political agenda, using the slogan #NoTo2030 to rally opposition to efforts aimed at extending the current political order.

title: Chivayo family registers estate with Master of High Court
summary: The family of the late socialite Wicknell Chivayo has registered his estate with the Master of the High Court, setting in motion the legal process to administer his business interests and personal fortune. According to The Sunday Mail, the estate was registered about three weeks ago, and an initial meeting has been held to discuss […]
content_text:
The family of the late socialite Wicknell Chivayo has registered his estate with the Master of the High Court, setting in motion the legal process to administer his business interests and personal fortune.

According to The Sunday Mail , the estate was registered about three weeks ago, and an initial meeting has been held to discuss the way forward.

However, no executor or executrix has been appointed yet. This means the formal process of identifying assets, establishing liabilities and determining how his wealth will be distributed is yet to start.

Senior officials at the Master of the High Court confirmed the development to The Sunday Mail but declined to disclose details of the estate, whose value is believed to run into millions of US dollars.

“We can confirm that the estate was registered about three weeks ago, and a first meeting was held. But the executor or executrix of the estate is yet to be appointed,” said an official.

Another official said the Master’s Office was not yet in a position to discuss the administration of the estate.

“We will get in touch with you when we are ready and have something to say about the estate, but as of now, we cannot give you the finer details of the estate,” he said.

Chivayo died alongside his wife, Lucy Muteke, in a helicopter crash on 30 September in Marondera.

He left behind two minor children with his former wife, Sonja Madzikanda, and a substantial estate whose administration is expected to attract considerable attention.

One of the main outstanding matters is a US$25 million matrimonial property and asset division dispute involving Madzikanda, which was awaiting determination by the Supreme Court.

Following Chivayo’s death, the matter was removed from the court roll pending the appointment of an executor or executrix to represent his estate. His lawyer, Sylvester Hashiti, confirmed the development.

“The matter was removed from the roll on account of appellant’s demise until such a time he is substituted by his executor or executrix who will represent him in court as concerns any claims against his estate,” said Hashiti.

Under Zimbabwe’s civil procedure, a deceased litigant cannot continue to participate in court proceedings, and a legally recognised representative must be appointed where litigation survives death.

Legal experts said Chivayo’s death does not automatically extinguish any claims Madzikanda may have against his estate. The outstanding dispute is expected to be one of the major issues the administrator will have to address.

Sources close to the matter said Madzikanda’s legal team intends to pursue its claims, including property division and maintenance, once an executor has been appointed.

title: South Africa’s AGOA Exit: Can Trade Diversification Protect Its Economy?
summary: SOUTH Africa is preparing for a significant change in its trade relationship with the United States after Washington announced plans to terminate the country’s eligibility for the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) from 1 January 2027. The decision removes a longstanding tariff advantage for selected South African exports, but it does not close the […]
content_text:
SOUTH Africa is preparing for a significant change in its trade relationship with the United States after Washington announced plans to terminate the country’s eligibility for the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) from 1 January 2027. The decision removes a longstanding tariff advantage for selected South African exports, but it does not close the American market. The distinction is important: the immediate challenge is not the loss of access to US customers, but the additional cost of serving them and the ability of exporters to remain competitive.

By Brighton Musonza

The scale of the exposure also needs to be understood in context. South Africa exported approximately US$1.7 billion in goods to the United States under AGOA in 2025, compared with US$4 billion in 2024. Those preferential exports represented around 10% of South African exports to the US and approximately 1% of the country’s total global exports. The figures suggest that the withdrawal is unlikely, on its own, to destabilise the national economy. However, the aggregate numbers conceal substantial exposure among particular manufacturers, agricultural producers and communities whose commercial models have been built around preferential access to the American market.

The central economic question is therefore one of distribution rather than simply national exposure. South Africa may absorb the shock at a macroeconomic level while individual exporters, suppliers and workers face considerable pressure.

The difference between losing AGOA and losing the US market

AGOA, introduced in 2000, provides eligible sub-Saharan African countries with preferential access to the US market for thousands of products. For South African exporters, the arrangement has supported trade in selected agricultural products, automotive components, manufactured goods, chemicals and other value-added products.

The withdrawal of eligibility does not amount to a trade embargo or an automatic prohibition on South African goods entering the United States. Exporters will continue to trade, but products that previously qualified for AGOA preferences will become subject to the applicable ordinary US tariff regime and any additional duties in force.

The cost will vary considerably by product. Agricultural economist Wandile Sihlobo has indicated that the additional tariff burden for many affected products could be around 3.4 percentage points. That is not a universal rate: the actual exposure depends on tariff classification, existing exemptions and any other duties applying to the product.

This distinction matters because some of South Africa’s largest exports to the US are not dependent on AGOA. Precious metals and minerals, which account for a substantial proportion of bilateral trade, generally do not rely on the programme for their existing tariff treatment. Some automotive, steel and aluminium exports are already subject to separate US trade measures, meaning the removal of AGOA may add little to the tariff burden those products already face.

The automotive industry illustrates this complexity. South Africa’s vehicle exports to the United States had already been affected by additional American tariffs. Industry figures cited by Reuters indicate that the US, Mexico and Canada together accounted for about 8% of South Africa’s automotive exports in 2025, with the US representing the largest component of that group. The withdrawal of AGOA is therefore another challenge for an industry already dealing with a more difficult trading environment, rather than an entirely new shock.

The broader implication is that the economic consequences will be concentrated in the products for which AGOA provided a meaningful competitive advantage.

Agriculture faces a more immediate commercial test

Agriculture is among the sectors where the loss of preferential access could have consequences beyond the headline value of exports. South African producers have developed established relationships with American importers, retailers and distributors. Some production and logistics arrangements have been structured around the requirements and seasonal opportunities of the US market.

Citrus is a particularly important example. South African fruit helps supply American consumers during periods when domestic production is limited. However, as Gerrit van der Merwe, chairman of the Citrus Growers’ Association of Southern Africa, told Reuters, some orchards were planted specifically for the American market. Redirecting this produce is not necessarily straightforward because alternative destinations have different phytosanitary requirements, consumer preferences, seasonal conditions and commercial specifications.

The challenge extends beyond farms. Export agriculture depends on an interconnected system of packhouses, cold storage, packaging suppliers, freight operators, ports, inspection services and distribution networks. If exporters lose orders or are forced to accept lower prices to remain competitive, the effects can travel through the entire value chain.

AgriSA estimates that South African agricultural exports to the US amounted to approximately US$504 million in 2025. Although this represents a relatively modest share of the country’s agricultural trade, the association has warned that national averages can obscure significant exposure in individual products and production regions. The US accounted for 28.85% of South African litchi exports in the 2025/26 season, illustrating how a destination can be strategically important to a particular industry even when it is not dominant in national export statistics.

For agricultural businesses, the immediate response will involve reviewing contracts, renegotiating prices, examining alternative destinations and assessing whether the additional tariff can be absorbed by exporters, importers or consumers. Where margins are already narrow, even a relatively modest increase in duties can affect investment decisions, employment and the viability of smaller producers.

South Africa’s ability to retain its American customers will consequently depend on more than the quality of its produce. Reliability, price competitiveness, certification, shipping costs and the ability to meet market-specific standards will become increasingly important.

Employment risks are concentrated, not uniform

The employment implications require careful assessment. Some public commentary has suggested that hundreds of thousands of jobs could be at risk. Such estimates should not be treated as confirmed job losses or as a forecast of the national employment impact.

Reuters reported on 3 November that Business Unity South Africa expected the number of affected jobs to be in the range of a few thousand. The Financial Times reported that officials had warned of up to 10,000 jobs being at risk. Other, substantially larger estimates have included indirect employment across supply chains and therefore use different assumptions and definitions.

These figures are not directly comparable. The actual impact will depend on how much of the additional tariff exporters can absorb, whether American buyers continue purchasing South African products, and how quickly businesses can secure alternative markets.

Nevertheless, the concentration of potential losses matters in a country already facing exceptionally high unemployment. A relatively small national employment shock can be severe for towns and industrial communities where a particular factory, agricultural export chain or processing facility is a major employer.

The Eastern Cape automotive manufacturing cluster and agricultural production areas in the Western and Northern Cape illustrate the importance of local exposure. A reduction in export orders can affect not only the principal exporting company but also component manufacturers, logistics businesses, contractors and workers whose livelihoods depend on the same commercial network.

The policy response should therefore be targeted. A national support package that does not distinguish between sectors, products and regions risks directing resources towards businesses that are not materially affected while leaving vulnerable export clusters without practical assistance.

Diversification is necessary, but markets cannot be replaced overnight

The South African government has identified export diversification as a central part of its response, with opportunities being pursued across the African Continental Free Trade Area, the European Union, the United Kingdom, India, China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and other markets.

This is economically sensible. A country with a broad export base and multiple commercial destinations is less vulnerable to unilateral trade decisions by any one government. However, diversification is a process of building commercial capacity, not simply identifying countries on a trade map.

New markets require regulatory approvals, product certification, established distributors, reliable transport routes, suitable payment arrangements and sustained demand. Agricultural exporters, for example, cannot necessarily redirect fruit originally prepared for the US market to another destination without meeting different phytosanitary and commercial requirements. Manufacturers face similar challenges where customers require specific technical standards, delivery schedules and after-sales support.

The European Union offers an established alternative trading relationship, supported by the EU-SADC Economic Partnership Agreement. The United Kingdom also remains an important market through its post-Brexit trade arrangements with Southern African partners. These relationships provide a foundation for diversification, but they do not guarantee that every product displaced from the US market can be absorbed at comparable prices and volumes.

The African Continental Free Trade Area offers a longer-term opportunity to expand intra-African trade. South African manufacturers have an established industrial base, financial infrastructure and logistics networks that could support greater regional exports. Yet the commercial benefits will depend on reducing non-tariff barriers, improving border efficiency, strengthening transport corridors and addressing the cost of doing business across the continent.

China is another obvious destination, given its scale and importance in global trade. However, it should not be regarded as an automatic substitute for the US market. Research published by Economic Research Southern Africa in June 2026 examined the potential for increased South African and Southern African Customs Union exports to China under a possible free trade agreement. Its modelling suggested that aggregate exports could rise by approximately 4%, a relatively modest response because many existing mineral and precious-metal exports already face low or zero tariffs.

That finding highlights an important structural limitation. Diversification towards China may expand opportunities, but simply redirecting existing commodity exports will not necessarily produce the industrial transformation South Africa needs. The greater prize lies in developing more competitive manufactured exports, processed agricultural products and higher-value services.

The US relationship is bigger than AGOA

South Africa also has to manage the diplomatic and investment implications of the decision. The commercial relationship between the two countries extends well beyond preferential trade access.

According to figures released by South Africa’s Department of Trade, Industry and Competition, bilateral trade reached US$28.8 billion in 2025. More than 600 American companies operate in South Africa, supporting approximately 134,600 jobs. South Africa also supplies 12 of the 50 minerals identified by the US as critical, as well as a significant share of the isotopes used in American cancer treatment.

These relationships create mutual commercial interests that neither government can easily disregard. American businesses have invested in South African operations, while South African companies have established investments and supply-chain relationships in the US. The loss of AGOA preferences could undermine parts of these arrangements, but it does not eliminate the underlying economic rationale for continued engagement.

The political dimension is more difficult. Washington has cited concerns about trade and investment barriers, corruption and issues affecting US national security and foreign policy interests. Pretoria, meanwhile, has argued that it made concessions during negotiations but that Washington subsequently introduced new issues beyond the scope of the discussions initiated in 2025.

Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau said on 3 November that the decision did not define the broader relationship between the two countries and that South Africa remained committed to constructive engagement. Government has also indicated that it will work with affected industries while pursuing new export destinations.

The immediate diplomatic priority should be to preserve channels of engagement and seek a more predictable framework for bilateral trade. South Africa’s strategic interests are not served by allowing a dispute over preferential market access to become a permanent deterioration in investment and commercial relations.

Equally, a negotiated solution cannot be built on the assumption that market access will remain insulated from political and regulatory disagreements. Businesses require certainty, and that certainty depends on a more stable framework for resolving trade disputes.

The deeper challenge is industrial competitiveness

The loss of AGOA exposes a broader weakness in South Africa’s export strategy: the need to increase the competitiveness, complexity and diversity of its productive economy.

Preferential trade arrangements can help exporters overcome tariff disadvantages, but they cannot permanently compensate for high logistics costs, unreliable infrastructure, weak productivity, regulatory uncertainty or insufficient investment in industrial capacity.

South Africa has significant advantages. It possesses a diversified industrial base, sophisticated financial institutions, established agricultural exporters, mineral resources, engineering expertise and relatively developed transport and commercial infrastructure. These capabilities provide a platform for adaptation.

However, the country also faces structural constraints. Manufacturing has been under pressure from electricity disruptions, logistics bottlenecks, weak domestic demand and limited investment in productive capacity. Port performance and rail inefficiencies raise the cost of moving goods to international markets. In this environment, an additional tariff can become more damaging because exporters are already competing from a relatively high cost base.

The response should therefore go beyond diplomatic negotiations and temporary financial support. South Africa needs a more deliberate export-led industrial strategy that improves productivity, lowers the cost of production and encourages firms to move into higher-value activities.

That means investing in modern manufacturing, agricultural processing, technology, engineering and supplier development. It also means making it easier for companies to import machinery and intermediate inputs where these improve productivity and export competitiveness. Industrial policy should focus on building firms capable of competing internationally rather than protecting inefficient production indefinitely.

The government’s Industrial Development Strategy will be judged by its ability to translate policy objectives into commercially viable investment, stronger domestic supply chains and a broader base of competitive exporters.

How South Africa can absorb the shock

The first priority is to establish precisely which products and companies are exposed. Exporters need clear information on the tariff treatment of individual product lines, the interaction with other US duties and the arrangements applying to goods already contracted or in transit. Without this clarity, companies may postpone investment, delay shipments or lose customers unnecessarily.

Second, government and business should pursue targeted support for sectors where the loss of preferences creates a demonstrable threat to employment and productive capacity. This could include export finance, trade insurance, assistance with market certification and support for companies seeking new distribution partnerships. Any intervention should be time-bound and linked to measurable improvements in competitiveness.

Third, South Africa should accelerate trade diversification without abandoning the American market. Maintaining existing commercial relationships remains important, particularly where South African products complement US production or supply specialised industrial requirements. The objective should be to reduce excessive dependence, not to replace one concentration risk with another.

Fourth, the country needs to address the domestic costs that weaken export competitiveness. More efficient ports, reliable rail services, predictable regulation, improved energy availability and faster certification processes would help exporters absorb tariff pressures and compete in markets where preferential access is unavailable.

Finally, Pretoria must recognise that trade policy and foreign policy are increasingly interconnected. The ability to negotiate commercially beneficial arrangements depends partly on the country’s wider diplomatic relationships and its credibility as a predictable investment destination. A more stable relationship with Washington would benefit both exporters and investors, even if the two governments continue to disagree on broader political questions.

A manageable national shock, but a serious test for business

South Africa is unlikely to face a national economic crisis solely because of its removal from AGOA. The programme accounted for a relatively small proportion of the country’s total exports, and most South African goods entering the US market were already traded outside its preferential framework. The continued demand for minerals, precious metals and other products provides an important buffer.

But the conclusion that the impact will be negligible would be equally mistaken. The withdrawal could reduce margins, weaken investment incentives and threaten employment in export-dependent industries. For particular agricultural producers and manufacturers, the loss of preferential treatment could be commercially significant even if the national trade figures suggest limited exposure.

South Africa’s ability to cope will ultimately depend on whether it treats the decision as a temporary diplomatic setback or as a warning about the risks of relying on preferential access in an increasingly fragmented global trading system.

AGOA provided a competitive advantage, not a permanent guarantee of market access. The next phase of South Africa’s trade strategy must be built on productivity, industrial depth, diversified customers and commercially sustainable exports.

The country has the economic scale and institutional capacity to adjust. The more difficult question is whether government, business and labour can coordinate the reforms needed to protect vulnerable industries while making the wider economy more competitive. That will determine whether the loss of AGOA remains a contained trade shock or becomes another obstacle to South Africa’s long-term industrial and employment ambitions.

About the writer

Brighton Musonza is a Zimbabwean business and economic commentator, writer and media entrepreneur, and the founder of The Zimbabwe Mail. He holds an MBA and a BSc in Business Management, with additional professional training in business analytics, finance and digital transformation.

His commentary focuses on Zimbabwe’s economy, regional and international trade, financial markets, investment, industrial development and public policy. He examines economic developments through the lens of business strategy, macroeconomics, institutional governance and the practical realities facing businesses and investors.

Based in the United Kingdom, Musonza writes about Zimbabwe’s economic transformation, the country’s position in Southern Africa, and the opportunities and challenges shaping its engagement with international markets. His work aims to encourage informed debate, challenge conventional assumptions, and promote a deeper understanding of the economic forces shaping Zimbabwe’s development.

Editorial Disclaimer

The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the writer, Brighton Musonza, and do not necessarily represent the official position of The Zimbabwe Mail, its editors, associates or contributors.

This article is intended for general information, economic commentary and public discussion. While reasonable care has been taken to present information accurately and draw on relevant sources, economic data, projections, estimates and policy developments may change. Interpretations and assessments of potential economic consequences represent the writer’s analysis and should not be treated as established outcomes.

The article does not constitute financial, investment, legal or commercial advice. Readers, businesses and investors should undertake their own independent research and seek appropriate professional advice before making decisions.
