title: ARDA Grain Deliveries Top 248 000 Tonnes as Zimbabwe Braces for El Niño Drought
summary: The Agricultural and Rural Development Authority (ARDA) has delivered more than 187,000 tonnes of summer cereals and 60,529 tonnes of winter wheat to the Grain Marketing Board (GMB), as Zimbabwe intensifies efforts to strengthen national food reserves ahead of an anticipated El Niño-induced drought. The […]
content_text:
The Agricultural and Rural Development Authority (ARDA) has delivered more than 187,000 tonnes of summer cereals and 60,529 tonnes of winter wheat to the Grain Marketing Board (GMB), as Zimbabwe intensifies efforts to strengthen national food reserves ahead of an anticipated El Niño-induced drought.

The authority has also set an ambitious target of cultivating 100 000 hectares during the 2026/27 summer cropping season, in a major production drive aimed at augmenting the country’s Strategic Grain Reserve and cushioning communities against potential food shortages.

The authority delivered 187,704 metric tonnes of summer cereals from the 2025/26 agricultural season to the GMB.

Of this quantity, 31,293.46 tonnes were channelled towards immediate milling requirements and price stabilisation.

ARDA has also delivered 60 529.3 tonnes of winter wheat, with harvesting still underway after commencing two weeks ago.

The authority said most of the harvested wheat was still on farms, undergoing bagging and grading, while some fields were yet to be harvested.

The figures underline ARDA’s contribution to national food-security preparations as Zimbabwe braces for a potentially difficult agricultural season.

Under its 2026/27 summer production programme, ARDA is targeting 100,000 hectares across its estates, A1 and A2 joint venture growers, irrigation scheme business units and clustered smallholder farmers.

Of the targeted hectarage, 60,000 hectares will be under irrigation, while the remaining 40,000 hectares will be planted using climate-smart varieties.

The programme is intended to strengthen domestic cereal production and further build the Strategic Grain Reserve against the threat of below-normal rainfall.

Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development Minister Dr Anxious Masuka recently warned that Zimbabwe was almost certain to experience below-normal rainfall during the coming season, with the Meteorological Services Department classifying it as a drought year.

Speaking at the 74th graduation ceremony at Gwebi College of Agriculture, Dr Masuka said the warming of the central South Pacific Ocean associated with El Niño was expected to exceed three degrees Celsius, pointing to a particularly strong weather phenomenon.

“So now we are almost 100 percent certain that we will have below-normal rainfall for Zimbabwe,” he said.

However, the minister assured the nation that Government was implementing measures to safeguard food security.

He revealed that the GMB had purchased 345 000 tonnes of various cereals by the previous day, exceeding the 328,000 tonnes distributed during the devastating 2024 drought.

“As of yesterday, we had actually purchased at the GMB 345,000 metric tonnes of various cereals. In 2024, when we had the worst drought, we distributed 328,000 metric tonnes,” he said.

“So we are well on our way to ensuring that should there be this unfortunate event, we will have enough of the strategic grain reserve to feed everyone.”

Government’s broader drought preparedness programme includes strengthening national and household grain reserves, promoting climate-smart agriculture, implementing livestock drought mitigation programmes and improving early-warning systems.

Under the livestock intervention, authorities plan to establish drought mitigation centres serving every seven to eight villages, equipped with permanent water sources, feeding facilities, livestock sales points and disease-control services.

Dr Masuka also called for improved post-harvest management, raising concern over maize losses that can reach 30 percent after harvesting.

He urged farmers and households to minimise food wastage and embrace innovation to withstand the anticipated weather challenges.

“Let’s invoke the Munhumutapa spirit, that entrepreneurial spirit, that innovation, so that Zimbabwe can come out stronger from this drought,” he said.

Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development, Professor Obert Jiri, has meanwhile urged farmers against panic planting or abandoning their fields over fears of an El Niño-induced drought saying the seasonal forecast should guide preparation rather than trigger premature decisions. He said farmers needed to conserve soil moisture, diversify crops and take advantage of favourable rainfall whenever it occurred.

“Farmers need to be ready and make the most of every drop of rain,” Prof Jiri said, urging them to monitor local weather conditions, assess soil moisture and seek guidance from agricultural extension officers before planting.

title: Ngwana clinic eases healthcare burden for pregnant women in Bulilima
summary: Pregnant women and other residents in Ward 21 of Bulilima District are set to benefit from reduced transport costs and improved access to healthcare following the commissioning of Ngwana Clinic, which brings essential medical services closer to the community. For years, residents had to travel about 10 kilometres to access healthcare at facilities such as […]
content_text:
Pregnant women and other residents in Ward 21 of Bulilima District are set to benefit from reduced transport costs and improved access to healthcare following the commissioning of Ngwana Clinic, which brings essential medical services closer to the community.

For years, residents had to travel about 10 kilometres to access healthcare at facilities such as Ndiweni and Matjinge clinics, placing a financial burden on families, particularly pregnant women, elderly people and those requiring regular medical attention.

Speaking at the commissioning ceremony on Friday, Ward 21 councillor Dolly Dube said the community initiated the clinic project in 2019 after recognising the difficulties residents faced in accessing healthcare at distant facilities.

She said some residents struggled to afford transport and other healthcare-related expenses, forcing them to endure difficulties when seeking medical assistance.

“We used to travel long distances to access healthcare at clinics such as Ndiweni and Matjinge, which is about 10km away. As residents, we realised that our community needed a health facility closer to where people live, so we came together and started the project. Accessing healthcare comes with a lot of expenses. Some people fall sick but do not have money for transport to travel to distant clinics or even to afford medical services. The establishment of this clinic will bring relief to many residents because healthcare services are now closer to them,” Dube said.

She said the clinic would particularly ease the burden on pregnant women who previously had to travel long distances to access maternity services.

“We are happy that the clinic is now closer to the community, especially for pregnant women who previously had to travel long distances to access maternity services. This will make it easier for them and other residents to seek medical attention without having to travel far,” Dube said.

Headman Sylvester Nkomo of Ward 21 said the vast geographical spread of communal areas made access to essential services difficult, with some villages covering extensive areas.

He said the establishment of Ngwana Clinic would significantly reduce the distances residents had to travel when seeking medical attention.

“The communal areas are too big. Though we call them villages, they are not equally the same. Some villages take quite a vast amount of land. So this institution here now is an advantage to the community because on medical grounds, it will be very near. So it helps the community a lot. To me, it benefits us,” Nkomo said.

Nkomo said the community also faced land ownership challenges when identifying a suitable site for the clinic, as some of the buildings and land in the area were considered government property.

He said the government had initially indicated that it could not release the land because it belonged to the State, delaying progress on the project.

“The establishment of the clinic was initially delayed by challenges over land ownership because there were two Government buildings already in the clinic. The government was saying it could not offer us the land because it belonged to the State. However, a solution was eventually found, allowing the project to proceed,” Nkomo said.

Resident Chemist Ncube said the clinic would ease the financial burden on households that previously spent money travelling to distant health facilities.

He said the proximity of healthcare services would allow residents to redirect money previously spent on transport towards other household needs.

“We used to spend money travelling to other clinics whenever we needed medical assistance. Sometimes people would need to go to a health facility but the challenge would be finding money for transport. Now that we have a clinic within our community, residents will be able to access healthcare closer to their homes. This is a great relief because the money that people used to spend travelling can be used to meet other household needs,” he said.

Ncube said pregnant women would particularly benefit from having healthcare services closer to their homes, given their need for regular medical attention.

“For pregnant women, this clinic is very important because they need regular medical attention during pregnancy. Having a health facility nearby will make it easier for them to seek assistance without the difficulties of travelling long distances. It will also benefit people who need regular check-ups and medicines because they will have a facility closer to their homes,” Ncube said.

title: Women Still Shut Out of Power as Gender Bias Undermines Africa’s Democracy
summary: Women who venture into politics also face violence and intimidation, including technology-facilitated gender-based violence, which further discourages their participation.
content_text:
ZANZIBAR – Discriminatory social norms, unequal power relations and growing gender-based violence continue to undermine women’s participation in political leadership across Africa, despite progress in representation and the adoption of laws promoting gender equality, United Nations and European Union officials have warned.

Speaking at the opening of a two-day Inter-Regional Dialogue on Advancing the Transformation of Gender Social Norms to Enhance Women and Youth Participation and Representation in Leadership and Decision-Making in Zanzibar, UN Women Representative in Tanzania, Julia Broussard, said women’s political representation remained disproportionately low, with entrenched attitudes continuing to influence who gets opportunities to lead.

Broussard said women occupy just over a quarter of parliamentary seats across sub-Saharan Africa, while in Tanzania they account for approximately 38 per cent of Members of Parliament.

However, she warned that progress in representation had not necessarily translated into equal influence in decision-making spaces.

“Beyond the numbers, discriminatory social norms and unequal power relations continue to shape who is seen as a legitimate leader, whose voice is heard and whose contributions are valued,” she said.

Citing the OECD’s 2023 Social Institutions and Gender Index, Broussard said 43.9 per cent of Tanzanians believed men made better political leaders than women, highlighting the attitudes that continue to reinforce gender inequality in public life.

She said such perceptions had practical consequences, affecting the opportunities women receive, the support they can mobilise and their ability to influence decisions.

Women who venture into politics also face violence and intimidation, including technology-facilitated gender-based violence, which further discourages their participation.

Tanzania’s Minister for Community Development, Gender, Elders and Children, Saada Mkuya Salum said women aspiring to political leadership continued to face social scrutiny and criticism that often left them with little opportunity to defend themselves.

“It’s not easy at all. They will write. They will comment. They will do everything. And you don’t have a chance actually to explain,” she said.

She added that although progress had been made in empowering women, the systems and attitudes that historically excluded them remained firmly entrenched.

“So even the journey, women journey much as enhanced, are empowered somehow, but the journey has never and I believe it’s not going to be that easy because of these systems that have been rooted,” Mkuya said.

The Minister said Tanzania was proud of the progress made but warned that discriminatory social norms, weak institutional support and inadequate assistance for female candidates continued to undermine meaningful participation.

“We’re proud of progress but they also tell us that when we are heading into the right direction we are not there yet and we will not get there as long as deep-rooted discriminatory social norms, institutions that support women’s advancement and inadequate support for women candidates continue to restrict their participation,” she said.

Mkuya also highlighted the additional burden placed on women by traditional household and caregiving responsibilities, which often leave them with less time and resources to build political networks, mobilise support and pursue leadership positions

European Union Ambassador to Tanzania and the East African Community, Jean-Marc Pisani, echoed the concerns, arguing that women’s underrepresentation was not primarily a question of legal frameworks or leadership capabilities, but of deeply rooted social attitudes and the failure to translate commitments into practice.

Pisani said women held an average of 27 percent of parliamentary seats and 26 percent of local government positions across sub-Saharan Africa.

Regional disparities remain significant, with women accounting for approximately 31 percent of parliamentary representation in East and Southern Africa, 20 percent in Central Africa and 16 percent in West Africa.

Rwanda, where women hold 64 percent of parliamentary seats, demonstrates what can be achieved through political will and strong institutions, he said.

“Norms are not a cultural footnote to democracy. They determine who can take part in it,” Pisani said, pointing to research showing that about half of the world’s population still believes men make better political leaders than women.

He warned that violence against women in politics was increasingly moving into digital spaces, where abuse, threats and disinformation targeting female candidates and leaders were becoming additional obstacles to their participation.

“These are not private harms. They are attacks on democracy itself,” he said.

Both officials called for a broader approach to gender equality, arguing that increasing the number of women in political institutions would not be enough without addressing the social and institutional barriers that limit their influence.

Broussard called for more inclusive political institutions, gender-responsive media coverage and the active involvement of men and boys in challenging discriminatory attitudes.

She also highlighted the importance of recognising young people, particularly young women, as agents of change rather than merely future leaders.

Pisani similarly urged men to take an active role in dismantling barriers by supporting women’s political ambitions, speaking out against harassment and sharing decision-making power.

He also challenged journalists to examine how media narratives shape public perceptions of leadership and influence what girls believe they can achieve.

“The stories a society tells about leadership shape what its girls believe they can become,” he said.

The two officials also pointed to ongoing interventions aimed at translating gender equality commitments into tangible improvements.

Broussard highlighted Tanzania’s legislative reforms, including the recognition of violence against women in politics as an electoral offence under the Presidential, Parliamentary and Councillors Election Act.

She also cited initiatives supporting women parliamentarians through partnerships involving the Uwongozi Institute and the European Union, as well as community engagement programmes with the Tanzania Media Women’s Association (TAMWA).

Pisani said the European Union had committed €90 million to its Gender Transformative Action programme, Breaking the Glass Ceiling, which supports gender-responsive policies, legal empowerment and community-level efforts to challenge discriminatory social norms.

The dialogue, bringing together participants from 23 countries, including journalists, women in politics and community leaders, is being convened by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA), with support from the European Union and UN Women.

The meeting seeks to facilitate exchanges on practical strategies for transforming gender norms and strengthening women’s and young people’s participation in leadership and decision-making.

title: President Chamisa: Confront Mnangagwa Regime, Stop Fighting Me…
summary: Tinashe Sambiri| Citizens leader Advocate Nelson Chamisa has taken a swipe at those who spend their energy attacking the opposition … Continue reading "President Chamisa: Confront Mnangagwa Regime, Stop Fighting Me…"
content_text:
Tinashe Sambiri| Citizens leader Advocate Nelson Chamisa has taken a swipe at those who spend their energy attacking the opposition instead of challenging the entrenched system of power, saying genuine leadership demands courage, sacrifice and conviction.

In a statement on Tuesday, Chamisa said leading a credible alternative against a dictatorship was a demanding and perilous task, not a walk in the park.

“Leading a credible alternative and genuinely challenging an entrenched dictatorship is a demanding, costly and often perilous undertaking. It is certainly no walk in the park,” Chamisa said.

He said true opposition requires tenacity and an unwavering commitment to the cause, which is why some people find it easier to target fellow opposition figures.

“It requires tenacity, conviction, courage, sacrifice and an unwavering commitment to the cause. Perhaps this is precisely why some find it easier to position themselves as the ‘opposition to the opposition’ rather than confront the difficult realities of challenging an entrenched system of power,” he said.

Chamisa added that attacking the opposition was less costly and less risky than confronting those in power.

“It is less costly, less demanding, less stressful and certainly less risky to be the opposition to the opposition,” he said.

He challenged critics to rise above petty attacks and focus on building a credible alternative that can translate citizens’ aspirations into a pathway to government.

“But genuine political leadership demands more than criticism of those seeking change. It requires the courage to challenge the status quo, the discipline to build a credible alternative and the determination to translate the aspirations of citizens into a viable pathway to government,” Chamisa said.

“The ultimate responsibility is not simply to oppose the opposition, but to confront the system that makes genuine opposition. Do better. Don’t just be the opposition to the opposition,” he added.

title: South Africa’s AGOA Crisis: What It Means for Zimbabwe’s Economy
summary: South Africa’s impending removal from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) is being treated largely as a diplomatic confrontation between Pretoria and Washington. For Zimbabwe, however, the implications are considerably wider. The decision exposes the vulnerability of an economy whose trade, manufacturing supply chains, fuel supplies, agricultural inputs and distribution networks remain deeply connected […]
content_text:
South Africa’s impending removal from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) is being treated largely as a diplomatic confrontation between Pretoria and Washington. For Zimbabwe, however, the implications are considerably wider. The decision exposes the vulnerability of an economy whose trade, manufacturing supply chains, fuel supplies, agricultural inputs and distribution networks remain deeply connected to its southern neighbour.

By Brighton Musonza

The immediate question is how South African exporters will absorb the loss of preferential access to the United States. The more important question for Zimbabwe is what happens when the largest economy in Southern Africa is forced to reorganise its trade relationships, redirect exports and reconsider the structure of its industrial supply chains.

Zimbabwe cannot afford to view this as somebody else’s trade dispute. Its economic relationship with South Africa is too substantial, too concentrated and too important to domestic production for the consequences to remain on the other side of the Limpopo.

Washington has notified Pretoria of its intention to remove South Africa from AGOA with effect from 1 January 2027. The programme, established in 2000, provides eligible sub-Saharan African countries with preferential access to the US market for thousands of products. South Africa became its largest beneficiary, building export industries around access to American consumers, particularly in automotive manufacturing, agriculture, food processing and selected industrial products.

The Southern African Agri Initiative estimates that 62,000 direct jobs could be at risk following the proposed withdrawal. Aluma Capital chief economist Frederick Mitchell has put the potential exposure considerably higher, estimating between 125,000 and 576,000 direct and indirect jobs. The wide range reflects different assumptions about the effects across supply chains, and should not be interpreted as a confirmed forecast of job losses.

The scale of the potential disruption is nevertheless significant. South Africa’s automotive industry, citrus and deciduous fruit producers, wine exporters and advanced manufacturing businesses have developed commercial relationships around the US market. Some agricultural producers have invested in orchards and production capacity specifically to serve American buyers. Redirecting those products to other destinations is not necessarily straightforward.

But the economic consequences will not stop at South Africa’s borders.

Zimbabwe’s exposure is much larger than the AGOA trade itself

Zimbabwe’s vulnerability begins with the structure of its external trade. South Africa is not simply a neighbouring country with which Zimbabwe exchanges goods. It is a major source of the machinery, fuel, food, chemicals, vehicles, plastics, steel and other industrial inputs that keep Zimbabwean businesses operating.

World Trade Organisation data, drawing on UN Comtrade, shows that South Africa supplied approximately 39.5% of Zimbabwe’s merchandise imports in 2024, equivalent to about US$3.77 billion. It also accounted for 27.6% of Zimbabwe’s exports, worth approximately US$2.05 billion.

Those figures reveal a relationship that is both commercially important and structurally imbalanced. Zimbabwe buys substantially more from South Africa than it sells there, leaving local businesses dependent on South African manufacturers, wholesalers and distribution networks for a considerable proportion of their requirements.

The composition of imports matters as much as the total value. Zimbabwe’s purchases from South Africa include cereals, machinery, mineral fuels, vehicles, plastics, iron and steel, electrical equipment and fertilisers. These are not merely consumer products that can be replaced without consequence. They are inputs into agriculture, mining, manufacturing, construction, transport and retail.

A disruption to South African production or distribution could therefore reach Zimbabwe through several channels. If manufacturers face higher costs, weaker export demand or reduced investment, those pressures may eventually be reflected in supplier prices, delivery times and the availability of industrial inputs.

This does not mean AGOA’s withdrawal will automatically make South African goods more expensive in Zimbabwe. The programme governs preferential access to the US market, not South African exports to Zimbabwe. The transmission would depend on how individual companies respond, whether they lose orders, how they reorganise production and whether the costs of adjusting their businesses are passed on to customers.

That distinction is important. Zimbabwe should prepare for possible spillovers without confusing a US trade preference decision with a direct tariff imposed on Zimbabwean imports.

The risk of a weaker South African industrial economy

The more immediate danger is that South African businesses exposed to the US market could experience weaker demand, lower margins and pressure to reduce operating costs.

The South African automotive sector illustrates the problem. Vehicle manufacturing is built around extensive supplier networks involving components, metals, plastics, logistics, engineering services and specialised labour. A reduction in export competitiveness can affect businesses well beyond the final vehicle assembly plants.

Zimbabwean companies supplying industrial materials, packaging, engineering services or other inputs into South African production networks could face indirect exposure where their customers are linked to affected export industries.

Agriculture presents another transmission channel. South Africa is a major regional producer and distributor of food. Its agricultural economy is connected to Zimbabwe through imports, wholesale markets, transport operators, packaging businesses and cross-border trade.

If South African fruit and agricultural exporters redirect products towards African markets after losing preferential access to the US, Zimbabwe could experience increased competition from imported produce. Local farmers and processors may face pressure in products where South African producers have advantages in scale, financing, technology and distribution.

This could be particularly challenging for Zimbabwean horticultural businesses seeking to expand commercial production. The country has ambitions to grow exports of citrus, avocados, blueberries, macadamia nuts and other high-value agricultural products. However, building a competitive export industry requires more than favourable growing conditions. It requires reliable logistics, cold-chain infrastructure, certification, access to finance and consistent market demand.

South Africa already possesses much of that commercial infrastructure. If its exporters intensify their search for regional customers, Zimbabwean producers will have to compete against companies with established supply chains and greater economies of scale.

The outcome could be a more competitive regional market, but not necessarily one in which Zimbabwean businesses automatically gain.

The opportunity hidden in South Africa’s trade difficulties

There is, however, another side to the argument. A restructuring of South African supply chains could create opportunities for Zimbabwean manufacturers and service providers capable of meeting the requirements of regional businesses.

South African companies may increasingly examine alternative sourcing arrangements, particularly where they can reduce costs, improve supply security or establish production partnerships elsewhere in the region.

Zimbabwe has an existing industrial base that could support some of this activity. Food processing, metal fabrication, packaging, chemicals, engineering, textiles, agricultural processing and mining-related manufacturing offer potential areas for deeper commercial cooperation.

The opportunity is not necessarily to replace South African manufacturers. It is to become a more useful part of their regional production networks.

For example, a Zimbabwean company producing packaging materials, industrial components or processed agricultural products could seek supply contracts with South African businesses. Mining companies operating across the region could also benefit from more integrated engineering, maintenance and equipment supply networks.

This is consistent with the direction of discussions at the South Africa–Zimbabwe Business Forum in August 2026. ZimTrade urged Zimbabwean companies to look beyond conventional exports and pursue opportunities in manufacturing, industrial supply chains, technology partnerships and regional distribution.

That is the correct strategic direction. Zimbabwe has spent too long treating exports largely as the movement of finished goods across borders rather than as an opportunity to participate in the production systems of larger regional economies.

However, investment will not follow political declarations. South African businesses will not relocate production or enter long-term supply agreements simply because Zimbabwe is geographically close. They will examine electricity reliability, currency and payment risks, taxation, labour productivity, infrastructure, border efficiency and the predictability of government policy.

Zimbabwe must compete on commercial terms.

The danger of becoming a dumping ground

One of the less discussed consequences of the AGOA decision is the possibility that South African exporters will redirect goods towards markets where they already have established commercial relationships.

Zimbabwe is an obvious destination because of its proximity, existing transport corridors and established distribution networks.

That could benefit consumers through greater product availability and competitive pricing. But it could also intensify pressure on domestic manufacturers already struggling with high production costs, expensive finance, unreliable electricity and competition from imports.

The distinction between healthy competition and the destruction of local productive capacity is important.

Zimbabwe needs imported machinery, raw materials and intermediate goods to support industrialisation. It does not need a trade structure in which local manufacturers are unable to compete with imported finished products because domestic production costs remain persistently higher.

If South African businesses redirect excess production into Zimbabwe, local firms could lose market share in sectors where they have the capacity to produce competitively. The result could be increased import dependence, reduced industrial utilisation and further pressure on employment.

Government therefore needs to monitor import trends carefully, while respecting regional trade commitments and avoiding arbitrary protectionist measures. The objective should be to improve the competitiveness of domestic producers, not to shelter inefficient businesses indefinitely.

Zimbabwe cannot simply inherit South Africa’s AGOA advantage

There is also a misconception that South Africa’s removal from AGOA could create an automatic opening for Zimbabwean exporters in the United States.

It will not.

Zimbabwe has not been designated an AGOA beneficiary. The withdrawal of South Africa’s eligibility does not automatically transfer its preferential access to another country. Zimbabwean exporters cannot claim AGOA treatment simply because they operate in the same region or supply goods previously exported through South African businesses.

Any attempt to use regional production arrangements to access preferential treatment would also have to comply with applicable rules of origin and US customs requirements.

This is an important limitation because it places the opportunity in the correct context. Zimbabwe may be able to supply South African businesses, attract investment into regional production or develop alternative export markets, but it cannot assume that South Africa’s lost trade preferences will become its own.

The country would need to pursue its own trade diplomacy and improve the competitiveness of its exports if it wants to expand access to international markets.

The regional trade imbalance is a strategic weakness

Zimbabwe’s dependence on South Africa also raises a broader question about the country’s industrial and trade policy.

A country that imports a substantial proportion of its manufactured goods from one trading partner is exposed to developments in that partner’s economy, even when the original shock occurs in a completely different market.

South Africa’s AGOA difficulties are an illustration of this vulnerability. A diplomatic dispute with Washington could influence the commercial decisions of South African manufacturers, agricultural exporters and investors. Those decisions could then affect Zimbabwe through prices, orders, employment, logistics and the availability of goods.

Zimbabwe’s 2024 trade figures underline the challenge. South Africa supplied nearly US$3.8 billion of imports, while Zimbabwe exported about US$2.05 billion to the market. The relationship is not inherently unhealthy; proximity and established infrastructure make South Africa a natural trading partner. The problem is the limited capacity of Zimbabwe’s domestic industrial base to supply more of its own requirements and compete for a greater share of regional demand.

The country must therefore distinguish between reducing dependence on South Africa and reducing trade with South Africa. The latter would be neither practical nor economically desirable. The objective should be to build productive capacity so that Zimbabwe can trade with its neighbour from a stronger commercial position.

That means producing more of the goods it currently imports, increasing the value added to mineral and agricultural exports, and developing businesses that can supply regional manufacturers.

Zimbabwe’s export structure remains heavily concentrated in primary commodities and mineral products. More value addition in minerals, tobacco, horticulture and other agricultural products would help diversify export earnings and create stronger links between mining, manufacturing and services.

SADC and AfCFTA need to become commercial instruments

The AGOA dispute also places renewed emphasis on the importance of regional trade integration.

The Southern African Development Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area provide frameworks through which businesses can expand markets, establish production partnerships and reduce some of the barriers to regional commerce.

But regional agreements alone cannot create competitive industries. Their value depends on whether companies can move goods across borders efficiently, obtain predictable customs treatment, secure payments and operate within consistent regulatory systems.

For Zimbabwe, the Beitbridge border remains central to this discussion. Delays, administrative costs and transport inefficiencies raise the cost of doing business with South Africa. A more efficient border environment would benefit exporters, importers, logistics companies and manufacturers on both sides.

The same applies to rail infrastructure, road networks, warehousing and access to reliable energy. Regional trade integration will remain largely theoretical if businesses cannot move goods at competitive cost.

Zimbabwe should also pursue stronger commercial links with Zambia, Mozambique, Botswana and other regional markets. Diversification does not require abandoning South Africa. It requires ensuring that South Africa is not the only practical route through which Zimbabwean businesses can source inputs, sell products or reach international markets.

The investment question

Perhaps the most important long-term consequence is what the AGOA dispute reveals about the relationship between trade policy and investment confidence.

South Africa’s access to the US market was not simply about the value of goods exported under preferential tariffs. It helped support investment decisions, production capacity, employment and long-term commercial relationships.

When access becomes uncertain, companies reassess where they manufacture, where they source inputs and which markets justify additional capital expenditure.

Zimbabwe should pay attention to that process.

The country has mineral resources, agricultural potential and a geographical position that could support regional manufacturing. Yet those advantages will not attract investment without credible property rights, predictable taxation, reliable energy, efficient transport and a stable framework for repatriating returns.

Investors compare locations. If South Africa becomes less attractive for particular export-oriented activities, Zimbabwe could be considered as an alternative production base. But that would require a demonstrable improvement in the investment environment, not simply the existence of a neighbouring country’s difficulties.

The lesson is that investment is attracted by competitive conditions, not by another economy’s misfortune.

A test of Zimbabwe’s economic strategy

South Africa’s impending AGOA removal is ultimately a reminder that trade access is never guaranteed. Preferential arrangements can be withdrawn, political relationships can deteriorate and established export markets can become less predictable.

For Zimbabwe, the danger is not that it will lose AGOA benefits it does not possess. It is that an important trading partner could face a period of industrial adjustment, with consequences for the businesses and consumers connected to its economy.

There are opportunities in the disruption, particularly in manufacturing partnerships, agricultural processing, regional distribution and industrial supply chains. But capturing them requires a more competitive domestic economy.

Zimbabwe needs to move beyond the rhetoric of import substitution and export diversification towards a practical industrial strategy built around productivity, investment and value addition. It must make it easier for businesses to produce locally, source competitively, cross borders efficiently and sell into regional markets.

South Africa’s trade difficulties could create openings for Zimbabwean companies. They could also expose the weaknesses of Zimbabwe’s own production base and intensify competition from redirected imports.

The difference between those two outcomes will be determined by Zimbabwe’s ability to respond commercially.

The real lesson from the AGOA dispute is therefore not that Zimbabwe should celebrate South Africa’s setback. It is that the country must build an economy capable of benefiting from regional opportunities without being destabilised by every shock experienced by its largest trading partner.

About the writer

Brighton Musonza is a Zimbabwean business and economic commentator, writer and media entrepreneur, and the founder of The Zimbabwe Mail. He holds an MBA and a BSc in Business Management, with additional professional training in business analytics, finance and digital transformation.

His commentary focuses on Zimbabwe’s economy, regional and international trade, financial markets, investment, industrial development and public policy. He examines economic developments through the lens of business strategy, macroeconomics, institutional governance and the practical realities facing businesses and investors.

Based in the United Kingdom, Musonza writes about Zimbabwe’s economic transformation, the country’s position in Southern Africa, and the opportunities and challenges shaping its engagement with international markets. His work aims to encourage informed debate, challenge conventional assumptions, and promote a deeper understanding of the economic forces shaping Zimbabwe’s development.

title: 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference: Global Gathering to Protect Earth’s Green Lungs
summary: HAIKOU, CHINA – Media OutReach Newswire – 3 November 2026 – From Nov. 18 to 22, 2026, a global gathering dedicated to protecting the Earth’s “green lungs” will take place in Haikou, Hainan Province, China: the 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference. A Hainan Gibbon (Nomascus hainanus) photographed in the Bawangling Area of the National […]
content_text:
HAIKOU, CHINA – Media OutReach Newswire – 3 November 2026 – From Nov. 18 to 22, 2026, a global gathering dedicated to protecting the Earth’s “green lungs” will take place in Haikou, Hainan Province, China: the 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference.

From the vast Amazon rainforest to the dense forests of the Congo Basin and the diverse landscapes of the Malay Archipelago, representative rainforests from around the world will come together with the National Park of Hainan Tropical Rainforest for dialogue and exchange. Under the theme “Global Treasures · Shared Future,” the conference embodies humanity’s shared commitment to protecting rainforests and pursuing sustainable development.

Tropical rainforests cover less than one-tenth of the Earth’s land area, yet they are home to more than half of the world’s plant and animal species. Hainan, China’s only tropical island province, is home to the country’s largest, most concentrated and best-preserved contiguous tropical rainforest on a continental island. Established in 2021, the National Park of Hainan Tropical Rainforest covers more than 4,269 square kilometers and protects over 95 percent of Hainan Island’s primary forests. Its forest coverage rate remains stable at 95.9 percent, while both its water and air quality excellence rates stand at 100 percent.

Over the past five years, this rainforest has continued to witness remarkable ecological achievements. The Hainan gibbon population has grown to 44 individuals across seven groups, making it the only gibbon population in the world to have shown sustained growth.

In addition, 91 previously undocumented wild plant and animal species have been recorded in the park. An integrated space-air-ground ecological monitoring system now provides round-the-clock, comprehensive monitoring and protection of the rainforest ecosystem. The “Bawangling Model” for Hainan gibbon conservation has also been recognized by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as a global model for protecting rare species.

The conference will explore how forests can serve as reservoirs of water, sources of food, generators of economic value and carbon sinks. Two keynote forums and four parallel forums will be held, bringing together participants for in-depth discussions on key topics, including water conservation and aquatic ecological security, the sustainable use of forest food resources, ways to unlock the value of ecological products, and carbon management in rainforests. The discussions will foster exchanges of ideas and the sharing of experience.

The conference will also focus on Hainan’s efforts to seek dual World Heritage recognition for its natural and cultural heritage. It will bring together global expertise to support the nomination of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest and the Traditional Settlement of Li Ethnic Group for inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List as a mixed natural and cultural heritage property. The initiative will explore new approaches to rainforest governance that uphold ecological protection as a firm priority while bringing tangible benefits to local communities.

In addition to the conference sessions, a series of supporting events will be held. “Rainforest Night,” a showcase of Hainan’s intangible cultural heritage, will offer an immersive audiovisual experience showcasing the distinctive traditions of the Li and Miao ethnic groups. The “Hidden Realms · Shared Life” Hainan Tropical Rainforest Photography Exhibition and the “Gifts of Nature” Ecological Products Market will showcase the rainforest’s natural beauty and innovative ways of turning ecological resources into tangible benefits. Field expeditions into the Hainan Tropical Rainforest, media tours, and the public-interest initiative “Breathe Deep in the Rainforest · Protect Our Shared Habitat” will take participants deep into the rainforest to experience the vitality of its ecosystems.

As the Hainan Free Trade Port approaches the first anniversary of the launch of island-wide special customs operations and the National Park of Hainan Tropical Rainforest marks its fifth anniversary, this conference will serve as China’s green calling card to the world and provide a platform for international dialogue and cooperation on rainforest conservation.

summary: GUANGZHOU, CHINA – Media OutReach Newswire – 3 November 2026 – Co-hosted across Guangdong, Hong Kong, and Macao from October 31 to November 2, the 2026 Greater Bay Area (GBA) Science Forum took place with a strong focus on future industries and cutting-edge technologies. Jointly guided by the Ministry of Science and Technology and the […]
content_text:
GUANGZHOU, CHINA – Media OutReach Newswire – 3 November 2026 – Co-hosted across Guangdong, Hong Kong, and Macao from October 31 to November 2, the 2026 Greater Bay Area (GBA) Science Forum took place with a strong focus on future industries and cutting-edge technologies. Jointly guided by the Ministry of Science and Technology and the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), this year’s event highlights national strategic leadership to accelerate the implementation of key policies and technological breakthroughs in the region.

The forum features an opening ceremony, a main forum, 15 specialized sub-forums, and 10 signature events. While the opening ceremony and main forum were held on November 1 in Nansha, Guangzhou, parallel sessions are rolling out across Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Huizhou, Dongguan, and Yangjiang, demonstrating a deeply integrated and synergistic approach to the event across multiple cities.

The opening ceremony witnessed the release of new support measures for the GBA International Sci-Tech Innovation Center, jointly introduced by relevant state ministries and central authorities. A key highlight is the commitment to fortifying the region’s original innovation capacity by supporting the development of a world-class cluster of major sci-tech infrastructures in the GBA. Furthermore, two national key R&D projects under the 15th Five-Year Plan, spearheaded by Guangdong Province, were officially launched: the “Advanced Biotherapeutic Technologies Project” and the “GBA International Sci-Tech Innovation Center Project.”

The ceremony also featured the signing of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Collaborative Innovation Joint Funding Program, as well as major sci-tech cooperation agreements between CAS and Guangdong Province, marking another solid step in translating national strategic visions into concrete actions.

Since its inception in December 2021, the GBA Science Forum has been successfully held for five editions. It has evolved into a premier high-level exchange platform and a vital showcase for the matchmaking and achievements of the GBA International Sci-Tech Innovation Center.

This year’s forum brought together four Nobel laureates, alongside distinguished academicians from home and abroad, young scientists, and leading tech entrepreneurs.

Together, they shared their latest research findings and visionary insights on critical topics, including cutting-edge scientific breakthroughs, future technological trends, and the deep integration of scientific and industrial innovation.

In recent years, the GBA International Sci-Tech Innovation Center has demonstrated robust innovation momentum and cultivated a thriving developmental environment. This vitality was globally recognized in September 2026, when the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) published its Global Innovation Index 2026 Top 100 Science and Technology Clusters, with the “Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou” cluster securing the number one spot globally once again.

title: Masvingo seeks relief from Operation Chenesa after hailstorm disaster
categories: Zimbabwe South; Masvingo City Council; Operation Chenesa
summary: Masvingo councillors have proposed engaging the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works to seek temporary relief from aspects of Operation Chenesa, arguing that residents need time to recover from the destruction caused by the October 5 hailstorm. The hailstorm damaged more than 13 500 properties, prompting the government to declare a state of national […]
content_text:
Masvingo councillors have proposed engaging the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works to seek temporary relief from aspects of Operation Chenesa, arguing that residents need time to recover from the destruction caused by the October 5 hailstorm.

The hailstorm damaged more than 13 500 properties, prompting the government to declare a state of national disaster, with efforts underway to assist affected households.

During a recent Full Council meeting, councillors unanimously agreed to approach the ministry and seek leniency in implementing the clean-up operation, saying enforcement could further burden residents who are still struggling to rebuild their homes and livelihoods.

Launched in September, Operation Chenesa is a government-led clean-up and environmental management campaign targeting, among other issues, informal trading activities and illegal structures.

Ward 2 councillor Benson Hwata said many residents were yet to recover from the disaster, with some depending on informal trading for their livelihoods.

“Our people are still not yet back on their feet after the hailstorm. We are appealing that our province be exempted from the wrath of the operation while we try to make things work. The situation of the people is dire,” he said.

“Most of them live on informal trading and some are part of those who have been operating at undesignated places and using illegal structures. But can they get more time to put their houses in order?”

Ward 9 councillor Bernard Muchokwa said the disaster warranted a temporary suspension of enforcement activities to give residents time to rebuild.

“It is international practice that in the event that there is a national disaster, all other operations have to be halted. There are other cities that we can draw lessons from which had to halt these kinds of operations after they had been hit by floods, landslides and earthquakes. Masvingo should not be an exception,” he said.

“We are asking for time to recoup from this loss we suffered, while we also make sure all that we have is put back in place.”

Ward 10 councillor Senengai Manyanga said the national disaster declaration should influence how other government programmes were implemented in the province.

“The President declared the hailstorm a national disaster. All other operations that are ongoing need to be halted until another declaration is made otherwise. We understand that Operation Chenesa is a nationwide campaign, but how do you come and further destroy infrastructure that was already destroyed by a natural disaster?” she said.

Responding to the concerns, Mayor Aleck Tabe said the local authority had a responsibility to provide alternative designated trading spaces before relocating vendors from their current operating areas.

He said council would engage the ministry to negotiate a scaled-down implementation of the operation in Masvingo.

“We have the mandate as the council to establish and build alternative designated areas for the vendors to move to. We cannot just let the people be without providing them with alternative areas,” he said.

“Of course, we have higher authorities that give us directives, but we must try and negotiate with them and ask for leniency. We could find resources from partners that could cushion our vendors so that they may legitimise their operations.”

Tabe said council, with the support of the town clerk, had already been engaging the minister over the province’s circumstances.

He, however, emphasised that the local authority remained bound by the law and could not abandon enforcement altogether.

“What we are trying to negotiate for is that we can have the operation scaled down in Masvingo. Of course, there are extreme cases where we can see that there is danger to people’s health and safety, that we have to do away with, but for mild cases we can plead for leniency,” he said.

title: Good News For Motorists: Harare City Council is slashing traffic penalties, clamping and tow-away fees
keywords: news
summary: Harare proposes lower traffic penalties as illegal-dumping fines soar HARARE — Harare City Council is proposing to cut some traffic-enforcement charges by half while sharply increasing penalties for illegal waste disposal, a mixed tariff package that would shift the cost of parking offences and rubbish dumping in the capital from January 2027 if approved. The […] The post Good News For Motorists: Harare City Council is slashing traffic penalties, clamping and tow-away fees first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
Harare proposes lower traffic penalties as illegal-dumping fines soar

HARARE — Harare City Council is proposing to cut some traffic-enforcement charges by half while sharply increasing penalties for illegal waste disposal, a mixed tariff package that would shift the cost of parking offences and rubbish dumping in the capital from January 2027 if approved.

The proposed traffic schedule reduces the prescribed enforcement penalty from US$20 to US$10 and the related administration charge from US$10 to US$5. At the same time, a number of waste-related penalties would rise steeply, including a proposed increase of nearly 178 per cent for dumping domestic rubbish from standard refuse containers or carts.

Residents have until November 30, 2026, to lodge objections to the proposed tariffs. The changes are scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027, subject to approval.

The new charges are set against a continuing struggle to remove rubbish from Harare’s neighbourhoods. A June 2026 account of council and waste-management data put the city’s daily waste generation at about 995 tonnes, while collection levels remained below half of the total. The resulting gap was estimated at more than 180,000 tonnes of refuse a year.

The same figures showed that Harare was operating 33 refuse trucks, compared with an estimated 120 needed for reliable collection across the city. Mbare, Glen View, Budiriro, Mabvuku and parts of the central business district were identified as areas with significant waste accumulation.

The city’s published refuse collection and sanitation schedule lists 37 suburbs across 5 zones, with collections scheduled from Monday to Saturday and daily collection in the central business district. The council identifies Geo Pomona Waste Management as its service partner and provides a hotline for missed collections.

Under the proposed enforcement tariffs, illegal discharge of domestic or industrial effluent would attract a US$1,500 penalty, up from US$616. Businesses caught dumping industrial or commercial waste in undesignated places would face a proposed US$950 charge, compared with US$385 at present.

The proposed penalty for dumping domestic waste from a motor vehicle rises from US$113 to US$300. For waste dumped from a standard refuse container or cart, the amount would increase from US$36 to US$100. That is a rise of US$64, or nearly 178 per cent.

Ordinary monthly residential refuse-removal charges are not changing under the proposal. Households in high-density areas would continue to pay US$8.97 a month for one weekly collection, while low-density households would continue to pay US$12.71.

The scale of the fines contrasts with the daily problems residents describe when collection does not happen. In Mabvuku, resident James Tofa said: “When trucks don’t come, people have nowhere to put the rubbish. It ends up in drains, open spaces and along roadsides.”

In Mbare, resident Kudzai Gwati described a familiar cycle of rubbish returning after it has been swept away. “Tomorrow it will be bigger,” she said.

Harare’s waste difficulties have prompted emergency clean-up efforts before. In 2024, the Government said the first phase of Operation Chenesa Harare had cleared more than 250,000 tonnes of garbage, but illegal dumpsites began appearing again in some areas after the initial operation ended. The Government then announced a second phase and said it was considering longer-term arrangements after the council requested central-government help with solid-waste collection.

At the time, Information Minister Jenfan Muswere said: “Despite the Harare City Council levying and collecting rates for the purpose of waste management and having adequate legislative provisions to support such functions and operations, it has continuously failed to provide functional systems for solid waste management.”

The proposed 2027 waste penalties add another enforcement measure to that record of clean-ups and service changes. Their practical impact will depend on both the city’s ability to identify offenders and the availability of regular collection, particularly in the high-density suburbs where the reported truck shortage and waste build-up are most severe.

For motorists, the tariff review also changes some wheel-clamping charges while leaving others untouched. Drivers of light vehicles in the central business district would continue to pay US$20 for clamping. The proposed charge for commuter omnibuses carrying more than 18 passengers falls from US$25 to US$20.

Clamping charges for conventional buses and lorries would drop from US$30 to US$20. Articulated heavy lorries would also pay US$20, down from US$30.

Tow-away charges for light vehicles would remain at US$20, while storage for light motor vehicles would stay at US$10. The council would retain an additional US$0.50 per kilometre when a vehicle is towed from outside the central business district.

The proposed reductions do not remove the city’s wider parking-enforcement system. Council enforcement agents currently issue tickets and may clamp or tow vehicles parked unlawfully or left in a bay after paid time expires. The draft tariff schedule revises specified penalties and vehicle-class charges; it does not propose abolishing clamping or towing.

Taken together, the proposals offer motorists lower charges in some categories but leave key light-vehicle costs unchanged. For waste disposal, they would make the financial consequences substantially heavier for households, motorists and businesses caught dumping rubbish or discharging effluent unlawfully.

The consultation period gives residents and businesses until November 30 to submit objections before the council’s 2027 tariff decisions are finalised. If adopted, the revised charges would begin on January 1, 2027, while residential refuse-removal fees would remain at their current proposed levels.

summary: A 45-year-old Nkayi man has been sentenced to life imprisonment for the brutal murder of his former lover after tracking her down following the collapse of an abusive relationship. The High Court sitting in Hwange also handed the man an additional five-year prison sentence for attempted murder after he stabbed a 72-year-old man in a […]
content_text:
A 45-year-old Nkayi man has been sentenced to life imprisonment for the brutal murder of his former lover after tracking her down following the collapse of an abusive relationship.

The High Court sitting in Hwange also handed the man an additional five-year prison sentence for attempted murder after he stabbed a 72-year-old man in a separate attack on the same night. The sentences will run consecutively.

According to the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA), the victim, Princess Janet Ncube, had ended her relationship with the offender while they were living in South Africa and returned home to Nkayi in December 2025 seeking refuge from the abuse.

Ncube, who worked as a cook at Inkisela Lodges in Nkayi, settled at her mother’s homestead in Mbondweni Village under Chief Tshugulu. However, her former partner refused to accept the break-up.

Prosecutors said the man relentlessly pursued Ncube, demanding that she return to him. When she refused, he allegedly threatened to kill her and members of her family. He also wrote a six-page handwritten note detailing his intentions before travelling to Nkayi, where he reportedly stalked both Ncube and her relatives.

The violence reached a tragic climax on 28 January 2026.

At around 8 pm, Ncube left Inkisela Lodges in the company of her new boyfriend. The offender confronted the pair and threatened the boyfriend, forcing him to flee for safety.

The court heard that the man then dragged Ncube towards the nearby ZESA Nkayi offices, where he launched a frenzied knife attack. He stabbed her 13 times, killing her at the scene.

Just 30 minutes after the fatal attack, the offender struck again.

Near Junction Down Stores, he attacked a 72-year-old man, stabbing him once in the back with the same knife. The elderly victim survived and was treated at Nkayi District Hospital.

Police investigations quickly led to the arrest of the offender. Detectives recovered a blood-stained Okapi knife believed to have been used in both attacks, as well as the handwritten note outlining the man’s plans.

content_text:
The City of Bulawayo has postponed the launch of Operation Hlanzeka, a campaign aimed at removing informal traders operating in unauthorised areas, to allow more consultations with affected groups.

In a public notice issued on Tuesday, Town Clerk Christopher Dube said the operation, which had been scheduled to begin on 1 November 2026, has been put on hold with immediate effect.

Dube said the city wants to engage further with traders, small businesses and other stakeholders before proceeding. The operation is now expected to resume in about two weeks.

The postponement gives informal traders more time to move from undesignated trading spots to officially approved areas. Traders are also being urged to remove illegal structures and relocate their goods before enforcement begins.

While acknowledging the important role played by micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in supporting livelihoods, the council said trading on pavements, parking bays, road servitudes and other unauthorised locations remains against city by-laws.

The local authority stressed that all traders should comply with council regulations by moving their businesses to designated trading sites.

Dube urged affected traders to cooperate with council officials during the transition period to ensure what he described as a smooth relocation process.

content_text:
Tinashe Sambiri| President Emmerson Mnangagwa has warned Zimbabwean diplomats against treating their foreign postings as opportunities for leisure, insisting that ambassadors and other representatives must demonstrate measurable results in the execution of their duties.

Addressing Zimbabwean diplomats in Harare on Monday, Mnangagwa delivered a stern message, declaring that serving in the diplomatic corps under his administration was not an opportunity for individuals to enjoy foreign lifestyles at the country’s expense.

“Under my Administration serving as diplomats is not ‘child’s-play’. Ndinoda madzimai nevarume vakatsunga, vakazvipira kushanda nesimba kuti nyika ibudirire. Avo vanofunga kuti varikuenda-kuholiday, bodo. Hamusi kuyenda kunze ikoko kunomwa mazambiringa. I demand results,” Mnangagwa said.

His remarks raised questions about the performance expectations facing Zimbabwe’s diplomatic missions, particularly at a time when the government continues to look to foreign engagement to attract investment, expand exports and secure international partnerships.

The President’s insistence on results also places renewed attention on whether Zimbabwe’s diplomatic network is translating official engagements, international meetings and overseas postings into tangible economic opportunities for the country.

Mnangagwa further emphasised the people-centred purpose of diplomacy, declaring: “Diplomacy exists for people.”

However, beyond the strong rhetoric and demands for commitment, the central issue remains the actual impact of Zimbabwe’s diplomatic engagements on ordinary citizens and the national economy.

For many Zimbabweans, the value of diplomacy will ultimately be measured not by speeches, overseas meetings or official declarations, but by tangible improvements in economic opportunities, investment, trade and the country’s international standing.

summary: Spanish second-tier footballer Jesús de Miguel has died after suffering serious injuries during a league match between CD Tenerife and FC Andorra on Monday. Tenerife and Andorra were level at 2-2 when Owono […]
content_text:
Spanish second-tier footballer Jesús de Miguel has died after suffering serious injuries during a league match between CD Tenerife and FC Andorra on Monday.

The 30-year-old striker sustained severe head and chest injuries following a heavy collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono deep into stoppage time.

Tenerife and Andorra were level at 2-2 when Owono raced from his goal to clear a long ball near the centre circle. His knee appeared to strike De Miguel, who collapsed and lay motionless on the pitch.

Medical staff treated the forward for several minutes before he was taken by ambulance from the Estadio Heliodoro Rodríguez López to hospital. Players from both teams were visibly shaken by the incident, with several Tenerife players in tears. The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.

De Miguel’s condition was initially described as stable but serious. However, Spanish media reported that he suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was revived by paramedics on the way to hospital. His condition worsened overnight, and he died on Tuesday at 7 AM GMT (8 AM local time).

Announcing the news, Tenerife said: “Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic death of Jesús de Miguel Alameda.

“There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, his loved ones and all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today.”

Following De Miguel’s death, the Spanish Football Federation postponed Tuesday’s Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina fixtures as a mark of respect.

Born in Madrid, De Miguel began his professional career with Leganés in 2015 and went on to represent several Spanish clubs, including Lugo, Fuenlabrada, Internacional Madrid, Unión Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.

He joined Castellón in 2023 and played a key role in their promotion to Spain’s second division, scoring 16 goals during the campaign. In 2025, he signed a three-year contract with Tenerife and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the club.

De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernández, who was born in 2025.

content_text:
CATHERINE MUROMBEDZI CORRESPONDENT

THE US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted tentative approval for the first generic version of lenacapavir, LEN. LEN is a twice-yearly injectable drug for HIV prevention. The generic approval secures a path to supply 120 low- and middle-income countries at US$40 per person per year.

​The generic version, developed by India-based Dr Reddy’s Laboratories, secured regulatory authorisation just 16 months after the FDA approved Gilead Sciences’ originator product.

Initial generic shipments are scheduled to reach priority markets by late 2026, followed by broader international rollout in 2027.

​The accelerated approval followed a strategy combining financial, technical and regulatory backing from global health non-profits Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) and Wits RHI. By filing a unified application for both HIV prevention and treatment indications under the FDA’s 505(b)(2) pathway, Dr Reddy’s secured priority review status, cutting years off the typical timeline for generic entry.

Under a voluntary license framework established with Gilead in late 2024, the US$40 annual price point aligns long-acting injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with the cost of daily oral preventive regimens.

​While early rollout initiatives have already placed over 125,000 individuals across 10 African nations on lenacapavir, global health groups emphasize that tentative FDA approval serves as a regulatory stepping stone rather than a complete distribution solution.

National regulatory agencies must now process local approvals, while international procurement bodies, including the Global Fund (GF) and the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), work alongside local health systems to establish delivery logistics and community distribution networks. ● Feedback: cathymwauyakufa@gmail.com

content_text:
Makhadzi Claims She Is Stranded and Being Held Against Her Will in Botswana

South African singer Makhadzi is reportedly being held against her will in Botswana, where she has been stranded since Saturday following a dispute with an entertainment promoter.

She has accused Gilbert “PP Wa Pimp” Seagile of taking her passport, vehicle and personal belongings, leaving her unable to return home.

In a live social media broadcast, the award-winning musician explained that the disagreement involves money owed from a previous performance and promotional arrangements for her upcoming One Woman Show.

Also Read: ‘God Protected My Voice’: Makhadzi Speaks Out After Surviving Car Accident

Makhadzi Recounts How Incident Unfolded

Makhadzi revealed that the confrontation happened while she was performing at an event.

She said her road manager alerted her to a group of men waiting outside, prompting her to leave the stage to find out what was happening.

According to Makhadzi, two men approached her, demanded her passport and attempted to take control of her vehicle.

She questioned their authority, arguing that they were not wearing police uniforms and had not produced identification documents, a warrant or a court order.

The singer alleged that her vehicle, passport and other belongings were subsequently taken.

Dispute Involves Botswana Promoter

The disagreement reportedly involves Seagile, whose company, Gilbert Promotions, has handled Makhadzi’s bookings and business dealings in Botswana since 2023.

The financial dispute is said to involve P50,000, approximately R60,582, as well as arrangements for a proposed One Woman Show in Botswana.

Seagile has been involved in the singer’s business dealings since she parted ways with Open Mic Productions.

He is also a prominent figure in Botswana’s entertainment industry and was recently elected chairman of the Association of Botswana Night Clubs and Bars (ABONIC), which represents businesses in the country’s nightlife, entertainment and hospitality sectors.

DIRCO Confirms It Is Handling the Matter

The controversy has drawn the attention of South African authorities, with the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) confirming that it is attending to the matter.

DIRCO spokesperson Clayson Monyela acknowledged the situation after the singer’s account circulated on social media.

“ We are attending to this matter. An update will be provided,” Monyela said.

content_text:
A 75-year-old man from Banga Village in Marange was found dead by the roadside last week in a case linked to excessive consumption of illicit alcohol.

The deceased has been identified as John Chimhutu.

Acting Manicaland provincial police spokesperson Assistant Inspector Wiseman Chinyoka confirmed the incident, saying police in Marange received a report about the discovery of the body.

Chinyoka said Chimhutu left his daughter’s homestead in Murehwa Village, under Chief Marange, at around 5 am on 26 October.

Later that morning, he was seen by Nyasha Mushati, who was on his way to the fields.

“He left his daughter’s homestead on October 26 at about 5 am in Murehwa Village under Chief Marange. Later that morning, he was seen by Nyasha Mushati, who was on his way to the fields. Chimhutu was carrying an illicit alcoholic brew and talking to himself,” said Assistant Inspector Chinyoka.

Witnesses became concerned after seeing him appearing disoriented while carrying the illicit brew.

The body was later found lying lifeless by the roadside at around 2 pm by Trymore Chimhutu of Banga Village, who reported the matter to Marange Police Station.

Police attended the scene, and the body was taken to Victoria Chitepo Provincial Hospital mortuary for a post-mortem examination.

Assistant Inspector Chinyoka said investigations into the circumstances surrounding the death are continuing.

Police have urged members of the public to desist from consuming illicit alcoholic beverages, warning that excessive consumption can have fatal consequences and pose serious health risks.

title: Zimbabwe treasury collects ZiG220 billion in 9 months
summary: Zimbabwe has raised over ZiG220 billion in nine months, bringing Treasury closer to its ZiG280 billion revenue target for 2026.
content_text:
Zimbabwe has generated more than ZiG220 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026. The latest figures put the Government within reach of its annual collection target.

Treasury aims to collect ZiG280 billion by the end of December. Therefore, the latest performance signals progress towards meeting that financial goal.

The strong collections come as authorities intensify efforts to boost domestic revenue. Meanwhile, economic activity continues supporting Government’s efforts to mobilise resources locally.

VAT Leads Zimbabwe’s Revenue Collections

Value Added Tax (VAT) emerged as the biggest contributor to Government revenue during the reporting period. Personal Income Tax followed, alongside Corporate Tax and Excise Duty.

These revenue streams remain central to Zimbabwe’s public finances. They provide funding for Government operations and various national development programmes.

According to the latest State of the Economy Report, the collections reflect ongoing domestic resource mobilisation efforts.

Treasury Confident of Meeting ZiG280 Billion Target

The Ministry of Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion remains optimistic about achieving its 2026 revenue target.

Treasury also views stronger domestic collections as essential for financing development projects. Furthermore, increased revenue could help reduce budget deficits.

The Government also hopes to limit its dependence on external loans, grants and credit lines.

Meanwhile, attention is turning towards the next fiscal year. The 2027 National Budget presentation is scheduled for November 19.

The upcoming statement will outline the Government’s spending priorities and economic plans for the year ahead.

title: Zimbabwe Set to Become Africa’s 14th-Largest Economy in 2026
summary: Zimbabwe is projected to overtake Cameroon and Tunisia in 2026, securing Africa’s 14th-largest economy position with GDP reaching US$65.92 billion.
content_text:
Zimbabwe is on course to rank among Africa’s biggest economies in 2026, according to new IMF projections.

The country is expected to record a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of US$65.92 billion. This would secure Zimbabwe the 14th position among Africa’s largest economies.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) published the projections in its October 2026 World Economic Outlook.

The forecast puts Zimbabwe ahead of Cameroon and Tunisia in the continental rankings. Cameroon is expected to record US$64.81 billion, while Tunisia follows with US$62.74 billion.

Meanwhile, South Africa retains its position as Africa’s biggest economy. Its projected GDP stands at US$489.08 billion.

Egypt follows with an estimated US$442.89 billion, while Nigeria occupies third place with US$386.67 billion.

Zimbabwe’s economic outlook and continental ranking

The IMF expects Zimbabwe’s economy to expand by approximately five percent in 2026. This growth projection comes as the country seeks to strengthen production and attract investment.

However, the rankings reflect nominal GDP rather than real economic growth. Nominal GDP measures the value of goods and services at current prices.

It also converts economic output into US dollars. Consequently, exchange-rate movements and inflation can influence a country’s position.

Therefore, a higher ranking does not automatically translate into improved living standards. Productivity, employment opportunities and stronger industrial output remain important measures of economic progress.

Mnangagwa calls for stronger regional economic partnerships

Meanwhile, President Emmerson Mnangagwa has urged African countries to strengthen regional economic cooperation.

He delivered the call during the 19th COMESA Business Forum in Harare on 20 October 2026.

The event took place at the Harare International Conference Centre. Mnangagwa highlighted the importance of deeper trade and investment partnerships among member states.

He said stronger regional partnerships were important in boosting production and creating opportunities across the region.

His remarks come as Zimbabwe seeks to expand its economic opportunities. Stronger regional cooperation could also help businesses access wider African markets.

Zimbabwe Overtakes Cameroon and Tunisia in New IMF Ranking of Africa’s Biggest Economies

This headline creates curiosity while highlighting Zimbabwe’s achievement. It also includes recognisable country names and a strong economic angle.
