summary: MK Party organiser Lastborn Shazi was shot dead at his home in Umzumbe, South Africa, while reportedly taking part in a virtual election-planning meeting.
content_text:
The uMkhonto weSizwe Party’s Ugu regional organiser, Lastborn Shazi, was shot dead at his home in Umzumbe, KwaZulu-Natal, on Monday night, as party officials prepared for Wednesday’s local government elections.

The party said Shazi had been taking part in a virtual meeting with its regional elections team. He suddenly stopped participating, and those on the call were then informed that a shooting had taken place at his home.

Party officials said they learnt of the incident at about 9pm and sent leaders to the homestead. The party has not identified a suspect or established a motive, and its spokesperson said it was not aware of any witnesses.

Party urges members not to speculate

KwaZulu-Natal spokesperson Mkhuseli Mlengane said the party did not yet know what had led to the shooting. “We are trying to avoid speculation,” he said, urging members to let investigators establish what happened.

The party called on the province’s Political Killings Task Team to conduct an urgent investigation and bring those responsible to justice. It described Shazi’s death as a devastating loss to his family, the party and the communities he served.

In its appeal for a thorough investigation, the party said: “No individual should lose their life because of their political involvement or organisational responsibilities.”

The MK Party also urged its members and supporters not to spread unverified claims or make allegations that could inflame tensions or compromise the investigation. Funeral and memorial arrangements are expected to be announced after the party consults Shazi’s family.

Killing adds to concern about election violence

Shazi was killed two days before South Africans went to the polls in local government elections. His death comes amid wider concern about political violence in KwaZulu-Natal, but no evidence has been reported linking his killing to his political work or to the election.

Two ANC members were shot dead while conducting a door-to-door campaign in Umgababa in October. A third person was injured in that attack. No connection between the Umgababa shooting and Shazi’s killing has been established.

EWN cited Julian Rademeyer, a senior adviser to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, as saying that 26 people had been killed in suspected politically motivated attacks since the start of 2026. The figure reflects suspected cases and does not establish the motive in Shazi’s case.

title: Sweden Praises Zimbabwe’s Economic Progress as Inflation Drops to Single Digits
summary: Sweden has praised Zimbabwe’s economic recovery, highlighting falling inflation and improved stability as key factors that could attract foreign investment.
content_text:
Sweden has recognised Zimbabwe’s improving economic conditions, raising hopes of increased foreign investment.

Swedish Ambassador to Zimbabwe Per Lindgärde highlighted the progress during a meeting in Harare on Friday. He met Vice President General (Rtd) Dr Constantino Chiwenga to discuss relations between the two countries.

Lindgärde pointed to declining inflation and improved macroeconomic stability as encouraging signs. He also stressed the importance of resolving Zimbabwe’s outstanding debts to international financial institutions.

Sweden Highlights Zimbabwe’s Economic Recovery

The Swedish diplomat believes continued economic improvements could strengthen Zimbabwe’s recovery. Furthermore, clearing external arrears could unlock access to affordable international financing.

He explained that an International Monetary Fund programme could provide crucial support. Such financing could help Zimbabwe develop infrastructure and accelerate industrialisation.

“I think we see positive developments happening in Zimbabwe in the economic sector. There is much more macroeconomic stability in the country since I came three years ago. We have seen that inflation is coming down. You have now single-digit numbers. I think it was 2.9% inflation in August. And that is something you haven’t had for many, many years. So I think you are moving in the right direction on the economic side. And that is also important for the arrears clearance process. Because I think that if the arrears to the multilateral organisations could be cleared, and that you eventually could get an IMF programme with concessional loans, that will help develop the country even further when it comes to building the infrastructure, which will be crucial for the industrialisation of the country,” Ambassador Lindgärde said.

His comments come as Zimbabwe continues pursuing its international re-engagement and economic recovery agenda.

Sweden Promises Continued Cooperation Despite Embassy Closure

Meanwhile, Sweden is preparing to shut down its diplomatic mission in Zimbabwe. The decision forms part of a wider restructuring affecting its diplomatic presence worldwide.

Four other African countries will also experience similar changes. However, Stockholm has assured Zimbabwe that the embassy closure will not end bilateral cooperation.

Swedish development assistance will continue through regional and thematic programmes. These initiatives will maintain support for areas including child protection and gender empowerment.

Lindgärde also highlighted ongoing cooperation between Swedish institutions and Zimbabwean authorities.

“There will be other streams of support coming to Zimbabwe from regional strategies, from thematic strategies. So there will be, for example, some support from some civil society organisations. And also cooperation between different authorities will continue. Like the Swedish Public Health Agency, they are on their way to signing an MOU with the Ministry of Health. So that cooperation will continue,” Ambassador Lindgärde said.

He believes Zimbabwe’s improving economic conditions could strengthen international confidence. Moreover, sustained progress could improve the country’s chances of attracting foreign direct investment.

title: Axe murder case collapses after judge rejects earwitness testimony
categories: Crime and Courts; Axe Attack; Earwitness Testimony; Herdboy
summary: A herdboy accused of axing his 62-year-old former employer to death has been acquitted at the Bulawayo High Court after a judge ruled that earwitness voice identification was “notoriously unreliable”. Justice Donald Ndirowei acquitted Mkhokheli Ndlovu of murder following a full trial last week. Ndlovu had been accused of killing Teboko Sebata at her homestead […]
content_text:
A herdboy accused of axing his 62-year-old former employer to death has been acquitted at the Bulawayo High Court after a judge ruled that earwitness voice identification was “notoriously unreliable”.

Justice Donald Ndirowei acquitted Mkhokheli Ndlovu of murder following a full trial last week.

Ndlovu had been accused of killing Teboko Sebata at her homestead in Chabeda Village, Zezani, on 13 November 2022. The State alleged that he struck her repeatedly on the head with a metal-handled axe.

Sebata had just returned from a cattle sale. She sustained fatal head injuries and a severed carotid artery. Her body was found the following day. A blood-stained metal axe was later found hidden inside a ventilator hole of a Blair toilet at the homestead.

The prosecution, led by Elaine Kanengoni and Mufaro Ndirarire, argued that Ndlovu killed Sebata, stole her small Nokia cellphone and fled the area.

He was only arrested 18 months later, in May 2024, for possession of cannabis in Zezani, when police realised he was wanted for the murder.

The State’s case relied heavily on circumstantial evidence and the testimonies of the deceased’s son, Lihlonolo Sebata, and a relative, Lafhisani Muleya. Both claimed that when they called the victim’s missing phone after the murder, a man answered.

Lihlonolo claimed he recognised the voice as Ndlovu’s, but admitted under cross-examination that he had only met Ndlovu twice for a total of six days.

Muleya claimed the caller identified himself as “Mukokeli” before hanging up, but admitted that his initial statement to the police made no mention of the call.

Investigating officer Detective Hilton Sibanda conceded in court that two years had passed before the investigation picked up, no forensic evidence linked Ndlovu to the axe, and the stolen phone was never recovered or linked to him through IMEI tracking.

In his defence, Ndlovu said he was at his rural home in Plumtree at the time of the killing. He acknowledged that Sebata owed him unpaid wages when he left her employment, but denied killing her or ever answering her phone.

Justice Ndirowei ruled that voice identification by earwitnesses is inherently fallible, particularly where the witness has had limited contact with the accused.

“In criminal law, the alleged identification of an accused by voice alone is generally highly fallible and notoriously unreliable,” he said. He noted that without forensic corroboration or recovered property, earwitness evidence alone cannot secure a conviction.

The judge said robbers could have targeted Sebata knowing she had cash from the cattle sale and later impersonated Ndlovu on the phone to divert suspicion.

“The question is not whether the accused person might have committed the offence, but whether the evidence excludes every reasonable inference consistent with his innocence,” he said.

He found Ndlovu not guilty and ordered his release.

title: CHECKOUT: Zimbabwe civil servants to receive 2026 bonuses in two instalments
summary: Zimbabwean civil servants will receive their 2026 bonuses in November and December. Find out how much they qualify for and what pensioners will receive.
content_text:
Zimbabwean civil servants will receive their 2026 annual bonuses through two separate payments in November and December.

The National Joint Negotiating Council (NJNC) confirmed the payment arrangements in a statement released on Monday.

Under the agreement, eligible government employees will receive their bonuses based on 100% of their pensionable emoluments.

This calculation covers basic salaries, in-service allowances and administration allowances.

Furthermore, the Government will divide the payments equally across the two months.

Workers will receive 50% of their bonuses in November, followed by the remaining 50% in December.

How Much Will Civil Servants Receive?

The NJNC clarified that employees in Grades A to D qualify for bonuses calculated at 100% of their pensionable emoluments.

Consequently, the final amounts will depend on each employee’s qualifying earnings.

The payment arrangement means civil servants will receive half their annual bonus before December.

They will then receive the outstanding balance during the following month.

Meanwhile, Treasury has approved a separate financial benefit for retired government workers.

According to the NJNC, Government pensioners will receive a flat cushioning allowance in December.

However, the council did not disclose the amount of this allowance.

Mthuli Ncube Reaffirms Government’s Bonus Commitment

The latest announcement follows assurances from Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube on Saturday.

He had pledged that the Government would honour its annual bonus commitment to civil servants.

Ncube also highlighted the Government’s decision to extend annual bonuses to traditional chiefs.

He said authorities introduced these payments last year to recognise their contribution to communities.

The minister described the development as historic, marking the first such arrangement since Zimbabwe’s independence in 1980.

“We have even started paying bonuses for our traditional chiefs, which has never happened since independence in 1980. We also recognise the good work that they do, and we were able to cover them as well. But civil servants’ bonuses, we are going to pay those,” he said.

The NJNC’s confirmation now provides civil servants with a clearer picture of their expected 2026 bonus payments.

title: Zimbabwe ConCourt reserves ruling on war veterans’ bid to challenge CAA3 directly
categories: Crimes & Courts; News; Politics; CAA3; Constitution Amendment No. 3; constitutional court; Eliphas Kawa; Hazvineyi Machingura; Lewis Uriri; presidential elections; Tendai Biti; War Veterans; zimbabwe constitution
keywords: CAA3; Constitution Amendment No. 3; constitutional court; Eliphas Kawa; Hazvineyi Machingura; Lewis Uriri; presidential elections; Tendai Biti; War Veterans; zimbabwe constitution
summary: Zimbabwe’s Constitutional Court has reserved judgment on whether two war veterans can directly challenge CAA3, which changes how the President is elected and extends presidential and parliamentary terms to seven years.
content_text:
The Constitutional Court has reserved judgment on whether two war veterans can take their challenge to Constitutional Amendment Act No. 3 directly to the country’s highest court, without first going through the High Court.

Eliphas Kawa and Hazvineyi Machingura appeared before the court on Monday, represented by Tendai Biti and Advocate Lewis Uriri. The court has not yet ruled on whether the amendment is constitutional; it is deciding whether to grant the applicants direct access.

What the veterans are challenging

Constitution Amendment No. 3 extends presidential and parliamentary terms from five years to seven and transfers the election of the President from voters to Parliament.

The veterans’ lawyers argue that the changes raise fundamental questions about citizens’ voting rights and the source of public authority. They contend that Parliament could not remove citizens’ right to elect the President directly without a referendum.

The applicants are also challenging the provision allowing the President to appoint 10 senators, arguing that it undermines the Constitution’s basic structure.

A separate case is also awaiting a ruling

This is distinct from an earlier direct-access application brought by six war veterans, represented by Professor Lovemore Madhuku, which was heard in September. In that case, the Constitutional Court also reserved judgment on whether the applicants could bring their constitutional challenge directly before it.

The newer case puts another challenge to CAA3 before the court. For now, the immediate question is procedural: whether Kawa and Machingura may bypass the High Court. The substantive arguments about the amendment would be considered later if direct access is granted.

The disagreement comes as relatives pursue provincial hero status for the late actor, with some […]
content_text:
Family Dispute Erupts Over Burial Place of Veteran Actor William ‘Gweshegweshe’ Matenga

The burial of veteran actor William “Gweshegweshe” Matenga could be delayed as his family remains divided over whether he should be laid to rest in Buhera or Harare.

The disagreement comes as relatives pursue provincial hero status for the late actor, with some family members favouring Warren Hills Cemetery in Harare while others want him buried at the family cemetery in Buhera.

The 65-year-old actor died on Saturday after succumbing to hypertension, leaving his relatives facing uncertainty over his funeral arrangements.

Also Read: Veteran Gringo Actor William Matenga, Known As Gweshe Gweshe, Dies At 65

Family Divided Over Final Resting Place

The disagreement reportedly emerged during discussions at Matenga’s funeral wake in Zengeza 5, Chitungwiza.

Some relatives believe the actor should be buried at the family cemetery in Buhera, arguing that being granted hero status does not necessarily mean he must be interred in Harare.

They reportedly pointed to other individuals who were accorded hero status but were still buried at their rural homes.

Meanwhile, another section of the family is considering Warren Hills Cemetery, particularly as an application for provincial hero status is being pursued in recognition of Matenga’s contribution to the liberation struggle and his service to the country.

“ There was a fierce meeting regarding Gweshegweshe’s choice of burial place, as some family members preferred that his remains be interred at the family cemetery,” an insider familiar with the developments told H-Metro .

The source added that some relatives felt they had a say in deciding where the actor should be buried, with no known instructions from Matenga specifying his preferred resting place.

Provincial Hero Status Application Could Delay Burial

Family spokesperson Peter Chafewa said the application for provincial hero status was still being processed, with the necessary paperwork yet to be completed.

He revealed that the War Veterans Association for Harare Province, where Matenga was also a leader, wanted clarity on his status before the burial could proceed.

“ The burial of Gweshegweshe is likely to be postponed since the War Veterans Association for Harare Province, where he was also one of the leaders, wants clarity on his status,” Chafewa said.

He said a team comprising Matenga’s son Kudakwashe, his former wife and other relatives had gone to town to process the documents, but they were still awaiting feedback.

Chafewa expressed hope that the process would be completed in time for the family to give the actor a burial befitting his contribution to the country.

Family Awaits Arrival of Children Based Abroad

The funeral arrangements are also dependent on the arrival of some of Matenga’s children who live outside Zimbabwe.

His son Lawrence, who works in Australia, and another son, Lloyd Matenga, an advocate based in South Africa, are expected to return for the burial.

Kudakwashe, who is studying Information Technology at the University of Zimbabwe, is already in the country and has been assisting his mother with the paperwork.

title: Masvingo City Council considers raising burial fees
categories: General; Governance; Cambria Cemetery; Cemetery; Graveyard; Lawn Cemetery; Mangwandi Cemetery
summary: Masvingo City Council is considering increasing burial fees to ease pressure on Mangwandi Cemetery, which is expected to run out of space by 20 August 2027 if current burial trends continue. According to the latest full council minutes, the cemetery is under growing pressure following the closure of Lawn Cemetery, which has increased demand for […]
content_text:
Masvingo City Council is considering increasing burial fees to ease pressure on Mangwandi Cemetery, which is expected to run out of space by 20 August 2027 if current burial trends continue.

According to the latest full council minutes, the cemetery is under growing pressure following the closure of Lawn Cemetery, which has increased demand for burial space at Mangwandi.

The first section of Mangwandi, commissioned in 1996, had a capacity of 1,416 graves. The second section, opened in May 2019, could accommodate 864 graves. As of September 2026, only 267 spaces remained.

“The cemetery is, however, experiencing increasing pressure due to growing demand for burial space, particularly following the official closure of Lawn Cemetery,” read the minutes.

The council said Cambria Cemetery was established as an alternative, but most residents are reluctant to use it because of its distance and accessibility. It is about 10km from the central business district.

“Although Cambria Cemetery had been established as an alternative burial facility, most of the residents do not prefer to use it because of its distance and accessibility considerations,” read the minutes.

The council also warned that the children’s section could be exhausted within a relatively short period if current trends persist.

To reduce pressure on Mangwandi, councillors proposed reviewing grave fees upwards, arguing that current charges are below market rates.

“On the need to reduce pressure on Mangwandi Cemetery, it was suggested to review grave prices upwards given that the current grave fees were too low taking into account the cost of graves in the market,” read the minutes.

Council resolved to direct the Director of Housing and Social Services to prepare a report on the proposed fee review and submit it to management for consideration.

Other measures proposed include encouraging residents to use Cambria Cemetery, fencing Mangwandi to protect graves and tombstones from damage by stray animals, and exploring the establishment of a private cemetery targeting high-income earners to reduce pressure on public burial facilities.

title: You won’t get all of it at once: Cash-strapped government reveals how civil servants’ 2026 bonuses will be calculated and paid
keywords: news
summary: Civil servants will receive their 2026 annual bonuses in two equal instalments, with half due in November and the remaining half in December, under payment arrangements announced by the National Joint Negotiating Council (NJNC). Government pensioners are also due a flat cushioning allowance in December, although no amount for the allowance was specified in the […] The post You won’t get all of it at once: Cash-strapped government reveals how civil servants’ 2026 bonuses will be calculated and paid first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
Civil servants will receive their 2026 annual bonuses in two equal instalments, with half due in November and the remaining half in December, under payment arrangements announced by the National Joint Negotiating Council (NJNC). Government pensioners are also due a flat cushioning allowance in December, although no amount for the allowance was specified in the announcement.

For public service employees in Grades A to D, the bonus will be calculated at 100 per cent of pensionable emoluments. The NJNC defined those emoluments as basic salary, in-service allowance and administration allowance. The statement did not provide a cash figure for the bonus, which means the amount will depend on each eligible employee’s relevant pensionable pay.

“The payment modalities for the 2026 Annual Bonus for members of the Public Service are as follows: Grades A to D bonus will be calculated at 100 percent pensionable emoluments (basic salary, in-service allowance and administration allowance),” read part of the statement.

“Payment will be staggered in two equal instalments, 50 percent will be paid in November 2026 and the remaining 50 percent will be paid in December 2026. The NJNC also noted that Treasury has approved a flat cushioning allowance for Government Pensioners payable in December 2026.”

The announcement sets out both the basis for calculating the bonus for Grades A to D and the timetable for payment. The first instalment will amount to half of the bonus, with the balance to follow the next month. It does not specify individual payment dates, or give further detail about how bonuses for grades outside A to D will be calculated.

The NJNC said the decision followed a meeting on November 2 at Kaguvi Building in Harare. The council reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to meeting its annual bonus obligations. Finance Minister Professor Mthuli Ncube had also told civil servants that the payments would be made, saying in an interview on Saturday that Government remained committed to honouring them.

The announcement comes as Treasury faces competing demands across the public sector. At the close of the 2027 National Pre-Budget Seminar in Bulawayo, Ncube said ministries, departments and agencies had submitted funding requests totalling ZiG974 billion, while the expenditure envelope available for the coming budget was ZiG347 billion. The requests were nearly three times the stated envelope, and the minister said ministries would have to work within the available limit.

“We know we have an envelope. We know we have to live within it. And, of course, ministers will ask for more. Why not ask for more?” Ncube said at the seminar.

He also described the Government’s approach as a cash budgeting system. “We use a cash budgeting system. We spend what we have. We live within our means.” Treasury said a strengthened Cash Management Committee would forecast cash flows one to two weeks ahead to align budget releases with funds expected to be available. Ncube acknowledged concerns about releases running ahead of cash receipts and said the committee would be used to improve coordination.

Treasury also said projects worth more than US$2 million would require its concurrence, as it seeks to control commitments and limit the accumulation of domestic arrears. The budget measures relate to wider government spending and the 2027 planning process; the NJNC’s bonus statement separately sets out the November and December payment schedule for this year.

Alongside the pay announcement, the NJNC formally adopted the Public Service Occupational Safety and Health Policy. The council said it would support the policy’s dissemination and implementation, as well as its monitoring and periodic review.

The policy was gazetted last year and replaced older legislation, including the Factories and Works Act and the Pneumoconiosis Act. It is intended to reduce workplace injuries, diseases and deaths across sectors. Among the protections described for workers is the right to refuse work that presents imminent danger without fear of punishment or dismissal.

By linking the policy’s adoption to its work on public service conditions, the NJNC has put workplace safety alongside pay in its latest round of decisions. The council’s stated commitment covers not only circulating the policy but also tracking how it is implemented and reviewing it periodically. The announcement did not set out a timetable for those activities.

Ncube has also said Government began extending annual bonus payments to traditional chiefs last year, recognising their role in communities. He described the payments as a first since independence in 1980 and said chiefs had been included alongside civil servants.

“We have even started paying bonuses even for our traditional chiefs, which has never happened since independence in 1980. “We also recognise the good work that they do and we were able to cover them as well. But civil servants’ bonuses, we are going to pay those,” he said.

For this year’s public service bonus, the clearest details are the calculation basis for Grades A to D and the split payment plan. Half is scheduled for November and half for December, while pensioners are due a flat allowance in December. The NJNC’s statement confirms the arrangement but gives no monetary value for the pensioner allowance and no exact payday for either instalment.

title: Rural women sink boreholes from savings groups money
summary: TINASHE TIRIVAVITWO NATIONS BEITBRIDGE – Women Savings Groups starting savings from as little as R10 a week are making a huge impact and transforming rural lives in Masera Ndambe in Zhove, Beitbridge District.Supported by Savings and Internal Lending Communities (SILC), an organization found by the Roman Catholic run Caritas, villagers are raising enough funds to […]
content_text:
TINASHE TIRIVAVI TWO NATIONS

BEITBRIDGE – Women Savings Groups starting savings from as little as R10 a week are making a huge impact and transforming rural lives in Masera Ndambe in Zhove, Beitbridge District. Supported by Savings and Internal Lending Communities (SILC), an organization found by the Roman Catholic run Caritas, villagers are raising enough funds to erect solarized boreholes at their homes. Some have bought furniture, they raise goats, start market gardens and look after and send orphans to school. Women from Masera Ndambe gave inspiring testimonies during International Rural Women’s Day celebrations held at Zhove Lodge a week ago. SILC representatives, Tapson Ndou said the testimonies are a proof that development does not start with big money. He said Mnangagwa’s mantra nyika inovakwa nevene vayo guides the groups. The celebrations were attended by over 70 people including SILC members, village heads, community leaders and councilors. The celebrations also mapped the way forward for members, including how to manage and spend their savings in 2027. In one of the testimonies a man who reluctantly joined a savings group, starting with subscriptions of just R10 a week said he bought a bed for himself for the first time in his life when he already had six children, courtesy of the savings groups. From there he bought a bicycle and his latest acquisition is a cow. Lukas Mulaudzi of Masera Ndambe said he was laughed at when he joined the SILC. Salfina Ndou who joined SILC in 2022 drilled a borehole at her home, thanks to the financial discipline she was taught by from SILC. Liketsoe Maseko, a widow from Masera Ndambe is looking after her orphaned grandchildren, thanks to financial skills and the savings groups, she joined. “I am a widow but because of SILC I am living well in the community. I take care of my orphaned grandchildren, I send them to school through a garden that I manage. I have a solarised borehole at the garden and I have crops throughout the year,” said Maseko. Through the Child Optimised Financial Education (COFE) programme supported by CARITAS, CRS and Government, 52 members were trained in budgeting, record-keeping and business analysis.

“I have managed to drill and install a solarised borehole at my house. I now have running water at my place and I have been taught to save the little that I have by SILC,” said Ndou. “One of the most important lessons we have learned through the SILC programme is that development does not necessarily begin with large amounts of money. It begins with a willingness to save, discipline, trust and a shared commitment to improve our circumstances,” said Ndou. He said villagers started saving as little as R10 and today some save up to R200 per week. “The journey from R10 to R200 in weekly savings is not simply about the amount of money involved. It represents growing confidence, improved financial discipline and a changing mindset towards investment and economic independence,” he said.Five Masera Ndambe SILC groups have turned savings into 120 goats – Mulalo 47, Phathutshelo 27, Vusanani 21, Khuthadzo 18 and Dzumbululo 7 – and are now discussing goat market proposals and climate-smart farming as part of their 2027 plan. “These 120 goats represent more than livestock. They represent the determination of rural people to invest in their future, protect their livelihoods and create opportunities for their families,” said Ndou. He said the groups have also ventured into other businesses. At Masera Ndambe, 35 members are engaged in vegetable gardens while six are involved in ICT services including Wi-Fi and Starlink internet. “We believe communities must take ownership of their development, mobilise their resources and work with relevant stakeholders to achieve lasting solutions. We are not asking others to do everything for us. We are seeking partnerships that strengthen our own efforts,” he said.

title: Hulengende Takes Zimdancehall by Storm as His Star Continues to Rise
summary: Zimbabwean dancehall musician Hulengende is emerging as one of the genre’s most talked-about performers with a growing catalogue of popular songs, strong digital visibility and increasingly large crowds at live shows helping to propel him into the spotlight. The musician, whose real name is reported […]
content_text:
Zimbabwean dancehall musician Hulengende is emerging as one of the genre’s most talked-about performers with a growing catalogue of popular songs, strong digital visibility and increasingly large crowds at live shows helping to propel him into the spotlight.

The musician, whose real name is reported as Ezbornwage Chidamajaya has built a following through his energetic delivery, street-inspired lyrics and a sound that blends Zimbabwean dancehall with Jamaican influences.

His rise has been reflected in the performance of his music on streaming platforms where songs such as Zunza Mupunduru, Kukwadabuka, Chingonzwisisa Baby and Waponda Moyo have attracted attention from fans of Zimdancehall.

His growing popularity was on display at Chitungwiza Aquatic Complex where a large crowd gathered to support the musician.

The turnout offered a strong indication that his appeal is extending beyond social media and into live entertainment.

Hulengende’s momentum has also been driven by the continued circulation of his music online. In October reports said his songs had surpassed five million views across digital platforms, highlighting the potential reach of his growing catalogue.

Tracks such as Fadza Madzimai helped introduce him to a wider audience while newer releases have given supporters more material to embrace.

His ability to keep releasing music has become an important part of his rise in an industry where public attention can shift quickly.

Hulengende’s emergence comes at a time when Zimdancehall continues to produce young performers competing for audiences through streaming services, social media and live shows.

His growing profile has also placed him in the middle of comparisons with fellow chanter Junior Spragga as fans debate who is best positioned to dominate the next chapter of the genre.

However, turning popularity into a lasting career will require more than viral songs and packed venues.

Consistent releases, professional management, reliable performances and investment in production and promotion will be crucial if he is to maintain his momentum.

For now, Hulengende’s growing audience suggests that he has become a significant presence in Zimbabwe’s dancehall conversation.

His challenge is to convert that attention into sustained commercial success and establish himself among the genre’s leading performers.

content_text:
Zimbabwe head coach Ramon Catalá has unveiled his final Warriors squad for the decisive Matchday Three and Matchday Four fixtures against Equatorial Guinea in the qualifying race for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON).

The two matches could prove pivotal in determining Zimbabwe’s fate in the qualification campaign for the tournament scheduled to be hosted jointly by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda in 2027.

title: ARDA delivers over 248 000 tonnes of grain as Zimbabwe builds food buffer against El Niño
summary: AS Zimbabwe intensifies efforts to strengthen national food reserves ahead of the El Niño-induced drought, the Agricultural Rural Development Authority (ARDA) has delivered more than 187,000 tonnes of summer cereals…
content_text:
AS Zimbabwe intensifies efforts to strengthen national food reserves ahead of the El Niño-induced drought, the Agricultural Rural Development Authority (ARDA) has delivered more than 187,000 tonnes of summer cereals and 60,529 tonnes of winter wheat to the Grain Marketing Board (GMB).

The authority has also set an ambitious target of cultivating 100,000 hectares during the 2026/27 summer cropping season, in a major production drive aimed at augmenting the country’s Strategic Grain Reserve and cushioning communities against potential food shortages.

The authority delivered 187,704 metric tonnes of summer cereals from the 2025/26 agricultural season to the GMB.

Of this quantity, 31,293.46 tonnes were channelled towards immediate milling requirements and price stabilisation.

ARDA has also delivered 60,529.3 tonnes of winter wheat, with harvesting still underway after commencing two weeks ago.

The authority said most of the harvested wheat was still on farms, undergoing bagging and grading, while some fields were yet to be harvested.

The figures underline ARDA’s contribution to national food-security preparations as Zimbabwe braces for a potentially difficult agricultural season.

Under its 2026/27 summer production programme, ARDA is targeting 100,000 hectares across its estates, A1 and A2 joint venture growers, irrigation scheme business units and clustered smallholder farmers.

Of the targeted hectarage, 60,000 hectares will be under irrigation, while the remaining 40,000 hectares will be planted using climate-smart varieties.

The programme is intended to strengthen domestic cereal production and further build the Strategic Grain Reserve against the threat of below-normal rainfall.

Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development Minister Dr Anxious Masuka recently warned that Zimbabwe was almost certain to experience below-normal rainfall during the coming season, with the Meteorological Services Department classifying it as a drought year.

Speaking at the 74th graduation ceremony at Gwebi College of Agriculture, Dr Masuka said the warming of the central South Pacific Ocean associated with El Niño was expected to exceed three degrees Celsius, pointing to a particularly strong weather phenomenon.

“So now we are almost 100 percent certain that we will have below-normal rainfall for Zimbabwe,” he said.

However, the minister assured the nation that Government was implementing measures to safeguard food security.

He revealed that the GMB had purchased 345,000 tonnes of various cereals by the previous day, exceeding the 328,000 tonnes distributed during the devastating 2024 drought.

“As of yesterday, we had actually purchased at the GMB 345,000 metric tonnes of various cereals. In 2024, when we had the worst drought, we distributed 328,000 metric tonnes,” he said.

“So we are well on our way to ensuring that should there be this unfortunate event, we will have enough of the strategic grain reserve to feed everyone.”

Government’s broader drought preparedness programme includes strengthening national and household grain reserves, promoting climate-smart agriculture, implementing livestock drought mitigation programmes and improving early-warning systems.

Under the livestock intervention, authorities plan to establish drought mitigation centres serving every seven to eight villages, equipped with permanent water sources, feeding facilities, livestock sales points and disease-control services.

Dr Masuka also called for improved post-harvest management, raising concern over maize losses that can reach 30 percent after harvesting.

He urged farmers and households to minimise food wastage and embrace innovation to withstand the anticipated weather challenges.

“Let’s invoke the Munhumutapa spirit, that entrepreneurial spirit, that innovation, so that Zimbabwe can come out stronger from this drought,” he said.

Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development, Professor Obert Jiri, has meanwhile urged farmers against panic planting or abandoning their fields over fears of an El Niño-induced drought, saying the seasonal forecast should guide preparation rather than trigger premature decisions. He said farmers needed to conserve soil moisture, diversify crops and take advantage of favourable rainfall whenever it occurred.

“Farmers need to be ready and make the most of every drop of rain,” Prof Jiri said, urging them to monitor local weather conditions, assess soil moisture and seek guidance from agricultural extension officers before planting.

title: Zimbabwe Turns to AIDS Levy to Safeguard HIV Response
summary: Zimbabwe is relying on domestic funding including its National AIDS Trust Fund to sustain HIV and AIDS programmes as countries seek to reduce their vulnerability to declining or unpredictable external support. Health and Child Care Minister Dr Douglas Mombeshora said predictable financing, accountability and national […]
content_text:
Zimbabwe is relying on domestic funding including its National AIDS Trust Fund to sustain HIV and AIDS programmes as countries seek to reduce their vulnerability to declining or unpredictable external support.

Health and Child Care Minister Dr Douglas Mombeshora said predictable financing, accountability and national ownership were essential to maintaining progress in the fight against HIV and AIDS.

He was speaking as he welcomed a Tanzanian delegation visiting Zimbabwe to learn about the country’s domestic financing mechanisms for its HIV response.

The exchange comes as both countries explore ways to mobilise more local resources to sustain prevention, treatment and care services.

“Zimbabwe recognises that a sustainable HIV response must be anchored in national ownership, predictable domestic financing, strong institutions and effective partnerships,” Dr Mombeshora said.

At the centre of Zimbabwe’s strategy is the National AIDS Trust Fund commonly known as the AIDS Levy which provides dedicated funding for national HIV priorities.

The fund operates through an annual work plan and budget approved by the Health Minister. About 50% of its resources goes towards treatment, care and support while 12% is allocated to prevention programmes.

The remaining funds support logistics, programme coordination, monitoring and evaluation and other activities required to deliver HIV services.

Dr Mombeshora said the levy helped address critical funding gaps while complementing allocations from the national Treasury and contributions from development partners.

“Our approach is to use these resources strategically to address critical programme needs and financing gaps, while complementing Government Treasury allocations and support from development partners,” he said.

However, the minister stressed that domestic financing should complement rather than replace international cooperation in the fight against HIV and AIDS.

Zimbabwe is also seeking to ensure that money allocated to HIV programmes translates into measurable improvements in service delivery and health outcomes.

Dr Mombeshora said the government monitored expenditure and programme performance through National AIDS Spending Assessments, annual health sector resource mapping, National Health Accounts and routine reviews.

The country also uses the Integrated Results-Based Management framework to link institutional performance and budget utilisation to agreed service delivery targets.

“Our guiding principle is that we must account not only for the resources spent, but also for the results achieved,” he said.

The government has adopted a multisectoral approach to HIV, involving ministries, local authorities, civil society organisations, communities, the private sector and development partners.

The approach is intended to improve coordination between national policy and implementation at provincial and district levels ensuring that resources reach communities that need services.

Dr Mombeshora said the engagement with Tanzania would allow both countries to exchange lessons on financing and managing their HIV programmes.

He cautioned that funding models could not be transferred directly from one country to another because of differences in economic conditions, institutional capacity and national priorities.

However, he said predictable funding, transparency, accountability and effective coordination remained central to sustaining progress.

“We therefore welcome this opportunity for Zimbabwe and Tanzania to exchange experiences and learn from each other’s approaches,” he said.

The visit is expected to give the Tanzanian delegation insights into Zimbabwe’s AIDS Levy, institutional arrangements and accountability systems, while providing an opportunity for Zimbabwe to learn from Tanzania’s experience.

Both countries face the challenge of maintaining essential HIV services while strengthening domestic financing and protecting gains made in prevention, treatment and care.

title: Harare 2027 budget proposes hike in shop licences, clinic and hospital fees
categories: General; Governance; 2027 City of Harare Budget; Bills; City of Harare; City of Harare Budget; Council Bills; Jubilation Shoko
summary: The City of Harare is proposing to increase shop licences, hairdressing and hawker fees as well as clinic, hospital and maternity fees in 2027, while water, sewerage and refuse charges will remain unchanged. The proposed tariffs were presented to council on Thursday by Finance and Development Committee chairperson Councillor Jubilation Shoko. Cllr Shoko said the […]
content_text:
The City of Harare is proposing to increase shop licences, hairdressing and hawker fees as well as clinic, hospital and maternity fees in 2027, while water, sewerage and refuse charges will remain unchanged.

The proposed tariffs were presented to council on Thursday by Finance and Development Committee chairperson Councillor Jubilation Shoko.

Cllr Shoko said the 2027 tariff framework seeks to balance financial sustainability with affordability.

“The proposed 2027 tariff framework seeks to balance the financial sustainability of municipal services with the need to keep charges understandable and affordable for households and businesses,” he said.

“The proposals retain several existing service charges while introducing selected adjustments.”

Under business licences and enterprise development, the shop licence for premises measuring 50 to 100 square metres will increase from US$300 in 2026 to US$350 in 2027. The charge for premises above 100 square metres remains at US$500.

Cllr Shoko said the proposed fees are aligned with the Model Fees Bylaws promulgated under Statutory Instrument 41 of 2026, which prescribes the maximum permissible charges for the various categories.

For hairdressers, the Class A charge will increase from US$230 to US$260, while Class B remains at US$173.

Non-food hawker fees will increase from US$55 to US$58, while food hawker fees remain at US$58.

The biggest increases are in health fees. Cllr Shoko said the adjustments are intended “to maintain primary healthcare delivery and medicines availability across our polyclinics and hospitals in compliance with WHO standards.”

Clinic fees for adults will increase from US$5 to US$7 and for children from US$3 to US$5.

Hospital fees for adults will increase from US$20 to US$30 and for children from US$10 to US$20. Maternity fees will increase from US$25 to US$30.

Water tariffs will retain existing rates for both conventional and prepaid customers. Cllr Shoko said the ongoing smart-metering programme will improve consumption records, support efficient billing and encourage responsible water use.

Residential water tariffs per cubic metre remain unchanged at US$1.80 for high-density conventional and US$1.89 for high-density prepaid, and US$2.23 for low-density conventional and US$2.34 for low-density prepaid.

Commercial fixed water charges also remain unchanged at US$50 for 0 to 100 cubic metres, US$75 for above 100 to 200 cubic metres and US$150 for above 200 to 500 cubic metres.

Sewerage and refuse collection charges also remain unchanged. Cllr Shoko said the charges support the operation and maintenance of sewer networks, wastewater treatment and refuse collection, which are essential to public health and environmental protection.

Residential sewerage remains at US$9 for high-density and US$13 for low-density. Commercial sewerage remains at US$17.20 per fitment.

Domestic refuse for weekly collection remains at US$9 for high-density and US$13 for low-density. Commercial refuse remains at US$26 to US$39 and industrial refuse at US$22 to US$39.

Refuse charges will continue to reflect the applicable customer category and service arrangement, with greater emphasis on efficient collection routes, fleet availability and complete billing coverage.

Business licences for premises above 100 square metres will remain at US$500, hairdressers Class B at US$173 and food hawkers at US$58.

Cllr Shoko said the success of the tariff proposals will depend not only on the tariffs approved but also on the full fiscal participation of all residents, improved collection efficiency and effective control of operating costs.

“Residents are therefore encouraged to honour their obligations,” he said.

Council Chairman Garisikai Moyo told Masvingo Mirror that six soccer and six netball teams made up entirely of school dropouts will compete. content_text:
InnBucks customers can now pay their DStv subscriptions through the mobile payment platform following the introduction of a new bill payment service aimed at making everyday transactions more convenient.

The service allows customers to renew their DStv subscriptions directly through InnBucks, eliminating the need to use separate payment platforms.

The launch comes as the English Premier League season continues and the UEFA Champions League gathers momentum, giving football fans an additional option for keeping their television subscriptions active.

The development also expands InnBucks’ growing portfolio of bill payment services, which already includes ZESA electricity tokens, ZINWA water bills, council rates, TelOne and Liquid Intelligent Technologies bills, as well as airtime purchases for Econet and NetOne.

Customers can also make payments for funeral cover through Nyaradzo and Doves, while school fees can be paid through ZB Bank.

InnBucks said the addition of DStv reflects its broader ambition to evolve beyond money transfers into an integrated financial services platform where customers can manage multiple everyday payments in one place.

The company said it would continue expanding its network of billers and introducing new services to simplify financial transactions for Zimbabweans.

title: Chaos At Gweshe Gweshe Funeral
summary: By Showbiz Reporter | A family dispute over the burial place of veteran actor William “Gweshegweshe” Matenga has exposed tensions surrounding … Continue reading "Chaos At Gweshe Gweshe Funeral"
content_text:
By Showbiz Reporter | A family dispute over the burial place of veteran actor William “Gweshegweshe” Matenga has exposed tensions surrounding his final send-off, with relatives divided over whether he should be buried in Buhera or at Warren Hills Cemetery in Harare.

The disagreement comes as the family pursues provincial hero status for the 65-year-old actor, whose death has also reignited conversations about the precarious livelihoods of Zimbabwean artists, many of whom spend decades entertaining the nation but die without financial security or adequate institutional support.

With no known written instructions from Matenga about his preferred burial place, some relatives are reportedly pushing for his remains to be interred at the family cemetery in Buhera, while others favour Warren Hills, pending the outcome of the provincial hero status application.

“There was a fierce meeting regarding Gweshegweshe’s choice of burial place, as some family members preferred that his remains be interred at the family cemetery,” said a source familiar with the discussions.

Family spokesperson Peter Chafewa said the burial could be delayed while the War Veterans Association processed the application.

“There is a team which left this morning to process his papers in town, but they are yet to give us tangible feedback,” he said, adding that the family was also awaiting the arrival of two of Matenga’s children based in Australia and South Africa.

Matenga, a former soldier and liberation war veteran, died on Saturday after reportedly succumbing to hypertension. He had experienced recurring health challenges, including prostate gland enlargement, which was diagnosed last year.

Beyond his celebrated acting career, Matenga was remembered as a community leader who championed peace and unity in Zengeza 5, Chitungwiza.

Former detainee and ex-combatant Patricia Mutuswa described him as a role model and a man committed to community cohesion.

“He was always a man of peace,” she said.

His death has also highlighted a longstanding challenge in Zimbabwe’s creative industry, where actors and other performers often work without reliable salaries, pensions, medical insurance or royalties, leaving many financially vulnerable in old age.

Matenga is survived by seven children. Mourners are gathered at No. 12 Mupangara, Zengeza 5, Chitungwiza, as the family awaits clarity on the burial arrangements.

title: United States set to remove South Africa, Rwanda from AGOA
categories: Africa; African Growth and Opportunity Act; AGOA
summary: The United States has announced plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a move that could deal a huge blow to exports from both countries and further strain their relations with Washington. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Monday, 2 November, that President Donald Trump had […]
content_text:
The United States has announced plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a move that could deal a huge blow to exports from both countries and further strain their relations with Washington.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Monday, 2 November, that President Donald Trump had notified Congress and the governments of South Africa and Rwanda of his intention to terminate their participation in the programme with effect from 1 January 2027.

According to Greer, an annual review conducted by the Office of the United States Trade Representative found that both countries were no longer meeting the requirements necessary to remain beneficiaries of AGOA.

“President Trump found that the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria,” Greer said.

He cited barriers to American trade and investment, as well as actions that Washington believes threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.

AGOA is a US trade programme enacted in 2000 that grants qualifying sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the American market for thousands of products. It has long been regarded as the cornerstone of US economic engagement with Africa and is credited with supporting exports, investment and employment across the continent.

Countries benefiting from AGOA must meet a range of eligibility requirements, including respect for the rule of law, political pluralism, workers’ rights, market-based economic policies and the removal of barriers to US trade and investment. Their eligibility is reviewed annually.

The Trump administration said it is concerned about barriers affecting US trade and investment, corruption, and what it described as threats to American national security and foreign policy interests by the South African government.

The decision comes amid deteriorating relations between Washington and Pretoria. The Trump administration has repeatedly criticised South Africa over several issues, including its foreign policy positions and domestic policies.

South Africa is expected to be the country hardest hit by the decision. It is the largest AGOA beneficiary and exported about US$1.7 billion worth of goods to the United States under the programme in 2025. Key exports include motor vehicle components, citrus fruit and wine.

In response, South Africa’s trade ministry said it will continue pursuing trade and investment opportunities with the United States and support sectors likely to be affected by the suspension.

For Rwanda, Washington’s concerns extend beyond trade. The Trump administration cited issues relating to trade and investment barriers, human rights, workers’ rights, political pluralism, the rule of law, and alleged threats to US foreign policy interests.

Analysts believe the decision is closely linked to growing tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The United States has accused Rwanda of backing rebel groups in the region and has already imposed sanctions on several Rwandan individuals and institutions.

Rwanda’s exports to the United States under AGOA are much smaller than South Africa’s and include products such as coffee and minerals.

If the decision takes effect, goods from South Africa and Rwanda will lose their duty-free access to the US market and could face import tariffs. This would make their exports more expensive and potentially less competitive in the United States.

For South Africa in particular, the loss of AGOA benefits could have serious consequences for industries that rely heavily on exports to the US market, including the automotive and agricultural sectors. Thousands of jobs linked to trade with the United States could be affected.

content_text: All our toiling is pointing out to the ultimate joy we shall have at the end of this life. The previous verse is encouraging us to persevere since we are encompassed by a cloud of witnesses and finish our race well. The prior verse gave the logical application of this knowledge. With all we have been given as proof—”so great a cloud of witnesses” —we ought to make every effort to “hold fast” setting aside sin and selfishness as we pursue whatever path God has placed in front of us. This is the essence of godly faith: to trust God with our future, despite how hard it might be in the present. Here, we see how Jesus again serves as the ultimate example of this. Christ also suffered hardship and persecution, as well as temptation, but never wavered in His resolve to do the will of God the Father. Christ’s entire ministry and the superiority of the new covenant are grounded in His example, which we should strive to follow. His willingness to endure those trials came from an understanding that God could, and would, “work together for good” all of those things. The end goal of Jesus’ obedience was to establish the purpose we should be striving for: the “city with foundations,” our ultimate victory and reward in God. Looking unto Jesus the author and perfector of our faith. In a world where many things are fighting to capture our eyes, let’s resist the temptation and look only to Jesus. Don’t look at the world, for the end of it is destruction in a hell of fire. We look up to Jesus, the author and perfector of our faith. A very good morning to you all, I wish you a blessed day in the Lord. Stay in love with God and men as well. I love you all. Amen!!!

title: Uebert Angel hits back at critics of VP Chiwenga
summary: Presidential Envoy and Ambassador-at-Large Uebert Angel has publicly defended Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga amid reports of renewed factional tensions within ZANU PF. Speaking to his Good News Ministry congregation on Sunday, Angel condemned what he described as vicious attacks on Chiwenga, dismissing them as political misconduct and a sign of intellectual bankruptcy. Angel said political leaders, […]
content_text:
Presidential Envoy and Ambassador-at-Large Uebert Angel has publicly defended Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga amid reports of renewed factional tensions within ZANU PF.

Speaking to his Good News Ministry congregation on Sunday, Angel condemned what he described as vicious attacks on Chiwenga, dismissing them as political misconduct and a sign of intellectual bankruptcy.

Angel said political leaders, including President Emmerson Mnangagwa and Chiwenga, should be open to criticism, but warned against what he called contempt disguised as legitimate scrutiny.

“Criticism is legitimate. You should. You must. People criticise me. They criticise the President. They criticise the Vice-President. It’s allowed. But contempt masquerading as criticism is diabolic. It’s evil,” he said.

He also questioned the logic of those who portray Chiwenga as a dangerous figure while publicly challenging him.

“If you say Chiwenga is dangerous, and you come out and oppose him publicly, you’re giving us a public review that he is not as dangerous as we thought,” Angel said.

The preacher further argued that President Mnangagwa’s continued confidence in Chiwenga should be enough to discourage public attacks on the Vice-President.

“If the President sees him fit to still be the Vice-President, it must be a sign that I, with my little mouth or big mouth, should hush,” he said.

Angel also castigated people joining the public criticism of Chiwenga, making specific reference to his former wife, Marry Mubaiwa, following her recent interview in which she levelled damaging allegations against the Vice-President.

Using a hypothetical divorce scenario to illustrate his point, Angel cautioned against taking sides in disputes between former spouses, arguing that doing so could be interpreted as undermining the authority and judgement of the person who initiated the separation.

title: Civil servants to get 2026 bonuses in two instalments

summary: Civil servants will receive their 2026 annual bonuses in two equal instalments in November and December, the National Joint Negotiating Council (NJNC) has announced. In a statement on Monday, the NJNC said the bonus for Grades A to D will be calculated at 100 per cent of pensionable emoluments, which include basic salary, in-service allowance […]
content_text:
Civil servants will receive their 2026 annual bonuses in two equal instalments in November and December, the National Joint Negotiating Council (NJNC) has announced.

In a statement on Monday, the NJNC said the bonus for Grades A to D will be calculated at 100 per cent of pensionable emoluments, which include basic salary, in-service allowance and administration allowance.

Fifty per cent will be paid in November and the remaining 50 per cent in December.

The NJNC said Treasury has also approved a flat cushioning allowance for Government pensioners, which will be paid in December.

The announcement follows assurances from Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube on Saturday that Government will pay civil servants’ bonuses.

Ncube said Government had also extended annual bonus payments to traditional chiefs from last year in recognition of their role in communities, describing it as a significant development and the first time since independence in 1980.

“We have even started paying bonuses for our traditional chiefs, which has never happened since independence in 1980. We also recognise the good work that they do, and we were able to cover them as well. But civil servants’ bonuses, we are going to pay those,” he said.

content_text:
CHITUNGWIZA – William “Gweshegweshe” Matenga spent what would become his final Friday in familiar company, talking about household electricity and playing snooker at a local spot in Zengeza 5. By that evening, the veteran actor had fallen ill. Within hours, his family was facing not only the sudden loss of a father and community figure, but a difficult dispute over where his body should be laid to rest.

Matenga, whose performance in the television series Gringo made him a household name, died on Saturday after being taken ill. His family and friends described a man who had been active and cheerful just before his final health crisis, even as he had been managing recurring medical problems.

The loss brought mourners to the family home at No. 12 Mupangara in Zengeza 5, Chitungwiza. But grief was mixed with uncertainty. Relatives were divided over whether Matenga should be buried at the family cemetery in Buhera or in Harare, where a provincial-hero application was being pursued.

The dispute became more difficult as relatives offered different accounts of what Matenga himself had wanted. A close relative said his wish was to be buried in Buhera. Another family spokesperson said he had spoken about being laid to rest at the Provincial Heroes Acre beside a comrade from the liberation struggle. Family members were also waiting for a letter said to contain his final wishes.

At the wake, relatives favouring Buhera pointed to the family cemetery and argued that people recognised as heroes had also been buried at their rural homes. Others looked to Warren Hills in Harare, where a provincial-hero burial was being considered. No single arrangement had been agreed when family spokesperson Peter Chafewa described the disagreement and the outstanding paperwork.

“There was a fierce meeting regarding Gweshegweshe’s choice of burial place, as some family members preferred that his remains be interred at the family cemetery,” said an insider familiar with the developments.

“The same relatives told us that they had a say in where Gweshegweshe should be buried. For now, there appears to be an impasse regarding his preferred burial place.”

The family was also waiting for the outcome of the application for provincial hero status. Chafewa said the paperwork had not been completed and that the War Veterans Association for Harare Province wanted clarity before the funeral could proceed.

“The burial of Gweshegweshe is likely to be postponed since the War Veterans Association for Harare Province, where he was also one of the leaders, wants clarity on his status,” Chafewa said.

“There is a team which left this morning to process his papers in town, but they are yet to give us tangible feedback. This team is made up of his son Kudakwashe, who is studying IT at the University of Zimbabwe, his former wife and a few relatives. It is my hope that the paperwork will be processed in time so that we can give him a decent burial befitting his status.”

The family was meanwhile expecting two of Matenga’s children to travel from outside Zimbabwe. Lawrence was working in Australia and Lloyd Matenga was based in South Africa, where he worked as an advocate. Kudakwashe, known as Kuda, was already helping his mother with the paperwork.

Another relative said Matenga had expressed a wish to be buried in Buhera, his rural home, while discussions about provincial-hero recognition were under way. A different account placed his stated wish in Harare. The family spokesperson said Matenga had spoken at a family wedding about his final resting place and that a letter setting out his wishes was expected to be delivered for the family to review.

Two weeks before his death, the spokesperson said, Matenga had told a relative: “If I die, I would like to be buried at the Provincial Heroes Acre alongside my comrade, Cde Musiiwa. We served together in the liberation war and the army until his death.”

The burial discussions unfolded as mourners tried to understand how quickly Matenga’s health had worsened. Chafewa said the actor had been dealing with health problems since the previous year. He had been diagnosed with prostate gland enlargement, which was later complicated by hypertension. The initial condition had been treated, but it returned.

Chafewa said he had spoken to Matenga the day before his death. Their conversation had been about fixing electricity, a subject that suited Chafewa’s work as an electrical engineer. Matenga had also spent time playing snooker at Limbani Shops, his favourite spot in Zengeza 5.

“The last time I spoke to him was last Friday when we were talking about something to do with fixing electricity since I am an electrical engineer myself. He was in a jovial mood that Friday and had played snooker at Limbani Shops in Zengeza 5, which was his favourite spot.”

Later that evening, Chafewa learnt that Matenga had become unwell. He said the actor was taken to hospital and pronounced dead on admission.

“I was shocked to hear that he was unwell around 9pm. He was pronounced dead upon admission. We have lost a giant in the creative sector, a community defender and a loving father who was always ready to unite his community. Life will never be the same without him because he was indeed a unifier who preached peace and harmony.”

Matenga’s influence reached beyond the screen. Neighbours and fellow war veterans remembered him as a steady presence in Zengeza and a man who tried to keep people together. Former detainee and ex-combatant Patricia Mutuswa, known by her liberation-struggle name Cde Chido, said she had known him since 1982, when they became beneficiaries of houses in the area.

“I have known him since 1982, when we became beneficiaries of houses in Zengeza. We used to meet during our meetings as war veterans in this area, and he was always a man of peace,” she said.

Mutuswa also recalled accompanying him to play snooker. She said she had been with him on the day he fell ill and described him as a leader, father figure and mentor.

“I grew up admiring him because he was indeed a friendly man who had the community at heart. I used to accompany him whenever he went to play snooker at Limbani Shops. I was with him on the day he fell ill. I am also here mourning our hero. He deserved this status, and I will forever cherish him as a leader, father figure and mentor.”

His former churchmate, Gogo Farai Mbuzi, also remembered him as a respected neighbour and community leader. She said mourners were waiting for the paperwork and the outcome of the application for provincial hero status.

“We never had problems with him, and I am glad that we are here mourning him. We await the processing of his papers and the outcome of Harare Province’s application for him to be accorded provincial hero status. He deserved it, and we will surely miss him.”

For colleagues, Matenga’s death meant the loss of a performer and a mentor whose work had helped shape one of Zimbabwe’s best-known television comedies. He played Gweshe Gweshe, the long-suffering boss of Lazarus “Gringo” Boora’s title character in Gringo. The role gave Matenga the name by which many viewers knew him.

After Boora’s death, Matenga continued the story in The Return of Gringo, working alongside Boora’s son, Taurai. Fellow actor Blessing “Mbudziyadhura” Chimhowa said Matenga helped guide the younger actor and remained committed to the productions.

“Whenever we were on set, he was always humble. He was very passionate about acting, so this is a great loss to everyone. We have lost a legend, a father figure, a friend and a teacher. His acting was so natural that people sometimes thought what they were watching was real life. “He was disciplined both on and off set. We only learnt later in life that he was a war veteran and had served in the army but he never showed off about his background.

“That is why I say we learnt humility from him,” he said. Mudziyadhura said Gweshegweshe’s commitment to the Gringo productions was evident.

“He was one of the people who worked extensively on the Gringo series. Even when his job demanded a lot from him, he would still find time for us.” He said Gweshegweshe had also taken a fatherly role in helping to continue the Gringo story after the death of Boora. After Gringo died, he started working on The Return of Gringo alongside the late actor’s son, Taurai Boora.

“Taurai is still young and Gweshegweshe was there to guide and father him. Gweshegweshe was at the centre of the Gringo story. “His death is a huge loss to the cast. May his soul rest in peace,” he said.

Chimhowa also voiced frustration that recognition often came only after a person had died.

“It is sad that in this country people are only recognised and given their flowers when they are gone. That is when everyone starts talking about them. I am not saying people should not attend funerals but using someone’s death to create content is not honourable,” he said.

The actor’s neighbours and fellow veterans gathered at the family home as congregants from St Agnes Roman Catholic Church helped coordinate funeral arrangements. Friends, fans and former comrades continued to arrive to pay their respects. The family said Matenga was survived by seven children.

The funeral plans remained caught between the family’s rural roots, the possibility of provincial recognition and the different memories of what Matenga wanted. Those close to him remembered the Friday when he was still joking, talking about a practical repair and playing snooker. By the following evening, his family was mourning him while trying to settle where the actor, soldier, father and neighbour would finally rest.

content_text:
Mosquito-net errand ends in rape allegation as 62-year-old man goes on the run

A 62-year-old man from Cold Comfort is being sought after a 16-year-old domestic worker reported that he raped her in his bedroom, where he had asked her to fix his mosquito net and make his bed.

Peterson Goredema is alleged to have called the teenager into his room on Friday under the pretext of asking for help with the household task. After she finished, he allegedly blocked her way out, locked the door, pushed her onto the bed and raped her without a condom. The maid tried to fight him off but was overpowered.

The reported assault has prompted a police investigation in Harare. The teenager was referred to Sally Mugabe Hospital for a medical examination, and the matter was recorded at Kuwadzana Police Station under RRB 7013028. Goredema had left his home by the time the complaint was made and had not been located in the account of the case.

The sequence described by a neighbour suggests the young worker faced further pressure after the alleged rape. The neighbour said Goredema locked the yard gate the next day, preventing her from leaving. When she asked to visit her sister, he allegedly refused and threatened to end her employment if she left.

“On Saturday Goredema locked the gate to prevent the maid from leaving the yard. She further asked for permission to go and see her sister, but Goredema prevented her from leaving and threatened her that if she left the house her job will be terminated. On Sunday she managed to sneak out and proceeded to her sister where she narrated her story.

“The two proceeded to Goredema’s place of residence where they were chased refusing to answer questions about the rape. After the two went to police, Goredema fled his house and is yet to be located,” said one of the neighbours.

The teenager managed to leave the property on Sunday and went to her sister, where she disclosed what had happened. The two returned to Goredema’s home to seek answers, but were chased away, according to the neighbour. They then went to the police. Goredema is said to have fled after they reported the case.

The allegation describes a domestic worker summoned to perform an ordinary household duty and then allegedly trapped inside a bedroom. It also places the teenager in a position of dependence: she was working in the household, and the neighbour says her employer threatened her job when she sought permission to leave. The available account does not say how long she had been employed there or whether she had previously raised concerns.

The Cold Comfort case is among several reports involving domestic workers and employers in Zimbabwe during 2026. In April, a 19-year-old maid in Southlea Park told police that her employer, Vengai Makawa, raped her after she went into his bedroom to change his three-year-old son’s nappy and make the bed.

The alleged attack was said to have happened on March 29, after Makawa’s wife left for work. The maid was leaving the bedroom when she met Makawa at the door. He allegedly pushed her back inside, overpowered her and raped her without protection. He then left the house and returned with emergency contraceptive pills, which he ordered her to take.

The case came to light after the young woman told a friend the following day. She later called Makawa to say she was leaving for a relative’s home. He allegedly urged her not to go and not to tell anyone. She recorded that conversation, then went to her relative’s home and reported the case to police. Makawa appeared in court charged with rape. No later outcome was included in the available report.

A separate case in Harare ended in a prison sentence in October. A 54-year-old man was jailed for an effective 15 years after being convicted of raping an 18-year-old domestic worker at his home in Ingwe Farm. The assault took place on August 30 while his wife was away on night duty.

The court heard that the man was in his bedroom with his five-year-old daughter at about 4am while the domestic worker slept on the sitting-room floor. He went into the sitting room to check his mobile phone, woke her and complained that his wife’s night shifts were boring him before demanding sex. When she refused, he removed her blanket and raped her. He later gave her US$1 for a WhatsApp bundle and told her to keep quiet.

The young woman reported the assault to a neighbour at about 6am. The neighbour accompanied her to the police station, leading to the man’s arrest and, later, his conviction and sentence. Unlike the Cold Comfort and Southlea Park cases, this case had reached a conclusion in court by the time it was reported: the accused had been sentenced to prison.

The details of the 3 cases differ, but each account places a domestic worker inside the employer’s home when the alleged assault took place. In Cold Comfort, the teenager says she was called to carry out a task in the employer’s bedroom. In Southlea Park, the worker had entered the room to care for a young child and make the bed. In Ingwe Farm, the worker was asleep in a shared living area when her employer allegedly approached her.

For the Cold Comfort teenager, the immediate focus is on her medical examination and the police investigation, while the man named in the report remains at large. Her sister accompanied her when she sought help, and the neighbour’s account describes the effort to leave the property and reach the police despite the alleged threat to her job.

The case number recorded at Kuwadzana Police Station is RRB 7013028. Police have not been reported as locating Goredema. The 16-year-old has been referred to Sally Mugabe Hospital for examination.
