content_text:
Five excavators were allegedly burnt down by artisanal miners at Wanderer Mine Site Number 4 in Shurugwi on Monday.

The mine, owned by Chengxi Mine, was the scene of violence after security personnel tried to drive local miners off the company’s gold claims.

Sources told Masvingo Mirror that the situation turned violent after security apprehended artisanal miners who had allegedly trespassed onto the premises. The suspects are said to have become aggressive, assaulted security staff and set machinery on fire before fleeing.

Some security personnel were reportedly admitted to a local hospital after being severely assaulted.

Midlands provincial police spokesperson Inspector Emmanuel Mahoko confirmed the incident to Masvingo Mirror and said the suspects were not yet accounted for.

“I can confirm that there is a violent incident which happened at Wanderer Mine. Machinery was burnt, but we are yet to get more details about the incident. Investigations are underway; officers are attending the scene,” he said.

title: You’re not going on holiday, I demand results: Unhappy President Mnangagwa tells Diplomats as ambassador shake-up gathers pace
keywords: news
summary: President Emmerson Mnangagwa has told Zimbabwe’s ambassadors that diplomatic postings are not a holiday, demanding measurable results as his government prepares a major reshaping of the country’s foreign service. “Serving on diplomatic missions is no child’s play, and it is certainly not a holiday. My administration demands tangible, principled, and pragmatic results,” Mnangagwa said in […] The post You’re not going on holiday, I demand results: Unhappy President Mnangagwa tells Diplomats as ambassador shake-up gathers pace first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
President Emmerson Mnangagwa has told Zimbabwe’s ambassadors that diplomatic postings are not a holiday, demanding measurable results as his government prepares a major reshaping of the country’s foreign service.

“Serving on diplomatic missions is no child’s play, and it is certainly not a holiday. My administration demands tangible, principled, and pragmatic results,” Mnangagwa said in a public statement after addressing ambassadors and heads of mission at the Harare International Conference Centre on 2 November.

The meeting followed a Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Trade senior management and ambassadors’ retreat held from 19 to 22 October. Its theme was “From Strategy to Results: Advancing Zimbabwe’s National Interests through Coordinated, Accountable and Results-Driven Diplomacy.”

The president’s message was directed at a diplomatic corps facing a broad reorganisation. Reports say up to 26 ambassadors may be recalled, retired or reassigned as the government seeks to shift foreign missions towards trade and investment promotion. The proposed changes would reach across a network of about 40 embassies and 10 consulates. Some recalled officials are expected to move to other postings rather than leave the service.

The size of the reported exercise makes the president’s call for accountability more than a general instruction. Missions are being asked to show what they can deliver for Zimbabwe, from new investment and export opportunities to stronger tourism links and support for citizens abroad.

Mnangagwa described embassies as “strategic platforms” for advancing national development. He said diplomats must promote trade, investment and tourism, work closely with government offices at home, and protect Zimbabwe’s interests through partnerships that offer benefits to both sides.

He also called for a more practical approach to foreign relations. Zimbabwe, he said, remains “a friend to all and an enemy to none”, but should not depend on any one country or bloc. Diplomats are expected to provide timely advice on international developments and agreements, while translating policy into measurable programmes at their posts.

The reshuffle has already begun to take shape in public. Rwanda has approved the appointment of Helliate Rushwaya, chairperson of the Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation, as Zimbabwe’s ambassador to Kigali. She is to replace Charity Manyeruke, who is expected to take up a posting in Ottawa, Canada.

Retired Lieutenant-General Engelbert Rugeje was among the ambassador-designates who attended the Harare engagement. He has also taken part in diplomatic induction and training ahead of deployment. His name has been linked to a possible posting in Maputo, Mozambique, although the assignment has not been publicly confirmed. Rugeje previously served as ZANU PF’s national political commissar and held senior military roles.

Other figures reported to be in line for diplomatic work include former Harare Metropolitan Province Minister Miriam Chikukwa and former Cabinet minister Mike Bimha. Barbara Mukahanana has also been named among officials moving into diplomatic posts. The UK ambassador, retired Colonel Christian Katsande, and Zimbabwe’s envoy to Australia and New Zealand, Joe Tapera Mhishi, have been mentioned among those expected to depart or be reassigned as the review proceeds.

The exact final list of recalled and incoming envoys has not been made public. But the new approach is clear in Mnangagwa’s instructions: foreign missions should help open markets for Zimbabwean products, draw capital into priority industries and support national development goals. Agriculture and horticulture, mining and value addition, manufacturing, energy and tourism are among the sectors identified for closer attention.

The instruction comes as Zimbabwe takes on a number of regional and international roles. The United Nations General Assembly elected the country to a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for 2027–28, with its two-year term due to begin in January 2027. In October, Mnangagwa took over from Kenya’s William Ruto as chair of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa Authority for a one-year term. Zimbabwe is also due to host the African Continental Free Trade Area Council of Ministers in 2027.

Those assignments will place Zimbabwean representatives in settings where trade, regional cooperation and international security are discussed. At the same time, Mnangagwa has asked the Foreign Affairs Ministry to review the National Diaspora Policy. He said diplomats should treat Zimbabweans living near or visiting their missions with humanity, describing the diaspora as a “vital pillar” in the country’s development.

The emphasis on consular care comes against the backdrop of risks faced by overseas missions. In June 2023, armed men raided and looted the office and residence of Zimbabwe’s ambassador to Sudan, Hilda Mafudze, in Khartoum during the conflict there. Mnangagwa’s latest instructions also call on missions to report promptly and remain alert to emerging threats.

Diplomatic work is also affected by changes in other countries’ representation. Sweden closed its embassy in Harare on 31 October 2026, following a decision to wind down its bilateral development assistance programme and manage relations through other regional arrangements. The closure underlines how overseas diplomatic presence can change, making the effectiveness and reach of Zimbabwe’s own missions a practical concern.

The president also directed heads of mission to manage public money carefully, maintain government property and follow administrative rules. He told them to work with ministries and agencies at home rather than operate in isolation, and to turn the resolutions of the ruling party’s 23rd National People’s Conference and the ministry’s planning workshop into targets.

Zimbabwe’s election to the Security Council and its leadership in COMESA give its diplomats new platforms, while the 2027 AfCFTA meeting will bring trade officials to the country. Mnangagwa’s challenge is for the missions to use those opportunities to produce gains beyond ceremony and protocol.

As ambassadors return to their stations, the president has set out the standard he expects: visible work on investment, trade, tourism, diaspora support and the protection of national interests. “Zimbabwe remains open for business, and global capital is safe here,” he said, urging the diplomats to make economic diplomacy part of the country’s development drive.

And being found in human form he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.*The Word of the Lord.**RESPONSORIAL PSALM* Taken from Psalm 22: 26b – 27, 28, 29 – 30, 31 – 32 (R.) 26aAnd the response is;*R/. You are my praise, Lord, in the great assembly.*My vows I will pay before those who fear him. The poor shall eat and shall have their fill.They shall praise the Lord, those who seek him. May their hearts live on forever and ever! *R/.*All the earth shall remember and return to the Lord, all families of the nations worship before him. *R/.*For the kingdom is the Lord’s, he is ruler of the nations. They shall worship him, all the mighty of the earth; before him shall bow all who go down to the dust. *R/.*And my soul shall live for him, my descendants serve him. They shall tell of the Lord to generations yet to come, declare his saving justice to peoples yet unborn:“These are the things the Lord has done.” *R/.**GOSPEL ACCLAMATION*Matthew 11: 28*Alleluia.* Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest, says the Lord. *Alleluia.**GOSPEL*“Go out to the highways and hedges, and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled.” *A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke (LUKE 14: 15 – 24)*At that time: One of those who sat at table with Jesus said to him, “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God!” But he said to him, “A man once gave a great banquet, and invited many; and at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come; for all is now ready.’ “But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it; please, have me excused.’ “And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them; please, have me excused.’ “And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. ’ “So the servant came and reported this to his master. Then the householder in anger said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and maimed and blind and lame. ’ “And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room. ’ “And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges, and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet. ”’*The Gospel of the Lord.*

Nokuti ndinokutaurirai kuti hapana kana nomumwechete waavo vakakokwa acharavira mabiko angu.’ ”

title: Envoys rally behind President’s foreign policy
summary: Wallace Ruzvidzo Herald Reporter FOREIGN Affairs and International Trade Minister Professor Amon Murwira has reaffirmed the centrality of President Mnangagwa’s authority in directing Zimbabwe’s foreign policy, urging the country’s envoys to operate with “one nation, one President, one message, one voice”. Speaking during President Mnangagwa’s meet-and-greet engagement with Zimbabwe’s ambassadors, ambassadors-designate and chargés d’affaires in […]
content_text:
Wallace Ruzvidzo

Herald Reporter

FOREIGN Affairs and International Trade Minister Professor Amon Murwira has reaffirmed the centrality of President Mnangagwa’s authority in directing Zimbabwe’s foreign policy, urging the country’s envoys to operate with “one nation, one President, one message, one voice”.

Speaking during President Mnangagwa’s meet-and-greet engagement with Zimbabwe’s ambassadors, ambassadors-designate and chargés d’affaires in Harare yesterday, Prof Murwira said the Ministry’s Strategic Planning Workshop, which preceded the engagement, had established a clear national command for implementation of strategies aimed at generating quantifiable results.

“Working in liaison with the relevant departments back home, you have a duty to advance our national development goals and transform the quality of life of our people,” he said.

Prof Murwira said the Constitution vested authority over the conduct of foreign policy in the President, adding that the foreign service, therefore, operated under his strategic direction.

“So we left the workshop very clear that we all act under your command in terms of foreign affairs. Your Excellency, the Constitution makes it very unambiguous that the foreign service serves directly under your command, and we say one nation, one President, one message, one voice,” he said.

Prof Murwira said the Second Republic had deliberately repositioned foreign policy as an extension of Zimbabwe’s domestic economic and security priorities, with diplomatic missions expected to facilitate investment, technology transfer, export market expansion and national security.

He said the Ministry was also being restructured to ensure it was “fit for purpose”, following the functional needs analysis approved by the President.

Prof Murwira said the Public Service Commission had responded positively to the directive to restructure the Ministry.

He also said Government was progressing with the proposed Foreign Affairs and International Trade Bill, whose principles had already been approved by Cabinet, with the Attorney-General now working on the legislation.

The Bill is expected to strengthen the Ministry’s statutory mandate while enhancing coordination among Government agencies in projecting “Brand Zimbabwe”.

Prof Murwira said the Ministry was also implementing the President’s directive to formally incorporate trade and investment promotion into the statutory mandate of Zimbabwe’s diplomatic missions.

This, he said, would ensure that ambassadors and other envoys were judged not only on traditional diplomatic functions, but also on their contribution to economic development.

“In alignment with your pronouncement of the doctrine of ubiquitous leadership, the guiding principle that everybody is a chairman, we have charged all envoys to exercise proactive stewardship, total ownership, and personal accountability in driving national economic results for the integrity, dignity, and prosperity of Zimbabwe”.

Prof Murwira said Zimbabwe would use its regional leadership responsibilities to convert regional integration into tangible economic benefits while leveraging its forthcoming United Nations Security Council tenure to promote peace and conflict prevention.

“We shall use our commission chairmanship, Your Excellency, to convert regional integration into tangible trade dividends and operationalise our United Nations Security Council strategy to stop conflicts before they erupt through peaceful mediation,” he said.

Dean of Ambassadors, Ambassador Ignatius Mudzimba, reaffirmed the foreign service’s commitment to promoting trade, economic, tourism, social and cultural co-operation.

“Special attention will be given to promoting education, science, innovation, and technology cooperation to strengthen local production, beneficiation, and value addition of Zimbabwean products for the international market.

“We equally commit to continue engaging our diaspora community to promote their interests in welfare and to harness their potential to support and contribute to the development of Zimbabwe,” he said.

title: ‘Firearm amnesty window still open until November 12’
categories: the latest articles; Paul Nyathi; Zimbabwe Republic Police
summary: Freeman Razemba Senior Reporter THE national firearms amnesty is still in force, with Zimbabweans in possession of unlicensed firearms and ammunition being given until November 12 to voluntarily surrender the weapons without facing criminal prosecution, police have said. The Zimbabwe Republic Police (ZRP) has urged individuals and institutions holding illegal or unregistered firearms to take […]
content_text:
Freeman Razemba

Senior Reporter

THE national firearms amnesty is still in force, with Zimbabweans in possession of unlicensed firearms and ammunition being given until November 12 to voluntarily surrender the weapons without facing criminal prosecution, police have said.

The Zimbabwe Republic Police (ZRP) has urged individuals and institutions holding illegal or unregistered firearms to take advantage of the amnesty before the one-month window closes, warning that physical checks and verification exercises will follow its expiry.

The amnesty, which runs from October 12 to November 12, 2026, was granted by President Mnangagwa in line with Article 12 of the SADC Protocol on the Control of Firearms, Ammunition and Related Materials.

In a statement, national police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said the amnesty remained valid and covered firearms held in a range of circumstances, including weapons left behind by deceased licensed owners.

“The ZRP reminds Zimbabweans that the national Firearms Amnesty, which was approved by His Excellency President Cde Dr ED Mnangagwa, is still valid till 12th November 2026,” he said.

“Zimbabweans or anyone in possession of unlicensed firearms, those left behind by late family members, and those with companies and gun clubs which are no longer operating are urged to take advantage of the amnesty and voluntarily surrender firearms at any nearest police station.”

The amnesty allows individuals and institutions to surrender unlicensed, smuggled or illegally acquired firearms and ammunition without being prosecuted, while those who comply will receive an official safe-custody receipt.

Comm Nyathi said police had also identified cases involving licensed firearm holders who were failing to renew their certificates or update their records, as well as cases where weapons were not being properly secured.

He said such lapses had contributed to the theft and misuse of firearms, with illegally held or stolen weapons subsequently being linked to serious offences including armed robbery and murder.

“Investigations reveal that some individuals continue to hold on to firearms despite changes in circumstances, such as company closures, inactive gun club membership and the passing on of licensed firearm holders,” he said.

He also warned licensed gun dealers and clubs against retaining unclaimed firearms surrendered to them for safekeeping, saying this was in contravention of the Firearms Act.

“All licensed firearm owners are urged to immediately update their records at local police stations in compliance with the Firearms Act, Chapter 10:09,” Comm Nyathi said.

“Those who comply will not face prosecution and will receive an official safe custody receipt. After the amnesty period expires, the Zimbabwe Republic Police will conduct physical checks and verification exercises targeting persons suspected of retaining illegal firearms,” he said.

The amnesty is part of efforts to strengthen control over firearms and reduce the availability of illegal weapons that can be used in violent crime.

Members of the public seeking guidance on the surrender process or safe-custody arrangements can approach their nearest police station, contact the National Complaints Desk on (0242) 703631 or send a WhatsApp message to 0712 800 197.

Source: ‘Firearm amnesty window still open until November 12’ – herald

title: MMCZ secures 9 new mineral export markets in diversification
categories: the latest articles; Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe; Nomsa Moyo
summary: Business Reporter The Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe has secured nine new export markets, led by fresh regional footholds for steel, coal and coke as part of an effort to diversify export destinations. According to a report by general manager Dr Nomsa Moyo, presented at the 2025 annual general meeting last week, the market expansion […]
content_text:
Business Reporter

The Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe has secured nine new export markets, led by fresh regional footholds for steel, coal and coke as part of an effort to diversify export destinations.

According to a report by general manager Dr Nomsa Moyo, presented at the 2025 annual general meeting last week, the market expansion drive has unlocked new trade corridors across southern and east Africa.

MMCZ is responsible for marketing all of the country’s minerals except gold and silver, which fall under the purview of Fidelity Gold Refinery, a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe. New export markets for Zimbabwean coal and coke have been secured in Malawi and Tanzania, while steel products have broken into key regional economies including the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Mozambique, Zambia, South Africa and Botswana, the report says.

“These achievements…strengthened trade relationships, expanded opportunities for local producers, enhanced market resilience and increased the contribution of beneficiated products, which accounted for 95 percent of total export value, reinforcing Zimbabwe’s position as a competitive and reliable supplier in global mineral markets,” Dr Moyo’s report says.

Bolstered by robust regional demand, steel exports nearly tripled to US$208,21 million during the 10 months to October 2026 – representing a 189,9 percent increase from US$71,82 million year-on-year. Meanwhile, coke sales grew 18,7 percent to reach US$179,54 million, compared to US$151,26 million previously. Beneficiated minerals accounted for 95 percent of total exports, reinforcing Zimbabwe’s position as a competitive and reliable supplier in global mineral markets.

While high-value minerals like lithium and platinum group metals continue to dominate aggregate export receipts – accounting for over 82 percent of cumulative revenue – bulk commodities such as coal, coke and processed steel are carving out an increasingly vital role within regional industrial value chains.

The entry of Zimbabwean steel into industrial hubs across the DRC, Zambia, Mozambique, South Africa and Botswana marks a major milestone for the country’s industrialisation and beneficiation push

The resurgence is heavily anchored by the coming online of mega-scale steel investments such as the Dinson Iron and Steel Company plant in Manhize, Mvuma.

With the facility operational, Zimbabwe is firmly poised to become a dominant regional steel hub, supplying heavy manufacturing, construction and infrastructural projects throughout Southern Africa.

At the same time, the strong uptake of Zimbabwean coal and coke has been heavily driven by surging energy and metallurgical demand from South Africa and wider regional markets.

The pursuit of new regional trade frontiers forms a core component of MMCZ’s risk mitigation strategy.

The report noted that while structural demand factors – such as global electrification and grid expansion – keep valuations firm, ongoing geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions continue to disrupt traditional supply chains. Addressing the shifting global trade landscape, the report cautioned that key markets such as the US and the European union have imposed high import tariffs on finished goods from China and other regions, triggering major shifts in global trade, supply chains and domestic economies.

By broadening its geographical footprint across the African Continental Free Trade Area framework and regional markets, Zimbabwe is effectively cushioning its mining sector against external trade shocks.

The report, however, cautioned that logistical bottlenecks continue to pose a threat to full market optimisation. The report specifically flagged inadequate road and railway networks to move bulk minerals as a primary operational barrier that risks making Zimbabwean products uncompetitive. To sustain the momentum of the newly opened markets, the MMCZ has prioritised enhanced regional collaboration, accelerated digital traceability systems and intensified surveillance at major ports of exit like Beitbridge and Forbes to curb illicit mineral leakages.

Source: MMCZ secures 9 new mineral export markets in diversification – herald

title: Govt, Invictus seal historic agreement
categories: the latest articles; Invictus Energy; Scott Macmillan
summary: Oliver Kazunga Senior Reporter ZIMBABWE’S ambitions to develop its domestic oil and gas resources have taken another step forward following the formal gazetting of the Petroleum Production Sharing Agreement (PPSA) governing the Cabora Bassa Project, providing a clearer framework for the long-term development of the country’s emerging petroleum industry. The agreement, published in the Government […]
content_text:
Oliver Kazunga

Senior Reporter

ZIMBABWE’S ambitions to develop its domestic oil and gas resources have taken another step forward following the formal gazetting of the Petroleum Production Sharing Agreement (PPSA) governing the Cabora Bassa Project, providing a clearer framework for the long-term development of the country’s emerging petroleum industry.

The agreement, published in the Government Gazette under General Notice 2101 of 2026 on Friday last week, completes the formal execution requirements following its signing between the Government, Invictus Energy, the Australia-headquartered company — and its 80 per cent-owned subsidiary, Geo Associates (Private) Limited in May this year.

While the signing established the agreement between the parties, its publication in the Government Gazette is an important step in giving the arrangement formal public and legal recognition.

It also brings the project closer to the stage where major investment decisions can be considered under an established regulatory and commercial framework.

Invictus Energy managing director Mr Scott Macmillan said:

“The formal gazettal of the PPSA is a landmark milestone for Invictus and the Cabora Bassa Project, completing the final formal step following the landmark signing of the agreement earlier this year.

“Importantly, it establishes the long-term fiscal, legal and commercial certainty required to underpin the substantial investment needed to advance the Mukuyu discovery through appraisal and towards development and commercial production.”

At the centre of the development is the Mukuyu gas discovery in the Cabora Bassa Basin, which Invictus has been exploring as part of its wider 360 000-hectare petroleum exploration portfolio in northern Zimbabwe.

The gazetting also carries an important message for prospective investors and financiers considering Zimbabwe’s petroleum sector.

Large-scale resource projects require more than geological potential and investors need confidence in the rules governing their capital, the allocation of project revenues and the contractual rights and obligations of all parties.

Thus, by completing the formal publication of the PPSA, the Cabora Bassa Project now has an established agreement that Invictus has indicated provides the framework for taking the project into its next phase.

However, the gazettal should not be confused with a final investment decision, the commencement of commercial production or an immediate flow of petroleum revenues into Government coffers.

Those milestones will depend on the outcome of further technical work and the ability to demonstrate that the project can be developed profitably.

The publication of the agreement represents a significant step in translating the country’s petroleum exploration ambitions into a more defined development pathway.

With the legal and commercial framework now formally established, attention will increasingly turn to whether the Mukuyu discovery can be developed into a viable producing asset and what that could mean for the country’s long-term energy security and economic growth.

Economic analyst Mr Kudzai Chidamba has welcomed the development.

“The formal gazetting of the Petroleum Production Sharing Agreement (PPSA) is a critical prerequisite for unlocking capital, though we must emphasise that moving from legal certainty to macroeconomic transformation requires overcoming major financial and infrastructural hurdles”, he said.

To the nation, the significance of the PPSA extends beyond the completion of an administrative process.

Petroleum exploration and production projects require substantial upfront capital, long investment horizons and considerable technical expertise.

Investors should have clarity on the legal, fiscal and commercial conditions under which resources can be developed, produced and sold before committing the billions of dollars that large-scale petroleum developments can potentially require.

A production sharing agreement provides the contractual framework governing how the economic benefits of petroleum production are distributed between the State and the investor.

Such arrangements generally establish how production costs are recovered, how remaining production is shared, and the fiscal and operational obligations of the parties.

They also provide a framework for managing the relationship between the Government and the private-sector developer over the life of a project.

This is particularly important as the project moves beyond exploration and towards determining whether the discovered resources can support a commercially viable development.

Last week, Invictus announced that it had completed the installation of a drilling rig at its second exploration well in the Cabora Bassa Basin, paving the way for drilling to begin at Musuma-1 later this month, a development that could expand Zimbabwe’s potential gas and condensate resource base.

The successful relocation of Exalo Rig 202 from the Mukuyu-2 wellsite to Musuma-1 is a significant step towards testing a new prospect that the Australian-listed energy company estimates could contain 1,2 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and 73 million barrels of condensate.

A discovery does not automatically translate into commercially recoverable reserves or immediate production.

Further appraisal drilling, engineering studies, infrastructure planning, financing arrangements and market development are typically required before a project can reach a final investment decision.

It is believed that the development of a commercially viable petroleum industry could have wider implications for Zimbabwe’s economy.

Domestic gas production, if established at scale, could provide an additional energy source for electricity generation and industrial activity, potentially reducing reliance on imported energy and improving the security of supply.

And the gas could also support energy-intensive industries, including manufacturing, mining and fertiliser production, depending on the volumes discovered, production costs and the availability of infrastructure.

There could also be benefits through investment inflows, employment creation, procurement opportunities for local businesses, skills transfer and future government revenues from petroleum production.

For a country seeking to expand industrial capacity, attract foreign direct investment and strengthen its energy security, the development of domestic hydrocarbon resources could form part of a broader strategy to diversify the economy.

So far, these benefits remain prospective and would depend on successful appraisal — the establishment of commercially recoverable resources — the availability of financing, infrastructure development — and the ability to secure viable markets for the gas.

Source: Govt, Invictus seal historic agreement – herald

title: Police invade Borrowdale, Hatcliffe communities
summary: Arron Nyamayaro Police and community groups marched through Borrowdale and Hatcliffe on Saturday, urging residents to report drug dealers and drug bases as efforts to combat substance abuse intensify. The march involved the Christian Community Policing Network, Business Against Drugs and Substance Abuse Forum, Zimbabwe Bikers Association, Crime Liaison Committees, the University of Zimbabwe and […]
content_text:
Arron Nyamayaro

Police and community groups marched through Borrowdale and Hatcliffe on Saturday, urging residents to report drug dealers and drug bases as efforts to combat substance abuse intensify.

The march involved the Christian Community Policing Network, Business Against Drugs and Substance Abuse Forum, Zimbabwe Bikers Association, Crime Liaison Committees, the University of Zimbabwe and primary schools.

A speech by Police Commissioner-General Stephen Mutamba, read by the officer commanding Harare Province, said 9,200 of the 12,000 suspects arrested between January and September were under the age of 35.

Mutamba said the fight against drug and substance abuse required a united community effort, warning residents not to assume the problem affected only other families.

“The fact that the fire has not reached your doorstep does not mean your house is beyond its flames,” he said.

He said drug and substance abuse was linked to domestic violence, theft, robbery and other serious crimes, including murder. It was also disrupting young people’s education and damaging careers, marriages and families, he said.

Mutamba expressed concern that some adults were contributing to the problem by abusing or selling drugs. He also said some people struggling with addiction turned to crime to fund their habits.

“The net is closing in, and the full force of the law awaits you,” he warned drug dealers and their accomplices.

He said police were working to identify and disrupt drug supply networks through intelligence-led policing, investigations and targeted operations at the country’s points of entry and exit. The police would also continue working with communities, schools and other institutions, he said.

Mutamba urged young people to shun drugs, focus on their education and protect their health, saying the country’s future depended on them. He called on parents, teachers, law enforcement officers, civic organisations and churches to work together to protect young people.

Source: Police invade Borrowdale, Hatcliffe communities – herald

title: Zim to advocate for peace at UN Security Council

summary: Columbus Mabika Herald Reporter ZIMBABWE intends to leverage its tenure as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council to encourage peaceful resolution of international conflicts through dialogue and strict adherence to the dictates of international law, including the principles of the United Nations Charter, Defence Minister Oppah Muchinguri Kashiri has said. She made […]
content_text:
Columbus Mabika

Herald Reporter

ZIMBABWE intends to leverage its tenure as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council to encourage peaceful resolution of international conflicts through dialogue and strict adherence to the dictates of international law, including the principles of the United Nations Charter, Defence Minister Oppah Muchinguri Kashiri has said.

She made the remarks yesterday at the graduation of the Junior Staff Course at the Air Force of Zimbabwe School of Academic training at Manyame air base.

The sentiment comes as Zimbabwe will serve a two-year term in the United Nations security council as a non-permanent member beginning on January 1, 2027 after receiving overwhelming 182 votes out of 191 in an election that was held in June in New York.

The commitment by Zimbabwe is also consistent with the African union Agenda 2063, particularly the aspiration of Silencing the Guns in Africa by 2063.

The need to resolve conflicts diplomatically came as the globe is experiencing continuous conflicts in recent times.

Minister Muchinguri-Kashiri said the world has in recent years witnessed an accelerated increase in conflicts in which dialogue and dictates of the international law should be applied.

“Against the backdrop of a global peace and security environment that is characterised by unmitigated conflicts, geopolitical competition, switching military alliances, rapid technological advancements and mounting pressure on multilateral institutions that are mandated to maintain international peace and security, Zimbabwe will use its tenure in the security council to diplomatically bring peace to the world.”

“The security situation in the northern parts of Mozambique remains of great concern, while in the north protracted conflict in Democratic Republic of Congo continues to present serious challenges to regional peace and stability.

“At the global level, the Russia-Ukraine war continues to affect international peace and security, with consequences reverberating beyond the immediate theatre of conflict, while the continuing confrontation involving the United States of America and Israel on one hand and Iran on the other, has the potential of a wider regional conflict that presents serious implications for international peace and security.”

Turning to the modernisation of the ZDF, she said Government is prioritising revamping the force capabilities through research and development and acquisition of modern technologies and equipment.

The objective is to strengthen indigenous technological capabilities and to develop appropriate military systems in order to progressively reduce dependence on external sources of supply.

“To accelerate the upgrading and modernisation programme, the Ministry of Defence has embarked on a massive transformation of defence economic activities which entails restructuring and revitalisation of business ventures under the Defence Procurement Fund which is managed by the Defence Procurement Board to augment the inadequate funding provided by Treasury,” she said.

On the course, she said the inclusion of allied students has far reaching effects in enhancing inter-operability.

“I am particularly pleased to note the inclusion in the course, of members from SADC Member States. This is consistent with the objective of enhancing interoperability between and among SADC Defence Forces through joint military exercises and training. SADC air forces have consistently conducted humanitarian exercises, the last of which was held in Zambia in September 2025,” she said.

Zimbabwe is set to host exercise “Blue Runde” in 2027, preparations for which are at an advanced stage.

On gender balance, she said it was worth noting that the ZDF was taking the lead as witnessed by a 35 percent female representation in the course.

“The gender distribution achieved by this course, 12 females out of the 34-student complement, a 35 percent representation, is particularly pleasing.

“This is a significant achievement for which the School of Academic and Staff Training must be commended. There is still room for improvement though until the ideal of 50 percent representation is achieved, for that is what is consistent with the Government’s policy on gender equality and inclusion as enshrined under Sections 17 and 56, of the Constitution of Zimbabwe,” she said.

Commandant Air Force of Zimbabwe School of Academic Training, Group Captain Lloyd Bamba said the school will do everything in its jurisdiction to ensure that it continues to offer quality training for officers in the quest to achieve national , regional and global peace.

Source: Zim to advocate for peace at UN Security Council – herald

content_text:
Freeman Razemba

Senior Reporter

NATIONAL carrier Air Zimbabwe is participating at the World Travel Market in London this week, taking its voice to the global aviation and tourism stage.

As the world’s most influential travel and tourism event for almost five decades, this year’s show is set to build on last year’s record‑breaking performance, with several new features and standout experiences across the show floor.

Taking place at ExCeL London from November 3-5, 2026, WTM London 2026 will once again act as the premier global meeting place for travel industry professionals, stakeholders and decision‑makers, drawn by an enhanced conference programme, an expanded schedule of networking events and unrivalled business opportunities.

Air Zimbabwe chief executive, Mr Edmund Makona, is set to participate as a speaker, contributing to an important industry conversation titled: “Connected Infrastructure – Can Aviation Growth and Destination Strategy Align?”

In a statement, Air Zimbabwe said: “The discussion will explore the relationship between aviation connectivity, infrastructure development and destination strategies in unlocking tourism growth and strengthening global travel markets.

“For Air Zimbabwe, this conversation resonates strongly with the airline’s role as a strategic enabler of Zimbabwe’s tourism, trade and investment ambitions, connecting the country to regional and international markets.”

As the national airline continues to expand its connectivity, including the resumption of direct flights between Harare and London after a 14-year hiatus, this engagement provides an opportunity to share perspectives on the role of aviation in driving destination growth and economic opportunities.

The airline’s Airbus A330-300 operates three weekly flights from the Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport to London Gatwick, departing Harare on Sundays, Wednesdays and Fridays, with return flights operating on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Air Zimbabwe is also planning to expand its domestic network, while pursuing additional international routes, including Dubai, Beijing and Guangzhou.

A 41-year-old inmate, Joshua Belden Swarts, has appeared in the Brakpan Magistrate’s Court after Hawks investigators allegedly found crystal methamphetamine worth R12,000 and three cellphones linked to him at Boksburg Correctional Centre.

Swarts was arrested by members of the Hawks’ Northern Cape Serious Organised Crime Investigation unit during an intelligence-driven operation under Project Ditto.

Project Ditto is an ongoing investigation launched in 2023 to dismantle identified drug networks operating in Kimberley and parts of Gauteng.

During a search of Swarts’ cell, investigators recovered two cellphones hidden under his pillow. A further search of his locker uncovered crystal methamphetamine, commonly known as Tik, with an estimated street value of R12,000.

The Department of Correctional Services had conducted an internal search a week earlier, during which another cellphone was allegedly found in Swarts’ possession, bringing the total number of cellphones linked to him to three.

He is also facing an additional charge of possession of a stolen motor vehicle. According to police, a vehicle allegedly found in his possession before his incarceration was identified as stolen during a Project Ditto takedown operation.

Swarts made a brief appearance in the Brakpan Magistrate’s Court, where the matter was postponed to 26 January 2027 for further investigation.

Hawks spokesperson Lieutenant Colonel Tebogo Thebe confirmed the operation and the charges.

title: Masvingo councillors raise alarm over delayed hailstorm relief
categories: Zimbabwe South; disaster relief; Masvingo City Council
summary: Masvingo councillors have raised concern over delays in government assistance to residents whose homes were damaged by hailstorms that hit the city on October 5, 2026, saying affected families are still waiting for promised support to rebuild their houses. content_text:
Masvingo councillors have raised concern over delays in government assistance to residents whose homes were damaged by hailstorms that hit the city on October 5, 2026, saying affected families are still waiting for promised support to rebuild their houses.

The concerns were raised by Ward 7 councillor Rivhard Musekiwa during a recent Full Council meeting, where he said residents were becoming increasingly frustrated after submitting quotations detailing the damage to their properties but receiving no communication from the government on when assistance would be provided.

Following the destruction caused by the hailstorm, the government announced plans to decentralise damage assessments across 11 affected wards, with homeowners required to submit Bills of Quantities to establish the cost of reconstruction.

The government also announced food assistance for vulnerable households, with 6,711 households earmarked to receive food and non-food items.

Cllr Musekiwa said the lack of updates had left councillors struggling to respond to residents seeking information about the promised assistance.

“We were promised help by the government but it has not yet come. Most of our residents lost their houses to the hailstorm. They were told to go and get quotations of the damage suffered. They did that a while ago but to date there has not been any communication on the way forward,” he said.

“The people keep coming back to us for updates, yet we do not have any. Would it be okay that we call the District Development Coordinator (DDC) to come and address us here, on behalf of the government, so that we can know what to tell the people?”

He urged the government to expedite the assistance programme and provide regular updates, saying the communication gap was undermining councillors’ ability to represent affected communities.

“As people’s representatives, it does not paint a good picture that we do not have answers to such pertinent questions. It will seem as if we do not care about the plight of our people. We expect the government to finish such important programmes,” he said.

Cllr Musekiwa said the declaration of the hailstorm disaster as a national disaster should have prompted urgent intervention, particularly with another rainy season approaching.

“When the hailstorms hit, a state of national disaster was declared. We expect this matter to be treated with urgency because people are in a dire situation. We have people with disabilities among those affected, who need extra care. As things stand, we are already approaching another rainy season. What is going to happen to our people who are already faced with this situation?” he said.

Responding to the concerns, Masvingo Mayor Cllr Aleck Tabe said several stakeholders, particularly businesses, had provided assistance to affected families, although the scale of the destruction meant more resources were required.

He said some businesses had donated building materials and helped construct cottages for families who lost their homes.

“I want to thank everyone who has come on board thus far to render assistance to our affected people. We received great assistance from various stakeholders, especially the business community. They came through with material and managed to build some cottages for some of the affected people. We are yet to have a consolidated list of the assistance we have received thus far,” he said.

Cllr Tabe said about 13,500 households had been affected and that the responsible minister was expected to visit the city to conduct further assessments and monitor resource mobilisation.

“As far as the government is concerned, we need to appreciate that at least 13,500 households were destroyed. This is a huge number. The minister is meant to come soon for further assessment and ensure that resource mobilisation is on track. We need to be patient,” he said.

He added that some vulnerable households had received food assistance through social welfare programmes, although available supplies were insufficient to cover everyone affected.

“Of course, we would have needed more because everyone was vulnerable at the time, but the hampers were not sufficient for everyone. Those who are already on the list of the social welfare were prioritised at the time,” he said.

Cllr Tabe said councillors had fulfilled their role by advising affected residents to obtain quotations for damaged properties and urged them to remain patient as the government mobilised resources.

title: Turning operational data into business performance
summary: Jackson T. Mashinge IN an increasingly competitive business environment, organisations are under pressure to deliver services faster, re­duce operating costs, improve accuracy and make better decisions. Process auto­mation through data…
content_text:
Jackson T. Mashinge

IN an increasingly competitive business environment, organisations are under pressure to deliver services faster, re­duce operating costs, improve accuracy and make better decisions. Process auto­mation through data analysis is emerging as a powerful way to achieve these ob­jectives. By combining operational data, analytical tools and digital technologies, businesses can move beyond manual, repetitive tasks towards intelligent opera­tions that are more efficient, consistent and responsive to change.

At its core, process automation through data analysis involves using information to understand how work is performed, identify inefficiencies and design digital workflows that execute routine activities with minimal human intervention. It is not simply about replacing paperwork with computers. It is about rethinking how work flows through an organisation, how deci­sions are made and how information can be used to improve performance.

For years, many organisations have re­lied on employees to capture information, transfer figures between systems, reconcile records, prepare reports and follow up on outstanding approvals. Although these ac­tivities are necessary, they consume valu­able time and expose businesses to human error, duplication and delays. When such tasks are automated using reliable data and clearly defined rules, employees can redi­rect their efforts towards strategic planning, customer service, problem solving and other activities that require professional judgement.

The journey towards effective automa­tion begins with understanding the process itself. Organisations often attempt to intro­duce technology before establishing why a process is inefficient. This can result in expensive systems that merely reproduce existing problems in a digital format. Data analysis offers a more practical starting point by revealing where delays occur, which activities create unnecessary work and what factors affect performance.

Consider a customer service depart­ment that consistently fails to resolve re­quests within its target turnaround time. Management may initially conclude that employees need to work faster or that addi­tional staff are required. However, an anal­ysis of transaction records and timestamps may reveal that requests spend most of their time waiting for assignment, approval or missing information. The real problem is therefore not necessarily employee pro­ductivity, but the way work is organised.

With this insight, the organisation can introduce automated validation, direct requests to the appropriate teams, send reminders for outstanding approvals and flag incomplete submissions for correc­tion. Instead of treating the symptoms of poor performance, the business addresses the underlying causes. This demonstrates how data transforms automation from a technology project into a targeted business improvement initiative.

Across industries, opportunities for au­tomation are expanding rapidly. Finance departments can automate reconciliations and invoice processing, while human re­sources teams can streamline employee onboarding and leave approvals. Supply chain departments can use transaction data to monitor stock levels and trigger replen­ishment alerts. Customer service teams can automatically classify requests and direct them to the appropriate specialists. In each case, the objective is to reduce unnecessary manual intervention while improving the reliability and timeliness of outcomes.

Digital platforms such as Microsoft Power Automate, robotic process automa­tion tools, database workflows and enter­prise integration systems make it possible to connect activities across multiple ap­plications. A transaction entered into one system can trigger validation, retrieve sup­porting information from another system, initiate an approval and update the relevant records automatically. More advanced solutions can analyse historical patterns to identify unusual transactions, predict potential delays and prioritise cases that require urgent attention.

However, the effectiveness of these technologies depends heavily on the qual­ity of the data supporting them. An auto­mated process is only as reliable as the in­formation it receives. Incomplete records, duplicate entries, outdated information and inconsistent formats can cause automated workflows to produce incorrect results at remarkable speed. Organisations must therefore establish appropriate data stan­dards, validation procedures, ownership responsibilities and access controls before expanding automation.

Equally important is the need to rede­sign processes before automating them. An inefficient process does not become effec­tive simply because it is digital. If an organ­isation has unnecessary approval layers, unclear responsibilities or duplicated data capture, automating every step may rein­force the inefficiencies rather than elimi­nate them. Management should challenge existing procedures, remove activities that do not add value and simplify decision making before introducing technology.

Successful automation must also pre­serve accountability. Not every decision should be delegated entirely to a machine. Routine transactions that meet established policy requirements may be processed automatically, while unusual, high risk or ambiguous cases should be referred to employees with the appropriate authority. For example, a system may automatically process a low risk invoice that matches an approved purchase order and delivery re­cord, but refer discrepancies or suspicious transactions for further investigation. This balance allows organisations to benefit from speed without compromising profes­sional judgement and oversight.

For business leaders, measuring the im­pact of automation is essential. Improve­ments should be demonstrated through clear performance indicators, including processing time, operating cost, error rates, transaction volumes, outstanding backlogs and compliance with service standards. Establishing a baseline before implemen­tation enables management to determine whether the investment is delivering mean­ingful results. Monitoring exception rates can also reveal where data quality needs improvement or where automated rules require adjustment.

Governance and risk management must remain central to the process. Auto­mated workflows should maintain clear audit trails, restrict access according to responsibilities and document the reasons for significant decisions. Where predic­tive models are used, organisations should monitor their accuracy, assess potential bias and ensure that important decisions can be reviewed by authorised personnel. Regular testing and monitoring are neces­sary to confirm that automated processes continue to operate as intended as business conditions change.

Beyond immediate efficiency gains, the greatest opportunity lies in turning automation into a source of operational intelligence. Every transaction, approval, exception and delay can generate valuable information about how an organisation per­forms. When this information is analysed consistently, leaders can identify emerging bottlenecks, anticipate capacity constraints and make better informed decisions. In­stead of waiting for monthly reports to discover that performance has deteriorated, management can use timely dashboards and automated alerts to respond before problems become more serious.

Ultimately, process automation through data analysis is not about removing people from the workplace. It is about removing unnecessary friction from the way work gets done. By allowing technology to handle predictable activities and directing human attention towards judgement, in­novation and complex problem solving, organisations can create a more productive and resilient operating environment.

The organisations that will gain the greatest value are those that treat automa­tion as a continuous improvement capa­bility rather than a once off technology investment. They will begin with reliable data, redesign processes around business needs, establish appropriate controls and continually measure outcomes. When these elements come together, operational data becomes more than a record of past activities. It becomes a practical instrument for improving decisions, strengthening accountability and achieving sustainable business performance.

l Mashinge has 15 years of experience in accounting, auditing, and finance. His expertise is in auditing, risk adviso­ry, strategy formulation, project assur­ance, monitoring and evaluation.

title: Why AI hosting should be decided by directors
summary: GODFREY NYONI THERE was a time when decisions about servers, software, and infrastructure be­longed entirely to the IT department. The rest of the organisation provided requirements, and IT delivered solutions.…
content_text:
GODFREY NYONI

THERE was a time when decisions about servers, software, and infrastructure be­longed entirely to the IT department. The rest of the organisation provided requirements, and IT delivered solutions. Business leaders set strategy, finance managed budgets, operations ran the day-to-day, and the technology team handled the technical plumbing that made everything run. That division of responsibility made sense when technology was a support function. It makes con­siderably less sense when technology is the busi­ness itself and it makes almost no sense at all when the technology in question is artificial intelligence infrastructure.

AI hosting is not a technical decision with business implications. It is a business decision with technical components. The distinction mat­ters, because it determines who sits in the room when the choice is made, whose concerns shape the outcome, and who bears responsibility when something goes wrong.

Organisations that continue treating AI host­ing as a procurement exercise for the IT team to resolve will make decisions that are technically sound and strategically inadequate. The IT de­partment can tell you which provider offers the best uptime and the most competitive pricing on GPU hours. It cannot, on its own, tell you wheth­er concentrating your AI workloads on a single foreign provider creates acceptable commercial risk, whether the data residency arrangements align with your contractual obligations to clients, or whether the cost structure of the hosting mod­el you are adopting will remain viable as your AI usage scales.

The financial implications of AI hosting deci­sions extend well beyond the technology budget. Unlike conventional web hosting, where costs are relatively predictable and contained, AI infrastruc­ture often uses consumption-based pricing that scales with usage.

An AI application that unexpectedly attracts high traffic, a model that processes more data than anticipated, or an automation that runs more fre­quently than planned can generate hosting costs that bear no relationship to the original budget estimate. Finance leadership needs to be involved not to approve a line item but to understand the cost structure, model financial exposure under dif­ferent usage scenarios, and ensure the organisation has controls in place to prevent infrastructure bills from becoming a surprise. This is not a conversa­tion the IT team should be having alone.

Legal and compliance considerations are equally significant. AI systems process data, and the terms under which that data is stored, accessed, and protected are governed by contracts, regula­tions, and legal obligations that sit well outside the IT department’s domain.

A business that hosts its AI workloads with a provider whose data centres sit in a jurisdiction with different data protection standards may be in breach of commitments made to clients, exposed to regulatory risk it has not assessed, or storing sensitive information under legal arrangements that the company’s own lawyers have never re­viewed.

In Zimbabwe and across Africa, data gover­nance frameworks are evolving rapidly, and the hosting decisions made today may intersect with regulatory requirements that did not exist when the contract was signed. Legal counsel needs to be part of AI hosting decisions from the beginning, not brought in to resolve problems after the fact.

Operations and customer experience leadership have an equally important stake. AI hosting quali­ty directly affects the performance of applications that serve customers, support internal workflows, and underpin operational capabilities.

When an AI system responds slowly, fails in­termittently, or degrades in accuracy because of infrastructure limitations, the consequences land in customer service queues and damaged relation­ships not the IT team’s ticket system. Leaders re­sponsible for operations and customer experience should be setting the performance standards that AI hosting must meet, and should be part of the decision about whether a given provider can actu­ally meet them.

Executive leadership has perhaps the most important role of all, and it is the one most con­sistently absent from AI hosting conversations in African organisations. AI infrastructure is becom­ing as strategically significant as any other major capital or operational commitment the business makes. The provider relationships established now, the data arrangements agreed to today, and the technical dependencies created through host­ing choices will shape the organisation’s options for years. An executive team that delegates this de­cision entirely to IT and procurement is abdicating strategic responsibility for a choice that will affect the business’s competitive position, its risk profile, and its operational resilience in ways that extend far beyond anything the monthly technology bud­get suggests.

This does not mean that the IT department should be sidelined. Technical expertise is indis­pensable in AI hosting decisions. The IT team understands the infrastructure requirements, can evaluate provider capabilities, assess security controls, and manage the implementation. What changes is not the IT team’s role but the compo­sition of the decision-making group around it. AI hosting decisions should be cross-functional, with IT leading on technical evaluation, finance modelling the cost exposure, legal reviewing the contractual and regulatory dimensions, operations setting performance requirements, and executive leadership providing strategic oversight.

For Zimbabwean organisations navigating this transition, the practical implication is straightfor­ward. Before the next AI hosting decision is made, ask who is in the room. If the answer is only the IT team and a vendor, the decision is not being made correctly. The organisations that will get AI infrastructure right are the ones that treat it with the same cross-functional seriousness they would apply to any other decision with this level of finan­cial, legal, and strategic consequence. That is not a technology standard. It is a governance one.

title: Zimbabwe sets sugarcane purchase price at US$72.40 per tonne
summary: HARARE — The Zimbabwean government has set the purchase price of sugarcane supplied by private growers to millers at US$72.40 per tonne under new regulations governing the sugar industry. The price is prescribed in Statutory Instrument 174 of 2026, published in the Government Gazette dated October 30. The regulations, issued by the Minister of Industry […]
content_text:
HARARE — The Zimbabwean government has set the purchase price of sugarcane supplied by private growers to millers at US$72.40 per tonne under new regulations governing the sugar industry.

The price is prescribed in Statutory Instrument 174 of 2026, published in the Government Gazette dated October 30.

The regulations, issued by the Minister of Industry and Commerce after consultations with the ministers responsible for agriculture and the Zimbabwe Sugar Association, establish a mandatory purchase price for cane supplied by private farmers.

Under the regulations, the US$72.40 price applies notwithstanding the terms of existing cane purchase agreements between growers and millers.

The government has also introduced payment requirements, directing millers to pay growers by the eighth day of the month following delivery unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

The regulations provide penalties for non-compliance, including fines or imprisonment of up to six months, or both.

Company directors, managers and principal officers who knowingly participate in breaches of the regulations may also be held personally liable.

The new pricing framework directly affects private sugarcane growers supplying Zimbabwe’s milling industry, particularly those operating in the Lowveld.

The Gazette does not indicate how the prescribed price compares with previous commercial arrangements or explain the formula used to determine the US$72.40 rate.

The regulations were made under the Sugar Production Control Act.

HARARE — The Zimbabwe Tourism Authority (ZTA) is seeking a service provider to promote the country’s tourism destinations through the television drama series Nyakasikana , as it explores entertainment-based destination marketing.

The initiative was disclosed in the Government Gazette published on October 30, 2026.

Under tender number ZTA/JAHDRAMA/01/2026, the authority is inviting companies to bid for destination marketing and promotion services through the drama series.

The closing date for submissions is November 13, 2026.

The proposed initiative would use television storytelling as a promotional platform, potentially allowing tourism destinations to feature within entertainment programming rather than relying exclusively on conventional advertising.

However, the Gazette does not specify which destinations will be promoted, the value of the proposed contract, the television broadcaster involved or the intended audience.

It also does not disclose whether the programme will involve new episodes, product placement or other promotional arrangements associated with the series.

Interested bidders must provide a company profile, valid tax clearance, certificate of incorporation and proof of registration with the Procurement Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe.

Bidding documents are available through the government’s electronic procurement platform.

The ZTA has not yet announced a successful bidder, and the Gazette does not indicate when the proposed promotional campaign would begin.

The initiative could provide an opportunity to showcase Zimbabwe’s tourism attractions through locally produced entertainment, although its effectiveness will depend on the eventual campaign design, audience reach and implementation.

title: Panic in Zimbabwe as men of God Prophet Angel and Apostle Chiwenga suddenly start supporting General Chiwenga (VIDEO)
keywords: news
summary: Prophet Angel and Apostle Talent Chiwenga shift tone towards General Chiwenga amid ZANU-PF tensions Prophet Uebert Angel has urged Zimbabweans to stop attacking Vice-President General (Retired) Constantino Chiwenga, in a public intervention that came days after Apostle Talent Chiwenga apologised for his confrontational preaching and praised the Vice-President. Angel delivered his remarks during a service […] The post Panic in Zimbabwe as men of God Prophet Angel and Apostle Chiwenga suddenly start supporting General Chiwenga (VIDEO) first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
Prophet Angel and Apostle Talent Chiwenga shift tone towards General Chiwenga amid ZANU-PF tensions

Prophet Uebert Angel has urged Zimbabweans to stop attacking Vice-President General (Retired) Constantino Chiwenga, in a public intervention that came days after Apostle Talent Chiwenga apologised for his confrontational preaching and praised the Vice-President.

Angel delivered his remarks during a service at his Spirit Embassy ministry on Sunday, November 1. Video clips from the sermon circulated online as tensions between Chiwenga and President Emmerson Mnangagwa continued to dominate discussion around ZANU-PF’s future leadership.

“The vitriolic attacks against Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga is a disgraceful exhibition of political impropriety and a display of intellectual bankruptcy,” Angel told his congregation.

He said political leaders, including Mnangagwa and Chiwenga, could be criticised, but argued that personal attacks should not be presented as ordinary political scrutiny.

“Criticism is legitimate. You should. You must. People criticise me. They criticise the President. They criticise the Vice-President. It’s allowed. But contempt masquerading as criticism is diabolic. It’s evil,” he said.

Angel also pointed to Mnangagwa’s decision to retain Chiwenga as Vice-President, saying the public should respect the appointment. “If the President sees him fit to still be the Vice-President, it must be a sign that I, with my little mouth or big mouth, should hush,” he said.

The preacher singled out Chiwenga’s former wife, Marry Mubaiwa, whose recent public comments about their relationship and the Vice-President had drawn attention. Angel cautioned against joining attacks made in the course of disputes between former spouses.

His intervention followed a volatile period in ZANU-PF. At the party’s annual conference in Chinhoyi in October, Chiwenga delivered a speech that raised questions about the direction of the government and the ruling party. He asked whether the mistakes that led to the emergence of the Second Republic were being repeated and called for an honest review of the party’s decisions.

The conference adopted resolutions supporting changes to ZANU-PF’s leadership timetable, including keeping Mnangagwa at the head of the party until 2030 and moving the next elective congress to 2029. The events at Chinhoyi brought the rift between the President and his deputy into sharper public view.

Apostle Talent Chiwenga, a vocal preacher who has spent years outside Zimbabwe, made his own shift in tone shortly before Angel’s sermon. In an address posted online in October, he apologised for the irritation caused by his style of preaching. He said: “I want to apologize, perhaps, for the first time in my life, for the irritations that I caused in the society because of my methods of preaching.”

In subsequent public messages, Talent Chiwenga praised Constantino Chiwenga’s leadership and said he intended to return to Zimbabwe. His remarks marked a change from his previous confrontational public stance towards the government and the Vice-President. The two preachers’ statements have prompted renewed attention to the way prominent religious figures speak about political leaders.

Angel’s own intervention has also been viewed against earlier comments he made from the pulpit. In July, he referred to an unnamed person he described as a future successor who was suffering from a hidden illness and was “walking, but dead inside”. The remarks were widely interpreted in the context of the succession debate, although Angel did not name Chiwenga.

The latest sermon came just days after a major development in the long-running court case involving Mubaiwa. She was removed from remand on October 27 after a regional magistrate refused a state request to postpone the proceedings. The case had remained unresolved for nearly 7 years.

Mubaiwa had faced an attempted-murder charge linked to Chiwenga’s hospitalisation in South Africa in 2019. Chiwenga was later treated in China, where he spent 4 months. Mubaiwa has had her right arm and left leg amputated since her arrest. Her release from remand followed delays in the case, and prosecutors would need to take further steps if they sought to bring it back before the courts.

The case has repeatedly brought the former couple’s private conflict into public view. Angel’s decision to refer to Mubaiwa during a political sermon placed the dispute alongside his appeal for Zimbabweans to stop criticising the Vice-President.

Another development affecting the political atmosphere was the death of businessman Wicknell Chivayo in a helicopter crash near Marondera on September 30. His wife, Lucy Muteke, and 3 other people also died. Chivayo had been associated with powerful figures in the ruling establishment, and his death was reported amid continuing debate over factional alignments within the party.

Angel said he was not taking sides between rival camps. He urged people to let Chiwenga carry out his duties as Vice-President and warned against turning political disagreement into personal abuse.

Together, the recent remarks by Angel and Talent Chiwenga have made the Vice-President’s political position a focus not only for party figures but also for religious leaders with national profiles. Their public statements came in the wake of the Chinhoyi conference, amid renewed questions about ZANU-PF’s leadership plans and the future relationship between Mnangagwa and his deputy.

Angel, who has been associated with President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s political camp and previously found himself on the opposite side of the political tensions involving Chiwenga, delivered the remarks during a church service at his Spirit Embassy ministry on Sunday.

His intervention has raised fresh questions about the shifting political dynamics surrounding Mnangagwa and his deputy, particularly following Chivayo’s death in a helicopter crash near Marondera on September 30, which claimed the lives of his wife, Lucy Muteke, and three other people.

Chivayo was widely regarded as a close ally of Mnangagwa and had cultivated relationships with several powerful figures within the ruling establishment including Angel himself.

His growing political and financial influence had previously become a source of friction between Mnangagwa and Chiwenga, who reportedly criticised Chivayo and other wealthy businessmen associated with the President.

The businessman was among individuals perceived to be within Mnangagwa’s political orbit, making his sudden death a significant development in an already volatile political environment.

Against this backdrop, Angel’s latest remarks defending Chiwenga have attracted attention, particularly given his previous public pronouncements about the Vice-President’s future.

In July, Angel sparked controversy after declaring during a church sermon that a person he described as the country’s future successor was suffering from a hidden illness and was “walking, but dead inside”.

Although he did not explicitly name Chiwenga, the remarks were widely interpreted in the context of Zimbabwe’s succession politics, with the Vice-President emerging as a central figure in the speculation.

While there is no established evidence linking Chivayo’s helicopter crash to the factional battles, his death has added another layer of uncertainty to an already tense political environment.

Some political commentators and social media users have speculated that individuals perceived to be aligned with Mnangagwa could increasingly feel vulnerable as succession tensions intensify.

Addressing his congregation on Sunday, Angel condemned what he described as vitriolic attacks against Chiwenga, dismissing them as political impropriety and intellectual bankruptcy.

“The vitriolic attacks against Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga is a disgraceful exhibition of political impropriety and a display of intellectual bankruptcy,” he said.

He acknowledged that political leaders, including Mnangagwa and Chiwenga, were open to criticism but warned against what he termed contempt disguised as legitimate scrutiny.

“Criticism is legitimate. You should. You must. People criticise me. They criticise the President. They criticise the Vice-President. It’s allowed. But contempt masquerading as criticism is diabolic. It’s evil,” Angel said.

He further questioned why individuals who portray Chiwenga as dangerous would openly challenge him.

“If you say Chiwenga is dangerous and you come out and oppose him publicly, you’re giving us a public review that he is not as dangerous as we thought,” he said.

Angel also invoked Mnangagwa’s authority, arguing that the President’s decision to retain Chiwenga as his deputy should discourage public attacks against him.

“If the President sees him fit to still be the Vice-President, it must be a sign that I, with my little mouth or big mouth, should hush,” he said.

The preacher also criticised those joining public attacks against Chiwenga, specifically referencing his former wife, Marry Mubaiwa, following her recent interview in which she made damaging allegations against the Vice-President.

Using a hypothetical divorce scenario, Angel warned against taking sides in disputes involving former spouses, arguing that doing so could be interpreted as undermining the authority of the person who initiated the separation.

His remarks come amid renewed political tensions between Mnangagwa and Chiwenga, which recently spilled into public view during the Zanu-PF Annual National People’s Conference in Chinhoyi.

Angel, however, rejected suggestions that his intervention was driven by factional considerations, insisting that he was not aligned with competing political camps.

He urged Zimbabweans to allow Chiwenga to discharge his responsibilities as Vice-President and support the country’s leadership without participating in what he described as political drama.

title: Good news for some Zimbabwean care workers in UK: five-year settlement route retained
