keywords: earned settlement; ILR; indefinite leave to remain; Migrant workers; National Insurance; Shabana Mahmood; social care visa; uk immigration; UK settlement rules; Zimbabwean care workers
summary: Some Zimbabweans working in UK social care may retain the five-year route to settlement if they came to or switched into the care route between 2022 and 2025, earned at least £25,000 and complied with their visa conditions.
content_text:
Zimbabweans working in the UK’s social care sector may still be able to apply for settlement after five years under the government’s newly announced policy — if they meet specific salary and visa conditions.

The concession applies to care workers who came to or switched into the social care route between 2022 and 2025, earned at least £25,000 a year in the sector and complied with their visa conditions. Those who qualify will be able to remain on the existing five-year path to indefinite leave to remain (ILR).

That is a significant change from the original proposal, which could have left some care workers facing a wait of up to 15 years.

“Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told MPs as she set out the new policy.

🚨 BREAKING: Shabana Mahmood confirms most social care migrants will now be exempt from waiting 15 years to settle in Britain https://t.co/sDtHJKZIEb

— Politics UK (@PolitlcsUK) November 2, 2026

A second chance for some care workers

The government also announced a route for care workers who did not fulfil their visa conditions. They will be able to apply for a new five-year care visa and will not be tied to their previous employer, giving workers with problematic sponsors the chance to find a legitimate provider.

After completing that new visa, they will be able to apply for settlement. The government estimates this group represents about a quarter of people who came to or switched into the social care route between 2022 and 2025.

The concession is not automatic for every Zimbabwean in Britain, or for every person working in care. The salary, time-period and visa-compliance conditions matter, and applicants will also need to meet the government’s broader settlement requirements.

What happens to other migrants?

For most other migrants, the standard qualifying period for settlement will rise from five to 10 years.

A five-year route will remain for people earning more than £50,000 and workers in public service professions such as doctors, nurses and teachers. Those earning more than £125,000 and people on certain high-talent schemes may qualify after three years.

Applicants will also be expected to meet requirements including having no criminal record, speaking English to a high standard, owing no money to the taxpayer and having made at least three years of National Insurance contributions.

The government says an immigration breach could extend the wait to 20 years. Reuters reported that people who entered the UK illegally by small boat could face a wait of up to 30 years. Some groups, including Hong Kong British nationals, overseas members of the armed forces, people with a British connection and those on legacy routes such as Windrush, will keep their existing settlement pathways.

When will the new rules take effect?

The announcement sets out the government’s policy, but reports on the statement did not give a precise date for when the revised Immigration Rules will take effect. The formal rules and any transitional arrangements will determine how the changes apply to people already in the UK.

title: ConCourt reserves judgment in Kawa and Machingura challenge to CAB3
categories: Crime and Courts; CAA3; CAB3; CDF; Constitution Defenders Forum; Eliphas Kawa; Hazvineyi Machingura; Tendai Biti
summary: The Constitutional Court of Zimbabwe has reserved judgment in a challenge to Constitutional Amendment No. 3 brought by Eliphas Kawa and Hazvineyi Machingura. The recently passed amendment extends President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s term by two years to 2030, postpones the next general election from 2028 to 2030, lengthens the presidential term from five to seven years […]
content_text:
The Constitutional Court of Zimbabwe has reserved judgment in a challenge to Constitutional Amendment No. 3 brought by Eliphas Kawa and Hazvineyi Machingura.

The recently passed amendment extends President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s term by two years to 2030, postpones the next general election from 2028 to 2030, lengthens the presidential term from five to seven years and scraps the direct election of a president, among other changes.

Kawa and Machingura cite the Minister of Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, Parliament, the President and the Attorney General as respondents.

The applicants argue that the amendment cannot take away their right to elect a president of their choice under Section 67 of the Constitution without a referendum. They further contend that the president’s appointment of 10 senators undermines the basic structure of the Constitution.

Mnangagwa signed the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment No. 3 Bill into law on 7 July 2026. It is now Act No. 6 of 2026.

When first tabled in the National Assembly, the Bill secured 216 votes, 29 more than the two-thirds majority required, while 42 CCC MPs voted against it.

Legal experts have questioned whether the amendment can lawfully apply to Mnangagwa’s current term without first being approved in a national referendum. The MDC has filed a separate urgent application at the Constitutional Court arguing that Section 328(6) required a referendum before the president assented.

The Kawa and Machingura application is one of several challenges to the amendments currently pending before the courts.

In a statement issued on Monday, 2 November, after the hearing at the Constitutional Court in Harare, the Constitution Defenders Forum (CDF) said it was awaiting the court’s determination.

“The Constitutional Court of Zimbabwe has reserved judgment in the matter brought by Eliphas Kawa and Hazvineyi Machingura, concerning Constitutional Amendment No. 3. We await the Court’s determination on this important constitutional matter,” the CDF said.

The Forum, led by former Finance Minister Tendai Biti, thanked citizens who attended the proceedings and those who expressed solidarity from across the country and abroad.

“We extend our sincere gratitude to every citizen who attended today’s court proceedings, as well as Zimbabweans at home and across the globe who expressed solidarity through various platforms and channels. Your support and commitment to the defence of constitutionalism are deeply appreciated,” it said.

“As the Constitution Defenders Forum, we remain resolute in our commitment to intensify and escalate our peaceful, lawful and constitutional efforts to restore constitutionalism in Zimbabwe.

“While we await the Court’s judgment, our determination to defend constitutional supremacy, democratic governance and the rights of the people remains unwavering. The struggle to restore constitutionalism continues!”

title: Zimbabwe gazettes landmark oil and gas deal for Cabora Bassa
categories: Mining; Cabora Bassa Oil and Gas project; Invictus; Invictus Energy; Invictus Energy Limited; Musuma-1; Muzarabani Oil And Gas Project; Muzarabini oil and gas project
summary: Zimbabwe has gazetted a Petroleum Production Sharing Agreement (PPSA) for the Cabora Bassa Project in the north of the country, setting the long-term rules that will govern how oil and gas will be explored, developed and produced. Gazetting the agreement means it has been formally published by the Government and is now law. It completes […]
content_text:
Zimbabwe has gazetted a Petroleum Production Sharing Agreement (PPSA) for the Cabora Bassa Project in the north of the country, setting the long-term rules that will govern how oil and gas will be explored, developed and produced.

Gazetting the agreement means it has been formally published by the Government and is now law. It completes the formal requirements for the deal between Zimbabwe, Australian Stock Exchange-listed Invictus Energy as the operator, and its subsidiary Geo Associates as the licence holder.

The PPSA is the main contract between Government and the company. It sets out the legal, tax and commercial framework for the entire life of the project – from exploration and appraisal to development and production. Without it, the project cannot move from searching for gas to actually producing and selling it.

The PPSA gives the company protection against future changes to laws or tax structures that could affect its investment. It also provides what the industry calls regulatory and fiduciary certainty – a clear and stable set of rules that banks and large energy partners need before they commit heavy funding.

Large-scale energy development requires what are known as farm-out partners – other companies that come in to share the cost and risk of development. Reaching the gazettal milestone gives those prospective strategic and financing partners the confidence to invest in advancing the Mukuyu discovery and unlocking the wider Cabora Bassa resource.

The PPSA is the formal contract both Invictus and the Government need to transition the pioneering Cabora Bassa project from exploration into commercial production.

After drilling its first exploratory wells, known as wildcat wells, at Mukuyu-1 and Mukuyu-2, Invictus confirmed that there is a working petroleum system in the basin.

The company estimates a portfolio-wide resource base of about 4.2 trillion cubic feet of gas and 264 million barrels of condensate on a gross mean unrisked basis. Condensate is a very light oil found together with gas. Broader basin estimates are even higher.

Following that discovery, Invictus is now in the appraisal phase. This is the next step after a discovery, where the company measures how big the resource is, whether it is commercially viable and how much can actually be recovered as reserves.

The company is also preparing to start exploration drilling at a new target in the same basin, called Musuma-1. Musuma-1 is a separate prospect that is estimated to hold about 1.2 trillion cubic feet of gas and 73 million barrels of condensate.

If appraisal and further exploration are successful, the Cabora Bassa Project would be Zimbabwe’s first commercial oil and gas development.

title: Bulawayo Oil Plant Nears Completion, Set to Create 400 Jobs
summary: A new oil processing plant in Bulawayo is nearing completion with the project expected to create up to 400 direct jobs and provide business opportunities for local farmers, transport operators and small-scale entrepreneurs. The facility, which is about 85% complete will process soya beans into […]
content_text:
A new oil processing plant in Bulawayo is nearing completion with the project expected to create up to 400 direct jobs and provide business opportunities for local farmers, transport operators and small-scale entrepreneurs.

The facility, which is about 85% complete will process soya beans into cooking oil, incorporating grain storage, oil extraction, refining and bottling operations in an integrated production system.

Fats & Feeds Sub-Manager Zacharia Mupachike said construction was progressing with about 65% of the required equipment having arrived at the site.

The investment is expected to strengthen the country’s manufacturing capacity by increasing domestic processing and adding value to agricultural produce.

The project includes storage tanks with a capacity of about 250 000 litres each and grain silos capable of holding approximately 5 000 metric tonnes apiece.

“These facilities are expected to provide substantial storage capacity for raw materials, helping the business manage supplies and support continuous production,” Mupachike said during a tour of the facility by the Minister of Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services, Zhemu Soda

The infrastructure is designed to support the handling of agricultural inputs and maintain a steady supply of raw materials for industrial processing.

The development comes as Zimbabwe seeks to expand domestic manufacturing, reduce reliance on imported finished products and increase value addition across key economic sectors.

The plant has already provided employment during its construction phase with 276 workers on site at the time of the visit.

Mupachike said most of the workers had been recruited locally while 25 were from outside the area.

Young people and women have also participated in construction activities while a local contractor from Bulawayo has been involved in the project.

Once operational, the facility is expected to employ between 300 and 400 people directly, although the final number will depend on the company’s staffing requirements and the scale of production.

The investment is also expected to generate indirect employment through demand for transport, vehicle maintenance, catering and other support services.

The facility is also incorporating renewable energy with solar panels being installed on rooftops and a separate solar power installation under development.

The system is expected to provide an additional source of electricity and potentially help manage energy costs and improve operational efficiency.

Reliable power supplies remain important for manufacturers seeking to maintain production and remain competitive.

Bulawayo has historically been one of the country’s major industrial centres and the new investment could help strengthen its manufacturing base.

title: Bosso fight back from a goal down to beat CAPS and book Chibuku Super Cup final spot

summary: Highlanders will face Hardrock in the Chibuku Super Cup final after beating CAPS United 3-1 on penalties in the second semi-final at Rufaro Stadium on Sunday. content_text:
Highlanders will face Hardrock in the Chibuku Super Cup final after beating CAPS United 3-1 on penalties in the second semi-final at Rufaro Stadium on Sunday.

The teams were deadlocked at 1-1 after 90 minutes.

CAPS United took the lead in the 61st minute when David Marowa unleashed a rising shot from the edge of the box that crashed in off the underside of the crossbar to beat Aron Ngwenya. The goal came after a scramble in the Highlanders box, with Bosso failing to clear a free-kick delivery and the ball falling to Marowa inside the area.

Ngwenya produced a point-blank save to deny United a second goal but picked up an injury in the process and was replaced by substitute goalkeeper Reward Muza in the 78th minute.

Highlanders had the final say 10 minutes from time. Andrew Mbeba swung in a free-kick that found Reason Sibanda at the far post, and the defender rose highest to head the equaliser and force a shoot-out.

Muza was the hero in the shoot-out, saving two spot-kicks. Nyasha Gurende had his effort saved, Obey Chirinda blasted over the bar, and Alleny Mukombedzi was also denied by Muza, with only Lloyd Njaliwa scoring for United from their first four kicks.

Highlanders were clinical, converting all three through Rainsome Pavari, Isaac Ngoma and Mongameli Tshuma to book their place in the final.

Hardrock secured the other final berth on Saturday after recovering from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 with FC Hunters.

Prince Dube struck twice in the final 10 minutes for Kelvin Kaindu’s side before they prevailed 5-4 on penalties.

The final will be played on 28 November at Hardrock’s Chahwanda Stadium in Kwekwe. The Video Assistant Referee system will be used for the first time in Zimbabwe during the match.

The event will be held in honour of the late actor Lazarus ‘Gringo’ Boora’s legacy in the entertainment industry.

The programme will feature a soccer tournament and a musical gala showcasing Zimbabwean musicians, gospel artists, content creators and other performers.

The event is expected to draw football enthusiasts, music lovers, artists and community members for a celebration combining sport, music and social interaction.

Beyond entertainment, the festival seeks to celebrate local talent, promote local culture and strengthen community ties by creating a platform for artists and other players in the creative industry to connect and exchange experiences.

The combination of football and live performances is also expected to provide opportunities for emerging and established entertainers to showcase their skills to a wider audience.

Community festivals have become an important platform for bringing people together while providing artists with opportunities to reach new audiences and build networks within Zimbabwe’s growing creative sector.

Organisers are expected to welcome attendee for a full day of activities, with the free-entry arrangement allowing members of the community to participate without paying an admission fee.

title: Nitefreak teams up with Dr Feel on Afro House project

The track will feature on Inner Visions, a compilation bringing together Zimbabwean producers, DJs and vocalists. The […]
content_text:
Bulawayo-born Afro House DJ and producer Nitefreak has teamed up with Zimbabwean DJ and producer Dr Feel on a new collaboration titled BYO 2 Luanda , featuring on a compilation celebrating Zimbabwe’s contribution to the global Afro House movement.

The track will feature on Inner Visions , a compilation bringing together Zimbabwean producers, DJs and vocalists. The project, released through South African label Mansa Musa, is scheduled to drop on November 27, 2026.

Nitefreak, born Bhekinkosi Melusi Mabhena, is among Zimbabwe’s most internationally recognised electronic music artists, with performances at major venues and festivals across Europe, North America, South America and Asia.

He has gained international recognition through tracks such as Gorah and his remix of Premier Gaou , both of which have surpassed 100 million Spotify streams.

His remix of the Magic System classic, produced in collaboration with Francis Mercier, has also achieved Platinum certification in France.

The collaboration with Dr Feel brings together two Zimbabwean artists whose work connects the country’s electronic music scene with international audiences.

The compilation features a wider group of Zimbabwean producers and DJs, including DJ Stavo, DJ MidTempo, Ryan Synth, MIčI, Reverb, TAPIWA and Simbai, among others.

Kenyan singer Victoria Kimani also features on the project, contributing vocals and songwriting to Joy , alongside Dr Feel and DJ Stavo.

The release comes amid growing international interest in Afro House, a genre rooted in African musical traditions that has gained increasing popularity at international clubs and festivals.

According to Splice and MIDiA Research’s Sounds of 2026 report, Afro House downloads on music-production platform Splice increased from approximately 760,355 in 2024 to 6.67 million in 2025.

Nitefreak has also built platforms to promote African electronic music, including HiNDE, launched in Zimbabwe in 2021 and subsequently expanded to cities such as New York, Miami and Mauritius.

Inner Visions is expected to spotlight Zimbabwean talent and strengthen the country’s visibility in the expanding international Afro House industry.

title: Promised Report, No Answers: Why Wicknell Chivayo’s Mysterious Accident Investigation Is Still Waiting as Police Await Other Agencies
keywords: news
summary: More than a month after the helicopter crash that killed businessman Wicknell Chivayo, his wife and three others, Zimbabwe’s police say they are still waiting for findings from other agencies before a consolidated investigation report can be issued. The Bell 430 helicopter went down at Kudenga Farm in rural Marondera on September 30, killing all […] The post Promised Report, No Answers: Why Wicknell Chivayo’s Mysterious Accident Investigation Is Still Waiting as Police Await Other Agencies first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
More than a month after the helicopter crash that killed businessman Wicknell Chivayo, his wife and three others, Zimbabwe’s police say they are still waiting for findings from other agencies before a consolidated investigation report can be issued.

The Bell 430 helicopter went down at Kudenga Farm in rural Marondera on September 30, killing all five people aboard. The deadline for a preliminary report, announced by the Government in the days after the crash, passed at the end of October without findings being made public.

Police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said the inquiry involved several state bodies and was not being handled by the Zimbabwe Republic Police alone.

“Remember, the government set up a team to investigate the matter, and we are waiting for other members to submit their findings before a consolidated report is issued,” Nyathi said. “It’s not solely the responsibility of the ZRP — other agencies are also involved.”

Nyathi gave no date for the report’s release. The delay leaves unanswered the central question of what caused the aircraft to crash, even as investigators have moved from the scene to a more detailed examination of the wreckage and records connected with the flight.

The helicopter was travelling from Gandami in Chikomba District towards Marondera after Chivayo had been visiting a property where construction work was under way. It crashed about 40 minutes after take-off. The five people named by police were Chivayo, his wife Lucy Muteke, her aide Sanelisiwe Magagula, pilot Captain Calvin Soda and co-pilot Captain Courage Mutavirwa.

An initial public account gave the number of people aboard as six. Police later confirmed there were five occupants and named them, a figure repeated in the Government’s Cabinet briefing on the crash.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe said early observations at the scene showed that fuel spilled after impact and a fire burnt grass around the wreckage. Those observations describe what happened after the helicopter hit the ground; officials have not announced a cause for the crash.

In its October 6 briefing, Cabinet said the preliminary on-site examination had been completed and the wreckage taken to the Government hangar at Charles Prince Airport. The aircraft was to undergo detailed forensic examination with international experts. Information Minister Zhemu Soda said the preliminary report would cover the wreckage, weather conditions, maintenance records, and information about the helicopter’s operator and crew.

The report was expected within 30 days of the September 30 accident. It was intended to provide an initial account of the inquiry’s findings, not simply a description of the scene. No public update has since set out what the forensic examination has established or whether investigators have completed work on the flight and maintenance records.

The wreckage was recovered after investigators finished at Kudenga Farm. The bodies were also badly damaged in the crash and fire, requiring forensic identification procedures before Chivayo and Muteke could be buried. The couple were laid to rest at Glen Forest Memorial Park in Harare. Magagula and the two pilots were buried separately.

President Emmerson Mnangagwa accorded Chivayo provincial hero status two days after the crash. Mnangagwa and Kenyan President William Ruto, who had both cultivated public friendships with the businessman, paid tribute to him after his death. The scale of the public response reflected the sharply divided views Chivayo had attracted during his life: some people celebrated his high-profile gifts, while others saw his conspicuous wealth and closeness to political leaders as emblematic of a system shaped by state contracts and patronage.

Chivayo was one of Zimbabwe’s most visible business figures. He posted images of luxury cars, designer clothes and meetings with political leaders on social media, and became known as “Sir Wicknell” for his public gifts of vehicles and money to musicians, church figures, sports personalities and political supporters.

His business career had long drawn scrutiny. In 2005, he was convicted in a money-laundering case and served 3 years of a 5-year prison sentence. He later founded Intratrek Zimbabwe, an engineering and construction company that secured a major contract to build the Gwanda solar power plant for state-owned Zimbabwe Power Company. The project remained stalled for years, and the company received an advance payment of about US$5 million.

The solar project became the subject of a criminal case involving allegations over the advance payment. Chivayo denied wrongdoing. The case was struck from the court roll in 2023 after delays by prosecutors, while a separate contract dispute ended with an order requiring the power company either to perform the contract or pay Intratrek US$22 million. Chivayo was acquitted of fraud in that matter.

His political visibility grew further in 2026 when he announced a US$3.6 million donation for Members of Parliament and senators, describing it as funding for constituency development. He later withdrew that pledge and offered US$5 million through ZANU-PF provincial structures, ahead of a proposed constitutional vote linked to extending Mnangagwa’s term in office. The donation became another flashpoint around Chivayo’s relationship with the ruling party and the access enjoyed by wealthy businesspeople with government-linked contracts.

The crash has brought that public attention back to the state agencies now responsible for explaining how the helicopter came down. At the time of the October Cabinet briefing, officials said the inquiry would draw on physical evidence from the wreckage as well as weather, maintenance, operator and crew records. Police now say they cannot issue a consolidated account until the other members of the investigation team submit their findings.

For the families of the five people who died, the investigation concerns the circumstances of a fatal flight. For the wider public, the unanswered questions remain attached to one of the country’s most prominent and divisive businessmen. More than 30 days after the Government set out its expected timetable, officials have not announced when the preliminary report will be released.

title: POLAD CAR CRASHES: Madhuku in accident on way to CAB3 challenger’s son’s funeral; vehicle extensively damaged after hitting trees (VIDEO)
keywords: news
summary: Constitutional lawyer and National Constitutional Assembly leader Professor Lovemore Madhuku escaped injury after his vehicle left a gravel road and struck trees in the Humani Ranch area of Chiredzi on Saturday, October 31. Madhuku was travelling from Harare to attend the funeral of 15-year-old Trevor, the son of Vhurande Mahlupeko, a National Constitutional Assembly member […] The post POLAD CAR CRASHES: Madhuku in accident on way to CAB3 challenger’s son’s funeral; vehicle extensively damaged after hitting trees (VIDEO) first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
Constitutional lawyer and National Constitutional Assembly leader Professor Lovemore Madhuku escaped injury after his vehicle left a gravel road and struck trees in the Humani Ranch area of Chiredzi on Saturday, October 31.

Madhuku was travelling from Harare to attend the funeral of 15-year-old Trevor, the son of Vhurande Mahlupeko, a National Constitutional Assembly member who is among the people challenging Constitution Amendment Act No. 3. The vehicle was extensively damaged in the crash, but Madhuku said he and another occupant were unharmed.

“I was travelling on a gravel road from Harare to Chiredzi to attend the funeral. They were waiting for me, and I was rushing to get there when the vehicle skidded, veered off the road and hit a tree. The vehicle was extensively damaged, but fortunately, the other occupant and I escaped without any injuries,” Madhuku said.

He described the road as gravel and said the vehicle skidded before going off the road and hitting a tree. Reports identified it as an Isuzu double-cab allocated to him by President Mnangagwa through the Political Actors Dialogue programme, known as POLAD. Madhuku later described the crash as not serious. “It wasn’t a serious accident,” he said.

The crash drew attention because of its timing and Madhuku’s role in several legal challenges to the constitutional amendment. Posts on social media speculated that the accident might have been deliberately caused to intimidate him or interfere with the court cases. Madhuku rejected that suggestion, saying the crash was caused by the vehicle skidding on the road.

“I have seen some speculation suggesting that there could have been foul play, with some people alleging that the accident might have been influenced by the Constitutional Amendment Act No. 3 court hearings. No, I am very much alive to what happened. It was an accident,” he said.

Madhuku was travelling to the village for the funeral of Mahlupeko’s son. Mahlupeko is a complainant in one of the Constitutional Court cases against the amendment, and Madhuku is representing him. The journey was therefore to a family funeral as well as an event involving a close colleague whose case he is handling.

The case is scheduled to be heard by the Constitutional Court on November 11. Mahlupeko is asking the court to invalidate the entire Act, arguing that 10 provisions were added to the final legislation after the original Bill had been published for public review. His challenge says the public did not receive the required 90-day notice to consider those provisions before they were introduced in Parliament.

The hearing is expected to consider that procedural challenge alongside a separate application by former opposition MP Prince Dubeko Sibanda. His case challenges the extension of presidential and parliamentary terms from five years to seven, including the application of the longer terms to current officeholders.

The amendment, signed into law by President Emmerson Mnangagwa on July 7, 2026, became Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment Act No. 3 of 2026. Its provisions extend the presidential and parliamentary terms and change how the President is selected. The legislation moves the next general election from 2028 to 2030 and replaces the direct election of the President by voters with selection through Parliament.

Madhuku has represented people challenging different parts of the changes. The applications have raised questions about the public consultation process, the effect of the term extension on leaders already in office, and the right of citizens to elect the President directly. Mahlupeko’s case centres on the route taken to pass the Act, while Sibanda’s focuses on whether the longer terms can benefit current officeholders.

The November 11 hearing will bring those two challenges before the court on the same day. The court is also due to hear another challenge on November 25, filed by the Movement for Democratic Change, which argues that removing the direct presidential vote required a national referendum.

The accident happened as preparations continued for the funeral and as the court cases moved towards their scheduled hearings. Madhuku’s damaged vehicle left him unable to continue the journey in it, but he said the crash did not injure him or the other occupant. The incident did not prevent him from making clear that he rejected claims of political interference.

His journey had begun in Harare and was taking him to Chiredzi to be with Mahlupeko and his family at a difficult time. The crash, in a rural area of the district, turned that trip into a frightening detour before the funeral. But Madhuku’s account was direct: the vehicle skidded on the gravel, left the road and struck a tree.

The vehicle sustained extensive damage, while its occupants escaped without injury. As the November hearing approaches, Madhuku remains part of the legal team pursuing the challenge brought by Mahlupeko, the bereaved father whose son’s funeral he had been travelling to attend.

title: He Cried in His Coffin… Uncles Had Warned Him! – Manicaland dead man sheds tears at his funeral, grave found tempered with
keywords: news
summary: A family in Hauna, Manicaland, is seeking answers after mourners said they saw tears streaming from the eyes of 26-year-old Walter Kupemba Jnr as he lay in his coffin. The following morning, relatives returning to his grave found marks on the fresh earth, footprints leading away and a stone shifted from its position at the […] The post He Cried in His Coffin… Uncles Had Warned Him! – Manicaland dead man sheds tears at his funeral, grave found tempered with first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
A family in Hauna, Manicaland, is seeking answers after mourners said they saw tears streaming from the eyes of 26-year-old Walter Kupemba Jnr as he lay in his coffin. The following morning, relatives returning to his grave found marks on the fresh earth, footprints leading away and a stone shifted from its position at the head of the grave.

Kupemba was buried last Friday after his health deteriorated rapidly. He died at Victoria Chitepo Provincial Hospital on Wednesday, leaving relatives struggling to understand both his sudden death and what they say happened during and after the funeral.

His mother, Gladys Tangwena, said staff at the funeral parlour first alerted the family to what appeared to be tears on her son’s face. She later saw the liquid herself when the coffin was opened. Family members wiped it away, she said, but it appeared again while she and her sisters carried out traditional rites observed by a deceased person’s mother.

“They wiped the tears away, but when my sisters and I later performed some traditional rituals observed by a deceased person’s mother, the tears started flowing again. It was not just a few drops. It appeared as if he was weeping, especially from the right eye. It was as though he was alive and crying. I was devastated and could not bring myself to view the body again,” she said.

Tangwena said other mourners who viewed the body also noticed what appeared to be tears. The family eventually went ahead with the burial, although she said the unusual sight had left them distressed.

The next morning, relatives returned for rumuko, a traditional ritual performed after burial. Tangwena said they found marks at the upper end of the newly covered grave, including what looked like footprints going away from it. A stone placed at the head of the grave also appeared to have moved.

“There were marks on the upper end of the grave that looked as if someone had sat there. We also noticed footprints leading away from the grave. Some appeared human, while others resembled those of a four-legged animal,” she said.

Her son’s death followed a swift decline that began after he came home from Sagambe complaining of a toothache. Tangwena said his neck later became swollen and he lost the ability to speak. When he was admitted to Victoria Chitepo Provincial Hospital, he could communicate only through sign language.

Walter had been working in Sagambe and was building a seven-roomed house, his mother said. She described him as hardworking and ambitious, and said the family had not expected to lose him so suddenly.

Tangwena said she was frightened by the circumstances and had considered leaving the family home with her two daughters. She also alleged that her son had previously been involved in a dispute with one of his uncles, whom she said had threatened him. She did not say that the uncle was responsible for his illness or for the events at the grave.

“I do not know what happened to my son or why these strange things are happening after his death. Sometimes I even think of leaving our home with my daughters because I am afraid,” she said.

Walter Kupemba Snr, the deceased man’s uncle and namesake, said relatives and community members had also seen what appeared to be tears at the funeral. He said the family wanted to understand what had happened and had begun consulting traditional healers. One was expected to visit their homestead. The relatives also planned to go to Sagambe to ask whether Walter Jnr had faced disputes or difficulties before he became ill.

“It was the first time I had ever seen such a thing. We were all shocked. As a family, we want to understand what happened and what caused his death,” Kupemba Snr said.

He said he had also seen the marks on the grave during rumuko. “It was shocking to find marks that looked as if someone had sat on a fresh grave. We also saw footprints leading away from it. We want to establish exactly what happened there,” he said.

The Hauna family’s account recalls other Zimbabwean funeral reports in which relatives and mourners described seeing tears on a deceased person’s face. The cases have been reported in different communities over several years, each with its own circumstances and family response.

In July 2020, relatives in Chigodora, near Mutare, said the body of 42-year-old Chandapiwa Makaza, also known as Chandapiwa Bushu, appeared to weep after being placed in a mortuary. The report said she had died following an incident in which she was attacked by a rooster. Her body was said to have appeared to weep 2 days after it was taken to the mortuary, as relatives and friends gathered for the funeral. The unusual sight added to the distress around a death that had already unsettled people in the area.

A later account of the rooster incident said the bird’s owner, Zvikomborero Takarinda, was expected to appear before a traditional leader’s court to explain what had happened. Acting Chief Zimunya said the matter had drawn attention because of the circumstances surrounding Makaza’s death. The funeral account and the subsequent traditional-court proceedings were separate developments, but both kept the case in public discussion in the months that followed.

Another reported case came from Mateta Village in Gokwe South in February 2014. Mourners viewing Alexander Zigara’s body said fresh tears appeared to be flowing from his eyes, briefly halting burial proceedings. Reports at the time said the 40-something man had been found dead in his bedroom hut the previous day and had not been known to complain of illness. Relatives consulted traditional healers, and some villagers took the apparent tears as support for claims that he had been bewitched. The next day, his grave was also said to have been disturbed. Those details were part of the reported family and village response; they were not described as findings from a medical examination.

A 2012 case involving 33-year-old Tsitsi Tekere was reported in Epworth. Mourners said tears rolled down her cheeks while her body was being transported from Chivhu to Harare. Her burial was already troubled by a dispute over where she should be laid to rest: people close to her said she had wanted to be buried in Chivhu, while she was ultimately buried in Epworth. On the morning of the burial, relatives also said the grave had filled with soil after it had been dug. Her father rejected the idea that the filled grave was mysterious and suspected a nearby resident following a confrontation over the site.

The earlier accounts show how a sight described as tears can become part of a family’s wider effort to make sense of a death, particularly when other upsetting events are said to have taken place around the funeral or grave. In Hauna, the family is now focused on finding out what happened to Walter Jnr before his death and what caused the marks they found at his burial place.

For Tangwena, the memories are inseparable: her son’s sudden illness, the apparent tears in his coffin and the signs on the grave the morning after the burial. Her relatives say they will continue asking questions in Sagambe and at their homestead as they seek answers about the young man they had expected to see complete the house he was building.

title: The Unseen Financial Opportunities Behind EI Nino
summary: When the sky holds back its rains, a nation is forced to look deeper at where its true economic resilience lies. Speaking from my perspective as a financial advisor, Treasury’s recent pre-budget adjustment scaling our 2027 economic growth forecast down from 5% to 3.5% anchored […]
content_text:
When the sky holds back its rains, a nation is forced to look deeper at where its true economic resilience lies.

Speaking from my perspective as a financial advisor, Treasury’s recent pre-budget adjustment scaling our 2027 economic growth forecast down from 5% to 3.5% anchored on the anticipated realities of an El Niño induced cropping season and tightening global financial conditions is not a sign of defeat.

Instead, it is a clarion call for strategic realism, fiscal discipline, and aggressive market innovation.

With over 60% of our population tied directly to agriculture , a dry spell in the fields naturally triggers a consumer consumption squeeze, rippling outward through retail, manufacturing, and financial services.

This climate driven contraction collides directly with global economic headwinds, including volatile international energy prices, high freight shipping costs, and tighter global credit conditions that inflate the price of imported goods.

For ordinary citizens and enterprises, this dual pressure creates real vulnerability.

Jobs in agriculture-dependent supply chains, formal agro-processing, retail merchandising, and traditional manufacturing face immediate risk as operating margins tighten and consumer demand contracts.

Similarly, small businesses and informal traders the backbone of our local commerce are grappling with rising operational costs, inventory replacement challenges, and declining customer purchasing power.

Yet, small businesses and informal enterprises can survive and thrive by pivoting toward lean inventory models, diversifying into fast-moving daily essentials, adopting digital record-keeping, and forming collaborative buying cooperatives to cut wholesale costs.

Looking at this as someone inside the insurance sector, this environment demands that we entirely rethink how we protect families and how we sell essential covers like life and funeral insurance.

In times of economic hardship, people view traditional long-term policies as expensive luxuries they can no longer afford.

To overcome this, we must change where and how we sell. We cannot wait in our offices in urban CBDs; we must meet people where their cash actually moves ,inside bustling market stalls, at artisanal mining trading hubs, and through community-based networks.

Funeral and life insurance must be sold not as abstract future investments, but as immediate, dignity-preserving shields for today.

When a household operates on hand-to-mouth cash reserves, the sudden burden of a funeral or a medical emergency can completely wipe out generations of savings.

To make insurance irresistible, we must introduce bite-sized, low-cost economy line micro-policies tied directly to everyday micro-transactions, such as mobile money platforms, grocery purchases, or weekly airtime deductions.

By partnering with trusted local structures like burial societies, savings clubs (rounds), and informal trader associations, we embed insurance into existing community trust frameworks.

True economic analysis requires looking past headline contractions to find where the wealth is migrating.

El Niño does not destroy national liquidity; it redistributes it. Trust me, a lot of people are going to make a lot of money in 2027.

While traditional farming faces immense pressure, shifting rural markets toward survival trade and diaspora support billions of dollars in physical cash flow dynamically through resilient, dollar-earning sectors.

The true liquidity engines of today are thumping loud and clear in our mineral-rich gold and lithium belts across the country , alongside a thriving international tourism sector in Victoria Falls and the Eastern Highlands.

For the financial and life insurance sectors, this environment presents an extraordinary opportunity to pivot.

Financial institutions must aggressively ring-fence their existing client bases through flexible policy terms and payment holidays while expanding into these high-liquidity informal and mining markets.

Ultimately, economic winters do not last forever. By aligning our financial strategies with liquid mining and tourism corridors, empowering small businesses to adapt, and delivering micro-insurance solutions that protect the everyday citizen, we can turn the El Niño challenge into our most transformative economic catalyst.

The views, analysis, and opinions expressed in this piece are shared strictly by Jeoffrey Ncube in his personal capacity as a storyteller, financial advisor, and digital marketing consultant, and do not represent the official policy, position, or endorsement of any employer, government institution, or affiliated organization.

title: 15 armed robbery cases in just 2 weeks: Man (30) terrorises Zimbabweans back home after being deported from South Africa
keywords: news
summary: BEITBRIDGE — A 30-year-old man deported from South Africa has appeared in court facing 15 armed-robbery charges over attacks allegedly carried out in Beitbridge within about 2 weeks of his return. Courage Siziba, also known as Tafadzwa, is accused of targeting residents, motorists and businesses between September 24 and October 8, 2026. The property involved […] The post 15 armed robbery cases in just 2 weeks: Man (30) terrorises Zimbabweans back home after being deported from South Africa first appeared on My Zimbabwe News .
content_text:
BEITBRIDGE — A 30-year-old man deported from South Africa has appeared in court facing 15 armed-robbery charges over attacks allegedly carried out in Beitbridge within about 2 weeks of his return.

Courage Siziba, also known as Tafadzwa, is accused of targeting residents, motorists and businesses between September 24 and October 8, 2026. The property involved in the Beitbridge cases includes R13,510, US$2,917 and more than 15 mobile phones and tablets.

Siziba told the court that he had been deported from South Africa because he did not have a passport. He said he had worked as a construction worker there. He is from Madhibhanjenje Village in Mberengwa.

The allegations describe a series of attacks across Beitbridge, including robberies in the New Medium Density suburb, an attack on a service station and an incident involving a 12-year-old girl. The court heard that Siziba is also accused of kidnapping the child and taking her to a bushy area.

The first incident in the court account happened at about 10pm on September 24 at a bus stop near Redan Service Station on the Beitbridge-Bulawayo Highway. Siziba and an alleged accomplice, Trust Mugombe, are accused of pointing pistols at Phillip Tamuka Mudare and Terminage John Mazita and taking US$55 and 2 mobile phones. Mugombe is still wanted by police.

The following day, Siziba allegedly went to New Medium Density. He is accused of firing a shot into the air before taking 2 phones from waitress Moreblessing Ruzvidzo. He is also accused of robbing Elliard Zhou of cash and a Samsung A07 mobile phone.

The State says further robberies followed in the same suburb. Hollen Kazamula, Kudzanai Nerufure and Audrey Zonke were allegedly robbed of amounts including R2,500, R3,000, R1,000 and US$50.

At about 3.20am on September 27, Siziba allegedly entered Energy Park Service Station while armed and forced staff to open the safe. The court account says US$2,382 was taken from the safe, along with US$70 and US$200 from workers. Police have separately described the service-station robbery as part of a wider series of attacks on businesses and motorists in the area.

The alleged attacks continued into October. On October 8, Sophia Gwinji was reportedly robbed of R6,310 and 2 phones, while Melody Gomwe was allegedly robbed of US$100 and an iPhone. A nurse in the Hawkflight area was also reportedly robbed of 4 phones, tablets and cash.

Some of the stolen property was recovered after detectives took Siziba to Bulawayo. The court account refers to the recovery of a Rossi revolver and a silver pistol. Police said a search after his arrest uncovered a Rossi .38 Special revolver loaded with 5 rounds, as well as 16 additional rounds of ammunition in his satchel.

Police say the investigation covers a longer period and a wider range of offences than the 15 Beitbridge robbery counts. Detective Inspector Rachel Muteweri, a spokesperson for the Criminal Investigations Department, said: “Between August 14 and October 8, 2026, the suspect, armed with a firearm, went on a robbery spree, targeting residential properties, business premises and motorists in and around Beitbridge,” she said.

In one case, Siziba allegedly hired a taxi driver on September 17, pretending he needed to collect a parcel. He is accused of driving away in the driver’s Toyota Spade, valued at US$9,000. The vehicle was later recovered intact in Beitbridge.

Police also say a vehicle valued at R250,000 was stolen from a carport in Beitbridge on September 26. It was later traced to Zvishavane after it had been involved in a crash and was recovered damaged.

The police account also links Siziba to 2 armed-robbery cases in Mberengwa. Property valued at US$38,215, R262,900 and ZiG13,000 was reportedly stolen in those cases. Police said property valued at US$35,100 and R250,000 had been recovered.

Siziba is facing 15 counts of armed robbery, as well as charges linked to kidnapping, rape, unlawful entry and theft, and motor-vehicle theft, police said. He was arrested on October 21. He appeared in court on October 23, and was later remanded in custody to November 2 to receive medical attention.

Police credited members of the public with providing information that led to his arrest. They also said Mugombe remained at large. The police statement said: “The Zimbabwe Republic Police commends members of the public for providing credible information that led to the suspect’s arrest.

“The Zimbabwe Republic Police is now on the trail of the outstanding suspect, Trust Mugombe. We are now appealing for information that may lead to his arrest.”

Siziba’s case is not the first to involve Zimbabweans returned from South Africa and robbery proceedings in Beitbridge. In 2023, four men who were based in South Africa were sentenced in Beitbridge to 12 years in prison each for armed robbery. They had been arrested at a roadblock in South Africa after robbing a pirate taxi driver and were found with firearms before being deported to Zimbabwe.

Another case this year involved Justin Mpofu, who was deported from South Africa after hiding there for 15 years. Zimbabwean detectives wanted him in connection with a 2010 murder and armed robbery in which a man was fatally shot and property was taken from a bottle store. After his return, he was arrested and appeared in court. The case concerns an older alleged offence for which he had been wanted, rather than a new robbery said to have taken place after his deportation.

The Beitbridge case comes as Zimbabwe and South Africa move to establish a system for transferring sentenced prisoners between the 2 countries. The governments signed a memorandum of understanding in August 2026. It provides for eligible prisoners to serve the remainder of their sentences in their home countries and also covers wider cooperation between correctional services.

South Africa has more than 4,000 Zimbabwean nationals in its correctional facilities, while Zimbabwe has just 12 South African prisoners. However, the figure of more than 4,000 describes the Zimbabwean prison population in South Africa; it is not a published number of people confirmed for immediate transfer. The agreement does not say that every Zimbabwean prisoner will be moved at once. Prisoners transferred under the arrangement would continue serving their sentences in Zimbabwe. This arrangement, however, will likely result in an increase in crime rate as some of these inmates may be forced by the tough economic situation in Zimbabwe to commit crimes that got them arrested in South Africa where they have been seeking greener pastures.

For Beitbridge residents, the alleged attacks attributed to Siziba unfolded over a short period and ranged from street robberies to attacks on homes, workers and businesses. Detectives are still seeking Mugombe, while Siziba remains in custody as the case proceeds.

title: Nine killed as private jet plunges into Florida neighbourhood and explodes
categories: Accidents; International; News; United States; Aviation; Florida; Greenacres; Learjet 60; National Transportation Safety Board; Palm Beach County; plane crash; Ron DeSantis; Sean Duffy
keywords: Aviation; Florida; Greenacres; Learjet 60; National Transportation Safety Board; Palm Beach County; plane crash; Ron DeSantis; Sean Duffy; United States
summary: Nine people have been killed after a private Learjet plunged into a Florida neighbourhood and exploded, leaving a large crater near homes and passing vehicles.
content_text:
Nine people were killed when a private jet plunged into a residential neighbourhood in South Florida and erupted into a massive fireball, narrowly missing homes and motorists.

The Learjet 60 crashed near Military Trail in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, at approximately 12.50pm local time on Sunday.

All nine people aboard the aircraft died, United States Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed. There were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries among people on the ground.

The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was travelling to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas.

Video footage of the incident showed the aircraft descending at a steep angle before striking the ground and exploding close to a busy roadway. The impact left a large crater, scattered wreckage across the surrounding area and damaged local infrastructure.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the crash as “cataclysmic”, saying the aircraft appeared to fall “like a missile”.

“It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road,” he said after visiting the scene.

Pilots reported icing and turbulence

Air-traffic control recordings and flight-tracking data indicate that the jet had been flying east at approximately 35,000 feet when its pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation.

The crew requested permission to climb by another 2,000 feet, but the situation deteriorated rapidly.

One of the pilots declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at thousands of feet per minute.

“We’re descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.

The jet reportedly descended about 27,000 feet in one minute and accelerated beyond its design limits before crashing.

Investigators have not established what caused the aircraft to enter the fatal dive. Although the crew reported ice and severe turbulence, officials cautioned that it was too early to determine whether weather conditions caused the accident.

Heavy rain and thunderstorms were reported in the area, while a flood watch remained in effect.

Hundreds evacuated

Approximately 600 residents from a nearby mobile-home community were evacuated while emergency teams secured the area and federal investigators prepared to examine the wreckage.

Officials said the crash damaged water lines and other infrastructure. Military Trail was closed in both directions, and local authorities warned that sections of the road could remain inaccessible for an extended period.

Witnesses described seeing debris scattered near houses and vehicles, while flames continued burning around the crater left by the impact.

One resident said the aircraft passed so close that it shook his house before crashing less than a kilometre away.

The Federal Aviation Administration has deployed personnel to assist the National Transportation Safety Board, which is leading the investigation.

Investigators are expected to examine the aircraft’s flight controls, weather conditions, maintenance history, cockpit communications and the pilots’ response to the reported icing and turbulence.

The identities of the passengers and crew had not been publicly released.

title: Sympathy is not evidence: Scrutinising Marry Mubaiwa’s claims against Chiwenga
categories: Editor's Choice; Opinion; Constantino Chiwenga; Emmerson Mnangagwa; Gabriel Manyati; Marry Mubaiwa; Pethidine; Simba Chikanza; succession politics; Zanu PF; Zimbabwe politics; ZimEye
keywords: Constantino Chiwenga; Emmerson Mnangagwa; Gabriel Manyati; Marry Mubaiwa; Pethidine; Simba Chikanza; succession politics; Zanu PF; Zimbabwe politics; ZimEye
summary: Marry Mubaiwa’s suffering deserves compassion, but her allegations against Constantino Chiwenga still require evidence, independent verification and careful political scrutiny.
content_text:
In the fevered theatre of Zimbabwean politics, timing is rarely accidental and character is seldom incidental. Marry Mubaiwa’s sudden emergence from seven years of legal limbo into a lengthy, emotionally charged interview with Simba Chikanza of ZimEye is no exception.

Within hours of a Harare magistrate removing her from remand in the attempted-murder case linked to Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga, she delivered a scathing account of their marriage, pethidine use, lost children and presidential unfitness.

The performance arrived less than a fortnight after Chiwenga’s pointed address at the ZANU PF conference in Chinhoyi, where he asked uncomfortable questions about whether the Second Republic was repeating the very mistakes it was created to correct, insisted the party belonged to the people rather than individuals, and called for change driven from below rather than imposed from above.

In the raw succession struggle now consuming the ruling party, Mubaiwa’s testimony functions less as personal catharsis than as convenient ammunition.

Yet before the public elevates a former model and serial marital participant into the arbiter of a Vice-President’s moral fitness, it is necessary to examine the witness herself.

Credibility is not conferred by wheelchair or amputation; it is earned through consistency of conduct. On that score, Mubaiwa’s record is instructive.

Her matrimonial history is a study in serial abandonment and contested claims. She left businessman Terrence Mandizha for then-football star Shingi Kawondera. That union, which produced a daughter, ended when she moved on to the then-Commander of the Defence Forces.

Kawondera has publicly alleged that she played a role in the dissipation of his wealth, including claims surrounding Pioneer Gas and the late Genius “Ginimbi” Kadungure – a relative of Mubaiwa’s through her father’s side.

Kawondera has described forgery of signatures and the loss of assets he says he helped establish. Mubaiwa has dismissed these accusations as fabrications, challenged him to produce evidence in court, and laughed off the suggestion that she and Ginimbi were strangers until Kawondera introduced them.

The dispute remains unresolved in the public domain, but the pattern is clear: relationships end, financial recriminations follow, and the former partner is left to litigate or lament.

The Chiwenga chapter followed a similar trajectory of ascent and collapse. A customary marriage in 2011, three children, the trappings of proximity to power, then acrimony, arrest, and years of litigation.

In 2022 a court found Mubaiwa guilty of forging documents that purported to formalise the union as a civil marriage without Chiwenga’s consent, a conviction that sits uneasily beside any claim to pure victimhood.

Separate allegations have surfaced over the years concerning the handling of security-team allowances during Chiwenga’s illness and other financial disputes.

These are not the footnotes of an otherwise spotless life; they form the texture of a public persona that has repeatedly collided with questions of integrity, loyalty and self-interest.

It is against this backdrop that her latest intervention must be weighed. The interview did not merely catalogue private pain; it delivered political payload. She questioned what kind of president a man who “does unjust things” would make.

She asserted that President Emmerson Mnangagwa knows she never attempted to kill Chiwenga. She linked her health catastrophe to years of alleged pethidine injections ordered by her husband. Claims of this gravity demand scrutiny, not uncritical amplification.

Medical causation between the disputed drug regimen and her amputations has not been independently established in the public record.

Contradictions appear even within her own account – the man she paints as cruel is also the man she acknowledges spent substantial sums on her treatment.

The narrative is long, dramatic and selectively detailed, the classic profile of a propaganda piece that risks collapsing under its own contradictions.

The political utility is harder to miss. Chiwenga’s Chinhoyi speech unsettled those pushing for an extension of Mnangagwa’s tenure beyond constitutional limits. It reasserted the principle that ZANU PF is not personal property and that leadership must remain accountable to the grassroots.

In the days that followed, factional temperature rose. Then, with exquisite timing, the ex-wife who had been legally constrained for nearly seven years was freed from remand and promptly given a high-profile platform to attack the vice president’s character, fitness for office and private life.

One need not invent a formal contract to recognise the convenience. In the zero-sum contest for the succession, a bitter former spouse with unresolved grievances and a willingness to speak is a ready-made asset.

Whether resources, protection or simple opportunity flowed from the Mnangagwa-aligned side is a question the public is entitled to ask; the pattern of benefit is already visible.

None of this requires one to defend every aspect of Chiwenga’s personal or political record. The vice president is a formidable and controversial figure whose own history invites rigorous examination.

But the principle at stake is larger than any individual: the quality of evidence and the character of the witness.

A woman whose marital career is marked by successive collapses, whose former partners have accused her of financial predation, who has herself been convicted of forging marital documents, and whose latest public intervention arrives at the precise moment it can inflict maximum political damage, is poorly placed to sit in moral judgement. Bitterness is not evidence. Timing is not coincidence. And a succession struggle does not convert private grievance into public truth.

Zimbabwe’s politics has long specialised in the weaponisation of personal history. The danger is that citizens, fatigued by factional noise, begin to mistake the loudest allegation for the most credible one.

Marry Mubaiwa is entitled to her pain, her health struggles and her desire to see her children. She is not entitled to rewrite the standards of evidence simply because her story serves a factional purpose.

Those who amplify her without interrogating her record do the country no service.

In the end, the question is not whether Chiwenga is perfect. It is whether the nation is prepared to let the least qualified witnesses define the terms of its most consequential political contest.

title: Reward Muza saves two penalties as Highlanders beat CAPS United to reach Chibuku final
categories: Football; News; Sports; Benjani Mwaruwari; Caps United; Chahwanda Stadium; Chibuku Super Cup; Hardrock FC; Highlanders FC; Reason Sibanda; Reward Muza; Rufaro Stadium; VAR Zimbabwe; Zimbabwe football
keywords: Benjani Mwaruwari; Caps United; Chahwanda Stadium; Chibuku Super Cup; Hardrock FC; Highlanders FC; Reason Sibanda; Reward Muza; Rufaro Stadium; VAR Zimbabwe; Zimbabwe football
summary: Highlanders beat CAPS United on penalties after Reason Sibanda’s late header forced a 1-1 draw. Substitute goalkeeper Reward Muza saved two spot-kicks to send Bosso into the Chibuku Super Cup final.
content_text:
Highlanders are through to the Chibuku Super Cup final after goalkeeper Reward Muza saved two penalties in a shoot-out victory over CAPS United at Rufaro Stadium.

The teams drew 1-1 in regulation time on Sunday. Highlanders converted all three of their penalties to win the shoot-out 3-1 and set up a final against Hardrock FC on November 28.

Sibanda’s late equaliser

CAPS United took the lead in the second half through Davison Marowa, whose strike put Highlanders under pressure.

Bosso kept pushing and drew level with about 10 minutes remaining. Andrew Mbeba delivered a free-kick into the box and substitute Reason Sibanda rose above the defenders to head home.

“When we conceded, we kept on believing,” Mbeba said after the match, adding that coach Benjani Mwaruwari had urged the players to keep pressing.

Muza steps up after goalkeeper injury

Highlanders’ route to the final was secured by Muza, who had come on after first-choice goalkeeper Aron Ngwenya suffered an injury late in the match.

Muza saved penalties from Nyasha Gurende and Alleny Mukombedzi. Obriel Chirinda sent his attempt over the bar, while Lloyd Njaliwa scored CAPS United’s only penalty.

Rainsome Pavari, Isaac Ngoma and Mongameli Tshuma all converted for Highlanders to seal the 3-1 shoot-out win.

Highlanders will now meet Hardrock in Kwekwe. Hardrock reached the final after recovering from a two-goal deficit to eliminate FC Hunters on penalties.

The final is scheduled for Chahwanda Stadium on November 28. The PSL says it is set to be the first local football match to use Video Assistant Referee technology.

title: 10-man Hardrock fight back from 2-0 down to reach Chibuku Cup final
categories: Football; News; Sports; Castle Lager Premier Soccer League; Chahwanda Stadium; Chibuku Super Cup; FC Hunters; Hardrock FC; Highlanders FC; Kelvin Kaindu; Prince Dube; Zimbabwe football
keywords: Castle Lager Premier Soccer League; Chahwanda Stadium; Chibuku Super Cup; FC Hunters; Hardrock FC; Highlanders FC; Kelvin Kaindu; Prince Dube; Zimbabwe football
summary: Hardrock FC fought back from two goals down despite being reduced to 10 men, drew 2-2 with FC Hunters and won on penalties to reach the Chibuku Super Cup final.
content_text:
Hardrock FC have booked a place in the Chibuku Super Cup final after staging a dramatic comeback against FC Hunters in Kwekwe.

The Castle Lager Premier Soccer League newcomers were trailing 2-0 and had been reduced to 10 men, but fought back to draw 2-2 before winning the penalty shoot-out at Chahwanda Stadium on Saturday.

Hardrock, who were playing Division One football last season, will now face Highlanders in the final on November 28 at their home ground.

Dube brace sparks comeback

Hunters appeared to be in control after taking a two-goal lead, leaving the hosts with a steep task in the second half. Hardrock’s challenge grew tougher when they were reduced to 10 men following a red card.

But the Kwekwe side refused to give up. Prince Dube scored twice, including a late equaliser, to take the semi-final to penalties. Hardrock then held their nerve from the spot to secure their place in the decider.

Coach Kelvin Kaindu said the team’s belief had helped them recover from a difficult position.

“I’m happy with the culture that we have developed to believe in ourselves that it is not over until it is over,” he said after the match.

Debut season brings final chance

Hardrock’s run to the final is a significant achievement in their first season in the top flight. The club has combined experienced players with younger talent and has also made its home ground a difficult venue for visiting teams.

The final will give the Kwekwe side a chance to pursue silverware in front of its supporters. Highlanders secured the other place in the final after beating CAPS United on penalties following a 1-1 draw.

Hardrock had already established itself as one of the season’s surprise stories, challenging established clubs in the league and advancing through the knockout competition. Now one match stands between the debutants and their first Chibuku Super Cup title.

title: Zimbabwe bowled out for 79 as Afghanistan complete T20I whitewash
categories: Africa Report; Politics; Sports; Top Stories
summary: SPORTS REPORTER Zimbabwe suffered a humiliating seven-wicket defeat to Afghanistan in the third and final Twenty20 International at Sharjah Cricket Stadium on Sunday, November 1, as the hosts completed a 3-0 series whitewash. The Chevrons were bundled out for just 79 runs in 14.3 overs before Afghanistan raced to 81 for three in only 8.1 […]
content_text:
SPORTS REPORTER

Zimbabwe suffered a humiliating seven-wicket defeat to Afghanistan in the third and final Twenty20 International at Sharjah Cricket Stadium on Sunday, November 1, as the hosts completed a 3-0 series whitewash.

The Chevrons were bundled out for just 79 runs in 14.3 overs before Afghanistan raced to 81 for three in only 8.1 overs, sealing victory with 71 balls to spare.

Afghanistan spinner Noor Ahmad was the chief destroyer, claiming five wickets for just 13 runs in 3.3 overs to dismantle Zimbabwe’s middle and lower order.

Zimbabwe’s batting troubles began early after Afghanistan elected to field.

Openers Innocent Kaia and Brian Bennett were dismissed cheaply, while captain Sikandar Raza managed just two runs as Zimbabwe slumped to 13 for three inside four overs.

Ryan Burl offered the only meaningful resistance, scoring 30 runs from 29 deliveries, including five boundaries.

Wessly Madhevere contributed 10 runs, but the rest of the batting line-up struggled against Afghanistan’s disciplined bowling attack.

Noor ripped through the Zimbabwean middle order, dismissing Madhevere, Tadiwanashe Marumani, Tafadzwa Tsiga, Newman Nyamhuri and Ernest Masuku as the Chevrons lost their final six wickets for just 23 runs.

Abdullah Tarakhail also impressed with figures of two wickets for 14 runs from three overs.

Chasing a modest target of 80, Afghanistan made light work of Zimbabwe’s bowling attack despite losing three wickets.

Ibrahim Zadran top-scored with an unbeaten 25 from 17 deliveries, while Sediqullah Atal struck 20 off 14 balls.

Azmatullah Omarzai finished unbeaten on 18 as Afghanistan comfortably reached their target.

For Zimbabwe, Ernest Masuku claimed two wickets for 21 runs in two overs, while Blessing Muzarabani picked up the other wicket.

The defeat completed a disappointing T20I series for Zimbabwe, who had earlier lost the opening match by 37 runs and the second encounter by 19 runs.

Zimbabwe’s latest batting collapse contrasted sharply with the second T20I, in which Raza had struck a remarkable 106 runs from 56 balls in a losing cause.

The two teams will now turn their attention to a two-match Test series, scheduled to begin on November 5.

Brief scores: Zimbabwe 79 all out (14.3 overs; Ryan Burl 30, Noor Ahmad 5/13). Afghanistan 81/3 (8.1 overs; Ibrahim Zadran 25 not out, Ernest Masuku 2/21). Afghanistan won by seven wickets.

Nguluvhe pushes for high rise buildings in Gwanda

by Staff reporter

Views

Matabeleland South Provincial Affairs and Devolution Minister Albert Nguluvhe has urged Gwanda Municipality to prioritise the construction of high-rise residential buildings to address the province's growing housing shortage, with more than 34,000 people currently on the housing waiting list.

Speaking during World Habitat Day commemorations held at Phelandaba Stadium in Gwanda on Tuesday, Nguluvhe said local authorities should embrace modern housing solutions that maximise limited urban land while providing affordable accommodation.

The commemorations, held under the theme "Adequate Housing for All", were organised in partnership with UN-Habitat.

Nguluvhe said the traditional approach of allocating large residential stands was becoming increasingly unsustainable, particularly as younger generations prioritised affordable housing over spacious properties.

"These young couples no longer care much about having garden space or big land, they just want accommodation that is affordable, so I urge you to look into it and focus more on having high-rise buildings," he said.

He said constructing multi-storey residential apartments would enable local authorities to accommodate more families on smaller pieces of land while reducing pressure on existing infrastructure.

The minister commended Gwanda Municipality for its ongoing housing development initiatives, saying the projects demonstrated encouraging progress towards addressing the accommodation crisis.

"I'm happy with the progress that Gwanda Municipality is making in terms of creating accommodation for residents. Mat South province as a whole has 34,000 on the waiting list. As I tour the projects in Gwanda, I'm happy with the progress, keep it up," Nguluvhe said.

Gwanda Mayor Thulani Moyo said the municipality was working with private developers to accelerate residential stand servicing and housing delivery.

Monerf managing director Elinas Gumbo confirmed that her company was developing more than 600 residential stands in the town, with infrastructure works nearing completion.

"We are developing over 600 stands and we are finishing up the servicing of stands and main sewer lines," Gumbo said.

However, Mayor Moyo expressed frustration over delays involving land held by the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) and AFC Bank, saying the failure to service the properties was holding back major investment projects.

He revealed that several investors were prepared to develop modern hotels and sporting facilities in Gwanda but could not proceed because of the outstanding land servicing issues.

"We have approached the Minister of State and told him about the delays by the RBZ and AFC in servicing the land they hold. We have ready investors to build state-of-the-art hotels and stadiums but we cannot proceed due to the hold-up," Moyo said.

The municipality hopes that resolving the land development challenges, alongside increased investment in high-density residential projects, will accelerate housing delivery and stimulate economic growth in the provincial capital.

The provincial housing backlog highlights the growing pressure on local authorities to provide affordable accommodation as urban populations expand and demand for serviced residential land continues to rise.

RBZ moves to ease ZiG cash shortages

by Staff reporter

01 Nov 2026 at 18:27hrs |

826

Views

The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) is introducing a new cash distribution monitoring system aimed at improving access to ZiG currency across the country, particularly in rural and underserved areas where businesses and consumers continue to struggle to obtain physical cash.

The central bank says Zimbabwe has sufficient ZiG notes and coins in circulation to meet demand, but uneven distribution and limited banking infrastructure have created shortages in some parts of the country.

In its latest ZiG Cash Distribution and Availability report, the RBZ identified logistical challenges and the concentration of banking services in major cities as key obstacles to ensuring that cash reaches the public efficiently.

"The central issue is not only how much cash is in circulation, but where it is held and how quickly it reaches the public," the central bank said.

According to the report, Zimbabwe currently has ZiG703.4 million in circulation against a total deposit base of ZiG32 billion, representing a cash-to-deposit ratio of 2.2 percent.

Although this falls slightly below the three percent benchmark considered optimal, the RBZ maintains that existing cash levels are adequate to support economic activity.

However, significant disparities remain in the geographical distribution of banking infrastructure.

Harare accounts for 54.2 percent of the country's 428 banking locations, while Harare and Bulawayo each have representation from 20 banking institutions.

In contrast, Matabeleland South and Mashonaland East have the lowest institutional coverage, with only seven banks represented in each province.

"Public consultations highlighted persistent challenges in cash access, availability and distribution, particularly in remote areas," the RBZ said.

To address the problem, the central bank is developing a Cash Distribution and Availability System (CDAS), designed to monitor cash movements and help financial institutions respond more effectively to shortages.

The system will enable banks to identify underserved areas, improve cash deliveries to branches and automated teller machines (ATMs), and monitor availability more closely.

Under the proposed arrangement, banks will also be encouraged to maintain minimum cash balances at branch level and introduce mechanisms for escalating shortages before they disrupt business operations.

The RBZ believes these measures will reduce excessive cash accumulation at central depots while ensuring that more currency reaches communities where it is needed.

The report reveals that banks currently hold ZiG490.4 million, representing 69.7 percent of the currency in circulation, while the public holds approximately ZiG209.3 million, or 29.8 percent.

Of the total cash supply, ZiG195.1 million, equivalent to 27.7 percent, is already held within bank branch networks and is therefore more readily available for withdrawals.

Another ZiG270.4 million, representing 38.4 percent, remains in central cash depots awaiting distribution to branches as demand arises.

"This indicates substantial cash capacity within the banking system to support continued public access to ZiG cash," the RBZ said.

The central bank expects the new monitoring framework to strengthen cash distribution, improve financial inclusion and support businesses that depend on physical currency for everyday transactions.

The initiative comes amid continued efforts to strengthen confidence in the ZiG currency and ensure that its availability matches the needs of consumers and businesses throughout Zimbabwe.

Rwodzi dedicates African award to Mnangagwa

by Staff reporter
