767

Views

Zimbabwe's Tourism and Hospitality Industry Minister Barbara Rwodzi has dedicated her Unstoppable African Minister of the Year Award to President Emmerson Mnangagwa and First Lady Auxillia Mnangagwa, crediting their leadership and support for the country's growing tourism industry.

Rwodzi received the prestigious continental recognition at the Africa Agenda Forum (TAAF) and Unstoppable African Awards ceremony held in Nairobi, Kenya, on Saturday evening.

The award was accepted on her behalf by Zimbabwe's Ambassador to Kenya, Winpeg Moyo, who was accompanied by Tourism and Hospitality Industry Permanent Secretary Dr Takaruza Munyanyiwa and Zimbabwe Tourism Authority chief executive officer Dr George Manyaya.

In a speech delivered by Ambassador Moyo, Rwodzi described the recognition as a tribute to Zimbabwe's collective efforts to transform tourism into a major contributor to economic growth, employment creation and national development.

"I receive this recognition not merely as a personal achievement, but as an affirmation of Zimbabwe's collective efforts to reposition Tourism as a strategic driver of economic growth and national development," she said.

The minister praised Mnangagwa for prioritising tourism under the Government's Vision 2030 development agenda and the National Development Strategy.

"I therefore acknowledge the visionary leadership of His Excellency, the President of the Republic of Zimbabwe, Cde Dr Emmerson Dambudzo Mnangagwa, who has placed Tourism at the centre of our economic transformation agenda," she said.

Rwodzi also paid tribute to First Lady Auxillia Mnangagwa, who serves as patron of the tourism and hospitality industry, for promoting Zimbabwe's cultural heritage, traditional cuisine, wildlife and tourist attractions.

She said the First Lady's initiatives had contributed to strengthening Zimbabwe's international tourism profile and showcasing the country's unique cultural identity.

The recognition comes as Zimbabwe intensifies efforts to diversify its tourism offerings beyond traditional wildlife attractions and natural wonders.

Under a 13-cluster tourism development model, the Government is promoting cultural and heritage tourism, religious tourism, sports tourism, gastronomy and Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions (MICE) tourism across the country's 10 provinces.

The strategy is intended to attract more international visitors, encourage investment and spread tourism-related economic opportunities to communities outside established destinations.

Zimbabwe has also received several international tourism accolades in recent years, including the Pacific Area Travel Writers Association's Destination of the Year Award for Natural Wonders at ITB Berlin in March 2025.

The country has also featured in international travel publications, including Forbes and Condé Nast Traveller, highlighting its attractions and potential as a global tourism destination.

Rwodzi said the latest recognition followed another milestone in her political career after she was named Zimbabwe's Overall Best Performing Cabinet Minister for 2025, becoming the first woman to receive the honour.

"This recognition comes at a particularly meaningful time in my journey. I was also honoured as Zimbabwe's Overall Best Performing Cabinet Minister for 2025, becoming the first woman to receive this recognition since its inception," she said.

However, she emphasised that the awards carried greater responsibility to deliver meaningful improvements in the tourism industry.

"I consider these honours a responsibility rather than a destination. They challenge us to do more, lead with purpose and demonstrate that transformative leadership can deliver tangible results for our people," Rwodzi said.

She dedicated the continental award to Zimbabweans, tourism industry workers and young African women aspiring to leadership positions.

The minister said she hoped the recognition would inspire more women across Africa to pursue leadership roles and contribute towards transforming their communities.

The award adds to Zimbabwe's efforts to raise its international tourism profile as the Government seeks to position the sector as a major source of foreign currency earnings, investment and employment.

I don’t think his statement should be stripped of its full context. Context and objectivity matters in such instances. Yes, he talked about […]
content_text:
DR ABIGALE MUPAMBI URGES ZIMBABWEANS TO REMAIN OBJECTIVE OVER SPEAKER MUDENDA’S ‘PORRIDGE’ REMARKS

By Dr. Abigale Mupambi

I have listened to the debate around Speaker of parliament Advocate Jacob Mudenda’s porridge remarks. I don’t think his statement should be stripped of its full context. Context and objectivity matters in such instances.

Yes, he talked about porridge. But he did not present it as the ultimate solution to the El Niño-induced drought ahead.

In my view, as a highly informed official sitting in a better position to know the magnitude of what is coming and its consequences at household level, the Speaker wanted to ignite consciousness – and he has already achieved that – and possibly inculcate a mentality of saving the little that may be available.

He appreciates the limitations of the national budget to fully mitigate the crisis, and sought to bring the public to the same level of reality using a pragmatic, relatable example near home.

We as citizens are fast developing a dangerous culture: brushing off serious issues, blaming, politicizing everything, and turning even livelihood matters into jokes.

Fellow citizens , let us sober up.

El Niño-induced drought is predicted ahead of us. That is a fact. Government has confirmed it and is mobilizing a US$500 million defence fund.

The question is not about porridge. The question is: what proactive propositions can we, as communities, put forward to survive the situation ahead?

This is the time to engage, collaborate, and meet Government halfway. All stakeholders must join hands. Objectivity must lead.

title: 26 Years After Land Reform, Why Is the New Farmer Still New?
summary: WHY FREE FARM INPUTS EVERY SEASON IS NOW UNSUSTAINABLE IN ZIMBABWE! ……..26 years after land reform, Zimbabwean farmers should be graduating from government support rather than remaining dependent on free inputs. By Dr. Abigale Mupambi Farming is the backbone of the Zimbabwean economy. It is not a social welfare programme. It contributes 12 percent to […]
content_text:
Farming is the backbone of the Zimbabwean economy. It is not a social welfare programme. It contributes 12 percent to GDP, provides 60 percent of raw materials for manufacturing, and sustains 67 percent of our population.

On that basis, I objectively differ with the continued model of Government fully funding farmers with seed and fertiliser every season. The model may be politically viable, but it is economically unsustainable.

The model was valid at inception. In 2000, when Fast Track Land Reform began, state-funded support was necessary. The new farmer had assumed a demanding national responsibility without capital or equipment. Government had to jump-start production.

That was 26 years ago. Twenty-six years down the line, the new farmer has remained new. It is time to graduate.

Year in, year out, we see the same queue for the same 10kg of maize seed and 50kg of Compound D, while Treasury strains an already heavily strained budget. For 2026/27: CBZ has set aside US$18m under NEAP, Treasury is building a US$500m El Niño fund (US$250m cash + US$250m grain), and US$5.7m has been raised from grain levies. The Presidential Inputs Programme targets 3.5 million beneficiaries and one million hectares under Pfumvudza.

This continuous scheme has crippled graduation. It has broken the farming cycle of producing, selling, saving and reinvesting.

First, it has killed financial inclusion. Why develop a bankable plan when inputs are free? Second, it has weakened private agro-dealer networks. Third, it has killed commercial discipline.

What we need now is a graduation model:

Tier One – Graduate (60%): Farmers with 5+ years delivery to GMB move from free inputs to title-deed-linked commercial finance. Use title deeds as collateral for tractors and irrigation at 7.5%, as CBZ is piloting. Inputs become a loan, not a grant.

Tier Two – Transition (30%): 50% subsidy, 50% loan repayable via Agricultural Revolving Fund in grain to build Strategic Grain Reserve.

Tier Three – Safety Net (10%): Elderly, persons with disabilities, youth-headed households remain on full support under Persons with Disabilities Act [17:01]. This is true inclusive gatekeeping.

Fiscal logic: Capitalise the Revolving Fund once with US$100m and enforce 80% recovery, it becomes self-sustaining in 3 seasons. Government saves US$150-200m annually on procurement and leakages. That saving can fund dams, roads, and ZIMRA digital systems to prevent a repeat of the ASYCUDA collapse that cut capacity from 500 to 100 trucks per day.

We must stop celebrating tonnes of seed distributed and start celebrating farmers who no longer need free seed.

The Presidential Inputs Programme succeeded in its historical mission. Its greatest success would now be to make itself unnecessary.

Dr. Abigale Mupambi is a renowed Political Scientist and an International Relations Expert who provide diverse insights in contemporay Global Affairs Analysis.

title: Government Considers Opening Nursing Training to Private Hospitals
categories: Health; Cimas Health Group; The Avenues Clinic
summary: Government is considering expanding private-sector participation in nursing education, a move that could allow more healthcare institutions to train general nurses and help address the country’s growing demand for skilled medical personnel. Health and Child Care Minister Dr Douglas Mombeshora said the Government intended to […]
content_text:
Government is considering expanding private-sector participation in nursing education, a move that could allow more healthcare institutions to train general nurses and help address the country’s growing demand for skilled medical personnel.

Health and Child Care Minister Dr Douglas Mombeshora said the Government intended to progressively open nursing training to private institutions, although the process would be guided by the outcome of an ongoing pilot programme at the Dr Auxillia Mnangagwa School of Nursing in Kadoma.

“The Ministry’s intention is to progressively open up private sector participation in nurse training beyond the current pilot project being undertaken at the Dr Auxillia Mnangagwa School of Nursing in Kadoma,” Mombeshora said.

He was speaking at The Avenues Clinic’s 23rd graduation ceremony, where 38 specialist nurses graduated after completing training in Intensive Care and Operating Theatre Nursing.

The clinic has since renewed its application for Government approval to introduce General Nursing Diploma training, arguing that expanding its programmes would strengthen the country’s nursing workforce.

Managing Director Sibusisiwe Ndhlovu said the institution was already investing US$200,000 annually in postgraduate nursing education, alongside improvements in medical infrastructure, equipment and clinical training.

Principal Nursing Officer Florence Ogwal said the clinic was also responding to changing healthcare needs through specialised programmes in Oncology and Palliative Care Nursing, introduced in January 2026.

“By strengthening local capacity, we can help more patients receive care close to home, with the support of their loved ones,” Ogwal said.

The Avenues Clinic has trained 347 specialist nurses since establishing its postgraduate nursing school, comprising 185 Intensive Care Nurses and 162 Operating Theatre Nurses.

The institution also offers subsidised training opportunities to nurses employed at Government health facilities and supports clinical attachments for University of Zimbabwe nursing students.Mombeshora commended the clinic’s contribution to nursing education and urged healthcare institutions to continue investing in specialist skills, particularly in critical care, oncology, emergency medicine and neonatal care.

The proposed expansion of private-sector participation comes as healthcare institutions seek to increase local training capacity and respond to the demand for qualified nursing professionals.

title: Wicknell Chivayo’s estate registered, but no executor appointed as US$25m dispute remains unresolved

keywords: Chivayo estate; deceased estate; estate administration; Lucy Muteke; Master of The High Court; Sonja Madzikanda; Wicknell Chivayo; Zimbabwe Supreme Court
summary: Wicknell Chivayo’s estate has been registered with the Master of the High Court, but no executor has been appointed. The estate’s assets and liabilities have yet to be formally accounted for, and a US$25 million dispute with his former wife remains unresolved.
content_text:
The estate of the late controversial businessman Wicknell Chivayo has been registered with Zimbabwe’s Master of the High Court, but the formal process of accounting for his assets and liabilities has yet to begin.

The Sunday Mail, in a report carried by The Herald, said the estate was registered about three weeks ago and an initial meeting was held. However, no executor or executrix has been appointed to take charge of its administration.

That appointment is a key next step. Until one is made, the estate’s assets and outstanding liabilities have not been formally established, and no distribution to beneficiaries can begin.

Officials at the Master’s Office confirmed the registration and initial meeting but declined to disclose details about the estate. Its value and the full composition of its assets have not been made public.

US$25m dispute still hanging over estate

One of the outstanding legal matters is a US$25 million matrimonial property and asset division dispute between Chivayo and his former wife, Sonja Madzikanda. The case had been awaiting determination by the Supreme Court when Chivayo died.

The US$25 million figure relates to the dispute; it is not a confirmed valuation of Chivayo’s estate. The estate’s overall value has not been disclosed.

The death of a person involved in court proceedings can require the estate to be represented before a case continues. With no executor or executrix appointed yet, the next steps in the dispute remain tied to the administration of the estate.

Two minor children among those affected

Chivayo died alongside his wife, Lucy Muteke, in a helicopter crash in Marondera on September 30. The couple left behind two minor children.

The estate process will need to establish what assets and liabilities Chivayo left behind before its eventual distribution can be determined. The Master’s Office has not disclosed who may benefit from the estate or when an executor or executrix might be appointed.

News

Mutoko Farmers Find New Hope in Traditional Grains

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

BY DELIGHT GUMA

Talent Humanikwa once relied on maize, but erratic rainfall and rising temperatures made the crop increasingly difficult to grow.

“I used to grow maize, but it did not do well because of the harsh weather conditions. A 20-kilogram bucket of maize would sell for about US$8,” says Humanikwa, a farmer from Kawere Village in Ward 4, Mutoko District.

She has since turned to finger millet, rapoko and groundnuts, which she says offer better returns in a changing climate.

The Zimbabwe Smallholder Organic Farmers Forum (ZIMSOFF) has trained Humanikwa and other farmers in Kawere to grow traditional grains, which are generally more tolerant of high temperatures and dry conditions than maize.

The programme is helping smallholder farmers adapt to climate change, strengthen food security and diversify their incomes, although water shortages continue to threaten their efforts.

A bucket of unprocessed finger millet, commonly known as rukweza, sells for about US$40. Once processed, the price can rise to US$70.

“These crops are nutritious and well suited to hot, dry conditions,” Humanikwa says. “They are gold because they offer farmers an opportunity to generate income while strengthening household food security, particularly as climate change and recurrent droughts continue to affect agricultural production.”

But even traditional grains need water.

The 2023/24 El Niño-related drought severely affected agriculture across Southern Africa. With another El Niño forecast for the 2026/27 season, farmers in Kawere are concerned about renewed rainfall shortages and the impact on their livelihoods.

ZIMSOFF has also trained farmers in income-generating activities, including fish farming, and provided guidance on water management. However, Humanikwa says the training cannot fully address their challenges without reliable water supplies.

“Water shortages remain a serious challenge, and our crops are dying because we do not have enough water to sustain them,” she says.

Shylet Macherenje, 33, who also grows small grains in Kawere, says unreliable rainfall and rising temperatures have exposed the vulnerability of smallholder farmers.

“Prolonged dry spells can damage crops and reduce harvests, threatening household food security and farmers’ incomes,” she says.

Finger millet and rapoko offer farmers alternatives to maize because they are generally more tolerant of heat and dry conditions. However, severe drought can still reduce their yields.

“Better access to water, suitable seeds, agricultural training and other forms of support would help us sustain production and protect our livelihoods,” Macherenje says.

In the same village, 27-year-old farmer Marvelous Chimana is combining horticulture with livestock farming. She keeps pigs, chickens, turkeys and cattle, and uses poultry manure as fertiliser.

“Livestock is an important source of food and income for our households. By diversifying our farming activities, we can reduce our dependence on a single source of livelihood and become more resilient when climate-related challenges affect crop production,” Chimana says.

She says combining crop production with livestock farming improves soil fertility and reduces dependence on purchased fertilisers.

“Combining horticulture, livestock and traditional grain production helps us make better use of the resources available to us. It also strengthens our ability to provide food for our families, even when one farming activity faces difficulties,” she says.

The initiative combines training in drought-resistant crops, agroecology, water harvesting and soil conservation with efforts to monitor public investment in irrigation, rural roads, storage facilities and markets.

Farmers are also being trained in Public Expenditure Tracking Surveys, which allow communities to examine how public funds are allocated and spent.

“Through this approach, farmers can follow how funds are allocated and used, identify implementation gaps and advocate for greater accountability in climate adaptation financing,” Chikowe says.

The programme aims to help farmers engage policymakers on agricultural budgets and climate adaptation plans, with particular attention to women and young people.

The need for accountability extends beyond Kawere. During the 2023/24 drought, Southern African Development Community leaders launched a US$5.5 billion humanitarian appeal to support affected member states. For farmers, the question is whether such resources reach the communities most affected by drought.

In Kawere, women preserve and share traditional seeds while maintaining knowledge of crop varieties suited to difficult growing conditions. Banners carried by ZIMSOFF and the Alliance for Food Sovereignty in Africa reflect this role. One reads, “Women: Africa’s Seed Custodians,” while another declares, “Seed Is Life.”

For Humanikwa, however, adaptation ultimately depends on access to water. Traditional grains may offer better returns and withstand dry conditions better than maize, but they still need sufficient moisture to grow.

“We do not have enough water to sustain them,” she says.

As farmers prepare for the 2026/27 season, water shortages remain an immediate concern in Kawere, highlighting the need for practical climate adaptation measures that support women smallholder farmers and protect their livelihoods.

title: Mutare supervisor jailed for stealing US$16,000 to fund own business
categories: Africa Report; Crime & Courts; Politics; Top Stories
summary: MUTARE — A 25-year-old woman who defrauded her employer of more than US$16,000 to finance her own retail business has been sentenced to an effective two years in prison. content_text:
MUTARE — A 25-year-old woman who defrauded her employer of more than US$16,000 to finance her own retail business has been sentenced to an effective two years in prison.

Michellene Muzenda, of Hobhouse One in Mutare, was sentenced to six years in prison by regional magistrate Anne Ndiraya on Tuesday.

Two years were suspended for five years on condition of good behaviour, while another two years were suspended on condition that she makes restitution.

Muzenda was employed as a supervisor by local businesswoman Nomsa Chave-Chiadzwa, with responsibilities that included collecting cash from automated teller machine operators, reconciling daily sales and maintaining financial records.

She also controlled access to a safe where daily cash collections were kept.

The fraud came to light in March 2026 after Chave-Chiadzwa ordered an audit of cash sales at two of her shops.

Another supervisor, Tendai Chitambirofa, discovered numerous discrepancies in records maintained by Muzenda, while an audit conducted by Muzenda herself reported no irregularities.

The matter was reported to police, leading to her arrest and the recovery of US$700 in cash.

On March 20, Muzenda led detectives to her shop at Tinmac Mall in Mutare, where police recovered merchandise believed to have been acquired using proceeds of the fraud.

The recovered goods included dresses, jeans, handbags, perfumes, shoes, underwear, towels and teddy bears.

Investigators also subjected her iPhone 13 to forensic examination at the Zimbabwe Republic Police Cyber Laboratory.

A subsequent forensic audit, covering transactions between November 2025 and March 2026, established that Muzenda had falsified daily cash sales records to conceal discrepancies between recorded sales and ATM data.

Prosecutor Chris Munyuku told the court that the fraud had prejudiced the employer of US$16,241.05, with an additional US$400 worth of merchandise involved.

Muzenda will serve two years behind bars, provided she complies with the conditions attached to the suspended portions of her sentence.

content_text:
HARARE — Shoe repair businesses in Harare could face a more than threefold increase in municipal charges next year as the city reviews tariffs for informal traders.

Under the proposed 2027 budget, the monthly charge for shoe cobblers and cleaners will rise from US$3 to US$10, an increase of approximately 233 percent.

The proposal is among several adjustments affecting informal businesses operating in the capital.

Canteens operating from sites approved by the City Health Department will also pay more, with monthly fees rising from US$30 to US$50.

However, the council is proposing reductions for certain categories of traders.

Fees for approved high-density tuckshops will decrease from US$30 to US$25 per month.

The hourly charge for parking at designated market sites will fall from US$3 to US$1.

Ordinary street vending charges will remain unchanged at US$1 per day or US$5 per week.

The council also proposes a US$10 trading fee per stall at People’s Markets, where no corresponding 2026 amount is shown in the tariff schedule.

The mixed adjustments could have different implications for informal traders depending on their businesses and locations.

The tariffs remain proposals, and ratepayers have until November 30, 2026, to submit objections.

HARARE — Harare City Council is proposing to halve its prescribed traffic enforcement penalty from US$20 to US$10 under its 2027 budget tariffs.

The municipality also wants to reduce the associated administration charge from US$10 to US$5.

The proposed reductions are contained in the council’s traffic enforcement tariff schedule, which also provides for changes to wheel-clamping charges.

Motorists driving light vehicles in Harare’s central business district will continue paying US$20 for wheel clamping.

However, the proposed clamping charge for commuter omnibuses carrying more than 18 passengers will decrease from US$25 to US$20.

Conventional buses and lorries will see their clamping charges reduced from US$30 to US$20, while articulated heavy lorries will also pay US$20, down from US$30.

Tow-away charges for light vehicles will remain at US$20, while storage fees for light motor vehicles will remain at US$10.

The council’s schedule also maintains an additional US$0.50 per kilometre charge for towing outside the central business district.

The proposed reductions come alongside increases in other municipal fees and penalties, including charges for illegal dumping.

The tariffs are scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027, if approved.

title: Avenues Clinic invests US$200,000 annually in specialist nursing training
summary: HARARE — The Avenues Clinic is investing US$200,000 annually in postgraduate nursing education, as the institution continues to expand specialist training programmes aimed at strengthening Zimbabwe’s healthcare workforce. The hospital graduated 38 specialist nurses at its 23rd graduation ceremony this afternoon, comprising 19 Intensive Care Nurses and 19 Operating Theatre Nurses drawn from central, district, […]
content_text:
HARARE — The Avenues Clinic is investing US$200,000 annually in postgraduate nursing education, as the institution continues to expand specialist training programmes aimed at strengthening Zimbabwe’s healthcare workforce.

The hospital graduated 38 specialist nurses at its 23rd graduation ceremony this afternoon, comprising 19 Intensive Care Nurses and 19 Operating Theatre Nurses drawn from central, district, private and mission hospitals across the country.

The clinic has trained a total of 347 specialist nurses since establishing its postgraduate nursing school, including 185 Intensive Care Nurses and 162 Operating Theatre Nurses.

The institution’s Managing Director, Sibusisiwe Ndhlovu, highlighted the hospital’s annual US$200,000 contribution to postgraduate nursing education, alongside investments in medical equipment, infrastructure and clinical training.

Speaking at the graduation ceremony, Principal Tutor Sophia Paso said the institution began training intensive care nurses in 1998 before introducing operating theatre nursing the following year.

She said the latest graduating class comprised three groups that had undergone specialist training between 2024 and 2025.

The January 2024 intake, comprising five Intensive Care Nurses and five Operating Theatre Nurses, recorded a 100 percent pass rate in their state final examinations.

Similarly, the July 2024 to June 2025 group, which included eight Intensive and Coronary Care Nurses and eight Operating Theatre Nurses, achieved a 100 percent pass rate.

However, the January 2025 group experienced challenges, with only one of the six Intensive Care Nursing students passing the initial state final examinations, representing a 16.7 percent pass rate.

All six Operating Theatre Nursing students from the same group passed their examinations.

Paso said the poor intensive care nursing results prompted an internal review of the school’s teaching and learning processes.

“This came as a shocker and a wakeup call to the teaching team and students who did a root cause analysis,” she said.

“The problem was identified and corrective measures implemented which saw all the five candidates passing” their supplementary examinations.

She said the experience demonstrated the importance of continuous assessment, evaluation and corrective action in maintaining nursing education standards.

Meanwhile, The Avenues Clinic has expanded its postgraduate training programmes to include Oncology and Palliative Care Nursing, which commenced in January 2026 following approval from the Ministry of Health and Child Care and the Nurses Council of Zimbabwe.

Principal Nursing Officer Florence Ogwal said the expansion was intended to respond to the country’s changing healthcare needs, particularly the growing demand for specialised cancer treatment and end-of-life care.

“By strengthening local capacity, we can help more patients receive care close to home, with the support of their loved ones,” Ogwal said.

She said the increasing complexity of medical procedures and advances in healthcare technology required continuous investment in specialist nursing skills.

The institution also provides subsidised training opportunities for nurses employed at government health facilities.

Its training partnerships include clinical attachments for University of Zimbabwe nursing students and collaboration with Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals in supporting open-heart surgery services and nursing attachments.

Ndhlovu highlighted ongoing infrastructure improvements at the hospital, including the refurbishment of medical and surgical wards, maternity facilities, intensive care, high-dependency and coronary care units.

The clinic has also renewed its request for Government approval to offer General Nursing Diploma training, seeking to expand beyond its existing postgraduate programmes.

Ogwal said the institution was prepared to collaborate with the Ministry of Health and Child Care, the Nurses Council of Zimbabwe and public-sector institutions to meet the required training standards.

“We respectfully renew our request for approval for The Avenues Clinic to train General Nurses,” she said.

Health and Child Care Minister Dr Douglas Mombeshora, who officiated at the graduation, said Government intended to progressively expand private-sector participation in general nursing training.

However, he said the process would be guided by evaluations of the ongoing pilot programme at the Dr Auxillia Mnangagwa School of Nursing in Kadoma.

“The Ministry’s intention is to progressively open up private sector participation in nurse training beyond the current pilot project being undertaken at the Dr Auxillia Mnangagwa School of Nursing in Kadoma,” Mombeshora said.

He commended The Avenues Clinic for its contribution to nursing education and urged healthcare institutions to continue investing in specialist skills, particularly in critical care, oncology, emergency medicine and neonatal care.

Paso thanked Medical Investments Limited management for its continued support of the nursing school, including during difficult periods.

The ceremony was attended by senior Government officials, nursing regulators, healthcare professionals and Cimas Health Group Chief Executive Officer Vuli Ndlovu.

The agreement was signed at the EU-Canada Summit in Montréal on 30 October 2026. It gives the EIB a legal framework […] Source
content_text:
News

EIB and Canada Open Door to Investment in Critical Minerals

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

BY NATHAN GUMA

The European Investment Bank (EIB) and Canada have signed an agreement that could bring more European investment into Canada’s mining sector, as both sides look to secure supplies of critical minerals.

The agreement was signed at the EU-Canada Summit in Montréal on 30 October 2026. It gives the EIB a legal framework to consider financing and providing technical support to eligible projects in Canada.

Critical minerals are expected to be among the first areas of cooperation, with potential investments covering mining, processing, refining and recycling.

For Europe, the partnership offers an opportunity to diversify its sources of minerals. Canada, which has significant mineral resources and mining expertise, stands to attract investment into projects across the sector.

EIB Vice-President Nicola Beer said the agreement would bring together the strengths of both sides.

“Europe and Canada have what each other needs,” Beer said.

“Canada has world-class resources and expertise, while Europe offers investment, technology and a huge market. This agreement can bring those strengths together. At a time when both sides of the Atlantic are working to reduce strategic dependencies, we want to turn our partnership into investment in real projects, from mining and processing to recycling. That is how we build supply chains that are not only more secure, but more competitive too.”

The deal follows a Letter of Intent signed by the EIB and Canada in Toronto in March. Since then, the bank has started engaging Canadian companies and public and private financial institutions to identify projects that could attract investment.

The EIB also plans to establish a presence in Ottawa to support its work in Canada.

Canada’s Finance and National Revenue Minister François-Philippe Champagne said the agreement would help attract investment into Canadian critical mineral projects and strengthen economic ties with Europe.

“Canada is a long-standing, like-minded ally, and natural partner for Europe,” Champagne said.

He said the partnership would help secure access to resources needed by both economies and reduce their strategic dependencies.

Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said Canada had the resources and expertise to expand its role in the global mining industry. He said the agreement could unlock investment while creating opportunities for workers, communities and Indigenous partners.

European Commission Executive Vice-President for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy Stéphane Séjourné said the partnership was intended to move beyond shared ambitions towards industrial investment.

He said combining Canada’s natural resources with European technology, expertise and capital could help develop supply chains stretching from extraction to refining and recycling.

Under the framework, the EIB can consider several forms of support, including loans, guarantees, equity and quasi-equity investments, as well as technical assistance. However, the signing does not mean that particular projects have already secured funding. Each proposed investment will still go through the bank’s appraisal and approval process.

The agreement builds on the EIB’s Critical Raw Materials Strategic Initiative, approved in March 2025 to support investment in secure and sustainable mineral supply chains and the implementation of the EU Critical Raw Materials Act.

The EIB Group, owned by the European Union’s 27 member states, signed €100 billion in new financing and advisory services in 2025, supporting more than 870 projects.

For Canada and Europe, the next step will be turning the new framework into actual investments in mineral projects.

content_text:
News

CAA3 reversal a daydream as implementation gathers pace

EFFORTS to reverse the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act, 2026 (CAA3) are a daydream, with the government insisting that implementation of the controversial constitutional changes is already under way after the amendment completed all constitutionally prescribed stages.

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

… government says constitutional changes have passed all legal stages

STAFF REPORTER

EFFORTS to reverse the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act, 2026 (CAA3) are a daydream, with the government insisting that implementation of the controversial constitutional changes is already under way after the amendment completed all constitutionally prescribed stages.

With judges and senators appointed under the new constitutional framework already sworn in, the government says there is no legal basis for attempts to overturn the amendment through repeated court challenges.

The latest challenge by six war veterans seeking to contest the presidential electoral system introduced under CAA3 has further intensified the legal battle, with the government arguing that the applicants are attempting to bypass established judicial procedures.

In an opposing affidavit filed by President Emmerson Mnangagwa, Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi and Attorney-General Virginia Mabiza, the respondents dismissed the latest application, maintaining that the amendment had already completed all the necessary legislative and constitutional processes.

Represented by lawyer Sylvester Hashiti, the respondents argued that the amendment had passed through all the required stages of enactment, making further challenges to its validity legally untenable.

“The Constitutional Amendment Bill No. 3 has now passed all legally prescribed stages and requirements for its enactment. Accordingly, any subsequent challenge to its validity is legally untenable and ought to be dismissed.”

The war veterans are challenging the presidential electoral system introduced under CAA3, which provides for the election of the President by Parliament rather than through a direct popular vote.

However, the respondents maintain that the applicants have failed to demonstrate why they should be granted direct access to the Constitutional Court instead of first approaching the High Court.

The Constitutional Court has reserved judgment in the application.

Addressing the court, Hashiti said the applicants had failed to comply with procedural requirements for direct access and had not established exceptional circumstances justifying the bypassing of the High Court.

“So, today we are arguing an application for direct access, where the war veterans are seeking leave from the court to approach it, to challenge the amendments, in particular the issues to do with the direct election of the President,” Hashiti said.

“Procedurally, the applicants did not comply with the rules, did not comply with the requirements required in an appeal of this nature.

“Secondly, the applicants did not set out on what basis they were approaching the court.”

He also questioned the applicants’ legal standing, arguing that they had not provided sufficient evidence to establish their interest in bringing the matter directly before the apex court.

“They did not prove their voters, they did not prove that they are presidential candidates, they did not prove any interest, even a public interest, on why they were approaching the court,” he said.

Hashiti further argued that the applicants had failed to demonstrate why their case deserved exceptional treatment by the Constitutional Court instead of following the ordinary judicial process.

“We also referred the court to the issue that on the substance of the application itself, there was no case set out as to why exceptionally the war veterans must come to the Constitutional Court and not the High Court,” he said.

“They should have gone to the High Court as a court of first instance, because that is the court which deals with matters as a first instance.”

The respondents also challenged the decision to cite Mnangagwa as a respondent, arguing that the President had no relevant legal interest in the dispute because his role in the enactment process had already been completed.

“The President has no interest, there is no justification for involving him in these things, because his function was already concluded and no one has challenged that the President was wrong in ascending to the throne.”

“So therefore the issues to do with the President are not necessary, they are simply for other reasons, but legally they are unnecessary.”

The government maintains that CAA3 has crossed the constitutional and legislative hurdles required for its enactment and is now being implemented, arguing that attempts to reverse the changes cannot succeed without meeting the established legal requirements.

With key appointments under the new framework already completed, the government is pressing ahead with implementation while insisting that litigants seeking to challenge the amendment must follow the prescribed judicial procedures.

title: Tax Relief Dominates As Parly Pushes For $150 Tax-Free Threshold
categories: Analysis; Budget; News; Abuja Declaration; Tax Free; Thresholds
summary: By Correspondent Parliament has proposed raising the tax-free income threshold from US$100 to US$150 and cutting transaction taxes, as demands for cost-of-living relief dominate the 2027 Pre-Budget Seminar. The proposals are contained in a consolidated report from nationwide public consultations presented by the Chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on Budget, Finance and Investment Promotion, Lincoln […]
content_text:
By Correspondent

Parliament has proposed raising the tax-free income threshold from US$100 to US$150 and cutting transaction taxes, as demands for cost-of-living relief dominate the 2027 Pre-Budget Seminar.

The proposals are contained in a consolidated report from nationwide public consultations presented by the Chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on Budget, Finance and Investment Promotion, Lincoln Dhliwayo.

The seminar, running from Wednesday to Saturday is meant to shape Parliament’s recommendations ahead of the 2027 Budget presentation by Finance Minister Prof Mthuli Ncube on 19 November.

According to Dhliwayo, the call to raise the tax-free threshold was the most consistent demand across all provinces.

“Anyone who earns $100 is not taxed anything.

“People were raising, they wanted that threshold to be raised up to $150,” he said.

Inflation Erodes Gains

Government raised the threshold to US$100 in the 2026 Budget.

However, citizens argue inflation has eroded its impact, with low-income earners still taking home below survival wages after PAYE deductions.

On fuel, stakeholders proposed that Government retain subsidies or reduce levies to keep petrol and diesel below US$2 per litre.

The report says participants from agriculture, mining, transport and SMEs warned that any increase would trigger price hikes across the economy.

The third proposal targets the Intermediated Money Transfer Tax (IMTT).

Parliament heard that the current rate of up to 2% on electronic transactions discourages formal transactions and penalises small businesses.

Further Cuts

Citizens want a further cut from the 1.5% ZiG rate introduced in 2026 to 1% or less for low-value transactions.

The proposals seek to make the local currency, ZiG, more accessible and affordable, and to reduce production and transport costs.

Finance Minister Ncube and Reserve Bank Governor Dr John Mushayavanhu are expected to respond to the proposals during the seminar.

Treasury has previously cautioned that tax cuts must be weighed against revenue needs.

Government collected ZiG137.8 billion against a ZiG124.4 billion target at mid-year 2026.

Parliament will adopt a final position paper on Saturday.

Under Statutory Instrument 153 of 2026, the 2027 National Budget must be presented no later than the third Thursday of November.

title: Mudenda Demands 15% Health, 20% Education Allocations As MPs Probe Missing Sugar Tax Millions
categories: Budget; Education; mthuli ncube; Mudenda; Pre-Budget Seminar
summary: By Correspondent Speaker of Parliament Jacob Mudenda has challenged Parliament to assert its oversight role by forcing the 2027 National Budget to meet international spending thresholds for health and education. Mudenda was speaking during the official opening of Parliament’s 2027 Pre-Budget Seminar in Victoria Falls. He urged MPs to also demand full accountability for billions […]
content_text:
By Correspondent

Speaker of Parliament Jacob Mudenda has challenged Parliament to assert its oversight role by forcing the 2027 National Budget to meet international spending thresholds for health and education.

Mudenda was speaking during the official opening of Parliament’s 2027 Pre-Budget Seminar in Victoria Falls.

He urged MPs to also demand full accountability for billions raised through sugar tax and health levies.

Mudenda said Treasury can no longer ignore benchmarks Zimbabwe has voluntarily signed up to.

Benchmarks

“We have the Abuja Declaration which requires at least 15% of the national budget to go to health.

“We have the Education 2030 Framework for Action which requires 15% to 20% to education.

“You must ensure that allocations to both sectors advance fulfilment of the benchmarks to which Zimbabwe has subscribed,” he said.

He warned that without decisive investment, Zimbabwe will fail to build resilience to climate and economic shocks, particularly for vulnerable rural populations.

Education

On education, Mudenda went further, calling for a specific vote for age-appropriate Artificial Intelligence literacy and a deliberate plan to close the digital divide.

“It is not enough to talk about AI in Harare.

“Rural communities must not be left behind in internet penetration and AI literacy if we are to prepare our children for the future economy,” he said.

The Sugar Tax Storm

The Speaker’s call for more money to social sectors dovetailed with explosive revelations from last week’s public budget consultations in Harare.

MPs questioned where health levy money is going.

According to submissions before the Portfolio Committee on Health and Child Care, beverages giant Delta Corporation alone paid US$32 million in sugar tax in 2024.

US$32.1 million was paid in March 2025, and US$30 million in March 2026.

These funds are part of a wider health levy basket that includes tobacco levies, health insurance levies and sin taxes.

Yet, MPs heard that Parirenyatwa and Mpilo Central Hospitals still require patients to purchase their own orthopedic implants.

Hospital Crisis

Prices for these range from US$4,000 to US$8,000 per implant.

Currently hospitals face chronic shortages of drugs and sundries.

“Citizens pay seven to eight health-related levies at the till, but only one reaches the sector.

“We need traceability.

“If a Zimbabwean pays sugar tax on a drink, they must see it become an implant, a cancer drug, or a working theatre,” said one MP during the consultation.

The Committee also demanded that Treasury ring-fence all health levies and channel them through a transparent Health Fund managed jointly with NatPharm.

The Bulawayo retreat will conclude on Saturday with a consolidated Parliamentary Position Paper.

It will contain binding recommendations for the Finance Minister.

The 4-day retreat is running under the theme “Accelerating Economic Transformation and Building Resilience to Climate and Global Shocks.

It is bringing together Finance Minister Prof. Mthuli Ncube, Reserve Bank Governor Dr. John Mushayavanhu, Committee Chairpersons, and development partners to shape the Budget before its presentation to Parliament on 19 November.

title: Q & A with City of Harare over 14 day ultimatum
summary: Following yesterday’s 14-day ultimatum for partially regularised settlements to have the owners fully comply, we have noted frequently asked questions from residents and the media. Our Corporate Communications Manager Stanley Gama responds to some of the issues raised: Source
content_text:
News

Q & A with City of Harare over 14 day ultimatum

Following yesterday’s 14-day ultimatum for partially regularised settlements to have the owners fully comply, we have noted frequently asked questions from residents and the media. Our Corporate Communications Manager Stanley Gama responds to some of the issues raised:

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

Following yesterday’s 14-day ultimatum for partially regularised settlements to have the owners fully comply, we have noted frequently asked questions from residents and the media. Our Corporate Communications Manager Stanley Gama responds to some of the issues raised:

Question: What prompted the City of Harare to issue the 14-day ultimatum, and how many property owners and beneficiaries of settlements across the City are affected by the enforcement measures?

Answer: The City is grappling with serious legacy issues in land management resulting from the 2004 Parallel Development Policy whose main focus was to provide decent and affordable human shelter. The policy was manipulated by land barons resulting in massive land invasions, and illegal development of settlements without adequate social amenities like water, sewer, schools and health facilities. The land barons continued in that modus operandi, duping many people of their hard-earned money. The City moved to regularise these settlements starting 2017, but some ignored the City intervention and continued with their illegal practice. The continued general state of lawlessness in the City in terms of land management forced the City to issue this warning for the final and last time. The level of disrespect for authority is appalling. We cannot have a City with land barons who resent authority. Land barons have gone too far. This enforcement action is meant to rehabilitate those who operate as if there is no authority in Harare.

Question: How many illegal structures are earmarked for demolition, which suburbs or settlements are targeted, and when will the demolitions begin once the deadline expires?

Answer: The City of Harare has no appetite to demolish people’s homes. We want to regularise them. Across the City very few properties can be negatively affected as they are developed in the sensitive areas and can not be regularised. Our initial assessment indicated that less than 100 properties across the City can be affected but the exact number will be informed by compliance levels and demolitions will commence at the expiry of the 14 day compliance period but as a last resort.

Question: How much are affected property owners expected to pay in regularisation penalties, land value charges and infrastructure development costs, and what payment arrangements has Council put in place to help them comply?

Answer: A minimum of USD 1,500 or equivalent in ZIG . The exact amount is determined by the levels of breach. Breaches are in various forms and shapes. Some have illegally built structures on properly allocated land, some have illegally built structures on private land and state land, some have illegally invaded Council land and built on it, whilst some have illegally constructed water and sewer reticulation and illegally connected their fittings to municipal services and are consuming Council services for free. All these attract different penalties. The City accepts payment plans and has even extended deadlines for payment of penalties to allow the affected more flexibility. However the City is alive to the reality that non compliance with the law must not be affordable otherwise the motivation to be law abiding can be diminished if non-compliance is not punitive.

Question: What progress has the City made in regularising the affected settlements, and what challenges have delayed compliance with requirements such as approved building plans, roads, water supplies and sewer infrastructure?

Answer: The City registered progress especially on those settlements developed on private land. The developers were forthcoming. Good examples are Chiremba Park, Masasa Park and Audor Investment in Southlea Park. But in the case of municipal and state land, progress has been slow because regularisation has not been paired or complimented with enforcement. The defaulting residents have not been forthcoming and hence our decision to escalate the compliance a gear up. The City is more than ready to facilitate this process. The City has decentralised its services including plan approvals in an attempt to engender the ease of doing business in the City.

Question: How will the City balance enforcement against illegal structures with protecting residents who may have bought stands in good faith from housing cooperatives or land developers, and what measures are in place to prevent further illegal land sales and construction?

Answer: The regularisation exercise is an exercise with a human face. We recognise that not all people are allergic to authority. Some are innocent victims. But they became complicit to their situation and this is why we have extended the regularisation hand to them to redeem themselves. It is up to them to own up and pay for the required penalties and have their illegal actions and investments legalised.

Conclusion: Plans are there to avoid further illegal activities. Enforcement will be immediate. Illegal construction is to stop forthwith. Law enforcement agents have been put on high alert and we will be working closely with them to ensure that we weed out bad apples.

News

Rugeje preps for diplomatic deployment

Despite his initial position to refuse deployment to Maputo, Mozambique, as ambassador, retired Lieutenant-General Engelbert Rugeje – who served in several high-ranking state and ruling party roles, including being Zanu PF national commissar – has of late been attending diplomatic induction and training sessions with several other civil and foreign service personnel.

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

Despite his initial position to refuse deployment to Maputo, Mozambique, as ambassador, retired Lieutenant-General Engelbert Rugeje – who served in several high-ranking state and ruling party roles, including being Zanu PF national commissar – has of late been attending diplomatic induction and training sessions with several other civil and foreign service personnel.

This comes as President Emmerson Mnangagwa has initiated a major diplomatic shake-up, with Helliate Rushwaya, former ZBC chairperson, being the first publicly announced and approved new appointment as Zimbabwe’s ambassador to Rwanda.

The Rwandan cabinet officially granted approval for Rushwaya to serve as ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Kigali, replacing Professor Charity Manyeruke who is being redeployed to Ottawa, Canada.

Reports indicate Mnangagwa is planning to recall, retire, or reassign up to 26 ambassadors – roughly half of Zimbabwe’s global network of 40 embassies and 10 consulates – to shift focus toward economic diplomacy.

This suggests Rugeje might soon be deployed on a foreign mission even though he initially resisted a plan to send him to Maputo as ambassador following the death of Victor Matemadanda in June.

Matemadanda, Regeje’s successor in Zanu PF as political commissar, was ambassador to Mozambique and Eswatini.

Following the death of Matemadanda, the position of Zimbabwe’s ambassador to Maputo and Mbabane has been shrouded in high-stakes political tension, following a pattern of consecutive envoys returning home in caskets.

The “Maputo assignment” has increasingly been viewed by insiders as a dangerous or punitive deployment — frequently termed a “graveyard shift” for retired military personnel linked to internal Zanu PF succession politics.

Retired Lieutenant-General Douglas Nyikayaramba was deployed to Maputo in 2019 and died two years later, officially from Covid-19 complications.

Matemadanda was thrown into the fray and he also died serving in that position.

As a result, the role has faced delays in being filled due to resistance within Zimbabwe’s security elite.

Mnangagwa reportedly offered the Maputo posting to Rugeje, a close ally of Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga, but he initially refused.

Rugeje broke protocol and turned down the appointment amid an intensifying succession battle between Mnangagwa and Chiwenga.

His refusal is widely attributed to acute security concerns after watching his two immediate predecessors die shortly after taking the post, combined with a reluctance to be politically exiled from Harare.

The deployment to Maputo is part of a broader political strategy by the Mnangagwa administration to clear Chiwenga-aligned military figures out of domestic politics by sending them abroad into the diplomatic corps.

Rugeje, widely seen as a cog in the wheel for the Chiwenga’s military faction, has been undergoing induction and training of Zimbabwean diplomats before their deployment abroad, primarily managed through the Zimbabwe Foreign Service Institute established under Presidential Proclamation.

The Zimbabwe Foreign Service Institute acts as the primary training and research arm for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Trade.

It utilises a hybrid model, combining face-to-face and virtual instruction, to train civil service and foreign service personnel.

The Zimbabwe Institute of Diplomacy is a complementary specialised body offering tailored programmes in international diplomatic protocol, public administration, formal and social etiquette, crisis management, and cross-cultural communication.

Training familiarises officers with Zimbabwe’s foreign policy doctrine, economic diplomacy, and national development frameworks and programmes.

It prepares envoys for multilateral and geopolitical readiness, and specific international postings such as courses for envoys designated for Zimbabwe’s upcoming tenure on the United Nations Security Council.

It also deals with protocol and etiquette issues.

title: Chiwenga’s Unravelling Was Political But Now Its Personal
categories: 2030 Agenda; Analysis; chiwenga; Colonel Minnie Baloyi; Mary Mubaiwa
summary: By Chenesai Mugwadi On Tuesday, 27 October, Harare Regional Magistrate Musaiona Shortgame released Marry Mubaiwa from remand. For 7 years she has been accused of attempting to murder Vice President Constantino Chiwenga by unplugging his life support in a Pretoria hospital in 2019. The State had asked for yet another postponement to November 25. The […]
content_text:
By Chenesai Mugwadi

On Tuesday, 27 October, Harare Regional Magistrate Musaiona Shortgame released Marry Mubaiwa from remand.

For 7 years she has been accused of attempting to murder Vice President Constantino Chiwenga by unplugging his life support in a Pretoria hospital in 2019.

The State had asked for yet another postponement to November 25.

The magistrate refused.

Seven years, he said, had caused her “mental, physical and financial prejudice.”

Outside court, the woman who went in as a former model and came out in a wheelchair, right arm amputated, left leg amputated, marriage gone, children gone, property gone, told reporters:

“We won.”

It is a human story before it is a political one.

And that is precisely why it is politically lethal for her former husband.

The Release Is Not The Point. The Interview Is.

Legally, Mubaiwa was removed from remand and the State can still proceed by way of summons.

It was not an acquittal on the merits.

The case collapsed under its own delay , after Chiwenga himself walked away from cross-examination by Beatrice Mtetwa in camera almost two years ago and never returned to the dock.

What matters now is what she said once she was free to speak.

In an interview with journalist Simba Chikanza hours after the ruling, Mubaiwa alleged that years of pethidine use, administered by a military nurse at Chiwenga’s arrangement, destroyed her health.

She alleged she was given a break only when she became pregnant.

Mubaiwa said, simply: “Chiwenga destroyed my mental health, my health and this is a man I took care of.”

These allegations have not been independently established.

They must be reported as allegations.

However, in Zimbabwean politics, credibility is not established in a laboratory but is established in the street.

Chiwenga Was Already Falling

This is the strongest editorial point, and the most misunderstood.

Marry Mubaiwa did not cause Constantino Chiwenga’s political decline.

That decline was already underway, driven by forces far larger than a marriage.

Since the 2017 coup that made him kingmaker, Chiwenga has struggled to convert military capital into political capital.

The succession matrix has shifted beneath him.

The ED2030 push, the open realignment of provincial chairpersons, the quiet demotion of his allies in the security sector, and his long absences for medical treatment have all narrowed his room.

His image as the disciplined, austere general does not survive easily in a ZANU-PF that now rewards deal-making, distribution, and the optics of economic stability.

He entered the succession race with structural weaknesses: a thin civilian base, a reputation for rigidity, and a health history that opponents whisper about.

Mubaiwa’s accusations do not create those weaknesses.

They are an accelerant.

From Party Power To Personal Credibility

The Mubaiwa story moves the succession question from “Who controls the party?” to “Who is this man?”

ZANU-PF succession battles are normally fought over institutions, war veterans, the commissariat, provinces.

They are about power.

They are rarely about character, because character is hard to litigate.

However, for the first time, Chiwenga’s opponents do not need to argue about constitutions or congresses.

They can argue about credibility.

If a man is accused by his former wife of orchestrating drug dependency that left her disabled, what does he do to his country?

It humanises the collateral damage of power in a way that communiques never can.

Zimbabweans have watched Mubaiwa’s physical deterioration for seven years, the wheelchair, the amputations, the court appearances while on remand.

She lost “almost everything during the seven-year legal fight.

Lost her marriage to Chiwenga, access to her children, her right arm and left leg.

Whether you believe her or not, you have seen her suffering.

Chiwenga’s political brand was built on being the man who protects the nation.

The image of a man who could not protect or is alleged to have destroyed his own household is corrosive.

It does not need to be proven to be politically effective.

That is why this is not a sideshow but the main show reframed.

The contest was already about whether Chiwenga could succeed.

Now it is also about whether he should.

title: Is the phone you’re buying stolen? GSM Zimbabwe launches a WhatsApp IMEI checker
categories: Gadgets & Apps; WhatsApp; GSM Zimbabwe; Hector Chikomba; IMEI Check
summary: If you’ve bought a phone in town recently, can you say for sure where it came from? Most of us can’t. That’s the gap GSM Zimbabwe is trying to close with a new WhatsApp bot that checks a phone’s IMEI and tells you what you’re really buying. The team gave me a few credits to […]
content_text:
If you’ve bought a phone in town recently, can you say for sure where it came from? Most of us can’t. That’s the gap GSM Zimbabwe is trying to close with a new WhatsApp bot that checks a phone’s IMEI and tells you what you’re really buying.

The team gave me a few credits to test the service with and I came away impressed. You send “Hi” to the bot (263790354368), give it the IMEI, pay with EcoCash and the report comes right there inside WhatsApp.

The problem it’s going after is quite significant in Zimbabwe even though it’s hard to quantify. There are a lot of fake and refurbished smartphones in Zimbabwe. Hector Chikomba, the founder of GSM Zimbabwe, says there’s also the huge problem of phones stolen in other countries showing up in Zimbabwe.

“We are seeing a massive trend of phones stolen in other countries and loan-defaulted phones being dumped in Zimbabwe,” he said in an announcement of the IMEI checker. Those phones, he said, often work perfectly on Econet and NetOne. So the buyer has no reason to suspect anything.

The trouble comes later. If this new owner takes that phone to South Africa, it may refuse to connect to networks there because its IMEI has been blacklisted on the GSMA database. Worse, if the phone was reported stolen in a robbery or hijacking case, or is still being tracked by the lender that financed it, an innocent buyer could end up having to explain how they came to have it.

Those lenders are the other trap. In South Africa, phones sold on credit through schemes like FoneYam and PayJoy can be locked remotely using Samsung’s Knox Guard when payments stop. GSM Zimbabwe says plenty of these devices are now being sold in Zimbabwe, and the person who pays for one has no idea it could be bricked.

Here’s an example of a genuine phone with an outstanding credit lock in South Africa.

For now the bot checks Apple and Samsung phones only. Other brands are coming, Hector says.

The report shows the phone’s real age, the manufacture date, the original purchase and activation date, and whether it’s still under warranty.

It tells you whether Apple or Samsung lists the device as refurbished or as a replacement unit. It even shows the phone’s original colour, which is a neat way to catch a device that has been put in a new housing. Then it looks for hidden locks: iCloud status, MDM corporate locks, carrier locks and Samsung Knox Guard.

Checking a phone costs $3, paid via EcoCash. You enter your EcoCash phone number, approve the prompt and the report follows.

Hector says he was moved to build it after watching Zim Tech Guy’s The Shocking Truth About Phones Sold as New in Zimbabwe . In it Zim Tech Guy claims that roughly 80% of smartphones sold as “brand new” in Zimbabwe are refurbished devices resealed in new boxes. That’s his figure and I’d love to see the data behind it. Still, nobody who has shopped for a phone in Zimbabwe will tell you the problem isn’t real.

GSM Zimbabwe itself grew out of repair work. Hector started out fixing computers before switching to phones. His reasoning was simple. When a computer breaks, people can put it aside for a while. A phone is something you need every single day.

Over the years he saw how hard it was for local technicians to find help and good information. So the team recently launched the GSM Zimbabwe Community , a platform built just for Zimbabwean phone repair technicians. It’s a place to post technical questions, share fixes and find files like schematics.

There’s a training angle too. A few years ago Hector ran a free short course on phone repair, and people have been asking for a full programme ever since. He says he’ll launch a full Cellphone Software Repair Course in December, aimed at giving young people a practical skill they can earn from.

If you’re about to buy an iPhone or a Samsung, especially one that’s “new” at a price that seems too good to be true, run the IMEI first. It takes a minute. You can start the bot here: wa.me/263790354368 .

title: Mliswa Gives ZACC 7 Days to Release Impounded Hilux and US$53k

He also accuses the anti-graft body’s officers of demanding a bribe and sitting on his complaint for three months. The vehicle, a white Toyota Hilux […]
content_text:
By Chiwoniso Mugwadi

Former MP Temba Mliswa has given the Zimbabwea Anti-Corruptipn Commission (ZACC) seven days to release his Toyota Hilux and account for US$53,000 he says was inside it.

He also accuses the anti-graft body’s officers of demanding a bribe and sitting on his complaint for three months.

The vehicle, a white Toyota Hilux GD6, Reg AAE 8748, Chassis, was intercepted at Lions Den Tollgate on 19 July 2026 on suspicion it was smuggled.

Mliswa says it was not.

Formal Accusation Against ZACC

In a formal complaint lodged on 24 July and received by ZACC the same day, Mliswa says he bought the vehicle from former Chegutu Rural District Council Chairman Tatenda Gwinji.

The deal is backed by a Council CEO letter dated 13 May 2024, an affidavit by Gwinji dated 14 May 2024, and a valid registration book from the Central Vehicle Registry.

Despite handing over the paper trail, Mliswa says he got no charge sheet or seizure inventory when ZACC seized the car.

Worse, he alleges, his driver received a call asking for money to clear the vehicle.

“Of grave concern is the fact that one of my drivers was allegedly approached… and requested to pay a bribe in order to facilitate the release,” Mliswa wrote to ZACC Chairman Honourable Reza.

“If true, this conduct strikes at the very foundation of the Commission’s mandate.”

Mliswa, who chairs the Southern African Parliamentarians Against Corruption (SAPNAC) accuses a named officer, Mr Tsindi, of leading a targeted campaign.

Corrupt ZACC Officials

“I wish to place on record my serious concern regarding the conduct of Mr Tsindi, whose actions appear to demonstrate a personal vendetta”.

He links Tsindi with a vendetta to protect corrupt officials in Hurungwe Rural District Council and Karoi Town Council.

“It is deeply troubling that corruption allegations involving institutions such as Hurungwe RDC and Karoi TC continue to attract widespread public concern.

“Yet there appears to be little visible enforcement action,” he said.

He alleges Tsindi even engaged the National Prosecuting Authority to stop arrests of suspects.

“Throughout my public life, I have consistently advocated for transparency.

“I remain prepared to submit myself to any lawful investigation.

“However, I cannot accept continued harassment, intimidation or the alleged solicitation of bribes.”

Mliswa’s lawyers, Masiya-Sheshe Associates, have set out five demands.

An independent probe into the bribe claim, investigation of Tsindi for abuse of office and interference with justice.

They also seek for confirmation of the Hilux’s legal status, final closure without harassment of family and workers, and disciplinary action if wrongdoing is found.

If ZACC fails, they warn of immediate court action for the vehicle, the cash and costs.

ZACC has not responded to questions at the time of publication.

News

CAA3 now at implementation stage — irreversible

With CAA3 now at the implementation stage, judges and senators appointed under the new constitutional framework have already been sworn in, as the government maintains that the amendment has passed all constitutionally prescribed stages and its implementation is under way.

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

…as same litigants flood courts with repeated challenges

STAFF REPORTER

THE government has declared the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act, 2026 (CAA3) irreversible, arguing that it has completed all constitutionally prescribed stages of enactment, as it pushes back against legal challenges to the new presidential electoral system.

The repeated court challenges to CAA3 have raised concerns over the same litigants flooding the courts with similar cases.

With CAA3 now at the implementation stage, judges and senators appointed under the new constitutional framework have already been sworn in, as the government maintains that the amendment has passed all constitutionally prescribed stages and its implementation is under way.

The position was set out in an opposing affidavit filed by President Emmerson Mnangagwa, Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi and Attorney-General Virginia Mabiza, who are opposing the war veterans’ application to bypass the High Court and directly challenge the constitutional changes in Constitutional Court.

Represented by lawyer Sylvester Hashiti, the respondents argued that the amendment had already passed through all the required legislative and constitutional processes, rendering the latest challenge legally untenable.

“The Constitutional Amendment Bill No. 3 has now passed all legally prescribed stages and requirements for its enactment. Accordingly, any subsequent challenge to its validity is legally untenable and ought to be dismissed.”

The six war veterans are contesting the presidential electoral system introduced under CAA3, which provides for the election of the President by Parliament rather than through a direct popular vote.

However, the respondents maintain that the applicants have not demonstrated why they should be allowed to approach the Constitutional Court directly instead of first taking their case to the High Court.

The Constitutional Court has reserved judgment in the application.

Addressing the court, Hashiti said the applicants had failed to comply with the procedural requirements for direct access and had not established exceptional circumstances warranting the bypassing of the High Court.

“So, today we are arguing an application for direct access, where the war veterans are seeking leave from the court to approach it, to challenge the amendments, in particular the issues to do with the direct election of the President,” Hashiti said.

“Procedurally, the applicants did not comply with the rules, did not comply with the requirements required in an appeal of this nature.

“Secondly, the applicants did not set out on what basis they were approaching the court.”

He also questioned the applicants’ legal standing, arguing that they had not provided sufficient evidence to establish their interest in bringing the challenge directly before the apex court.

“They did not prove their voters, they did not prove that they are presidential candidates, they did not prove any interest, even a public interest, on why they were approaching the court,” he said.

Hashiti further argued that the applicants had failed to demonstrate why their case warranted exceptional treatment by the Constitutional Court instead of following the ordinary judicial process.

“We also referred the court to the issue that on the substance of the application itself, there was no case set out as to why exceptionally the war veterans must come to the Constitutional Court and not the High Court,” he said.

“They should have gone to the High Court as a court of first instance, because that is the court which deals with matters as a first instance.”

The respondents also challenged the decision to cite Mnangagwa as a respondent, arguing that the President had no relevant legal interest in the dispute because the process leading to the amendment’s enactment had already been completed.

“The President has no interest, there is no justification for involving him in these things, because his function was already concluded and no one has challenged that the President was wrong in ascending to the throne.”

“So therefore the issues to do with the President are not necessary, they are simply for other reasons, but legally they are unnecessary.”

The respondents maintain that CAA3 has completed the constitutionally prescribed enactment process and that its implementation should proceed in accordance with the law, arguing that any further challenges must meet established legal and procedural requirements. They insist that the applicants should follow the ordinary judicial process rather than seek exceptional direct access to the Constitutional Court, as the government presses ahead with implementing the constitutional changes.

UN Turns to Forecasting, Early Aid as Intense El Nino threatens millions

Published

on

By

By Nathan Guma

The United Nations is using improved climate forecasting and early humanitarian funding to prepare for an exceptionally strong El Niño expected to worsen droughts, floods and food insecurity across Africa and other parts of the world.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned that the current El Niño could reach unprecedented strength, with sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific potentially rising to 3.8 degrees Celsius above average between November 2026 and January 2027.

The event is expected to peak towards the end of 2026, but its effects could continue long afterwards, disrupting rainfall and temperature patterns across several regions.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said parts of East Africa were more likely to experience wetter-than-normal conditions during the October-to-December rainy season, increasing the risk of heavy rainfall and flooding.

“We are already witnessing extreme weather events and expect this to multiply and cascade as El Niño intensifies,” she said during a joint press conference by the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and the WMO in Geneva.

Southern Africa faces the prospect of drier conditions from November, which could affect crop production, water availability and rural livelihoods as the region enters its typical rainy season.

Parts of Southeast Asia are also expected to experience warmer conditions and rainfall deficits, increasing pressure on agriculture and water supplies. Drought risks are also expected to rise in parts of Central America, the southern Caribbean and the Amazon.

The United Nations estimates that 50 million people could face increased hunger as El Niño compounds existing humanitarian crises, including conflict, displacement and rising food prices.

However, the UN says improved forecasting and early intervention could help reduce the damage by giving governments and aid agencies time to act before extreme weather triggers humanitarian emergencies.

“A powerful El Niño does not have to be a recipe for humanitarian disaster,” Saulo said, stressing the importance of science-based information, early warnings and decisive action.

Funding for affected countries

Tom Fletcher, the UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, said forecasting capabilities had improved since the previous El Niño, creating opportunities to prepare communities more effectively.

He said the UN had released more than $50 million from its Central Emergency Response Fund to support 11 countries facing the anticipated impacts, with humanitarian coordinators instructed to use pooled funding to prepare for the crisis.

The strategy, known as anticipatory action, involves using forecasts and risk assessments to deliver assistance before disasters cause widespread damage.

These measures include providing cash to vulnerable households, helping farmers and herders protect crops and livestock, and moving humanitarian supplies to safer locations before floods cut off roads.

“The African Development Bank estimates that it will cost African countries between 10 and 20 billion US dollars and drive down GDP by between 1 and 2%,” Fletcher said.

“First, we must prepare people who are in the path of El Niño,” he added.

“Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya need cash and supplies ahead of heavy rains. Southern Africa needs seeds and livestock before planning windows close. Central America needs immediate livelihood assistance, while Asia and the Pacific must prepare for droughts, floods, and cyclones,” he said.

Data sharing

Fletcher also urged scientists to share data, forecasts and advice with humanitarian agencies, while asking countries with disaster-response capabilities to place them on standby.

“The forecasting has moved on rapidly. And we’re applying the lessons we learned from previous crises. We’re using the best technology we can get our hands on to ensure that communities are as resilient as they can be,” he said.

He also called on the scientific community to contribute to the UN’s efforts to coordinate data and expertise.

“To the scientific community, please join our cell, which we’ve activated today, to share data, forecasts, and advice on the humanitarian response. We need that detailed work to help countries reduce the danger,” he said.

title: War Veterans Have Started Agitating For War But Will It Work This Time?
summary: By Fanuel James The statement this week by the War Veterans Pressure Group led by Rueben Zulu, endorsing Vice President Constantino Chiwenga and denouncing what it called intolerance at the Chinhoyi Conference, has been dismissed by some as the noise of a briefcase formation.
