content_text:
By Fanuel James

The statement this week by the War Veterans Pressure Group led by Rueben Zulu, endorsing Vice President Constantino Chiwenga and denouncing what it called intolerance at the Chinhoyi Conference, has been dismissed by some as the noise of a briefcase formation.

In the context of past experiences, that would be a mistake.

To understand its significance, you must rewind to 2014.

The ED Template And How It Started

When Emmerson Mnangagwa was isolated, humiliated and eventually fired in November 2017, it was not the Central Committee that first defended him.

It was the war veterans.

Chris Mutsvangwa, then as now a polarizing figure, turned the Zimbabwe National Liberation War Veterans Association into a political battering ram.

They held press conferences that Mugabe’s government declared treasonous.

War veterans boycotted and issued communiques calling the Party “adrift.” They framed their defence of one man as a defence of the liberation legacy itself.

Their language then: “We did not fight to create a dynasty.” “The Party has been hijacked by counter-revolutionaries.” “The principles of the struggle are being betrayed.”

Their language now, by Zulu’s group: “We did not fight to replace colonial authoritarianism with indigenous authoritarianism.”

“The Party has drifted from people-centered decision making.” “Organized booing replaced comradely debate.”

The vocabulary may be different but the grammar is identical.

The Three-Act Structure of a ZANU PF Split

Every succession battle in ZANU PF, so far, follows a three-act structure.

Act One: The incumbent secures a resolution to extend his rule. In 2014 it was the push for Dr Amai to succeed and today it is the 2030 resolution.

Act Two: A war veterans faction breaks ranks, claiming the legacy is under threat. In 2016, they were dismissed as “dissidents” and expelled. This week, Zulu’s group has already been dismissed as “briefcase.”

Act Three: The dispute moves from the Party constitution to the national Constitution itself.

Then, it was about whether Mugabe could anoint his wife; now, it is about Constitutional Amendment No. 3 of 2026.

The Human Factor: A Pact That Became Personal

What makes this moment human, and therefore dangerous, is that the actors know each other intimately.

Chiwenga and Mnangagwa are not Mugabe and Mnangagwa.

They planned November 2017 together in the same room with one a political strategist and the other the military guarantor.

Their pact was personal before it was political and when that kind of pact frays, the fallout is never procedural. It is personal.

And like in 2016, the war veterans are again positioning themselves as the conscience, not a faction.

Is It a Repeat? No. It’s More Volatile

In 2017, the war veterans had a clear popular grievance to weaponize, the excesses of the G40 and the evident frailty of an ageing leader.

They also had the security establishment behind them, and a frustrated populace ahead of them.

Today, the war veterans defending Chiwenga do not have the centre of power and so are defending from the periphery.

The security establishment is not monolithic, the economy is more fragile, and the instrument they are challenging, a constitutional amendment through public hearings, is far more sophisticated than a simple expulsion letter from Mazowe.

Therefore this not the preamble to Operation Restore Legacy II and most definitely the tanks will not roll for a press statement.

However, it is a preamble to something ZANU PF has always struggled to contain: the moment when a succession dispute stops being about personalities and starts being framed as a struggle for the soul of the liberation movement.

In 2017, that framing worked once the war veterans convinced the rank and file that ED was the Party and the Party was ED. The rest was logistics.

Zulu’s group is attempting the same alchemy with Chiwenga but whether they have the capacity to pull it off is another question.

title: DevFest Harare 2026: Zimbabwe Steps Into the Agentic Era
summary: We’ve all probably heard about the “agentic era” for some time now. It has been release after release of different forms of AI agents with new capabilities and specialties. But most of these are built for people in the U.S and other first world countries. I think it is important to ask what these agents […]
content_text:
We’ve all probably heard about the “agentic era” for some time now. It has been release after release of different forms of AI agents with new capabilities and specialties. But most of these are built for people in the U.S and other first world countries. I think it is important to ask what these agents mean, particularly in the Zim market. How can they help given the realities of our economy, environment and culture? Well Google Developer Group is hosting an event, DevFest, covering these issues. The event is taking place on the 24th of October. Just 2 days from now! And to be honest I think you should be there. Because I will!

The theme running through the whole agenda is AI agents: software that doesn’t just answer questions but actually does work. That’s the conversation happening in every tech company in the world right now. On DevFest day, Harare gets to have that conversation on its own terms, with speakers from across the continent who are building it for African realities.

The day is going to be seriously packed. It is expected to run from 08:00 to 16:00 with six sessions from Google Developer Experts coming in from Nigeria, Kenya, Zambia and South Africa, five local speakers, a talk from and a group discussion to close it out. So with that being said here’s what I’m really excited for.

The Google talk. Allela from Google Southern Africa opens the day at 09:10. I want to hear what Google is actually planning for developers in this region, and Zimbabwe in particular.

AI agents for African SMEs. James Mwai from Kenya is showing how small businesses can put agents to work using Google’s ADK. This is the talk I think business owners in Harare need to see. And I think there are a lot of questions needing answers for this one. Is it affordable for SMEs to actually do this? Do these agents truly bring value or they are just over hyped, etc

USSD and voice workflows. Umar Faruq Zubairu from Nigeria is talking about USSD and voice, the technology that still reaches people without smartphones, which i think is quite useful in Zim.

Third World Solutions for Third World Problems. Simon Muzariri’s title alone needs no further explanations. And as I had stated before most of the solutions being built in Silicon Valley are usually for the U.S. So basically we need to take things into our own hands.

The group discussion. This one gives the audience the chance to lay down their opinions, ask questions and get answers. And I think this is a much more efficient way of learning and gives the chance to understand what you are being taught.

So what is my take on all of this? Well I have built apps and software myself so I’m looking at this agenda as someone who ships things, not just as someone who covers events. What excites me most is that this lineup isn’t copying Silicon Valley. Look at the topics: AI for SMEs, cutting cloud costs by running AI in the browser, USSD for people without smartphones, solving Third World problems with Third World solutions. These are talks about building for the continent we actually live on, where data is expensive, power is unreliable and most customers are small businesses.

I also think the timing matters. AI agents are moving fast, and there is a real risk that Africa ends up only consuming tools built elsewhere. A day like this is how we avoid that. When a student in Harare watches someone from Lusaka or Nairobi show a working agent, building one doesn’t feel like an impossible thing all of a sudden.

As a media partner, I’ll be there from setup to the group photo. Expect live stories through the day, interviews with the organisers and speakers, a highlight reel, and a full vlog of the day from my point of view.

If you’re a developer, a student, a founder or just curious about where AI is heading in Zimbabwe, come through. And if you can’t make it, follow along. I’ll bring the day to you.

See you at DevFest Harare.

October 24, 2026 , Harare Institute Of Technology, Harare

title: Here Is Why Mudenda and Parliament’s Visit to House of Commons Has More Meanings
summary: The recent visit to UK’s House of Commons by a Parliamentary delegation led by Speaker Jacob Mudenda has signalled the latest massive change in relations between the two countries. The visit was more than protocol but politics, performed in the oldest language of the British state: parliamentary recognition. For 26 years, Zimbabwe’s relationship with Westminster […]
content_text:
The recent visit to UK’s House of Commons by a Parliamentary delegation led by Speaker Jacob Mudenda has signalled the latest massive change in relations between the two countries.

The visit was more than protocol but politics, performed in the oldest language of the British state: parliamentary recognition.

For 26 years, Zimbabwe’s relationship with Westminster has been defined by rupture which has seen sanctions, walkouts, megaphone diplomacy, and the bruising memory of the Fast-Track Land Reform.

The last time Zimbabwe was this close to the Commons, it was as a subject of debate, not a guest in the Speaker’s Gallery.

From Executive Isolation to Parliamentary Diplomacy

President Mnangagwa’s re-engagement policy has largely been an Executive affair characterised by meetings with diplomats, investor roadshows and UNGA handshakes.

It has yielded incremental thaws but also easy reversals, because Executive relations are transactional and hostage to electoral headlines.

Meanwhile, Parliamentary diplomacy is different as it is institutional and harder to cancel.

When Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle invites Mudenda he is extending recognition to an institution, not an administration.

While you can sanction a government; you cannot easily un-invite a Parliament that seats both ZANU PF and CCC in the same delegation.

The composition of the delegation was also telling. Three ZANU PF MPs – Webster Shamu, Mercy Mugomo, Noah Mangondo – and two from the opposition CCC – Vivian Chitimbe and Concilia Chinanzvavana.

The Commonwealth Cipher

No one in Whitehall will say it outright, but Westminster is the antechamber to the Commonwealth which Zimbabwe left in 2003.

Itapplied to return in 2018 but that application has sat in limbo, caught between UK reservations over electoral reforms and Harare’s frustration at what it sees as moving goalposts.

Mudenda’s itinerary is instructive as it includes meetings with the British Group of the Inter-Parliamentary Union, the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association UK Executive, the Foreign Affairs Committee chaired by Dame Emily Thornberry, and Minister for Africa Kirsty McNeill.

Such an itinerary is not tourism but is the plumbing for a Commonwealth return.

Britain alone cannot readmit Zimbabwe as it needs consensus but it can stop blocking the re-entry.

The Dividend for Both Houses

For Mudenda, the significance is gravitas as the longest-serving Speaker in SADC, chair of SADC-PF’s strategic lobby for a regional parliament, and architect of Zimbabwe’s Parliamentary Training Academy.

In Westminster, being feted in the State Dining Room alongside Mother of the House Diane Abbott it reframes him as a regional statesman.

It strengthens his hand to push institutional reforms – stronger committee oversight, better legislative drafting, AI and technology transfer, which was explicitly on the agenda.

For the UK, the significance is equally pragmatic.

With Gillian Lever, the new Ambassador to Harare, tasked with people-to-people and trade ties, London needs a functional interlocutor that is not State House.

Parliament has just become that player.

With Zimbabwe endowed with lithium, a diaspora of 150,000+ in the UK including the only Zimbabwean-heritage MP Adam Jogee who was on the guest list, and a strategic position in an Africa increasingly courted by Russia and China, re-engaging via Parliament allows London to hedge without endorsing.

The Uncomfortable Truth

However, the situation still appears a long way from the cordial relations of the past before the Commonwealth exit and Land Reform.

The same reports that welcomed Mudenda in London this week noted that the UK’s thaw with Harare is still conditional; governance, constitutionalism, and electoral credibility.

While Parliamentary diplomacy can launder image it cannot legislate legitimacy.

So the real test is not whether Mudenda was photographed in Westminster Hall but whether the institutional practices he observed travel back with him to Mount Hampden.

If they do, then the Carriage Gates were not just opened for a day but for a direction.

If not, then this was exquisite protocol – and protocol alone.

title: What Was Chiwenga’s Endgame After The Chinhoyi Landmine?

In a party where speeches are usually an orgy of praise-singing, Chiwenga did something unprecedented: he asked what the coup was for. “Chii chakaita kuti Second Republic ivepo? Kwaive kugadzirisa […]
content_text:
By Fanuel James

Vice President Constantino Chiwenga did not go to Chinhoyi on 16 October to introduce President Emmerson Mnangagwa only but to indict him.

In a party where speeches are usually an orgy of praise-singing, Chiwenga did something unprecedented: he asked what the coup was for.

“Chii chakaita kuti Second Republic ivepo? Kwaive kugadzirisa zvakaipa zvanga zvichiitika kumashure.

“Hatisi kudzokorora here kuita zvatakambotadza? Ndomubvunzo watinofanira kuzvivunza.”

That Shona sentence, delivered at the 23rd ZANU PF National People’s Conference at Chinhoyi University of Technology, is the most dangerous sentence spoken in ZANU PF since 2017.

To understand Chiwenga’s endgame, we must understand what he was trying to stop in Chinhoyi.

The battle was not about a speech but about three resolutions.

Mnangagwa’s allies wanted and managed to get the Conference to adopt resolutions that included.

Align the ZANU PF constitution with Constitutional Amendment Act No.3 which extends the presidential term from 2028 to 2030.

Move the party’s elective congress from 2027 to 2029 and declare Mnangagwa the sole, uncontested candidate to lead ZANU PF in 2029.

Chiwenga allegedly blocked those resolutions at Politburo level but failed to block them at the Conference. By Saturday 17 October, they were adopted.

So did Chiwenga lose?

As Hopewell Chin’ono correctly observed this week: “General Chiwenga gave a powerful speech that got the media and the country talking, but it earned him nothing, because the very changes he was trying to stop were adopted.”

Christopher Mutsvangwa dismissed him as “a loose bolt in a car engine.”That is the short game.

The long game is different.

Chiwenga’s Chinhoyi speech was not aimed at winning a vote in Chinhoyi but at three audiences outside that hall.

The military and war veterans.

Chiwenga opened by invoking the Chinhoyi Battle of 28 April 1966 – seven ZANLA heroes dying a few kilometres from the venue.

“Our party belongs to the people, never to individuals we are merely temporary custodians… what legacy are we leaving?”

In ZANU PF language, “individuals” and “mazvake mazvake” is code for the new oligarchs.

While he did not mention Kudakwashe Tagwirei by name, everyone in that hall knew the recent elevation of Tagwirei into the Politburo on the same day was what he meant when he warned Zimbabweans should not become “hewers of wood and drawers of water, surviving from the benevolence of a privileged few.”

He has called that class zvigananda before.

He is telling the generals and the veterans: The 2017 coup was not to replace one family business with another.

The constitutionalists and the people

The most calculated line was: “Change must be driven by the people, not imposed from above.

“You may recall, Your Excellency, that the voice of the people is the voice of God.”

That was Mnangagwa’s own 2017 slogan thrown back at him.

Chiwenga is positioning himself not as a coup plotter, but as a constitutionalist.

He did not say “I want to be President” but said: “Are our resolutions truly coming from the people? Do our conferences authentically capture the voices of the grassroots?”

If Mnangagwa’s endgame is to be elected by Parliament in 2030 without a popular vote, Chiwenga’s endgame is to make that process look illegitimate before it happens.

He is creating a record that he objected.

History

Chiwenga knows he was outmanoeuvred when Mnangagwa removed the running mate clause in 2023.

That clause would have made the VP an elected running mate who cannot be fired.

By removing it, Mnangagwa made Chiwenga an appointee who serves at the pleasure of the President.

From that moment, Chiwenga’s legal route to succession died.What is left?

The political route: to be seen as the last general standing who warned the party it was relapsing.

The panic that followed proves the shot landed.

ZBC and Star FM posted his speech, then scrubbed it from their platforms and restricted comments.

If it was a meaningless speech by a “loose bolt”, why delete it? Chiwenga’s endgame is not to win a vote in 2026.

He lost that in Chinhoyi.

His endgame is to ensure that if the Second Republic collapses under the weight of 2030, personal empires, and imposed change, history records that he stood up in Chinhoyi.

It is the defense he never got to make in 2017 because Mugabe never got a trial.

Chiwenga is making sure that when the next reckoning comes, there will be a transcript.

title: Botha Mine moves to report its own conduct to ED, shooting Itself in the foot
summary: By staff reporter In a move that has left officials and industry watchers in shock, Botha Gold Mine – the Bindura operation facing a litany of fraud allegations – has reportedly authored a glossy report to the Office of the President and Cabinet (OPC) purporting to be a victim of the very state-owned entity it […] Source
content_text:
News

Botha Mine moves to report its own conduct to ED, shooting Itself in the foot

Published

on

By

Share

Tweet

By staff reporter

In a move that has left officials and industry watchers in shock, Botha Gold Mine – the Bindura operation facing a litany of fraud allegations – has reportedly authored a glossy report to the Office of the President and Cabinet (OPC) purporting to be a victim of the very state-owned entity it is accused of stealing from.

The document dated 16 October 2026, titled “Systematic Disadvantage of Botha Gold Mine,” now circulating in Harare, paints Botha as a small 32-hectare miner being bullied by Freda Rebecca Gold Mine, a subsidiary of Mutapa Gold Resources under the sovereign wealth fund Mutapa Investment Fund.

The move raises a fundamental question: why would a company facing such serious allegations seek presidential intervention without first addressing the mounting evidence against its operations?

The allegations against Botha

Investigations by NewsHawks, supported by court filings and official correspondence, have placed Botha at the centre of a bitter dispute over Mining Lease 21 (ML21), held by Freda Rebecca Gold Mine.

According to court documents, Freda Rebecca alleges that Botha submitted coordinates for claims Botha 1-4 that materially differed from the original registration data, allegedly shifting the claims into portions of ML21.

The company argued that the coordinates were fraudulent and violated Section 5 of the Gold Trade Act [Chapter 21:03].

Court filings further allege that artisanal miners extracted gold from Freda Rebecca’s lease believing they were operating on Botha’s claims, while Botha allegedly received 30 percent of the proceeds.

The allegations remain subject to due process, but they raise serious questions about the company’s attempt to portray itself as the aggrieved party.

Approval withdrawn

On April 29, 2026, Mashonaland Central Provincial Mining Director Tendai Kashiri informed Botha that its Siting of Works approval, granted on April 21 for claims Botha 1-4, registration numbers 46035-38, had been “withdrawn and nullified”.

The reversal followed objections by Mutapa Gold Resources over allegations of fraud, forgery and abuse of office surrounding the approval.

Mutapa welcomed the decision, arguing that the document had been used to support an alleged attempt to extend Botha’s operations into Freda Rebecca’s lease.

Botha’s reported complaint about the withdrawal therefore cannot be separated from the allegations that prompted the regulatory intervention.

The US$40 million question

The Ministry of Mines’ position further complicates Botha’s victimhood narrative.

In sworn court papers, Kashiri stated that Botha had never acquired mining rights within ML21, warning that mining activities in the area would violate the law.

The Environmental Management Agency (EMA) also reportedly intervened after observing operations outside the coordinates of the approved mining plan.

Meanwhile, a Ministry summary cited in documents relating to the dispute estimates that approximately 271 kilogrammes of gold, valued at US$40 million, was unlawfully collected from State ground.

Mutapa Gold Resources alleges that the extraction prejudiced State-owned resources under its management. The allegations must be tested through due process, but the financial stakes make the dispute too serious to dismiss as a mere administrative disagreement.

A risky appeal to ED

By approaching the Office of the President and Cabinet (OPC), Botha appears to be seeking intervention from the very office responsible for overseeing the State’s interests.

If the company believes it has been unfairly treated, it must produce evidence and address the allegations surrounding its coordinates, withdrawn approval and operations within ML21.

The OPC must assess the complaint on its merits, without political pressure undermining regulatory oversight or judicial processes.

A glossy report cannot erase court filings, nullify official correspondence or resolve disputed mining rights.

content_text:
By Correspondent

The Constitutional Court has dismissed an application by Moreprecision Muzavazi and Pardon Gambakwe seeking direct access to challenge the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment No. 3 Act.

The court ruled that the applicants should have approached the High Court first.

The unanimous judgment was delivered by Deputy Chief Justice Paddington Garwe, seating with Justices Ben Hlatshwayo and Bharat Patel.

In their verdict they ruled that the applicants had failed to demonstrate that it was in the interests of justice for the Constitutional Court to hear the matter as a court of first and last instance.

Reasons For Ruling

The applicants had sought leave under Section 167(5) of the Constitution to challenge a resolution adopted at the ZANU PF National People’s Conference in Mutare in October 2025.

It resolved to extend presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years.

They argued that the resolution, which gave rise to the CAA3 infringed citizens’ political rights and violated Section 328(7) of the Constitution.

The section prohibits amendments extending term limits from benefiting an incumbent.

They also sought to challenge Constitution Amendment No. 2 of 2021, which removed the running-mate clause and expanded presidential powers in judicial and prosecutorial appointments.

Speaking outside the court, Muzavazi said the bench was hostile and unwilling to allow the applicants to make substantive presentations on the merits of the case.

“We’ve just come out of the Constitutional Court, where we are challenging CAB2 and CAB3.

“The Constitutional Court has dismissed both cases and said that we should have approached the High Court.

“The court was very hostile, they were not willing to even allow us to make a presentation.

“They were adamant that we should have approached the High Court,” he said.

Muzavazi added that approaching the High Court was an exercise in futility and accused the judiciary of acting as an extension of the executive.

He said the dismissal marked a sad day for Zimbabwe and was evidence that the judiciary, like the legislature, was captured.

The dismissal adds to a string of challenges to CAB3 that have been struck off on procedural grounds.

In May, the Constitutional Court dismissed separate applications by six war veterans and by former Binga North MP Prince Dubeko Sibanda.

Both sought to halt CAB3 while it was still before Parliament.

The court ruled that those challenges were premature.

The CAA3 was signed into law by President Emmerson Mnangagwa on July 7, 2026, and published as Act No. 6 of 2026.

Among other changes, the Act extends terms of office for the President and Parliament to seven years

It introduces a parliamentary electoral college for the election of the President and establishes an independent Delimitation Commission.

The Act also creates the office of Judge President of the Supreme Court, and provides for 10 additional senators appointed by the President.

However, it remains the subject of other pending challenges before the Constitutional Court.

These include a case by war veterans led by constitutional lawyer Lovemore Madhuku, who argue that the changes to presidential election procedures required a national referendum under Section 328(7).

title: MaDeals wins $7,000 at the Innovation Expo: what’s behind the startup, future plans?
categories: Startups; Innovation Expo 2026; MaDeals; Melusi Chiripowako; Ray Vines; Tech Startups; Zimbabwe startups
summary: MaDeals, the Zimbabwean marketplace app founded by Melusi Chiripowako, also known as Ray Vines, won $7,000 at the Innovation Expo & Conference 2026. We look at how the app works, its users, its challenges and what comes next.
content_text:
If you have been on Zimbabwean social media for a while, you probably know Ray Vines . He started making short comedy clips around 2019 (personal favourite: the bestie video), and his real name is Melusi Chiripowako. These days, you might have come across him again as the founder of MaDeals, a marketplace app. MaDeals won the $7,000 Start Up Category at the Innovation Expo & Conference 2026, under the Financial Inclusion, Smart Postal Services and SME Market Access category. The prize was US$7,000, presented by the Ministry of ICT, Postal & Courier Services and POTRAZ.

We had written about the app before, so we contacted Ray to find out what has changed, how the business is doing and what the app looks like today.

What MaDeals is

MaDeals shows you buyers, sellers and service providers near you on a live map. You can buy and sell products, hire someone for a job, run an auction or exchange items (might try the last one).

There is also a request feature. Rather than scrolling through listings looking for something, you post what you need and nearby sellers send you offers. It sounds like InDrive for goods and services in that regard. Then there is MaDeals AI. You can type something like “cheapest plumber near me”, and it searches the available listings and recommends options.

According to Melusi, the app has more than 30,000 registered users, around 4,000 products and 1,000 services listed. He also says interest is coming from South Africa as well.

The numbers behind the numbers

Ray told us that around 4,000 people use MaDeals each month. That is roughly 13% of the people who have signed up. He also says about 25 deals are completed every day across purchases, services, auctions and barter combined. That works out to around 750 deals a month if the daily figure holds.

And I wanted to know a little more about what those numbers look like in practice. How many of those sellers are actually making sales? Are buyers coming back, or are they trying the app once and forgetting about it?

Melusi said that building an active marketplace has been one of the biggest challenges so far.

Why it won

This is the part I found most interesting. Ray says the judges liked that MaDeals deliberately includes the informal sector, particularly vendors and small traders, rather than focusing only on registered businesses.

Many vendors who used to operate in the CBD have been pushed out and have struggled to find customers. MaDeals gives them another way to list their products and be found by people looking to buy.

There is something else worth noting about the award. Despite the category’s focus on financial inclusion and smart postal services, MaDeals does not yet handle payments or deliveries within the app.

Buyers and sellers arrange both themselves, and the startup has no courier partnerships yet. Ray says in-app payments are coming and that the team is negotiating with a bank to make them possible.

How it makes money

Listing and buying on MaDeals are free. Sellers can pay to promote their listings, starting at US$1 a day. Ray says more than 100 sellers have paid for promotions so far.

The startup also plans to introduce seller subscriptions, paid verification and small transaction fees later on.

What about scams?

Ray says MaDeals verifies sellers using a council trading licence and national ID. More than 20 sellers have gone through the process so far. Users can also report suspicious activity in the app, and the team can suspend accounts that break the rules.

The app’s store listing says it also warns users when someone asks them to pay before collecting an item.

Ray advises users to check reviews and, where possible, collect and pay for items in person.

The verification process is still at an early stage, though. With more than 30,000 registered users, just over 20 verified sellers is a relatively small number. We also do not know how many scam reports the team has received or how it has dealt with them.

The prize money

The US$7,000 has not been paid out yet, according to Ray. He says there are no conditions attached by the Ministry, and the plan is to put the money towards technology improvements and user growth.

It will be interesting to see what the team does with it, particularly given the challenges Ray described around getting people to use the app regularly.

Why not just use Facebook or WhatsApp?

This was our obvious question. Zimbabweans already buy and sell through Facebook Marketplace, WhatsApp groups and personal networks. Why would someone download another app to do something they can already do?

Ray’s argument is that Facebook and WhatsApp are global platforms, while MaDeals is built around what is near you. He also points to auctions, barter and service requests, which bring several ways of buying and selling together in one place.

Where things stand

MaDeals is running and looks promising. A year from now, Ray wants MaDeals to be the go-to platform for buying, selling and finding services in Zimbabwe’s major towns. We will be checking back.

Have you tried MaDeals? Did you find what you were looking for, or did you end up back on WhatsApp groups or Facebook Marketplace? Let us know in the comments.

title: Chiwenga Delivers Most Explicit Rebuke of ED’s Govt So Far
summary: By Fanuel James Vice President General (Rtd) Constantino Chiwenga has delivered his most direct criticism yet of President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s administration, calling for orderly change driven by the people and warning against individualistic rule. Addressing the 23rd ZANU-PF National People’s Conference on Friday Chiwenga insisted that ZANU PF belongs to the people and not to […]
content_text:
By Fanuel James

Vice President General (Rtd) Constantino Chiwenga has delivered his most direct criticism yet of President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s administration, calling for orderly change driven by the people and warning against individualistic rule.

Addressing the 23rd ZANU-PF National People’s Conference on Friday Chiwenga insisted that ZANU PF belongs to the people and not to individuals.

“Our party belongs to the people, never to individuals,” Chiwenga said.

He said while change was unavoidable, it must follow the party’s established procedures.

“While change is inevitable it must be orderly.

“In our party structures and guided by our constitution. Change must be driven by the people and not imposed from above,” he said.

In a pointed reminder to President Mnangagwa, Chiwenga invoked the President’s own mantra.

“You may recall your excellence that the voice of the people is the voice of God.

“As such we must remain true to that promise and carry with us the voice of the people,” he said.

Chiwenga said the party must return to its founding values of discipline and collective service.

“Discipline, accountability and selfless service must define our trajectory superseding disjointed and individualistic approaches,” he said.

Quoting the Chinese revolutionary leader, he added:

“Chairman Mao said, ‘individual desires and private virtues are meaningless outside their relationship to the collective.’

“He then concluded in Shona: “Mazvake mazvake ahana kwaanotisvitsa.”

The remarks are Chiwenga’s most explicit intervention since the passage of Constitution Amendment No. 3 and the ongoing debate over the extension of political terms from 2028 to 2030.

While he did not mention President Mnangagwa by name beyond the honorific, it was clear the speech was a clear rejection of attempts to personalize the party and the state.
