title: No Data? No Problem: How to Make Video Calls on Econet Using Airtime
summary: Good News! Econet’s VoLTE (Voice over LTE) has come with a bonus most people haven’t noticed: you can now make a video call straight from your phone’s normal dialer. And no you don’t need a data bundle, WiFi or WhatsApp. It’s a regular phone call, just with video. Here is how to make a video […]
content_text:
Good News! Econet’s VoLTE (Voice over LTE) has come with a bonus most people haven’t noticed: you can now make a video call straight from your phone’s normal dialer. And no you don’t need a data bundle, WiFi or WhatsApp. It’s a regular phone call, just with video.

Here is how to make a video call on Econet using airtime, with no data or WhatsApp

Three things have to be in place:

Econet on both sides. It only works when you call another Econet number.

An Android phone. It didn’t work on the iPhones we tested.

VoLTE switched on, on both phones.

So how do you switch on VoLTE

Open Settings on your phone.

Go to Mobile networks. On Samsung phones it’s Settings → Connections → Mobile networks.

Turn on VoLTE calls (some phones call it “4G calling” or “Enhanced 4G LTE mode”).

Menu names differ a little between phone brands. If you can’t find it, search “VoLTE” in your settings.

Now after setting up everything this is how you can make the video call

Open your normal Phone app.

Dial the Econet number you want to call.

Tap the video call button, or start a voice call and switch to video once it connects.

That’s it. No app or data needed.

Why it’s useful Only the caller pays. The person you’re calling doesn’t need airtime or data to answer, and both of you can be offline. Which is a different story On WhatsApp, both of you need data. It works when your bundle runs out. If you have airtime but no data, you can still see the person you’re calling. It’s easy for people who don’t use apps. Parents and grandparents can answer it like any normal call.

How much does it cost?

Econet hasn’t published a rate for VoLTE video calls yet. In Kenya, Safaricom charges video calls at the same rate as a normal voice call. If Econet does the same, it would cost about 4 cents a minute, the current Econet-to-Econet voice rate. That would be cheaper than a WhatsApp video call on a daily bundle, which works out to roughly 6 cents a minute because WhatsApp video uses about 10MB a minute. On a big monthly bundle, WhatsApp can be cheaper though.

Tip: check your airtime balance, make a one-minute video call, and check again. That will tell you the real cost on your line.

The limitations Econet only. You can’t video call NetOne or Telecel numbers this way. Those networks would first need to launch VoLTE and agree with Econet to connect their systems. No iPhones. Apple doesn’t support this type of network video calling on any network, including in Kenya where Safaricom has offered it since 2021. You need 4G. If your phone drops to 3G, the video call won’t connect.

Now go try it yourself and tell us what you think in the comments!

title: MIS: The Startup That’s Trying To Make It Easier To Find Medicine In Zim.
summary: Back in 2021, we covered a startup on a mission to change the way we search for medicine. In Zim, it’s quite common for patients to go from pharmacy to pharmacy, prescription in hand, trying to find what they need. Medical Information Service, founded by Dr Dudzai Mureyi, set out to make that search easier […]
content_text:
Back in 2021, we covered a startup on a mission to change the way we search for medicine. In Zim, it’s quite common for patients to go from pharmacy to pharmacy, prescription in hand, trying to find what they need. Medical Information Service , founded by Dr Dudzai Mureyi, set out to make that search easier using technology. A lot has changed since we last wrote about them, so let’s dive in.

For recap’s sake, Medical Information Service (MIS) is a Zimbabwean WhatsApp-based health platform founded by Dr Dudzai Mureyi . It helps people find medicine easily and compare costs across different pharmacies. That’s valuable if you ask me, especially in a country where advertising isn’t allowed in the pharmaceutical industry.

Although we only wrote about it in 2021, MIS actually started in 2015, so it has been running for a while now. In that time, it has been through some battles, as you’d expect for any business that has been around that long. What sets it apart from other startups, though, is that it has fought court cases against government bodies.

Entering a heavily regulated field with a new innovation almost guarantees legal problems. So, of course, the Health Professions Authority of Zimbabwe and the Pharmacists Council of Zimbabwe took MIS to court in 2017 and 2018. They argued that MIS had broken the rule that prevents pharmacies from advertising their medicine. Fortunately, MIS won. Twice. And it kept operating. It’s unusual, and quite impressive, for a small, newly launched startup to take on two government bodies and come out on top. Fast forward to today, and MIS is still running.

So what has changed since then? First things first, MIS has changed how people search for medicine on its platform. For most of its existence, the process was manual. A person would type in what they wanted, and the request would be sent to pharmacy staff, who would then reply with what they had in stock and at what price. As you can see, it was a bit of work.

In the first quarter of this year, MIS automated the process. It now has a WhatsApp bot, which you can find on its website. Everything is automated from start to finish: you answer a series of questions, and the results come back to you from its databases. The WhatsApp integration is a smart move, and I think more Zim startups should follow suit. Why? People of all ages and backgrounds are familiar with WhatsApp, and people who can’t afford WiFi can usually afford a WhatsApp bundle.

The service itself is simple to use. You send a WhatsApp message to the bot with the name of the medicine you need (or just a photo of your prescription) plus the area you’re in. MIS then checks with its network of pharmacies, which report back on what they have in stock and what it costs. You quickly get a list of pharmacies and prices. It costs nothing to use beyond your WhatsApp data, and it can even tell you which of those pharmacies accept your medical aid.

For all the talk about medicine, that isn’t all MIS offers. In fact, I was quite shocked at how many types of service providers it has under its belt. These include ambulances, police, dentists, lab tests and 24-hour emergency rooms. So it’s not just about medicine, it offers quite a lot.

While we’re on providers, the other thing that has changed is traction. Back in 2021, MIS had about 200 pharmacies. When we spoke to her, Dr Mureyi confirmed that it has grown to 416 providers in total (individual pharmacies plus other providers such as ambulances) across 32 provider types. On top of that, the bot has handled 1,566 queries since it launched in the first quarter of this year. So it’s safe to say MIS has grown.

As for the business model, Dr Mureyi wouldn’t disclose much. Since patients use it for free, the money probably comes from the providers. Either way, it’s safe to say money is coming in one way or another.

MIS fought legal battles and had to learn firsthand what it takes to run a business like theirs in a country like Zim. That work arguably opened the door for competitors like Cloomi , Kumbacare and MCAZ , who I’d like to think have had a much smoother ride. They run a similar model, and they use WhatsApp too. Imitation is flattery, I guess.

MCAZ is the bigger and more notable competitor. It’s the government body that decides which medicines are allowed in the country, and it has now adopted Dr Mureyi’s idea and built its own national medicine price platform. In a report, MCAZ even cited her legal victory as the reason it’s allowed to do so. Dr Mureyi, however, has no affiliation with the organisation.

With all that said, MIS has been at it for a long time, so there’s a good chance it will keep going. Whatever the future holds, it’s clear that MIS built something the market and the industry actually needed.

title: Did Customer Experience Slowly Become the Biggest Thing Any Business Can Sell?
categories: Business; Startups; Customer Experience; customer service; Entrepreneurship; Techzim Smartphones; Zimbabwean businesses
summary: You might not beat a bigger business on price or size, but you can compete on how people feel when they deal with you. Customer experience may be one of the most valuable things any business can sell.
content_text:
One of the most interesting things I have realised about myself is that, provided I have enough money, I would always choose to buy from someone with good customer skills over someone who is just cheaper.

I have noticed this behaviour of mine even when it comes to supermarkets I go to, tuckshops I buy from or even the musika where I find myself buying vegetables. The idea behind it, at least from what I can understand, is that these people make it so easy to interact with them that the experience becomes about more than just what I am buying.

We have heard similar stories countless times at Techzim Smartphones , and I thought it was worth writing about. Stories about our customers continuously buying from us because they love how we work with them through the process of getting a new phone and how much of a genuine interaction we have with them in the process. How someone who just thought of trying this new phone retailer can find themselves having an interesting conversation about technology and life in general until they have to convince themselves to leave.

In the process, we have made countless friends and return customers. We have had pilots come in for smartphones, army officers, executives, hustlers, students and everyone else with hope for a better future. But beyond all these titles and differences, they are just people. And people love beautiful interactions with other people.

I think what makes this much easier is why we sell smartphones . Limbikani always talks about why our smartphone business was to make smartphone buying in Zimbabwe risk-free. He says that our business was never made to be a once-off transaction and never will be. It is the start of a relationship between Techzim and our customer.

If you have ever interacted with him, he usually says, “This is the start of the relationship with you, your family and everyone who you interact with because when you go out there”. There is always a story you have beyond just the smartphone, smartwatch, tablet or anything like that.

I still think this can be implemented in every other business you might have and is very important when your business is starting. You might not beat a big company on size or price, but you can beat them on how people feel when dealing with you.

What do you think?

title: Zimbabwe’s Embassy Has a Cybersecurity Problem Hiding in Plain Sight
summary: Whenever I see a serious cybersecurity lapse, I believe it must be called out. Cybersecurity is not a luxury, particularly when we are talking about a sovereign state, diplomatic missions and official government communications. A document issued by the Embassy of the Republic of Zimbabwe in London, dated 28 September 2026, provides a typical example. […]
content_text:
Whenever I see a serious cybersecurity lapse, I believe it must be called out. Cybersecurity is not a luxury, particularly when we are talking about a sovereign state, diplomatic missions and official government communications.

A document issued by the Embassy of the Republic of Zimbabwe in London, dated 28 September 2026, provides a typical example. The embassy’s own notice for its consular outreach programme lists consularzimlondon@yahoo.co.uk as one of its official contact addresses. The embassy’s current website also publicly lists both zimlondon@yahoo.co.uk and consularzimlondon@yahoo.co.uk , alongside its government address, zimlondon@isp.gov.zw

Why is a sovereign state using a free Yahoo Mail account for official diplomatic and consular communication?

I am not suggesting that the mere use of Yahoo proves that a foreign government is reading Zimbabwe’s emails. That would be an allegation requiring evidence. But it is precisely the kind of unnecessary third-party dependency that a government dealing with sensitive diplomatic, consular and potentially national-security information should be examining.

Yahoo’s own privacy documentation says that Yahoo systems may analyse and store communications content, including incoming and outgoing email. Yahoo also states that information can be transferred, processed and stored in countries other than the user’s own, including the United States and that it may be required to disclose personal data in response to lawful requests from public authorities.

The issue is not whether Yahoo is a reputable company. It is whether the Government of Zimbabwe should be placing official diplomatic correspondence on a consumer email platform when it has the ability to operate controlled government email infrastructure.

There is an even greater irony here. Zimbabwe frequently speaks about sovereignty, national security and the strategic threat posed by foreign powers. Yet cybersecurity sovereignty is not achieved by making speeches. It is achieved by controlling your infrastructure, your identities, your communications and your data.

A government embassy should have properly managed government email addresses, strong authentication, encryption where appropriate, centralised security monitoring, retention policies, access controls, audit trails and clearly defined data-residency and incident-response arrangements.

Diplomatic communication should not depend on a free email address. And this is not simply an issue for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Ministry responsible for ICT and the country’s cybersecurity authorities should be asking how many other government departments, diplomatic missions, parastatals and public institutions are conducting official business through Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook.com or other uncontrolled consumer accounts.

If the answer is significant, then Zimbabwe has a much bigger cybersecurity governance problem than one embassy email address.

Government communications should be brought under a properly secured national government email and communications architecture.

We cannot demand digital sovereignty while outsourcing parts of our official communications infrastructure to consumer platforms.

Zimbabwe is a sovereign state. Its official communications should look and operate like the communications of a sovereign state.

This is precisely why cybersecurity professionals must sometimes be uncomfortable. If we see the vulnerability, we must say so before someone exploits it.

The Embassy’s current website also confirms the Yahoo addresses cited above and also lists its government email address, so the issue can and should be addressed transparently by the relevant authorities.

Engineer Jacob Kudzayi Mutisi +263772278161

title: Starlink Ground Station Coming to Zimbabwe in Early 2027, Says ICT Minister
categories: Broadband; Starlink; Gorund Station; Willard Shoko
summary: Zimbabwe is getting a Starlink ground station. ICT Minister Tatenda Mavetera says SpaceX has concluded an agreement with one of the local Starlink dealers to set one up in the first quarter of 2027. She said this on X in reply to Willard Shoko, the independent Starlink researcher who has been pushing for a ground […]
content_text:
Zimbabwe is getting a Starlink ground station. ICT Minister Tatenda Mavetera says SpaceX has concluded an agreement with one of the local Starlink dealers to set one up in the first quarter of 2027.

She said this on X in reply to Willard Shoko , the independent Starlink researcher who has been pushing for a ground station since before Starlink was licensed here. He has tagged the Minister, the Starlink team, and anyone who would listen, again and again.

“There is no policy nor directive preventing Starlink from setting up a ground station in Zimbabwe,” the Minister wrote, adding that government will monitor progress and play a facilitating role.

According to POTRAZ’s latest sector report , Starlink carried 197.78 Petabytes of data in Q1 2026. Shoko points out that’s about 2PB a day , more than Econet, NetOne and Telecel combined (179.33 PB). Starlink did this with about 86,000 subscriptions. The mobile networks have 13.5 million.

By our calculations from the POTRAZ figures, Starlink carried almost a quarter of all internet traffic in Zimbabwe in Q1 2026, and 31.85% of fixed internet traffic. Spread over the quarter, that’s an average of about 200 Gbps, around the clock. For comparison, the report puts TelOne’s entire equipped international capacity at 245 Gbps. Starlink traffic grew 17.58% in the quarter. If that pace holds, Zimbabwean Starlink users will pass 1 Exabyte this year, as Willard has forecast.

All of that traffic currently leaves through ground stations in other countries.

Why does a ground station matter?

So your Starlink dish talks to a satellite, and the satellite passes your traffic down to a ground station connected to fibre and the internet. Zimbabwe doesn’t have one, so our traffic travels to ground stations elsewhere in neighbouring countries first. It’s a longer trip that adds latency, the bit of lag you feel on video calls and in games.

To pass traffic down quicker Starlink satellites need a ground station within range. When there’s none nearby, newer satellites relay traffic between each other using lasers to reach a station further away. Older satellites without lasers can’t do this effectively reducing their effectiveness when they are over Zimbabwe. So a ground station in Zimbabwe would let more of the satellites passing overhead serve local users directly, adding capacity and cutting latency.

A local Point of Presence (PoP) would go further. It would keep local traffic inside Zimbabwe, allow peering with local ISPs, and make it possible to cache content like YouTube and Netflix locally. That is, as a Starlink customer your YouTube video would actually be sourced from a local server at Liquid, TelOne or Dandemutande, making your internet experience much faster.

What about Harare?

Harare and Bulawayo sold out within weeks of Starlink’s September 2024 launch. The “sold out” label came off in February , but residential customers still only get offered expensive Priority plans or a waiting list.

A ground station will help, but it won’t solve this alone. Harare’s problem is mostly too many users in one small area for the satellites overhead to serve.

Yes, bringing older satellites into play adds some capacity, but the bigger relief will come from Starlink’s new V3 satellites , which each have about ten times the capacity of the previous generation. A ground station and V3 satellites together could finally open Harare to ordinary residential customers.

title: Got an idea for one of Zimbabwe’s big problems? There’s $5,000 on the table
categories: Startups; Hacklab; Startup Challenge; UN; UNFPA
summary: If you’re between 18 and 35 and you’ve been sitting on an idea that could fix something real in this country, this one is for you. The Ministry of Youth, working with the UN Youth Group (chaired by UNFPA), has opened applications for the Zimbabwe Youth Innovation HackLab 2026. It’s tied to the National Youth […]
content_text:
If you’re between 18 and 35 and you’ve been sitting on an idea that could fix something real in this country, this one is for you.

The Ministry of Youth, working with the UN Youth Group (chaired by UNFPA), has opened applications for the Zimbabwe Youth Innovation HackLab 2026. It’s tied to the National Youth Empowerment Strategy 2026 to 2030 . The problem areas to be worked on were agreed on at a workshop back in July by government, UN agencies and civil society.

There are three categories. The first is youth health and well-being, covering things like health financing, service delivery gaps and digital access to health information. The second is economic empowerment, which is about skills mismatches, getting into formal employment and support for entrepreneurs. The third is green jobs and climate resilience, including access to green opportunities, finance and technology.

The winner in each category gets a USD 5,000 seed grant. They also get business development support, pitch coaching and some national and regional visibility.

You don’t need a finished product. A concept, an early prototype or an early pilot all qualify. What the judges want is an idea that responds to a real problem and goes after its root cause. Fully operational businesses aren’t eligible unless they’re pivoting to tackle a root cause in a materially different way.

You can apply alone, but teams of 2 to 5 are strongly encouraged. Every member has to be 18 to 35 and ordinarily resident in Zimbabwe. Teams that are at least 40% female get priority. You can only enter one category, so choose carefully. Being a student, an employee or tied to an NGO or company is fine, as long as your institution doesn’t own the idea.

The application form asks for a problem and solution summary of up to 500 words and an innovation description of up to 800 words. You’ll also need to explain the root cause you’re targeting, give a 12-month implementation plan and a budget estimate, and write a short note on how the idea touches SRHR, gender equity or disability inclusion. It’s worth drafting all of that before you open the form.

Here’s the timeline. Applications close on 20 October at 23:59 CAT. Finalists will be notified and briefed on 23 and 24 October. Pitching happens on 4 and 5 November in Harare at the National Youth Symposium, and the winners are announced there too.

Apply here: https://forms.gle/qXG6oVCC87Dq82TR9

If you know someone with an idea like this, send it to them.

title: Menard Mutingwende on Building ZimLedger, Finding Paying Customers and the Business of Tech
summary: ZimLedger started with a simple problem, Menard Mutingwende wanted an easier way to analyse his EcoCash transactions. What began as a tool for turning EcoCash statements into useful data soon became something much bigger. Mutingwende realised that while the idea was technically interesting, it wasn’t necessarily a business. “I told myself truthfully, it’s a cool […]
content_text:
ZimLedger started with a simple problem, Menard Mutingwende wanted an easier way to analyse his EcoCash transactions.

What began as a tool for turning EcoCash statements into useful data soon became something much bigger. Mutingwende realised that while the idea was technically interesting, it wasn’t necessarily a business.

“I told myself truthfully, it’s a cool idea, but no one will pay for this,” he says.

That realisation pushed him to think beyond graphs and transaction analysis and ask a more important question: *What problem would people actually pay him to solve?*

The answer eventually became ZimLedger , an all-in-one financial management platform designed around the needs of small businesses in Zimbabwe.

Today, the platform has more than 10 000 Google Play installs and a sign-up base of more than 10 000 users. Customers who want the full service pay $5 a month after a seven-day trial.

For Menard, however, the numbers are only part of the story. The bigger lesson is about building technology that solves a real problem and building a business around it.

Finding the gap

Menard says much of the existing accounting software is geared towards larger companies that can afford accountants.

Small businesses often need the same basic financial information but don’t necessarily have the resources or expertise to produce it.

ZimLedger brings several functions into one platform: business and customer ledgers, financial statements, payroll, quotations, invoices and personal finance tools.

The idea is particularly relevant in an environment where business and personal finances can often overlap.

Rather than requiring a small business owner to use separate applications for payroll, invoices, customer accounts and financial tracking, ZimLedger attempts to put those functions under one roof.

From an idea to a product

ZimLedger launched in August 2025 as a website and APK before eventually making its way onto Google Play.

The product has also evolved largely through customer feedback.

Users asked for features such as customer ledgers and team accounts, including different permissions for different employees. Menard says those requests influenced the direction of the product after launch.

And unlike many subscription businesses where payments are automatically deducted from a card, ZimLedger customers generally have to make their monthly payments manually through EcoCash.

For him, that makes the decision to subscribe particularly significant.

If someone chooses to pay every month, the product has to keep delivering enough value for them to make that decision again.

What many devs overlook

For Menard, one of the biggest lessons from ZimLedger is that technology alone doesn’t make a business.

“First, solve a problem,” he says. But solving the problem isn’t enough. Founders also need to ask whether there are people willing to consistently pay for the solution.

He also challenges the idea that launching an app is enough to attract customers.

“You build something, you launch it, and it doesn’t go viral the way it happens in the movies,” he says.

Marketing, he says, has to be treated as part of building the business. ZimLedger has used paid advertising as well as content marketing, including a WhatsApp channel that has grown to around 10 000 followers by sharing business and personal finance content.

Building for the business, not just the technology

Menard’s own background has helped shape that approach.

He has a master’s degree in financial engineering and previously ran StartupBiz Zimbabwe, an online business that has been publishing since 2015. That experience exposed him to another important distinction: once-off revenue versus recurring revenue.

It is one reason he favours the subscription model for ZimLedger.

But perhaps the most interesting part of his journey is where it began.

The first version wasn’t a grand fintech vision. It was simply an idea for analysing EcoCash transactions.

The turning point was recognising that *a technically impressive product isn’t necessarily a commercially viable one*.

As Menard puts it:

“No one will pay for nice graphs.”

For Zimbabwe’s growing community of developers and tech entrepreneurs, that may be the more important lesson behind ZimLedger.

title: An Open Letter to African Leaders on Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Digital Sovereignty and the Protection of Africa’s Future
categories: Artificial Intelligence; Africa; African Union; Cybersecurity; Digital Sovereignty; Zimbabwe Information and Communication Technologies; Zimbabwe Institution of Engineers
summary: The AI threat that Africa cannon ignore The Chairperson of the African UnionThe African Union Commission Heads of State and Government of the African Union Member States Your Excellencies, I write to you as a former Chairman of the Zimbabwe Information and Communication Technologies (ZICT) a division of the Zimbabwe Institution of Engineers (ZIE), with […]
content_text:
The AI threat that Africa cannon ignore

The Chairperson of the African Union The African Union Commission

Heads of State and Government of the African Union Member States

Your Excellencies,

I write to you as a former Chairman of the Zimbabwe Information and Communication Technologies (ZICT) a division of the Zimbabwe Institution of Engineers (ZIE), with many years of experience advocating for greater awareness of cybersecurity and information technology issues across Africa. Over the years, I have published numerous papers and articles on the growing threat of cyberattacks and cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and I have also organised and held cybersecurity conferences and awareness initiatives aimed at bringing together stakeholders to discuss the growing risks facing our digital society.

I have consistently warned that Africa cannot afford to underestimate the consequences of cyber threats or remain overly dependent on technologies and digital infrastructure developed outside the continent.

Today, I believe we have reached another critical moment. Artificial Intelligence Has Changed the Threat Landscape. The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces an entirely new dimension to cybersecurity and national security. Warnings from individuals working at the forefront of AI research including concerns that sufficiently advanced AI could potentially pose an existential threat to humanity should be taken seriously.

Whether the most extreme predictions ultimately materialise or not, one fact is already clear: AI has the potential to dramatically increase the speed, scale and sophistication of cyber threats. Africa is therefore more vulnerable than ever before.

Many African countries continue to face challenges including limited cybersecurity investment, shortages of highly skilled cybersecurity professionals, inadequate digital infrastructure, insufficient protection of sensitive data and dependence on foreign technology platforms.

The AI dimension could amplify these vulnerabilities considerably. Africa Cannot Afford to Wait. Our continent must not treat AI simply as another technological development. AI is becoming a strategic capability with implications for national security, defence, banking, healthcare, elections, energy, telecommunications, agriculture, education and critical national infrastructure. A sophisticated adversary equipped with advanced AI could potentially identify vulnerabilities, automate attacks and operate at a speed and scale that traditional cybersecurity teams may struggle to counter.

Africa therefore needs a coordinated continental response. We cannot continue relying solely on individual countries attempting to defend themselves in isolation. Africa Must Develop Technological Sovereignty.

Your Excellencies, Africa must also confront a fundamental strategic question: Who owns the technology upon which Africa’s future will depend? If African countries remain primarily consumers of AI technologies developed elsewhere, we risk repeating a familiar pattern in which Africa provides data and markets while intellectual property, infrastructure and much of the economic value remain outside the continent.

Africa must become a creator, developer, owner and responsible regulator of AI technology. We need greater investment in African AI research, computing infrastructure, cybersecurity capabilities, data centres, digital skills and African-owned technology companies. Our universities must be empowered to train the next generation of African AI scientists, engineers and cybersecurity specialists.

A Continental AI and Cybersecurity Strategy

I call upon the African Union to consider establishing or strengthening a continent-wide initiative focused specifically on the intersection of Artificial Intelligence, cybersecurity and national security.

Such an initiative could include:

A continental AI and cybersecurity threat-monitoring centre.

Greater intelligence sharing between African states.

Joint cyber-defence exercises.

Protection standards for critical national infrastructure.

Continental AI safety and governance standards.

Investment in African-owned AI and cybersecurity technologies.

Training programmes for African cybersecurity professionals.

Stronger protection of African government and citizen data.

Cooperation between African universities, governments and technology companies.

Emergency mechanisms for responding collectively to major cyber incidents.

This is ultimately not simply a technology issue. It is about protecting Africa’s people and Africa’s future. Africa’s Black and Arab populations, together with all of the continent’s diverse communities, deserve to enter the AI era with security, dignity and technological sovereignty.

We cannot allow Africa to become one of the easiest regions to destabilise because we failed to invest sufficiently in protecting our digital infrastructure. At the same time, we must not allow fear of AI to prevent Africa from embracing its enormous potential. Africa must embrace AI but Africa must also understand, control and protect itself from its risks.

Your Excellencies, I have spent years raising awareness about cyberattacks and cybersecurity threats. Through published articles, cybersecurity conferences and other awareness initiatives, I have consistently sought to draw attention to the risks facing our increasingly connected societies. The emergence of increasingly powerful AI makes those warnings more urgent.

The question before Africa is no longer whether AI will affect our continent. It will. The question is whether we will be prepared.

History has repeatedly demonstrated the consequences of technological dependence. We now have an opportunity to ensure that the next technological revolution is different.

Africa must invest. Africa must collaborate. Africa must develop its own expertise. Africa must protect its data. Africa must strengthen its cybersecurity. And Africa must have a seat at the table where the future of Artificial Intelligence is being decided.

I respectfully urge the African Union and every African Head of State and Government to treat the AI and cybersecurity threat as a matter of continental strategic importance and to begin an urgent dialogue on how Africa can protect its people, economies, infrastructure and sovereignty.

The continent should not wait for a catastrophic cyberattack or an AI-related crisis before taking action.

The time to prepare is now not after the crisis.

Yours faithfully,

Engineer Jacob Kudzayi Mutisi

title: Local Developer Turns Zimbabwe’s Favorite Card Game Into A Mobile App
summary: If you give most Zimbabweans a deck of cards, the game they will instantly think of is MaCards or Makasa. The fast paced game that most of us grew up playing at school with fellow students or at home with a group of friends. For the most part we have only played that game physically. […]
content_text:
If you give most Zimbabweans a deck of cards, the game they will instantly think of is MaCards or Makasa. The fast paced game that most of us grew up playing at school with fellow students or at home with a group of friends. For the most part we have only played that game physically. However, Tendai Karuma who is based in Norton, has decided to turn playing cards into a mobile app game, Makasa Cards .

It’s available on iOS and Android, and even has a web version. Normally when you hear “online card game,” you think of Blackjack, Klondike, or FreeCell. These are games that confused most of us, with rules nobody ever properly explained. Speaking for myself, I still don’t know how any of those are played. Fortunately, Tendai has given us one we already know and actually enjoy.

Don’t get me wrong, Makasa Cards isn’t the first to do this. As a matter of fact the card game that we play has been played exactly the same or almost similarly by many people from all over the globe. In fact it is a variation of Crazy Eight which originated in the US and has since been adopted and changed to the game we play now.

Within Zimbabwe itself, I haven’t yet seen any app competing in the space Makasa is. In the region there is some competition, Apps like Matatu , Kadi Saba and Kadi , built by developers in Kenya and Uganda, which offer similar games to Makasa.

The concept of bringing local iconic games came off as interesting to me so I decided to take my time to see how the game works. The whole mission was to check whether the game was just another vibecoded AI slop or something that really does work.

Makasa has a number of play modes. There’s standard online matches against other human players. There’s a campaign mode that takes you through story-driven levels, an Offline mode for practicing against the computer, and daily Challenges that hand out rewards for logging in and completing goals.

Maka also has tournaments. The site says you can “climb the ranks and win big prizes” playing a dedicated Weekend Tournament. We haven’t played this one yet so nothing to share on it. Makasa has made it clear, however, that there’s no gambling involved.

Business model wise, right now it’s free to play the games. There are some Google adverts that show in the app. But given their current numbers, this return from that is likely very low. So it’s not clear what funds the “big prizes” you get for winning competitions. Maybe in the future a new subscription model will be introduced to the game.

There’s also a lighter social layer. You earn an in-game currency called $MD as you play, which goes toward unlocking cards for your Collection. You can add friends, see who’s online, and challenge them directly. If you have played chess on chess.com you’re probably familiar with this already.

On the numbers, Makasa is still quite small. The site puts it at over 1,200 players already competing, Google Play lists it north of 1,000 downloads with 269 reviews and a 4.7-star rating. The app was last updated just days ago, so Tendai is still actively building on it, rather than having walked away after launch like many of us devs & vibercoders.

Quite interesting to see someone working on something outside the usual Marketplace apps, CV-writing ones, InDrive for X apps, food delivery apps, and literal InDrive clones .

.

title: Econet to phase out 3G by end of 2027
summary: Econet has said it’s planning to switch off 3G network by end of next year. The company says it will then gradually phase out 2G as it shifts its focus to faster 4G and 5G services. Econet CEO, Douglas Mboweni, said in a release we received today: “Our plan is to shut down 3G first, […]
content_text:
Econet has said it’s planning to switch off 3G network by end of next year. The company says it will then gradually phase out 2G as it shifts its focus to faster 4G and 5G services.

Econet CEO, Douglas Mboweni, said in a release we received today:

“Our plan is to shut down 3G first, by the end of December 2027. Only a small proportion of our customers remain on 3G, as most are now using 4G and 5G. We are encouraging those still on the older technology to migrate to the higher-speed technologies.

We must give rural customers more time to replace their phones while supporting them with affordable handsets and flexible payment terms. We will first upgrade network coverage and then help customers in rural communities migrate to 4G as the minimum standard. That work is already underway.

Econet says it plans to pour hundreds of millions into more 4G and 5G infrastructure.

According to its announcement today, maintaining several generations of mobile technology simultaneously puts pressure on spectrum allocation (what mobile operators buy for tens of millions from government, to be able to operate a mobile network). It’s expensive because it’s a limited resource. Econet says freeing up some of this spectrum allows it to use it for 4G and 5G services.

The latest Zimbabwe telecoms sector performance report by the sector’s regulator shows Econet has more 3G base stations than 4G ones. Here’s the breakdown of its base stations by technology:

2G – 2,981

3G – 2,071

4G – 1,951

5G – 353

It seems 3G still does some heavy lifting on the Econet network. In fact, 74 more 3G base stations were added between last December and March this year. So it’s surprising the company says “only a small proportion of its customers are on 3G.”

Whatever the case, Econet needs enough 4G coverage to replace whatever those 2,071 3G base stations currently provide. Which maybe explains those hundreds of millions Econet says it needs to spend.

Econet isn’t unusually early. Rwanda is targeting June 2027 for its 3G shutdown, while South Africa has set the same December 2027 deadline as Econet.

Customers with 3G-only smartphones will be affected by this 3G shutdown. December 2027 is still some 15 months away and the big unknown is how many Econet subscribers will still be using 3G-only devices by then. If that number remains significant as the deadline approaches, the company will face the difficult task of getting those customers onto 4G devices or reconsidering the deadline.

Complicating this further is that Econet’s move comes when, globally, prices of smartphones have skyrocketed owing to an AI-driven RAM crisis. It’s so bad it’s being called the “ RAMageddon “.

It’s estimated the crisis will persist, and might actually get worse, for another year or so as the AI demand grows. What this means is that many will not be able to upgrade their devices.

To be clear, it’s not necessarily that these 3G-only phones will stop working come January 2028. Econet says 2G will remain for longer, so compatible phones should still be able to fall back to 2G. For internet access though, 2G’s so slow it might as well not be there for the average user’s needs.

Econet also said in its release that it’s stepping up its fight against “grey handsets.” Econet says they now have the capability to detect such smartphones and that when they connect to the network, they’ll alert the customer and also let authorities know, “to help curb the practice.”

The term “grey handset” usually means genuine phones imported through unofficial channels or intended for another regional market (in Zimbabwe’s case usually Asia and the Middle East). Econet, however, appears to be using it differently here. It describes grey handsets as devices sold as smartphones but which don’t actually meet their advertised specs, essentially the questionable or outright fake smartphones that are fairly common on the local market. You can check out a video we did of a fake iPhone 17 Pro Max , earlier this year. These fake iPhones are really just bottom of the barrel Android phones, pretending to be what they’re not.

If you’re buying a smartphone between now and December 2027, it’d be really unwise to buy one that doesn’t support 4G. Econet commands about 75% of Zimbabwe’s mobile subscriptions, and in 15 months it intends to make 4G the minimum viable standard for decent mobile data on its network.

You can read the full release here .

title: Runtime Is Selling Local Domains For $2 A Year
categories: Startups; domains; Ngaatec; Ngaavongwe Ndasowampange; Runtime; ZISPA
summary: This one was a bit of a surprise. We have been paying our provider $10 a year. It’s not that we didn’t know local domains could be cheaper. There are providers, offering them at half that. But $2 a year makes you stop to check something out. To try it out and see if it […]
content_text:
This one was a bit of a surprise. We have been paying our provider $10 a year. It’s not that we didn’t know local domains could be cheaper. There are providers, offering them at half that.

But $2 a year makes you stop to check something out. To try it out and see if it delivers as advertised. It did. Runtime registered our new domain and got it working for the price of a kombi trip to the CBD. Well a round trip…

It’s exciting because it makes it easier for anyone to get started with something online with their own web app.

Runtime.co.zw was started recently by Ngaavongwe Ndasowampange who has already been providing web and app development hosting in Zimbabwe for a while on Ngaatec . He told us is drawing on the experience he’s had from that work with customers who need services to establish themselves online.

He said in response to some questions we sent him: “I wanted to experiment with a different approach. Make the entry point extremely simple and affordable, then build useful infrastructure and developer tools around it. That’s where Runtime came from. You should be able to have an idea today, get a domain and start building.”

AI vibe coding tools have made starting something extremely simple and low cost. Even on a free tier you can explain your idea to these tools and have them create something of a rough version 1 of your app. Something to help you test if it’s worth pursuing further. Being able to get a domain easily to start with, can’t hurt.

We tested Runtime with the registration of a domain, and the process, save for a few hiccups with ZISPA requirements (turns out you can’t register a one letter domain) went smoothly.

The one thing they definitely need to improve on is the EcoCash payment process which is still manual; that is you do a money send, then send proof of payment to Runtime. This part feels like we’re back in 2013. It’s more of a headsup for you reading this. Personally, for a $2 domain, it’s a bother, not a pain 🙂

title: MSU Student Accused in US$1.1 Million CABS Cybertheft
categories: Cybersecurity; Finance; CABS; hacking; Malware; Sabelo Malunga; SUPREMO
summary: In what is one of Zimbabwe’s largest reported financial cyber heists, a 24 year old Midlands State University student was brought before the courts for hacking and stealing US $1,136,179 from a local bank, CABS. According reports, the student, Sabelo Malunga, did attachment at CABS, and apparently exploited the access gained during his time there […]
content_text:
In what is one of Zimbabwe’s largest reported financial cyber heists, a 24 year old Midlands State University student was brought before the courts for hacking and stealing US $1,136,179 from a local bank, CABS.

According reports , the student, Sabelo Malunga, did attachment at CABS, and apparently exploited the access gained during his time there to install SUPREMO, a remote access software that then enabled his access after he had left. He apparently downloaded SUPREMO onto a CABS machine in January this year while still on attachment.

After his attachment ended (on 23 February), he could access the CABS systems and he used that access to plant malware tools that would create fraudulent Visa and ZIPIT transactions.

The Visa transactions were international ATM transactions linked to CABS-issued debit cards for $210,500 and they were discovered on 27 March. The transactions were flagged by Visa but the money had already been lost.

The bank’s IT team discovered the malware on 13 April and an internal reconciliation uncovered the ZIPIT transactions, some 1,911 of them, used to transfer US $925,679 to EcoCash, InnBucks, CBZ and Ecobank. This amount was also not recovered.

From the dates, it looks like the student had access for an estimated 4+ weeks.

There’s no mention about whether the transactions would siphon money from other bank customer accounts or a different pool of money within the bank’s system. There’s also no mention of how CABS’s endpoint cyber-security tools did not catch this remote access earlier.

According to the report, CABS used the services of a South African digital forensics company to “contain and eradicate the malware and investigate the breach.”

The student has not yet been asked to plead and was remanded in custody until Thursday. This means all these are just allegations for now.

The remote access software used in the attack, SUPREMO, is a legitimate tool similar to TeamViewer, AnyDesk, or Chrome Remote Desktop. However, while SUPREMO has built-in security measures and encryption, it has been exploited by hackers and scammers for unauthorized access to victims’ computers. The feature usually used is a feature where it can configured to start at system boot, allowing unattended remote access.

title: EcoCash is Winning The Download. Can It Win The Daily Habit?
