summary: The EcoCash SuperApp has crossed the 500K+ download milestone on Google Play, with a 4.3 rating from roughly 2,700 reviewers. That is impressive early traction, especially for a new Zimbabwean app. EcoCash has supported the push with a referral programme that rewards both the referrer and the referred user. It is also migrating customers from […]
content_text:
The EcoCash SuperApp has crossed the 500K+ download milestone on Google Play, with a 4.3 rating from roughly 2,700 reviewers.

That is impressive early traction, especially for a new Zimbabwean app.

EcoCash has supported the push with a referral programme that rewards both the referrer and the referred user. It is also migrating customers from the old EcoCash app to the new platform.

Those moves suggest that the SuperApp is strategically important to the company. But downloads alone do not tell us whether the bet is paying off. Many people may have downloaded it simply to continue making EcoCash transactions.

The real test, and what EcoCash is likely weatching, is whether they are using the features that actually make it a SuperApp; the Chat, the Explore social feed.

Both features have really strong existing competition in Zimbabwe from Meta. Chat is dominated by WhatsApp and the social feeds are dominated by Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and increasingly WhatsApp Channels. Competing for attention with these platforms will be super hard.

EcoCash can spend to incentivise installation, but can it build a new daily habit? Are Chat and Explore useful enough to justify the investment?

title: Econet’s AI Deployment Finds 1 Million Customer Phones Throttled at Wrong Data Speed
categories: Artificial Intelligence; Connectivity; 4G; 5G; AI; Econet; Smartphones
summary: Econet CEO, Douglas Mboweni has said the company recently discovered a lot of customers were using the internet at the wrong speed. The company credits the discovery to the deployment of AI on the network to help uncover issues customers are facing. Said Mboweni in a release to the media: “We recently discovered that more […]
content_text:
Econet CEO, Douglas Mboweni has said the company recently discovered a lot of customers were using the internet at the wrong speed. The company credits the discovery to the deployment of AI on the network to help uncover issues customers are facing.

Said Mboweni in a release to the media :

“We recently discovered that more than a million handsets had been configured at the wrong speed, preventing customers from properly accessing services such as TikTok and YouTube or watching short videos without buffering. With AI, we can now identify the affected handsets. We will in fact soon advise customers on how to change their settings or invite them to visit our shops for assistance.”

Mboweni called this a “breakthrough”, which just says how much of an impact it has on the company. Customers having connectivity problems on their devices is not a good thing for Econet. Customers happily consuming data means more revenue for Econet. Doesn’t make business sense for the company to invest in the latest network infrastructure (5G and 4G) only for this capacity to not be used. This could unlock internet bandwidth use and revenue growth, essentially sweating its investment in infrastructure.

The company also said it’s implementing some 20 artificial intelligence initiatives to improve business operations and customer experience.

This likely refers to internal deployments under the main company itself and not necessarily new products under the new AI focused subsidiary , Econet AI. Products like EcoAI Tokens . Or it could be both network stuff and new products given today’s press release mentions the 100 AI engineers recruited for Econet AI that was first mentioned last month .

Econet also mentioned two other breakthroughs: the ability to trace network faults in minutes rather than hours or days, and instantly diagnosing phone problems (even when customers aren’t aware an issue exists).

The company has said it’s investing significantly in AI. Mboweni said today “We now have access to AI capabilities at a scale unmatched in Africa, supported by our own cloud infrastructure, which is being deployed right now, as we speak.” The company separately announced this week that it has moved its entire digital operation to Google Cloud Platform, suggesting where this infrastructure footprint is being built.

Definitely interesting times. I’m not clear yet how everything is connected. Where Econet Infrastructure starts and ends. Where Google infrastructure starts and ends. What of Liquid Intelligent Technologies with its Microsoft bias in cloud platforms? And where Econet InfraCo fits in all this.

title: Why Your Phone Has Barely Any Local Apps: The Zimbabwean Startup Problem
summary: Over the past few weeks I’ve been digging into Zimbabwean startups. I came across all kinds of them, tackling problems across every field you can think of. What struck me was how little it seemed to matter how well designed, engineered, or marketed the product was. Most of these startups just were just simply not […]
content_text:
Over the past few weeks I’ve been digging into Zimbabwean startups. I came across all kinds of them, tackling problems across every field you can think of. What struck me was how little it seemed to matter how well designed, engineered, or marketed the product was. Most of these startups just were just simply not doing well.

Every year a fresh crop of Zimbabwean tech startups launches mostly with a post on X, LinkedIn and Facebook. They get a bunch of likes and comments, the team behind the startup gets excited. The founder is convinced that they are the one that breaks the pattern. Eighteen months later the startup is nowhere to be seen.The collapse isn’t dramatic or sudden but it’s slow and quiet. The website suddenly stops getting updated and the social media accounts go silent.

A quick look at your phone’s homepage can show you how exactly bad it looks. Most of us barely have any local apps on our phones. The only ones we usually have are backed by already big companies like Econet and Simbisa. With the exception of your friend’s vibecoded app you have in the name of support of course.

It’s not that Zimbabweans lack good ideas or technical skill. Startup Blink Report ranked Zimbabwe 117th out of roughly 118 countries surveyed in 2025, with only a couple of dozen startups tracked in the entire country. Highlighting how startup growth in Zimbabwe is stunted.

There are plenty of reasons that cause these frustrating failures of startups and for the most part it’s not just limited to Zimbabwe only. Most African startups run into the same wall. But a few of these problems hit Zimbabwe especially hard.

First off there are no real investors looking to fund promising local startups. Ask most of Zimbabwean founders where the venture capital is and you’ll get a confused look. Most of the ideas that these startups are trying to build need real money to run, not LinkedIn comments. Company registration, actually building the product, cloud hosting, developer salaries, data bundles, marketing, and the diesel to keep servers running through load shedding all cost money nobody’s handing out.

Sadly the money is very hard to get. Most startups end up quietly leaving the scene after realizing that they had heavily underestimated the operating costs. Especially at the early stages when little to no revenue is coming in.

At the same time looking for global venture capital is almost a dead end. Only a handful of African startups have managed to do that. Most of the money flows to American and Chinese startups. And the rest goes to European startups. So at the end of the day Zimbabwean startups are left to figure out everything on their own with barely anything in their bank accounts

The other reason why the tech space in Zim feels underwhelming right now is also because the talent leaves as fast as it’s trained . The same skills that would make someone a strong technical co-founder here make them an easy remote hire for a company overseas. Every developer who leaves is also a potential mentor, angel investor, or second-time founder who won’t be recycling their experience back into the local ecosystem the way it happens naturally in more established hubs.

The regulatory side doesn’t do founders any favors either. Registering and running a company here comes with more paperwork and cost than it probably should. There’s also no Startup Act or anything like it, no framework offering young companies breaks on tax, IP protection or licensing the way countries like Tunisia and Senegal have already set up for theirs.

Founders also share the blame when it comes to their failures. Most founders fall in love with the code, get too technical and underperform on the business side of their startups. Most forget to ask themselves a simple question before they start,” does anyone really need what we are creating?”. Or at least they simply lie to themselves.

There’s also a copy-paste culture where the fifth ride-hailing app or e-commerce clone launches with basically nothing separating it from the four before it. The Zim tech space is saturated with the same apps that do the same things. Sometimes a small research is all it takes to avoid getting into an already saturated market.

Even when a product is genuinely good, getting people to actually use it is its own fight. Zimbabweans already have trust issues, from scams and e-commerce experiences that promised convenience and couldn’t deliver, and that kind of skepticism doesn’t disappear just because a new app has a nicer interface.

With all that being said Zimbabwean startup founders still have a lot to learn. However some of the hiccups they face are out of their control and only direct interference from the government in the form of policy, funding, or a regulatory environment that actually works might be of help. Even though there have been some policies like National ICT Policy 2022–2027 , POTRAZ ICT Innovation Drive Fund and National ICT Innovation Fund. Most of them have turned out to be empty promises that don’t yield much result.

I have no doubt whatsoever that a new wave of Zimbabwean tech startups that grow into genuine industry giants is coming. It’s just a matter of when, not if.

title: Why smartphones prices are increasing so much
summary: Most of you have noticed that the prices of smartphones and laptops have been going up. Especially the entry level ones. This is the case wherever you buy your devices from. As Techzim, we sell smartphones to our community and are seeing this first hand. We retailed the Samsung Galaxy A07 with 128GB storage and […]
content_text:
Most of you have noticed that the prices of smartphones and laptops have been going up. Especially the entry level ones. This is the case wherever you buy your devices from.

As Techzim, we sell smartphones to our community and are seeing this first hand. We retailed the Samsung Galaxy A07 with 128GB storage and 4GB RAM at $110 around March this year. It has been going up gradually and this week that phone is now $160! It’s crazy. It brings back the hyperinflation trauma for most of us.

It’s happening at such a scale globally that people are now referring to this crisis as “ RAMmageddon .”

The situation is so bad that RAM has become the most expensive component in a smartphone.

We would like to answer what we can in this article and make recommendations. If you have any questions, please do ask in the comments so we address them.

Why are smartphones prices going up so drastically? What’s going on?

So, there’s a global RAM shortage right now. it actually started at the end of last year. The effects had not reached us but now we are getting hit too.

What’s causing this RAM Shortage?

The crisis hasd been caused by the sudden growth and need for more AI infrascturture. RAM is an important component in the chips needed for AI so companies like Google, Amazon, Meta (Facebook, WhatsApp), Microsoft, Oracle are buying a lot of them for their data centres. These companies are generally called Hyperscalers.

And there is not even enough for them so the demand is increasing. When demand is high and supply is low, prices increase.

There are just a few companies that make RAM chips globally. These companies supply everyone (phone makers, laptop makers, these Hyperscalers)

Is there profiteering going on as well?

It’s hard to say, but likely. Situations like these create opportunities for some companies to want to profiteer by raising prices above and beyond.

Some manufacturers of these RAM were sued for taking advantage of the supply shortage by price-fixing. taking advantage doesn’t just happen at manufacturer level, even distributors can do this. It is possible they are doing it at global, regional and even local country level.

When will the prices stabilise?

It will take a long time. At least a year from now. Likely more.

The few companies that make RAM have already started expanding so that they can make even more RAM chips, but this process takes years. It’s said it takes at least 2 years to bring up a new RAM factory.

What’s our advice then?

If you’re planning to buy a new phone or laptop (especially entry level ones), don’t assume the price you have seen in a shop will be the same price about a week or month later. The prices may be higher.

If you have some cash and want to buy a phone or laptop, wherever you buy, buy right away and don’t wait.

If you plan to upgrade your laptop with additional RAM, do it right away. Waiting for the prices to stabilise means you will wait a long time.

title: MaDeals: another promising marketplace app. Success or bust?
summary: After taking a long break from social media, viral comedy personality Melusi Chiripowako, better known as Ray Vines, came back to our screens reinvented. His new project isn’t a TikTok video but a marketplace app that has gained quite a bit of traction over the past few months. The MaDeals app. MaDeals works as a […]
content_text:
After taking a long break from social media, viral comedy personality Melusi Chiripowako, better known as Ray Vines , came back to our screens reinvented. His new project isn’t a TikTok video but a marketplace app that has gained quite a bit of traction over the past few months. The MaDeals app.

MaDeals works as a location-based marketplace where sellers post whatever they have, from second-hand goods to services. It is basically a C2C platform where anyone can decide to sell or buy at any given time. MaDeals makes it so that buyers browse a live map to see what’s available near them, rather than scrolling through a generic feed.

You chat directly with the seller inside the app, agree on a price, and arrange to meet and pay with hard cash or using EcoCash which is supported on the app.

What Madeals is trying to solve isn’t new. A lot of startups have tried the same thing both locally and internationally. The more recognisable competitors being Facebook Marketplace which runs the same consumer to consumer model and has a much bigger audience. OfferUp is also part of the competitors and is the one MaDeals resembles the most with its live map feature.

They have quite grown their user base thanks to their good marketing strategies. There is a variety of goods and services being offered across the platform and some people claim to have actually sold their goods on the platform which is a good sign.

As for the local market, while a huge chunk of it is still held by Facebook Marketplace and Whatsapp Groups, Classifieds.co.zw is a clear dominant platform in the market offering a huge amount of goods and services. Other platforms that are in the same market include Buyorsell , Zimexapp , EasyBuy , theDirectory and of course the Econet fumble Ownai.

As you can see the market is saturated and a lot of these platforms fight for crumbs left by the Facebook Marketplace, Whatsapp Groups and Classifields. Most of these marketplace platforms came in and then disappeared without a trace. In fact in 2021 we covered Marketsquare which looked promising at the time but hasn’t really grown much since then.

One of the reasons why most of these C2C apps don’t take off is trust. On a C2C platform anyone can post their products and for newer apps there is no telling if they are legit or not. So scamming can be common among these marketplace apps so people try to stay far away from them as possible.

Even Facebook Marketplace follows the same C2C model. A person can go check the seller’s profile and look at comments and decide whether they are legit or not.

MaDeals can achieve what others could not. That is if they maximise on Ray Vines’ popularity. For the most part that is what has gotten them this far. The marketing effort they are putting is also impressive and is something that most of the failed marketplace startups simply could not do.

Their application is somewhat easy to use but the live map feature can be confusing at times. The bloopers showing the sellers location can be saturated at one place especially in the CBD and it gets hard to see who is who.

As for their business model, posting a service or good is free. The same goes for buying and requesting services. However the App Store listing shows in-app purchases ranging from small donation tiers up to $69.99. And promotional packages that let sellers pay to boost a listing for anywhere from a day to a month, priced between $9.99 and $49.99.

Their business model can become tricky as people’s donations don’t tend to be enough to keep a business running. And promotional packages are easily ignored by people, especially in Zim.

Whether people take to Madeals probably comes down to trust more than features. Zimbabweans already have Facebook Marketplace, WhatsApp groups and Classifields for buying and selling locally. But having a known face like Ray Vines at the front could work in Madeals’ favour in a way a random new app never gets. But sadly a popular face can only get you so far.

At the end of the day, people are going to prioritize quality and convenience. The Madeals team has a tough battle ahead of them. Only time will tell if they follow the marketplace app trend, or carve their own path.

title: Econet launches ecoAI Token, taking the Data Bundles concept to AI
summary: Most of you probably know about Econet AI already. It’s a new Econet company that’s just focused on AI and the group is taking this effort pretty seriously. The company has it’s own CEO (Navdeep Kapur) and has publicly been on a recruitment drive for a 100 AI engineers. You can read about Econet AI […]
content_text:
Most of you probably know about Econet AI already. It’s a new Econet company that’s just focused on AI and the group is taking this effort pretty seriously. The company has it’s own CEO (Navdeep Kapur) and has publicly been on a recruitment drive for a 100 AI engineers .

You can read about Econet AI the company on the website dedicated to it here econetai.co.zw . I’ve been confused about the strategy and direction of this new company (too many B2B products where I assumed Econet would leverage its B2C strengths but that’s a story for another day) so it was quite pleasant to see them introduce a consumer product.

This week, the company introduced ecoAI Token , an AI aggregator.

You use it to chat with the top AI models: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Mistral. It’s not free. You use your airtime or EcoCash to pay for tokens.

Econet AI is selling tokens like Econet the network sells data bundles: 10 cents a day, 70 cents a week, $3 a month.

The onboarding to start using ecoAI is incredibly easy and straightforward. You enter your Econet number, you receive an OTP and you’re in! The company already has your information from the network side. In fact it’s so easy it made me uneasy.

Once you’re in, you select the package ( bundle? I’ll use this bundle language for ease but it’s not their language ) you want, confirm your EcoCash payment and you’re done. Their FAQ says eligible users can get a free tier, but doesn’t say how.

Once you’ve paid, you can chat with the AI models and use up your tokens. For example, I bought the 10 cents daily bundle and got 5000 tokens. I started what’s clearly an expensive conversation, comparing responses from the different AIs available, and my 5000 tokens were gone in 2 messages. So, wrong bundle for me.

When you run out, you can just top up with another AI bundle, just like data bundles.

If you use this frequently it will be clear how many tokens you need for your work. Can’t say right now if ecoAI is more expensive or cheaper than the competition. Actually I can. Without a free tier, it automatically costs more. Competing AI aggregators like Poe have a free tier.

But ecoAI is not just competing with other AI aggregators, there’s the frontier models themselves. Why would I use ecoAi when I can just use Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT directly? All the frontier models have free tiers, some of them offering unlimited text chats.

OpenAI, for example, now offers free users unlimited text chats with GPT-5.6 Luna, a model the company says produces 62% fewer factual errors than the GPT‑5.5 it replaces. Why would I buy the GPT 5.5 bundles that ecoAI is selling?

In addition, ecoAI doesn’t have the latest models. Their Claude only goes up to the 4.x versions, which is not the best. Why would I pay to access an older model when I can pay Anthropic directly to access the latest and more powerful ones like Fable 5 and Opus 5? Especially considering both Claude and ChatGPT let me fine-tune how much thinking the model does, a feature ecoAI just doesn’t have. Controlling this thinking effort impacts price, which would make using ChatGPT and Claude directly potentially cheaper.

So if ecoAI is not cheaper, then the utility is elsewhere? The quick switching between models? I’m already a heavy user of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Switching between them is just a tab click away, so switching models is definitely not a problem.

If it’s not the model switching, then maybe the payments ease? Is the micro-payment the innovation here? While I can already pay for Claude using my EcoCash Virtual Mastercard I can’t pay for for just 10 cents of it’s brain. Maybe there are lots of Zimbabweans who will find paying 10 cents at a time is more practical than forking $20 at once? But aren’t these people catered for by the leading models’ free tiers? ChaptGPT has unlimited, Claude resets every few hours, and Poe resets every 24 hours, making the ecoAI’s daily bundle redundant.

Or I just don’t get it.

Or maybe they’re going zero rate this so Econet customers can use it without buying data bundles?

Anyway, ‘why use this’ aside, there’s the issue of the product experience itself. I loved the payment and ease of login. The presentation of the product could improve but it is usable and will improve. There has been some complaints that it’s vibe coded as if vibe coding, itself is a bad thing.

I think as long as the person prompting is taking care to create a great product, whether it’s vibe coded or not doesn’t matter. Unless the argument is there’s no way to produce a good vibe coded product. But anyone who says this clearly hasn’t been vibe coding, or is just a sour developer struggling to find themselves in these new times.

It’s a new product and I think it will improve. Right now, I personally have no need for it. Keen to hear the use cases you are seeing. Please do comment.

title: BantuBuzz: A startup promising to connect Influencers with brands.
summary: A new startup has found its way on my desk and it’s an interesting one. If you have a significant following on social media platforms or you are looking to promote your brand this might be of interest to you. BantuBuzz, is a promising Zimbabwean platform that might have found a way to create earning […]
content_text:
A new startup has found its way on my desk and it’s an interesting one. If you have a significant following on social media platforms or you are looking to promote your brand this might be of interest to you. BantuBuzz , is a promising Zimbabwean platform that might have found a way to create earning opportunities for content creators. While also giving brands a platform to look for influencers who can promote their brands and products.

BantuBuzz calls itself “Africa’s premier creator-brand collaboration platform,” and behind it is Blessing Mokoena , a Zimbabwean entrepreneur. The idea is that creators from across multiple social media platforms, like X, TikTok and Instagram, can go on BantuBuzz and post their profiles, listing details like their follower count, how much they charge for a video promo, and what their niche is. Brands or people looking to collaborate can then pick whichever creator fits and work with them directly.

As for their business model it seems as if they charge both brands and creators to be on their platform.For the brand pricing model the prices vary from $0 to $399.Your plan affects the number of active campaigns, active collaborations and team members you can have.

The creator pricing model is more lenient. The plans start from $0 to $19, with limitations of how many “portfolio items” you can put, verified badge availability and priority search placement depending on the plan chosen.

This can be very helpful to creators when you realize that most people who get into content may not have the right information on how deals with brands are done. Let’s say a boy in Highfields starts making skits in his bedroom just for fun and he manages to get a significant number of followers from it. All of a sudden brands start reaching out. Even with a lousy offer he can end up making videos for said brand and ends up being taken advantage of without even noticing.

Being a marketplace means BantuBuzz naturally helps both creators and brands discover prices and each can see where they fit. A creator can simply observe what other creators of the same follower count range charge . While brands can see how much a certain type of creator is likely to charge without having to overpay.

It also gives niche creators a real shot at being discovered by brands. Usually, it’s social media algorithms doing the work of surfacing creators to brands, and that algorithm tends to favor whoever’s already popular. Feeds are also tuned to the tastes of whoever is viewing making the discovery of niche creators.

If you’re not showing up on people’s screens regularly, you barely get any offers, no matter how good your content actually is.

This can work against, say, someone who just opened a small hospitality business and wants to promote it. They likely don’t know which creator, out of thousands, is actually the right fit to push their brand. A platform like BantuBuzz, where creators list their niche and rates upfront, at least gives that business owner a place to go looking.

As always I had to visit their site to see what exactly they had going on for them. They have a good number of creators which is more than 80, some with followers in the hundreds of thousands. These include creators from different platforms like Facebook, X, Tiktok, Instagram and YouTube. This can provide variety for early brands who are trying to test out the platform. Hopefully BantuBuzz can keep increasing their creators, especially the ones with huge follower numbers to attract big brands.

The competition against BantuBuzz isn’t stiff, locally at least. In fact, my research shows that no one in Zimbabwe is doing quite what BantuBuzz does yet. But Bantu is not just targeting Zim. They are positioning themselves as the bridge between African content creators and brands.

On the continent, there is some competition. Kenyan platform Wowzi offers this and is already well ahead, having raised a few million dollars in funding and has worked with huge brands such as Netflix, Google and CocaCola. Even so, BantuBuzz still has an edge in the Zim market, since local brands are almost always going to look for local creators who resonate with their audience far better than an outsider would. Local might actually be their super power, as they plan to expand beyond. Indeed there are probably local brands looking to do regional promotions, as well as global brands that would love a single platform from which they can coordinate an Africa-wide campaign.

BantuBuzz has quite some potential. Their main focus now must be towards bringing bigger and more recognisable names to the platform. The problem they are solving is real and hopefully they are the one of the Zimbabwean startups that can make it big.

title: Rera: Whatsapp-based platform which takes reminding work off your shoulders?
summary: Imagine never having to chase someone for getting work done again. You say what needs to happen once, the recipient gets messaged, followed up with, kept on track and you only hear about it again if something actually needs your attention. That world might already exist, thanks to a new Zimbabwean platform called Rera. Rera […]
content_text:
Imagine never having to chase someone for getting work done again. You say what needs to happen once, the recipient gets messaged, followed up with, kept on track and you only hear about it again if something actually needs your attention. That world might already exist, thanks to a new Zimbabwean platform called Rera.

Rera is a Whatsapp-based follow through assistant by Timothy Sabelanga. So what it does is you make reminders for people on what you would normally forget, or get too busy to do. Rera can then follow up, coordinate with the right people and keep track. It only reaches out to you on matters that need your attention.

“The idea came from noticing how much of everyday life happens through chat, but how much work still remains with the person who started the conversation. You can message someone, “Remember to do this at 7,” but you still have to remember to check whether they did it. I started asking: What if you could hand that responsibility over and move on? That became Rera.” Timothy spoke about the inspiration behind Rera.

I took a look at their website and they managed to provide the platform’s use case in a very brief and specific way. Rera’s use case actually makes sense to me . Their site splits it into work, family, errands, friends and home. At work you can use it to chase a colleague who’s gone quiet on work supposed to be done. At home it’s the sibling who never does the one errand you asked for until you’ve reminded them four times.

Rera can also be integrated with home devices that can be used on the internet. These include smart TVs, smart speakers and smart geysers. The home example they show on their site is my favourite though, telling it to make sure the geyser switches off at 10.

As far as my research goes, Rera is the only platform doing this specific thing in Zimbabwe. Of course there’s WappGPT, Siri and Alexa which are somewhat in the similar space. They all have reminder features but it’s how far they go which differentiates them from Rera. While Siri and Alexa may allow you to set reminders for people, they simply do not go out of their way to follow up.

As for WappGPT they fall short on one specific thing that makes Rera what it is. On WappGPT you set reminders for yourself and then the assistant starts to remind you until you do that thing. However, Rera allows you to set reminders for other people. Let’s say you want to remind your coworker to do a certain task you just tell Rera and just like that your coworker won’t rest until they do what they are supposed to.

I tried Rera out to experience its services firsthand. I was able to set a reminder for my younger sister to do her studies at 6pm. The bot was easy to use and by just sending my request as a text like i would to a friend the reminder was set. She even complained about its persistence afterwards.

As for their business model Timothy assured that currently Rera is being opened for free so they can actually see what people would use it for in the real world. However the longer-term model is going to be subscription based.” The basic experience can remain very easy to try, while more advanced capabilities around ongoing follow-up, coordination, integrations and higher usage can become paid features. I don’t want to force a business model before we understand what users value enough to pay for,” Timothy explained his plans for the business model.

Overall Rera can be of use on the day to day basis of people’s lives. The fact that they are WhatsApp based also helps keeping in mind that data prices in Zimbabwe can sometimes be expensive and as per a poll in our WhatsApp Channe l a lot of people depend on WhatsApp for collaboration. It’s now up to Rera on how well they will perform in the unpredictable tech market of Zimbabwe.

title: When last did you take a Tap&Go ride?
summary: So while on my way to work I came across a Kose billboard advertising their ride-hailing services. I remember asking myself how they were going to compete with other platforms already in the market like Indrive, Tap&Go and Bolt. Just when I was in the middle of a brainstorm I came to a realization, it […]
content_text:
So while on my way to work I came across a Kose billboard advertising their ride-hailing services . I remember asking myself how they were going to compete with other platforms already in the market like Indrive, Tap&Go and Bolt. Just when I was in the middle of a brainstorm I came to a realization, it had been a long time since I had seen a Tap&Go car around.

I remember last year when they officially launched, they had very attractive offers that were threatening to their competitors. These included a free starlink wifi access during your ride and a very generous discount system. A lot of people were going crazy over the platform and the marketing was just top-tier. I honestly thought it was game over for InDrive and it was time for them to pack it up.

Now that some time has passed ,it looks like InDrive is doing just fine and is still leading the market.

My reasoning behind this is people have already familiarized themselves with InDrive since their launch in Zim back in March of 2023.This gave them an advantage of a 2 year headstart which helped them better understand the space and optimize their app to meet the needs of Zimbabwean customers.

A poll in our community made it clear that the majority of people still rely on InDrive on a day to day basis with just a few showing their commitment to Tap&Go. Some even highlighted the fact that InDrive simply has better marketing compared to Tap&Go. Shockingly Bolt even had a comfortable vote lead against Tap&Go even though Bolt’s presence and marketing at times may feel underwhelming.

Another reason that could also explain the slow start of Tap&Go is their different business model.Unlike their competitors Tap&Go operates more like a taxi company that has an app while other platforms focus more on connecting independent drivers with riders.This means Tap&Go own all of the cars their drivers use. They officially launched with a total of 60 cars and meeting the high demands of transport with just 60 cars in the busiest city of the country can become very hard and make them look unreliable. Not to mention they also operate in Bulawayo. Meanwhile their competitors had already recruited a very large number of drivers without having to own a single car making it easier for them to meet a very high demand of transport.

A look inside their pricing model can also be explanatory to their current situation.Zimbabweans love negotiating the price down.Unfortunately, Tap&Go only has a fixed pricing model, so if you’re even 50 cents short of the price shown, it’s basically game over . This also affects the drivers who at times may think that the ride must cost a little more than the recommended price and may feel like they are being taken advantage of.

In all fairness Tap&Go falling short to platforms like InDrive and Bolt can also be attributed to its competition’s very strong global reputation. In fact, according to InDrive on their own blog they reported that they were the second most downloaded ride hailing app globally from 2022 to 2026. To be honest it really takes some work to beat that.

So after all has been said and done just last week after the Kose billboard incident I did see about 2 of Tap & Go cars driving around. That’s still a lot less activity from them compared to what they are actually capable of achieving especially with the aggressive rise of the ride-hailing platforms over the recent years.So do you think Tap&Go still has a chance to claim the number 1 spot?

title: Why Our Data Protection Regulations Need Review
summary: The Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe (POTRAZ) announced that mandatory compliance inspections of data controllers will commence on 1 September 2026. The inspections will span both the public and private sectors, targeting banks, insurance companies, healthcare providers, schools, local authorities, telecommunications companies and many other organisations that process personal data. The sweeping nature […]
content_text:
The Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe (POTRAZ) announced that mandatory compliance inspections of data controllers will commence on 1 September 2026. The inspections will span both the public and private sectors, targeting banks, insurance companies, healthcare providers, schools, local authorities, telecommunications companies and many other organisations that process personal data.

The sweeping nature of the compliance requirements prompts us to question whether our current regulatory approach is the right one.

Data protection is not the problem

Few would disagree that personal data needs protection. So, Zimbabwe’s Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] was an important milestone. Enacted in 200, it introduced long overdue protections for personal information, established data subject rights and designated POTRAZ as the country’s Data Protection Authority.

However, the subsequent Cyber and Data Protection (Licensing of Data Controllers and Appointment of Data Protection Officers) Regulations, 2024 (SI 155 of 2024) went further to introduce mandatory licensing fees for data controllers and required many organisations to appoint Data Protection Officers (DPOs).

This brought significant recurring compliance costs making data protection a cost of doing business across the entire economy. This counters government’s recent efforts to reduce the cost of doing business in the country.

We borrowed from the GDPR—but not its philosophy

Zimbabwe’s legislation certainly draws inspiration from the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The terminology and concepts are familiar and both frameworks claim to adopt a risk-based approach. Yet, the implementation is vastly different!

The GDPR is fundamentally accountability-driven whereas Zimbabwe’s framework is primarily licensing-driven. Under the GDPR, organisations are not required to obtain permission from the regulator before processing personal data. Instead, they are expected to assess the risks created by their processing activities, implement safeguards that are proportionate to those risks, and demonstrate compliance if challenged.

The Zimbabwean regulation takes a different route. It requires organisations to obtain licences, pay annual fees and appoint Data Protection Officers before undertaking any processing activities.

Assumed risk not actual risk

The biggest difference is how Zim’s current framework interprets risk.

The GDPR deliberately avoids fixed numerical thresholds when determining whether processing presents significant risk. Instead, regulators consider several factors together:

the nature of the data;

the scale of processing;

the purposes of processing;

the context in which processing occurs; and

the potential impact on individuals if something goes wrong.

In contrast, Zimbabwe’s licensing obligations are tied largely to prescribed categories and processing thresholds based on the number of data subjects. This results in organisations with very different risk profiles facing broadly similar compliance obligations.

One size for all regulation

Consider a small private medical practice. Its patient records are undoubtedly sensitive, but it serves a relatively small number of patients, has limited staff and operates within a constrained budget and pre-existing regulations. Under the current framework, that clinic is required to obtain a data controller licence and engage a Data Protection Officer. Whereas in the E.U it would not be required to do so

A school, a pharmacy, a local NGO and a growing software startup find themselves navigating comparable licensing requirements with a bank or insurance company despite having fundamentally different operational risks and financial capacity. The current data regulatory framework ignores that the scale, complexity and potential consequences of a data breach are vastly different even though they may handle the same number of data subjects.

The impact on startups

This has a negative bearing on Zimbabwe’s technology ecosystem.

For many startups, the first objective is to build a minimum viable product (MVP), validate a market and secure investment. Every additional regulatory obligation increases the cost and complexity of reaching that milestone. Under the current framework, a founder developing a healthcare app, educational platform or logistics solution needs to also budget for data controller licensing fees and DPO-related costs before engaging in any data collection or processing. Some founders have responded by obtaining DPO certification themselves simply to satisfy compliance requirements—an investment that can cost over US$1,250 before they have acquired a single customer. Large corporations can absorb these costs whereas early stage startups often cannot. When regulation creates significant upfront fixed costs, it unintentionally favours established incumbents over innovators.

Regulation should enable innovation, not discourage it

Zimbabwe’s recently launched National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026–2030) recognises that the country’s regulatory environment must evolve to make Zimbabwe “AI-ready.” It explicitly calls for achieving an appropriate balance between protecting personal data and enabling innovation. That balance is essential. As POTRAZ begins nationwide inspections, there may be no better time to revisit whether our data protection regulations are achieving that balance.

Good regulation should scale according to risk. A revised framework could retain strong protections for citizens while adopting a genuinely risk-based model. Regulatory obligations such as licensing or DPO appointments should reflect the nature, scope, context and purpose of processing rather than relying primarily on broad categories or numerical thresholds. This reduces unnecessary compliance costs for low-risk organisations while allowing regulators to focus on where the greatest risks actually exist.

Dr Marlon-Ralph Nyakabau

Medical Doctor, Digital Health Consultant, Public Policy Analyst

title: Did Econet just change their airtime credit system?
summary: So my cousin came to me last week to recharge his airtime balance using my phone because of the Econet airtime credit he had for a long time now. He had been doing this for quite some time and in fact a lot of people did the same. It usually went like this: he buys […]
content_text:
So my cousin came to me last week to recharge his airtime balance using my phone because of the Econet airtime credit he had for a long time now. He had been doing this for quite some time and in fact a lot of people did the same.

It usually went like this: he buys data using my phone and then sends it to his number to avoid Econet recovering the money and just like that he gets to use the bundle with no repercussions. This time around it didn’t go quite as planned. He bought the data as always but somehow it wasn’t working.

Just as he was about to contact customer support, a text message from Econet popped out “Dear customer, just now you have reimbursed USD$0.20 Of Credit Loan, and left unpaid amount USD$0.40”.

The voice bundle never reached his phone instead Econet took their 20cents and reminded him he had 40cents more left to pay. We quickly brushed it off until I came across a lot of videos and posts across social media talking about the same experience.

From my research, Econet now doesn’t wait to take their money when you accidentally recharge airtime directly to your phone after forgetting your outstanding debt. Instead when your credit is due they simply wait for the next time you try to buy data bundles. It doesn’t matter if you do it from your friend’s phone or directly from Ecocash. Let’s say you buy a 20cents voice bundle on credit so you now owe Econet 40cents. The next time you try to buy a $1 Whatsapp bundle using Ecocash or another phone they will first take their 40 cents and inform you that you are left with 60cents and if you still want to buy your data bundle you will have to top up 40cents. The old tricks and techniques have been patched.

Quite a number of our community members have had the same experience as my brother. In fact some have reported that at times Econet had taken more money than what was owed to them. To my knowledge it doesn’t look like Econet had informed its customers on their new airtime credit system beforehand. They are still yet to speak about it, with that being said all the conclusions I made are from testimonies across the web and our community.

People across social media have different mixed opinions when it comes to the new credit system. With some even joking “Econet yakutora chero mari irikuseri kwepouch kana une chikwereti”. However one thing we can all agree on is, it’s just business.

title: AI Collaboration In Music
categories: Artificial Intelligence; Grace Wave; Kure Kure; Magic Wacho; Ndakainamatira Nyaya; Suno AI
summary: Art and creativity have always had a complicated relationship with technology particularly in emerging markets across the world where adopting new things lack proper funding. Tech has never waited for creative industries to catch up, how music is made, recorded, distributed and consumed has constantly changed. The music industry has moved through cassettes to CDs, […]
content_text:
Art and creativity have always had a complicated relationship with technology particularly in emerging markets across the world where adopting new things lack proper funding. Tech has never waited for creative industries to catch up, how music is made, recorded, distributed and consumed has constantly changed. The music industry has moved through cassettes to CDs, analogue recording to digital recording as well as from physical distribution to mp3s to piracy and streaming. Each change disrupted the system in its own way.

The most profound change now is rooted in Artificial intelligence, what makes it different is that the disruption is no longer limited to how we consume the art, but AI is increasingly sitting inside the creative process. AI isn’t basically a replacement for artists, it is mostly a collaborative tool, an instrument that can be used during creativity. We have already seen this happen locally. Zimbabwean creatives have already experimented with AI to come up with music, developing sounds and exploring ideas that previously required a lot of resources.

Some AI collaborated pieces have even found their ways onto local radio playlists with listeners sometimes surprised to discover that what they were humming to be an AI collaborated piece of work. Of note is Ndakainamatira nyaya by Grace Wave and Kure Kure by Magic Wacho . The tracks have demonstrated how an AI assisted piece can find an audience and achieve significant traction.

One very popular application in creating music is Suno AI . The app is readily available on play store and is very easy to use. Once you install it you are prompted to create a free account so that you start creating stuff. You choose the type of voice you want it to use, type of melody and you can tweak on bass and other sounds that may interest you. You simply upload the lyrics, and, in a moment, you have a song which you can import to your memory if you are a premium user.

An important aspect to take note of is that the tech is already here and people are listening, instead of the question being whether AI should be used in creative arts or not, perhaps we should be asking how we could use AI without losing human creativity, culture and identity that makes our music unique. Technology has never been the enemy of creativity.

Technology will force an industry to adopt and become part of the ecosystem. AI will follow the same path, artists who understand it rather than simply resist it may ultimately have an advantage. The real challenge being whether AI is adopted early, creatively and intelligently enough to shape what comes next, and this is not only for the arts sector but other sectors as well like the farming sector and medical sector to mention a few.

title: Zim Universities Should Let Students Work Remotely For Attachment, Says ZimWorX Co-Founder

In a release sent to Techzim, Oliver said remote work is now commonplace, even in Zimbabwe, and that “Internship policies of higher learning institutions should reflect this reality.” Currently, Zim universities only recognise attachments (known […]
content_text:
ZimWorX co-founder JW Oliver has argued that Zimbabwean universities need to allow students to work remotely for their industrial attachment. In a release sent to Techzim, Oliver said remote work is now commonplace, even in Zimbabwe, and that “Internship policies of higher learning institutions should reflect this reality.”

Currently, Zim universities only recognise attachments (known as internships elsewhere) where students work on-site at their host companies. Some, like Bindura University of Science Education , allow students to do their attachment outside Zimbabwe, but in person, and the student has to foot the travel bill of the lecturer carrying out the assessment.

The way it works here is that the student’s university supervisor has to physically visit the workplace to assess the student’s work in person. Seems the issue with remote work is that universities don’t have the mechanisms to assess someone working for a US-based company from their living room in Mabvuku. It’s a policy thing really.

The problem with the current setup is that many students who fail to get on-site attachment end up having their studies delayed. And Zimbabwe doesn’t exactly have lots of employment opportunities at the moment. It’s a tough time to be a student.

Oliver says it doesn’t have to be this way. “The world is changing. The days when working for a company automatically meant being physically present at its premises are gone. Work can now be done from anywhere in the world. Industrial attachment policies in Zimbabwe’s colleges should match this reality.”

“The entire purpose of an internship is to prepare a student for the day-to-day realities of the work environment. If work has shifted from only being done on-site to also being done remotely, shouldn’t the learning experience reflect this?”

Oliver co-founded ZimWorX which we are told now “employs” some 1300 Zimbabweans. ZimWorX is structured as an Employer of Record for these Zimbabweans, which just means it connects them to remote jobs in the USA and UK and takes responsibility for things like processing salaries, and compliance with labour laws. In ZimWorX’s case, they also provide a place for these remote workers to work from (for reliable high speed internet, power etc…)

There are a few other companies like this locally, but ZimWorX looks like the largest. Typical roles people fill for ZimWorX clients include receptionists, executive assistants, accountants, paralegals, and marketers.

There are also many Zimbabweans working remote jobs they find directly on the internet, like graphic design, software engineering, and English language teaching.

title: Will New Startup, Propertyzone, Manage to Transform Property Shopping In Zimbabwe?
summary: The frustration that comes along with house hunting, conversing with agents and finally deciding to buy a property is something I am not familiar with but can only imagine how tiring it can be. An interesting startup landed on my desk just last week and they are promising to make life easier by providing a […]
content_text:
The frustration that comes along with house hunting, conversing with agents and finally deciding to buy a property is something I am not familiar with but can only imagine how tiring it can be. An interesting startup landed on my desk just last week and they are promising to make life easier by providing a more secure and efficient way for buyers to get the property they need.

So PropertyZone is this Zimbabwean property listing platform built by a dev outfit called Sparkline Labs . It does the usual matching of property buyers and tenants with real estate agents with a bit of a twist. Neighbourhood reviews and, according to them, a tight handle on who gets to list a property. They also say they have designed the app so that agents get more qualified leads. They officially launched earlier this year in February.

PropertyZone are not alone in this market; they have to face established names like Property.co.zw , Propertybook and Property24

In their messages to us, one of the founders said about why they are working on the app: “Most listing sites here work the same way, they push as many inquiries as possible to the agent, regardless of fit. Over time agents get conditioned to a flood of low-quality inquiries from people who could have disqualified themselves before ever calling, if they’d had the right information upfront”

When you open the app, you can see how they are trying to do things differently, and honestly, it’s surprising the incumbents seem to have overlooked some of this. It’s clean, deliberately designed, and overall easy to navigate. The landing page makes it very clear that only EAC-registered (a governing body that oversees real estate practice) agencies could sell properties, prohibiting unregistered individuals from doing the same. On competitor platforms, it appears individuals can post properties.

The standout neighbourhood review feature we mentioned earlier is called “ Where to Live .” This section helps buyers decide which suburb best fits their needs. It consists of a suburb ranking system for each city, determined by ZESA stability, internet services available, road quality, traffic into CBD, amenities, water and such. Each suburb has reviews and comments from community members, giving buyers a clearer, more unbiased sense of the place. Buyers or tenants looking to relocate to a suburb can also ask the community questions about the place.

I even noticed that in the section there were about 2 reviews of the place I live, Highfields. I could tell that the comments were somewhat authentic as they were very descriptive of the area in a human way and I could instantly recognise my home. This removed the skeptical thoughts I had about the reviews as I know it’s possible for someone to use AI generated text.

As useful as the Where To Live feature is, I could not help but notice some flaws with it. It’s a new platform yet to grow the number of reviews and that clearly affects the accuracy of the ranking systems. A score is a better reflection of reality when there are many reviews to aggregate. This becomes a problem especially when some places get few overly negative or generous reviews.

The rest of the features are what you’d expect and get from other property listing sites per-listing legal data, including tenure type, title deed status, and zoning. They also provide per-listing utility data showing borehole/water reliability, solar setup, ZESA/grid reliability, and internet speed. But it feels PropZone is doing this on a deeper level than the incumbents though, which was definitely a plus in my books. This makes it much easier for buyers to rule out or prioritize properties.

Propertyzone’s business model is built around agencies, not property seekers. Buyers or tenants use the platform for free while agencies have to pay to get their properties listed.This is basically the model that most of its competitors are using and from what I’ve seen it has worked perfectly so far.

According to PropertyZone they have managed to attract 16 agencies and around 132 agents since their launch in February. You can feel there are still few agents when you browse around the site. The traditional big names (Seef, Knight Frank, Guest & Tanner, Pam Golding, Pocock etc…) aren’t listed there yet. However they have not disclosed the number of successful property deals or users they have had.

In conclusion, PropertyZone claims they have introduced a safer, more convenient way for property seekers to buy or rent. However PropertyZone’s argument could collapse the instant the features that differentiate them are adopted by their competitors. The real question is whether they’ll win over enough users first, or whether competitors will copy their features before PropertyZone gets the chance to grow.

title: Is this startup the answer to the unorganized advertisement of events?

content_text:
Finding new events for you and your friends to enjoy can be a hustle. I usually spend a lot of time searching through instagram just to find that one new thing i might like.The alternative being scrolling on tiktok and by chance landing on an event ad. The new startup KoopyKwacho could be the solution to these problems.

KoopyKwacho, a web app created by Jimmy Chirinda is a platform that helps with the discovery of upcoming events by putting them in one place. Jimmy’s background in photography inspired the idea that came alive 2 years ago as an Instagram page and evolved to the website it has become today.

“As a photographer and content creator, I attend and cover many events across Zimbabwe. I noticed that people were constantly asking, “What’s happening this weekend?” or “Where can I find events?” Jimmy said about the inspiration.

I managed to visit the website and from what I could see the landing page of the website is clean and easy to navigate through with clear options but the bright colors used for the design can be a bit distracting.

Another interesting feature I noticed was their AI powered assistant which can be of great help. I managed to plan for an event with its help and most of the details and responses it gave me were spot on. The assistant is a strong feature if used well.

I could not help but notice that the number of events were low especially in places outside Harare, with some only having 1 event .This poses a bigger threat to their startup’s survival as users may become less likely to come back and of course in return event organisers and advertisers will not take the web-app seriously.

KoopyKwacho also faces intense competition. In recent years, numerous Zimbabwean web apps offering similar services have entered the market, making it difficult for users to distinguish one platform from another. Despite this growing competition, many of these platforms have struggled to achieve sustained success.

According to Chirinda they gained1100 visits with 80 registered users within 10 days of their web app launch. They are aiming to catch the eyes of sponsors and advertisers for their revenue.

KoopyKwacho is a platform I can see myself using although there is still some polishing that could be done especially in the quantity and quality of events available. Their success will also be determined by how well they can manage to market the platform and gain users who still use the traditional ways of Instagram, Tiktok or word of mouth like myself.

As the holidays near , the people’s response to the website at the busiest time of the year will be a clear tell on whether the website sticks or is ignored like all the others.

HARARE - Calls are growing for Zimbabwe and Russia to strengthen cooperation against human trafficking and deceptive recruitment schemes as President Emmerson Mnangagwa prepares for bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trafficking experts and opposition figures say the meeting should produce concrete measures aimed at tracing financial flows linked to alleged recruitment networks that have reportedly targeted Zimbabweans with promises of employment opportunities abroad.

The issue has gained prominence following reports that Zimbabwean citizens were allegedly recruited through fraudulent overseas employment schemes and later found themselves in military-related activities in Russia.

According to figures cited in public discussions surrounding the matter, Zimbabwean authorities have confirmed deaths and cases involving Zimbabweans affected by questionable foreign recruitment arrangements, prompting investigations and efforts to establish the identities of some victims.

Trafficking in Persons expert Zororai Nkomo said authorities should focus on tracking financial transactions connected to recruitment networks while ensuring that potential victims receive protection and support.

"The UN press statement suggests that the Zimbabwean nationals were recruited with the promise of employment but subsequently found themselves in the military, contrary to what they had been led to believe. From a Trafficking in Persons perspective, this raises serious concerns about possible trafficking for the purpose of forced military service," Nkomo said.

He argued that authorities should avoid automatically treating returnees as offenders without first determining whether they were deceived, coerced or exploited.

"Returnees must not automatically be labelled mercenaries or prosecuted simply because they were found in military service. Each case must be assessed individually," he said.

Nkomo proposed stronger cooperation between financial intelligence authorities, law enforcement agencies and international partners to identify recruitment networks and suspicious financial transactions.

Among his recommendations are enhanced financial intelligence sharing, tighter oversight of recruitment agencies, stronger verification of overseas employment opportunities and support programmes for affected individuals.

Opposition leader Senator Jameson Timba said the bilateral talks should result in greater transparency regarding the circumstances under which Zimbabweans ended up in foreign conflicts.

"First, a full and verifiable account of every Zimbabwean recruited into Russia's military operations, including those killed, injured, missing or still deployed. Second, a credible joint criminal investigation into the recruitment networks, their financiers and facilitators," Timba said.

He also called for measures aimed at facilitating the safe return of Zimbabweans who may wish to leave conflict zones and support for affected families.

However, Permanent Secretary for Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services Nick Mangwana declined to discuss the agenda for the meeting in advance.

"Zimbabwe and all its sisterly nations discuss all matters of mutual interest through established diplomatic channels and we have never, nor will we ever, engage in megaphone diplomacy or grandstanding," Mangwana said.

"His Excellency, President Emmerson Mnangagwa and Russian President Vladimir Putin are due to meet on the 30th. It would therefore be disrespectful and diplomatically improper to pre-empt or speculate on the content of bilateral engagements between two Heads of State before they have even met."

The issue comes at a time when governments across the region are increasingly concerned about human trafficking, labour exploitation and deceptive international recruitment practices.

Zimbabwe recently issued a warning to citizens against fraudulent overseas job offers and urged job seekers to verify recruitment agencies before accepting employment opportunities abroad.

Analysts say any future cooperation between Zimbabwe and Russia is likely to focus on combating trafficking networks, protecting citizens from exploitation and improving information sharing between authorities.

Starlink plans direct-to-cell service for Zimbabwe

by Staff reporter

20 Oct 2026 at 20:18hrs |

3277

Views

Zimbabwe has been listed among more than 150 countries where SpaceX's satellite internet service, Starlink, plans to offer its direct-to-cell mobile connectivity service, branded Starlink Mobile.

The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Starlink's application for a global mobile roaming service on September 17, 2026, allowing the company to carry international voice, data and internet traffic across US borders through interconnections with affiliated entities in other countries.

The FCC document identifies 29 African countries where Starlink holds or has applied for permission to provide telecommunications services, including Zimbabwe, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mozambique and Namibia.

Apart from Namibia, which has faced regulatory hurdles over local ownership requirements, the countries listed have granted Starlink permission to operate within their jurisdictions.

However, the FCC approval does not automatically grant Starlink permission to provide telecommunications services in every country listed. Local regulatory requirements will still apply.

Starlink Mobile is designed to connect compatible mobile phones directly to satellites when conventional cellular network coverage is unavailable. Rather than operating as a standalone cellular network, the service currently relies on partnerships with terrestrial mobile operators, including T-Mobile, Rogers Communications, Deutsche Telekom and Optus.

As of September 2026, Starlink had confirmed plans to introduce its direct-to-cell technology in more than a dozen African countries, primarily through partnerships with Airtel Africa.

In March 2026, MTN Zambia became the first cellular operator to complete field testing of Starlink Mobile, successfully conducting the country's first satellite-based data session and mobile money transaction using MTN Zambia's licensed spectrum and Starlink's low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation.

The technology could potentially extend mobile connectivity to remote and underserved communities where traditional telecommunications infrastructure is limited, although the timing of a commercial launch in Zimbabwe has not been confirmed.

Despite the anticipated expansion, Starlink's direct-to-cell technology has limitations. Satellite signals cannot reliably provide direct connectivity inside buildings because walls and roofs can weaken or block the signals.

Customers seeking Starlink's conventional satellite internet indoors generally need an external satellite antenna connected to an indoor router through Wi-Fi or an Ethernet connection.

Although Starlink has secured mid-band spectrum in the 1.7GHz to 1.9GHz range, which offers better obstacle penetration than higher-frequency signals, the considerable distance between satellites and users on the ground remains a challenge.

The planned expansion could nevertheless mark a significant development for mobile connectivity in Zimbabwe, particularly in rural areas where conventional cellular coverage remains limited.

TSCZ urges journalists to dig deeper into road safety

by Simbarashe Sithole

Views

HARARE - Traffic Safety Council of Zimbabwe (TSCZ) managing director Munesu Munodawafa has challenged journalists to move beyond reporting road accident statistics and produce investigative stories that examine the causes of crashes, promote accountability and contribute to improved road safety.

Speaking at a road safety workshop for journalists in Harare on Friday, Munodawafa said the media plays a critical role in raising public awareness, influencing policy decisions and encouraging responsible behaviour among road users.

"The media plays a pivotal role in our country, so as journalists you should do in-depth stories on road safety," he said.

Munodawafa urged journalists to go beyond reporting the number of fatalities and injuries resulting from road accidents and focus on uncovering the underlying factors contributing to the country's road safety challenges.

He said comprehensive reporting should explore issues such as the condition of road infrastructure, vehicle roadworthiness, driver behaviour, enforcement of traffic laws and the effectiveness of road safety policies.

According to Munodawafa, journalists should use their platforms to question whether relevant authorities are doing enough to prevent accidents and improve safety for motorists, passengers, cyclists and pedestrians.

He also called for reporting that promotes accountability, supports evidence-based policymaking and highlights practical solutions aimed at reducing road traffic injuries and fatalities.

Munodawafa urged journalists to investigate why accidents occur, whether existing regulations are being enforced and what interventions could help prevent future tragedies.

He said road safety reporting should strive to contribute to long-term improvements rather than simply documenting accidents after they happen.

The workshop comes amid continuing concerns over road safety in Zimbabwe, where road traffic crashes continue to claim lives and affect livelihoods.

Beyond the immediate loss of life, accidents often leave families without breadwinners, increase financial burdens on households and place additional pressure on healthcare services.

Survivors may also face long-term disabilities, rehabilitation costs and loss of income.

Munodawafa said effective road safety reporting requires journalists to connect individual accidents to broader issues involving public policy, infrastructure development, law enforcement and the responsibilities of transport operators and road users.

Road safety experts have consistently highlighted the need for stronger driver training programmes, improved road infrastructure and stricter enforcement of traffic regulations.

The media, he added, can play an important watchdog role by following up on promised road improvements, investigating allegations of corruption in traffic enforcement and assessing whether safety campaigns translate into measurable reductions in crashes.

Munodawafa said reducing road carnage requires a preventive approach involving government departments, local authorities, police, transport operators and road users.

He noted that Zimbabwe's road safety ambitions will depend on sustained public education, safer road designs, regular vehicle inspections, effective law enforcement and improved emergency response systems.

Ultimately, he said, success should be measured not by the number of workshops held but by a reduction in deaths and serious injuries on the country's roads.

Chipinge South CCC legislator Clifford Hlatshwayo has called for the removal of Shona as a subject in schools in Chipinge, arguing that learners should be taught in their indigenous Ndau language.

Speaking at the Matlharihasi Festival held at Hakamela Stadium in Chipinge South last Friday, Hlatshwayo described the teaching of Shona in a predominantly Ndau-speaking community as a form of colonisation.

He also called on the government to deploy Ndau-speaking teachers in the area to promote indigenous languages and preserve local cultural heritage.

"What pains me is that we are being forced to learn a language that is alien to us. We are Shanghani, we are Ndau, let us learn our language. Learning in Shona is colonisation. Government should support our indigenous language," said Hlatshwayo.

The legislator also criticised the introduction of Mbende Jerusarema dance as a compulsory component of the new Heritage-Based Curriculum, arguing that it did not reflect the cultural traditions of communities in Chipinge.

"We don't want our children to be taught Jerusarema dance, it's not their culture, we have our own dances and our children should be taught those dances in schools," he said.

Chief Gezani, one of the traditional leaders who attended the festival, backed Hlatshwayo's position, saying education in indigenous languages would help children understand and preserve their cultural identity.

"I support the MP. Teaching our children in their indigenous language will enable them to know and understand better their culture. This will help preserve the culture," said Chief Gezani.

Chief Tshovani of Chiredzi also supported the call for cultural representation in schools, saying his community's popular Xibelani dance should be taught to learners.

The festival was attended by traditional leaders from Chiredzi and Chipinge South, as well as representatives from the Gonarezhou Conservation Trust, Chilo Gorge and Save Valley Conservancy, among other stakeholders.

Coltart refuses to sell out to Geo Pomona

by Staff reporter

Views

Bulawayo Mayor David Coltart has insisted that any proposed waste-management partnership with Geo Pomona must be affordable to residents, as the city intensifies scrutiny of the company's financial and contractual terms before committing to an agreement.

Coltart made the remarks on Wednesday after leading a council delegation on a tour of Geo Pomona's waste-management facility in Harare, where officials inspected waste sorting, landfilling and leachate treatment operations.

The delegation included Deputy Mayor Edwin Ndlovu, Town Clerk Christopher Dube, councillors and senior council officials.

Although Coltart acknowledged the potential benefits of introducing similar waste-management capacity in Bulawayo, he said the financial implications remained the biggest consideration.

"The critical thing for us, though, is what will it cost, and is it affordable for us?" he said.

He emphasised that the city was not opposed to working with Geo Pomona but would not sign an agreement without understanding the precise terms and how the proposed arrangement would be funded.

Council technical teams have already assessed the company's operations, with the next stage involving a detailed financial analysis.

Geo Pomona is among three companies shortlisted through a procurement process initiated by Bulawayo City Council in 2025. A pre-feasibility study was subsequently submitted to the Zimbabwe Investment and Development Agency.

The process is unfolding against the backdrop of a September directive by Local Government Minister Daniel Garwe, reflecting a Cabinet decision, instructing Bulawayo to engage Geo Pomona to address challenges at the city's overwhelmed Richmond Landfill, commonly known as Ngozi Mine.

The 30-hectare landfill, which opened in 1994, has exceeded its intended lifespan and continues to experience fires, gas emissions and other environmental and public-health concerns.

However, Coltart has maintained that any partnership must comply with Zimbabwe's procurement laws and protect residents' interests.

He has previously argued that Bulawayo's waste collection system remains relatively functional, with the city's more pressing requirements centred on waste separation, processing and disposal.

Geo Pomona's existing Harare arrangement has reportedly targeted the processing of approximately 650 tonnes of waste daily at US$40 per tonne, translating to an estimated annual cost of nearly US$9 million.

However, these figures do not establish what a potential Bulawayo agreement would cost.

The company's proposed waste-to-energy plant is also still at the planning stage and is not yet operational.

Meanwhile, residents' associations and civic organisations have called for transparency regarding the proposed costs, implementation timelines and competitive bidding process before council enters into any agreement.

Informal waste pickers who depend on activities at Ngozi Mine have also expressed concerns about the potential impact of changes to landfill operations on their livelihoods.

No agreement has been signed and no new cost figures have been announced following Wednesday's tour.

Council is expected to consider the findings of its financial assessment before deciding whether to proceed with further negotiations or prepare a draft memorandum of understanding.
