Zimbabwe set for bumper wheat harvest

by Staff reporter

01 Nov 2026 at 18:21hrs |

514

Views

Zimbabwe is poised to harvest at least 600,000 tonnes of wheat this season after farmers delivered nearly 570,000 tonnes from 83 percent of the planted area, raising expectations of another bumper harvest as the country strengthens its food security.

The Government has urged farmers to accelerate harvesting operations and complete the exercise by Friday, November 6, ahead of anticipated rains that could damage crops and compromise grain quality.

Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development Permanent Secretary Professor Obert Jiri said farmers had harvested 108,569 hectares out of the 130,316 hectares planted during the 2026 winter cropping season.

The harvested area has so far produced an estimated 568,581 tonnes, with an average national yield of 5.2 tonnes per hectare.

Zimbabwe exceeded its initial winter wheat planting target of 125,000 hectares by 5,316 hectares, reflecting increased production capacity and continued investment in irrigated agriculture.

"So, as of yesterday, we had harvested 108,000 hectares of the 130,000 hectares that we grew. And out of that 108,000 hectares, we had harvested almost 570,000 metric tonnes," Prof Jiri said.

"We hope that by the end of this coming week, we will be finished. We hope to reach at least 600,000 metric tonnes when we do the harvesting."

With approximately 21,747 hectares still awaiting harvesting, authorities have deployed 482 combine harvesters across the country.

The machines are collectively harvesting an estimated 14,000 hectares daily, raising hopes that the remaining crop will be collected before the onset of significant rainfall.

Mashonaland West leads in wheat production, having harvested 163,918 tonnes from 26,610 hectares, with an impressive average yield of 6.2 tonnes per hectare.

Mashonaland Central follows with 140,579 tonnes from 23,827 hectares, representing 94 percent of its planted area.

Mashonaland East has produced 104,070 tonnes, while the Midlands has recorded 61,051 tonnes.

Manicaland has harvested 44,400 tonnes, with Matabeleland South contributing 25,740 tonnes, Masvingo 15,098 tonnes and Matabeleland North 13,726 tonnes.

Matabeleland South has recorded particularly strong yields, averaging six tonnes per hectare, with provincial Agricultural and Rural Development Advisory Services director Shupikai Sibanda expressing satisfaction with progress.

"Currently we are at 98 percent and most of the wheat on bigger hectares is now done and now harvested. We are just left with a few pockets that we need to harvest," she said.

"Our yields are looking good, averaging around six tonnes per hectare and we are happy with what we have harvested so far."

In Matabeleland North, provincial Agricultural and Rural Development Advisory Services director Sibangilizwe Dlodlo said harvesting was nearing completion, with most districts expected to finish by November 6.

However, farmers in Umguza are expected to require an additional week.

Prof Jiri said Mashonaland West and Mashonaland East had the largest outstanding harvesting areas, but prevailing dry weather conditions were expected to support harvesting operations.

Farmers have been encouraged to expedite harvesting, threshing, transportation and storage to minimise losses and ensure that grain reaches designated collection points in good condition.

The anticipated bumper harvest comes as Zimbabwe seeks to consolidate its wheat self-sufficiency while responding to rising demand from the country's expanding milling and food-processing industries.

According to Prof Jiri, national industrial wheat requirements have increased significantly over the past three years, rising from less than 360,000 tonnes to more than 552,000 tonnes annually.

He attributed the growth to population increases, changing consumption patterns and expansion in food-processing capacity.

Despite producing enough wheat to meet overall domestic requirements, Zimbabwe continues importing specialised varieties, particularly hard wheat used by millers for blending and other industrial purposes.

Prof Jiri explained that these imports remain necessary because certain processing operations require wheat with specific quality characteristics that are not yet sufficiently available locally.

The Government is therefore seeking to increase production while encouraging the cultivation of wheat varieties that meet the requirements of domestic processors.

"We are now wheat self-sufficient and we are proud of that fact. We will continue to ensure that in terms of wheat, we continue to be self-sufficient and to produce enough for ourselves and hopefully for export as well," Prof Jiri said.

The projected 600,000-tonne harvest would exceed the country's current estimated industrial requirement of 552,000 tonnes, potentially creating a surplus of approximately 48,000 tonnes, although specialised imports will remain necessary.

Authorities believe sustained investment in irrigation, mechanisation and improved seed varieties will be critical to maintaining wheat self-sufficiency and positioning Zimbabwe as a potential exporter of the crop.

Gwanda-Maphisa road project stalls

by Staff reporter

01 Nov 2026 at 18:22hrs |

789

Views

Construction of the strategic Gwanda-Maphisa Highway in Matabeleland South has slowed significantly, with only one of the six contracted companies currently operating on site as authorities work to resolve outstanding contractual issues.

The delays have raised concerns among motorists and local communities who had hoped the long-awaited road rehabilitation project would improve transport links, reduce travel distances and stimulate economic activity across the province.

Matabeleland South Provincial Roads Engineer Mangisi Nkomo confirmed that five contractors were currently off-site, with most awaiting the review of their agreements before resuming construction.

He said JRG Goddard was the only contractor actively working on the highway, concentrating on a 10-kilometre stretch, while Difflock Construction was expected to resume operations on its allocated 30-kilometre section.

"We have one contractor on the ground who is JRG Goddard working on their 10km stretch where they are working on the subgrade. We are also expecting another contractor, Difflock Construction, to resume. These have a 30km stretch," Nkomo said.

"Some of the contractors are not on the ground as they are awaiting reviewing of their contracts. This has slowed down progress but we are expecting the issue to be finalised soon."

The Gwanda-Maphisa Highway is regarded as one of Matabeleland South's most important infrastructure projects, providing a shorter route between Gwanda, Maphisa and several surrounding districts.

Minister of State for Matabeleland South Provincial Affairs and Devolution Albert Nguluvhe expressed concern over the slow progress and pledged to intervene to ensure that all contractors return to work.

He described the highway as a critical economic corridor whose completion would significantly improve connectivity and reduce transport costs.

"This road is the heartbeat of Matabeleland South. With its completion, we are reducing travel distances by over 150 kilometres to some areas, which is transformative for business and service delivery," Nguluvhe said.

He said the road would provide a shorter route to Maphisa for travellers from Gwanda, Beitbridge, Insiza and Masvingo, while opening up new opportunities for businesses and communities.

"It will also improve intra-district connectivity and unlock more business opportunities within the province. It's therefore imperative that this road is completed as soon as possible," he said.

"Works have now slowed down but I will work tirelessly to ensure that they gather pace."

Construction resumed last year as part of major infrastructure projects undertaken ahead of the 2026 Independence Day celebrations hosted by Matabeleland South.

The highway connects several important economic centres, including ARDA Antelope Estate, Makwe Irrigation Scheme, two border posts and tourism destinations in Matobo.

Once completed, the road is expected to improve access to markets for farmers, facilitate mining activities, boost tourism and make it easier for residents to access essential services.

The project forms part of the Government's broader road rehabilitation programme, which includes the Plumtree-Maitengwe, Bulawayo-Kezi, Plumtree-Tsholotsho and Beitbridge-Bulawayo highways.

These infrastructure developments are among the initiatives being pursued under Zimbabwe's Vision 2030 economic development agenda.

However, motorists have expressed frustration over the slow pace of construction, warning that prolonged delays could undermine the anticipated economic benefits.

Motorist Ben Ncube said communities had welcomed the resumption of construction last year but were becoming increasingly disappointed by the lack of visible progress.

"We had high hopes when we saw construction of the road resumed last year but now we are discouraged because there isn't much work being done," Ncube said.

"We appeal to relevant authorities to see to it that this project resumes and this time is completed."

Authorities have expressed optimism that the outstanding contract reviews will be finalised soon, allowing construction to resume across the affected sections of the highway.

Fuel companies begin selling in ZiG

by Staff reporter

01 Nov 2026 at 18:19hrs |

1835

Views

Fuel companies in Zimbabwe have started selling petroleum products in Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG), although transactions remain largely restricted to bulk purchases as suppliers seek local currency to meet their statutory tax obligations.

Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) Deputy Governor Dr Innocent Matshe revealed the development during the 2027 Pre-Budget Seminar in Bulawayo, saying some fuel distributors were increasingly accepting ZiG payments from wholesale customers while continuing to sell fuel in United States dollars at retail outlets.

The move comes as the Government considers proposals to maintain fuel subsidies aimed at keeping pump prices below US$2 per litre and reducing production costs across key economic sectors.

Dr Matshe explained that fuel companies receiving most of their revenue in US dollars were finding it necessary to generate ZiG to settle their Quarterly Payment Date (QPD) tax obligations.

"You will realise that there are some fuel companies today that are selling fuel in ZiG. Unfortunately, they are only selling it in bulk," he said.

"Why, you may ask? It's because these companies, they do not want to put this fuel in the pump, but they also need this ZiG for their QPD payments."

He said the arrangement allowed fuel distributors to obtain local currency without immediately extending ZiG transactions to ordinary motorists at service stations.

"If they are receiving payments in US dollars and they are required to pay QPD in ZiG, they need to find a way of generating that ZiG," Dr Matshe said.

"So what they have opted to do in the interim is to sell it in wholesale in ZiG."

The development highlights the growing role of statutory payment requirements in creating demand for the local currency in Zimbabwe's predominantly US dollar-driven economy.

Although wholesale fuel transactions in ZiG represent a step towards wider acceptance of the currency, motorists are yet to benefit significantly from the arrangement because most retail fuel sales remain denominated in foreign currency.

Expanding ZiG fuel sales to service station pumps could provide consumers and businesses with additional payment options while strengthening the local currency's use in everyday commercial transactions.

Meanwhile, Parliament's Budget, Finance and Investment Promotion Committee chairperson Lincoln Dhliwayo said proposals had been submitted for the Government to continue subsidising fuel to cushion businesses and consumers against rising operating costs.

"There was a proposal to ensure that the Government continues to subsidise our fuel so that it is made below two dollars, so that at least the cost of production and also the cost to consumers is somehow reduced," Dhliwayo said.

Fuel prices remain a major factor influencing production costs in Zimbabwe, particularly in agriculture, mining, manufacturing, transport and logistics.

Farmers depend on diesel for land preparation, irrigation equipment and transporting produce to markets, while mining companies require substantial fuel supplies to operate machinery and move minerals.

Manufacturers and transport operators also face significant fuel-related expenses, which are often passed on to consumers through higher prices for goods and services.

Keeping fuel prices below US$2 per litre could therefore provide relief to businesses and help contain inflationary pressures, although the financial implications of maintaining subsidies would need to be considered against other national budget priorities.

The proposal remains under consideration, with no final decision announced on the continuation, structure or funding of the proposed subsidies.

As preparations for the 2027 National Budget gather momentum, policymakers face the challenge of encouraging greater use of ZiG while ensuring that energy costs remain affordable enough to support economic growth.

The emergence of ZiG-denominated wholesale fuel transactions could signal a gradual shift towards broader local currency acceptance, particularly if fuel distributors eventually extend the arrangement to retail customers.

Zimbabwe readies new policy that will entrench property rights

by Staff reporter

01 Nov 2026 at 18:18hrs |

583

Views

Zimbabwe is finalising a new land policy aimed at strengthening property rights for thousands of farmers resettled on former white-owned commercial farms, marking a significant shift in the country's land reform programme more than two decades after the controversial farm seizures.

Lands and Rural Development Minister Vangelis Haritatos said the policy, which is expected to receive Cabinet approval before the end of the year, would provide greater security of tenure while ensuring that the land redistribution programme remains irreversible.

Speaking in an interview in Bulawayo, Haritatos said the Government was putting the finishing touches on the policy, which is expected to transform agricultural land administration and create new opportunities for investment in the farming sector.

"The policy guarantees that the land reform is irreversible and moves us safely into a transformative rural economy," Haritatos said.

"We are already on the final draft."

The proposed reforms come 26 years after former President Robert Mugabe's government embarked on the fast-track land reform programme, which saw thousands of white commercial farmers lose their properties to newly resettled black farmers.

The programme, launched in 2000, was justified by the Government as a necessary measure to correct colonial-era land ownership inequalities that had left much of Zimbabwe's productive agricultural land concentrated in the hands of a white minority.

However, the often chaotic redistribution process disrupted commercial agricultural production, contributing to a sharp decline in farm output and leaving many beneficiaries without secure, bankable land tenure.

For years, resettled farmers have struggled to access affordable financing because their land tenure documents have generally not provided the same collateral security as conventional title deeds.

The new policy is expected to address some of these longstanding challenges by strengthening tenure arrangements and improving the administration of agricultural land.

Haritatos said the Government wanted to establish a more transparent and inclusive land management system that protects legitimate landholders while broadening participation in agricultural development.

He told lawmakers that the policy would consolidate the gains of land reform by "promoting an inclusive, transparent and equitable land-administration system that protects legitimate landowners and expands opportunities for women, youth and vulnerable groups."

The reforms are also expected to support efforts to attract investment into agriculture, improve productivity and encourage farmers to undertake long-term development projects.

However, the precise ownership rights, transfer conditions and collateral arrangements that will be provided under the new policy have yet to be publicly detailed.

The developments come as Zimbabwe continues efforts to compensate former commercial farmers who lost improvements on their properties during the land reform programme.

In 2020, the Government signed a US$3.5 billion compensation agreement with representatives of former white commercial farmers as part of efforts to resolve longstanding property disputes and rebuild relations with international creditors and investors.

Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube said the Government had so far disbursed approximately US$800 million through a combination of cash payments and Treasury bills.

The compensation programme forms part of Zimbabwe's broader efforts to address historical disputes arising from land reform and improve confidence in the country's investment environment.

Land ownership and security of tenure remain central issues in Zimbabwe's agricultural sector, where farmers require access to financing for irrigation infrastructure, mechanisation, livestock development and other capital-intensive investments.

The Government believes stronger land rights could help unlock the economic potential of resettled farms while safeguarding the redistribution gains achieved since 2000.

If approved by Cabinet before year-end, the new policy could represent an important milestone in Zimbabwe's efforts to move beyond land redistribution towards a more commercially productive and financially sustainable agricultural sector.

The success of the reforms will, however, depend on how the new tenure arrangements are implemented and whether financial institutions recognise the resulting land rights as acceptable security for agricultural lending.

Zimbabwe road carnage claiming 5 people every day

by Staff reporter

16 Sep 2022 at 18:00hrs |

5934706

Views

Five people die through road traffic accidents in Zimbabwe every day while the country loses US$406 million per year to the carnage, Transport and Infrastructural Development minister Felix Mhona has said.

Mhona said this while announcing the closure of Mbudzi round about in Harare to pave way for the construction of a more modern traffic interchange intersection.

"In Zimbabwe, the average number of crashes per year between 2010 and 2021 was 40 180 and the average number of people dying as a result of road crashes was 1 858 per year.

"Put differently, five people die every day on the roads in Zimbabwe and this translates to 153 persons killed per month.

"The country loses about US$406 million annually from an average forty thousand road traffic crashes every year, and this is estimated to be nearly 3% of GDP," Mhona said.

Globally, added the minister, 1.35 million people are killed annually from an average 3 700 people who lose their lives through the misfortunes daily.

The road crashes involve cars, buses, trucks, motorcycles, bicycles and pedestrians.

"More than half of those killed are pedestrians, motorcyclists, or cyclists.

"Currently, cyclists and pedestrians make up 43% of road traffic fatalities in Africa.

"As motorcycles have become more popular as a relatively affordable means of transport, motorcycle fatalities are also on the rise.

"Crash injuries are estimated to be the eighth leading cause of death globally for all age groups, and the leading cause of death for children and young people," he said.

According to police statistics, 2 480 pedestrians were killed in hit-and-run accidents by motorists.

The number of motorists who hit pedestrians or other vehicles on the roads and sped off without stopping to render assistance is now on the increase with police recording about 2 500 hit-and-run accidents in the first half of 2022, which saw the country lose 984 lives on the roads.

National police spokesperson Assistant Commissioner Paul Nyathi said in total, 102 road traffic accidents were recorded this year compared to 157 recorded during the 2021 Heroes and Defence Forces Holidays.

"We are worried about an increase in hit-and-run road traffic accidents that are occurring countrywide," Nyathi said.

In the first half of the year, 984 people were killed while 5 103 others were injured in 25 309 road traffic accidents recorded, 759 of them fatal, between January and June this year.

During the same period last year, 867 people died while 3 410 were injured in 20 679 road accidents recorded.

Police blame accidents on speeding, inattention, misjudgement, reversing and overtaking errors.

by Staff reporter

Views

The death of a Zimbabwean woman in a Krugersdorp hospital has left a deep scar among Zimbabweans who are desperate to receive health services in South Africa.

Luyanda Moyo, 21, is a Zimbabwean immigrant who visited South African medical centres to give birth but was allegedly met with poor treatment and lack of attention because of her nationality.

Moyo gave birth at the Yusuf Dadoo hospital in Krugersdorp to a baby weighing 4kg.

Despite complaining of pain and excessive bleeding, she alleged that the medical staff in the maternity ward did not pay attention to her.

Luyanda's uncle, Gibson Tshuma, told "The Star" that she was so neglected to the point of being the last patient in the ward.

"The Star" understands that nurses found Luyanda dead hours after giving birth.

Luyanda Moyo, 21, is a Zimbabwean immigrant who visited South African medical centres to give birth

She was in so much pain that she apparently told nurses that she would rather die than bare the pain she was in.

Her family is calling for an investigation into her death.

Tshuma said the family was concerned that the statements uttered by Limpopo Health MEC, Phophi Rmathuba, could have caused the staff at the hospital to have a negative attitude towards illegal Zimbabwean seeking medical attention in parts of South Africa.

Tshuma said when they found Luyanda's body in the hospital her clothes were covered in blood.

The hospital failed to explain what happened to Luyanda.

"Based on the messages on her cellphone she was overdue and she was given an inducing pill even though they acknowledged that the baby was too big for her to deliver naturally," Tshuma said.

"The Star" listened to some voice notes that Luyanda shared with her mother before she died.

In some of them the young woman was describing the unbearable pain she was in to his mother.

"It's so painfulâ€¦ they haven't checked on me, I think they will come today," Luyanda said in a voice note to her mother.

Luyanda's baby boy survived and is with his grandmother but the family said it was still left with a million questions concerning how Luyanda died.

"We are demanding answers as to what happened, we are not getting clear answers.

"They induced her even when they had observed an operation was necessary and then she was ignored when she was bleeding to death," Tshuma said.

The family is preparing for Luyanda's body to be transported back to Zimbabwe where her funeral will take place.

The family said it was concerned that if ordinary South Africans suffered poor service at hospital, the situations was worse for foreign nationals.

The Gauteng Department of Health did not respond to "The Star" questions by late afternoon yesterday.

by Staff reporter

06 Aug 2022 at 05:43hrs |

4468132

ZIMBABWE is tightening security at all border points in a bid to end unauthorised crossings from organised criminal gangs, including child traffickers, Information minister Monica Mutsvangwa has said.

Speaking at the launch of Anti-Child Trafficking Documentary on Thursday, Mutsvangwa said government was proposing stiffer jail sentences to those who are found guilty of trafficking.

"We have had issues with our porous borders. However, government is tightening all crossing points so that we stop human trafficking syndicates which have been preying on children. Government is also currently formulating stiffer jail terms," she said.

According to the 2019 Trafficking in Persons report, Zimbabwe is a Tier 2 country and was placed on the Office to Monitor Child Trafficking in Persons watchlist in 2019.

A Tier 2 country is a country that does not meet the minimum standards set by the office, but is making efforts to do so.

According to the United States embassy 2021 Trafficking Report, traffickers are also preying on children locally and exploiting them for cheap labour in farms and

mines.

The report also lists Zimbabwe as a source, transit and destination country for trafficked women and children.

In 2016, a truck carrying 57 Malawian children was intercepted in South Africa after the driver and his two accomplices had successfully navigated their way through both the Mozambique and Zimbabwe border posts.

Lupane State University students win innovation prize

by Staff reporter

07 Aug 2022 at 07:27hrs |

4469270

Views

LUPANE State University (LSU) scooped the top award at the Enactus awards ceremony organised and hosted by Boost Fellowship in Harare on Friday to walk away with $400 000.

The Entrepreneurial Action for Others Creates A Better World for Us All (Enactus) competitions were tightly contested by eight Zimbabwean universities.

The competition, which is meant to empower students at universities with entrepreneurial skills returned to in person participation after it has been held virtually in the past two years owing to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Boost Fellowship director and country leader for Enactus Zimbabwe Cleopatra Makoni said the competitions were organised to adequately prepare students from universities with innovative skills after they leave the learning environment.

"We are excited to showcase the innovative projects that our students have implemented in their communities to change lives and leave a lasting positive effect that will impact our whole country.

"Our youths are the future of this country," Makoni said.

"We observed that while most schools and universities across the world generally provide a wide ranging academic education, many students find themselves inadequately prepared for the opportunities and the challenges beyond the classroom."

The Enactus has 38 members across the globe including Zimbabwe and are held annually in every country where the winners will progress to the world cup.

This year's world cup will be held on October 30, to November 2 in the Caribbean island of Puerto Rico.

LSU Enactus team president Amanda Hove expressed gratitude to her team, which she said will represent Zimbabwe well at the world cup.

"I am happy that we won a tight competition and I want to promise Zimbabwe that we will not disappoint at the world cup competitions where we will battle it out with other 37 global champions," Hove said.

Midlands State University and University of Zimbabwe Enactus students were first and second runners up respectively.

The runners up received $240 000 and $160 000 as prize money respectively.

Zimbabwe is at peace, says Mnangagwa

by Staff reporter

23 Sep 2022 at 04:56hrs |

5180583

Views

PRESIDENT Emmerson Mnangagwa yesterday said his government was committed to ensuring peace during elections as political temperatures have risen ahead of the 2023 general elections.

The country has already recorded isolated incidents of political violence, with the opposition alleging that it is being targeted by suspected ruling Zanu-PF supporters.

The run-up to the March by-elections was marred by political violence that claimed the life of an opposition Citizens Coalition for Change (CCC) activist.

Addressing delegates at the United Nations (UN) General Assembly in New York, United States yesterday, Mnangagwa said Zimbabwe was a peaceful country.

"As my government continues to entrench democracy, good governance and the rule of law, we are committed to vibrant, competitive and peaceful political contestations. Zimbabwe is a peace loving country," Mnangagwa said.

Human rights watchdogs have, however, predicted a violent run-up to the 2023 elections.

Turning to southern Africa, Mnangagwa appealed for UN support to fight Islamic terrorist activities in neighbouring Mozambique.

"The spread of terrorism and intensification of old conflicts on the African continent and throughout the world have been a setback to our quest to "silence the guns," he said.

"In southern Africa, we remain seized with insecurity and terrorist insurgency in northern parts of Cabo Delgado (Mozambique) and conflicts in parts of the Great Lakes Region.

"Emboldened by our Sadc regional philosophy that â€˜an injury to one is an injury to all', we continue to pool our resources to fight terrorism and other threats to peace, security and stability in our region. We appeal to the United Nations to render the requisite support to our efforts to restore peace in the affected areas," he added.

Meanwhile, two Zimbabwean nationals have been selected to champion the UN's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Activist and You Tuber Varaidzo Kativhu and HIV/Aids advocate Paul Ndlovu are now part of the UN flagship initiative of the Office of the Secretary General's envoy on youth, which recognises exceptional young people around the world.

They were selected alongside 15 other young people from across the globe.

"This next cohort of young leaders for the SDGs hail from all corners of the world and work across all pillars of the UN, including sustainable development, human rights, and peace and security," the UN said.

"The group who are all between the ages of 17 and 29 years old include an aspiring astronaut, medical doctor and fashion designer, paralympic medalist, poet, artists, climate entrepreneurs, peacebuilders, gender justice advocates, and education innovators, among others."

UN Secretary-General's Envoy on Youth Jayathma Wickramanayake said: "Even amid the ongoing pandemic, climate crisis and global instability, these young people demonstrate immense resilience, resourcefulness and leadership in finding innovative solutions to the world's biggest challenges."

Since its launch in 2016, the initiative has collectively reached millions of young people around the world.

RULING Zanu-PF party deputy youth secretary John Paradza yesterday threatened to unleash party youths against the opposition Citizens Coalition for Change (CCC) as political tempers flare ahead of the 2023 elections.

Paradza was addressing scores of youths in the capital yesterday.

The defiant Paradza said the party would unleash violence in defending the revolutionary party, adding that as youth, they were going to defend the party.

"We have noted that CCC is unleashing violence against us, but starting from today, I am unleashing my dogs," he said.

"As youths, our mandate is to defend the revolutionary party and we are going to make sure we defend our party. CCC burnt houses in Chitungwiza and we are not going to fold our hands watching them unleashing violence," he said.

Zanu-PF supporters and CCC activists clashed in Nyatsime over the death of CCC activist Moreblessing Ali.

Tempers are rising ahead of the 2023 elections after a CCC rally was blocked in Chegutu over the weekend, with the opposition party blaming Zanu-PF for barricading Pfumojena Stadium where the rally was to be hosted.

Paradza added that President Emmerson Mnangagwa would unveil residential stands to the youth.

"I have met the President and he said he was going to unveil stands to the youths. It is the President's vision to give youths stands and also to have employment," he said.

Zanu-PF Harare central youth chairperson Emmanuel Mahachi also said they were going to defend the party.

"We are not going to fold our hands and we are going to defend our party through fighting because we rule this country," Mahachi said

In his vote of thanks, youth secretary for administration Tendai Chiwetu said he was aware of ministers and legislators who were working against Mnangagwa.

"We have people who seem to like President Mnangagwa, but they don't like him. We are going to make sure that they are not retained as central committee members as we approach the elections," Chiwetu added.

CCC youth assembly spokesperson Stephen Chuma said: "We, as CCC, believe in non-violence approach to solving problems. It's very unfortunate that in this modern era, we have a political party that believes in violence as a strategy.

"We are a peace-loving citizens' movement, but that does not make us weak or cowards. No one has monopoly of violence and we want to send the message clear to Emmerson Mnangagwa, John Paradza and Zanu-PF thugs that any attempts to drive the nation into anarchy will be resisted."

He added: "We know that Zanu-PF wants to use violence to drive this nation into anarchy so as to effect a state of emergency in order to postpone the upcoming general elections. They know they are going to lose elections so they are running scared and are now resorting to violence."

Police spokesperson Assistant Commissioner Paul Nyathi said: "I will have to get the information from Officer Commanding Harare Province and get back to you on the matter. I was not at work today (yesterday)."

Animal rights body takes swipe at Ramaphosa

by Staff reporter

24 Jun 2022 at 07:37hrs |

1083664

Views

Anyone involved in trophy hunting has some level of moral disconnect, so the fact that President Cyril Ramaphosa was potentially involved in other crimes was not surprising.

This is the view of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), a non-profit animal rights organisation, in reaction to criminal investigations into Ramaphosa after millions of US dollars "concealed" in furniture on his Phala Phala farm in Limpopo were stolen - allegedly by a gang of Namibian nationals with the assistance of his domestic worker.

Ramaphosa is being investigated for alleged money laundering, defeating the ends of justice and kidnapping the suspects who were allegedly interrogated and breaching the Prevention of Organised Crime Act, no 121 of 1998 ("Poca") and the Prevention of Corrupt Activities Act No12 of 2004 ("The Corruption Act").

Ramaphosa has only confirmed that the matter was reported to the head of his security, and not the police.

It remains unclear whether Sars and the SA Reserve Bank have launched their investigations in relation to the breaching of the country's laws around foreign currency.

In 2020, the same year of the theft of the money, PETA conducted an undercover investigation which revealed Ramaphosa's alleged hidden connections and investments in the trophy hunting industry, after a hunting Safari owner was caught on video stating that the president had bought a 50% stake in their company.
